sites.name: Xerxes (Ahasuerus) Royal Inscriptions
sites.subtitle: Trilingual royal inscriptions of Xerxes I · 486-465 BCE
sites.date: Reign of Xerxes I, 486-465 BCE. Individual texts are undated; they are placed in the reign by the king's name and titulary ('Xerxes the great king... son of Darius the king, the Achaemenid')
sites.date_basis: Name and filiation in the texts; the Elephantine papyri independently date documents by Xerxes' regnal years (Cowley no. 2: year 2 of Xerxes = 484 BCE) and equate year 21 of Xerxes with year 1 of Artaxerxes I (465 BCE; Cowley no. 6).

discovery.when: XPa and other Persepolis texts known to European travellers since the 17th-19th centuries; XPh found 26 June 1935
discovery.who: XPh: Oriental Institute (University of Chicago) Persepolis expedition (E. Herzfeld; E. F. Schmidt)
discovery.where: Persepolis (Gate of All Nations, palaces, stone tablets of XPh); Mount Elvend near Hamadan (XE); the citadel rock at Van, eastern Turkey (XV)

sites.location: XPa, XE and XV are carved in situ (Persepolis, Ganjnameh near Hamadan, Van citadel). The XPh stone tablets (two Old Persian, one Akkadian, one Elamite) were found at Persepolis in 1935; their present museum location was Not confirmed in a published museum record.

physical.material: Carved stone (building and rock-face inscriptions); XPh on stone tablets shaped like clay tablets
physical.script: Old Persian cuneiform, Elamite cuneiform, Babylonian cuneiform (trilingual)

overview: Xerxes I (Old Persian Xšayāršā), son of Darius I, ruled the Persian empire 486-465 BCE. His royal inscriptions are carved in three languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. They follow a set formula: praise of Ahura Mazda 'who created this earth, who created yonder heaven, who created man, who created welfare for man, who made Xerxes king', then Xerxes' titles and descent from Darius, then a statement of building and a prayer for protection.

The Gate of All Nations text (XPa), repeated four times above the winged bulls of the Persepolis gateway, says Xerxes built 'this colonnade (for the representatives) of all countries'. The Van rock inscription (XV) says Darius had the niche cut but left it uninscribed, and Xerxes ordered the text written. The 'Daiva inscription' (XPh), found on stone tablets at Persepolis in June 1935, records a cultic reform: it condemns the worship of the daivas (rival gods) and enforces the worship of Ahura Mazda (as summarized by Barnea 2025; the full XPh text is not cited here from a public-domain translation).

None of these inscriptions mentions Esther, Mordecai, Haman, Jews or Judah. The biblical link is the king's name: Hebrew 'Ahasuerus' (ʾAḥašwērôš) is a Hebrew rendering of Persian Xšayāršā, whose Aramaic form appears in the Elephantine papyri. The inscriptions show the court titles, the scale of the empire and the religious ideology of the king whom Esther and Ezra 4:6 call Ahasuerus.

text.quote: Says Xerxes the great king: By the grace of Ahura Mazda, this colonnade (for the representatives) of all countries I made; much else (that is) beautiful (was) done throughout Persia which I did and which my father did.
text.translation: H. C. Tolman, Ancient Persian Lexicon and the Texts of the Achaemenidan Inscriptions (1908), 'Xerx. Pers. a', §3, p. 39

evidence: XPa: 'Four times repeated on propylaea of Xerxes above the sculptured winged bulls; Persian, Elamite, Babylonian' (Tolman 1908, p. 39).

Standard titulary: 'I (am) Xerxes the great king, king of kings, king of the countries possessing many kinds of people, king of this great earth far and wide, the son of Darius the king, the Achaemenide' (Tolman 1908).
XV (Van): Darius 'commanded to dig out this place where he did not make an inscription written; afterwards I commanded to write this inscription' (Tolman 1908).

XPh: found at Persepolis 26 June 1935 on stone tablets, two with the Old Persian text, one Akkadian, one Elamite; first full publication of the original texts by E. Herzfeld, Archäologische Mitteilungen aus Iran 8 (1936) 56-77 (Kent 1937).

Elephantine: an Aramaic contract is dated 'the 28th of the month Paophi in the 2nd year of King Xerxes' (Cowley no. 2, 484 BCE); Cowley notes the Aramaic spellings of the name against 'OP Khshayarsha'.
Elephantine Cowley no. 6 equates year 21 of Xerxes with year 1 of Artaxerxes I (465 BCE), fixing the end of the reign.
questions: Is the Esther story's Ahasuerus the historical Xerxes? The name equation rests on the consonants of Hebrew ʾḤŠWRŠ and Persian Xšayāršā / Aramaic forms of the same name in Elephantine papyri; Ezra 4:6 places an Ahasuerus between Darius and Artaxerxes, the order of Darius I, Xerxes I, Artaxerxes I. S. Dalley (Esther's Revenge at Susa, OUP 2007) argues from Assyrian words, phrases and customs in the book that the story's roots go back to 7th-century Assyria and Susa. The Persian inscriptions themselves are silent on any queen named Esther or Vashti.

What did the Daiva inscription reform? J. Degen (JNES 83/1, 2024) reads XPh against Assyrian royal models ('an heir of Assyria?'). G. Barnea (Iran and the Caucasus 29/2, 2025) centres the reform on the repeated phrase artācā brzmniy and offers a wider translation using onomastic, epigraphic and archaeological data. Which country or sanctuary the reform targeted is not settled by the texts read here; identifications proposed in the literature (Babylon, Egypt, elsewhere) are inference.

Did Xerxes rebuild or destroy temples? The Daiva inscription condemns daiva worship (Barnea 2025) while the Gate text claims building. Neither mentions Jerusalem. Any link to the accusation against Judah and Jerusalem 'in the beginning of his reign' (Ezra 4:6) is an inference, not something the inscriptions state.

biblical.tie: 'In the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign, wrote they unto him an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem.' The verse sits between Darius (4:5) and Artaxerxes (4:7), the same order as Darius I - Xerxes I - Artaxerxes I in the Persian records and the Elephantine date formulas.

Ahasuerus reigns over many provinces from Susa and imposes tribute on land and isles. Xerxes' titulary 'king of kings, king of the countries possessing many kinds of people, king of this great earth far and wide' is the Persian self-description of the same scale of rule. The inscriptions do not mention Susa's court events or any person in Esther.

'The fourth shall be far richer than they all ... he shall stir up all against the realm of Grecia': a Persian king rich and campaigning against Greece fits Xerxes' place in the royal sequence. The Xerxes inscriptions do not narrate the Greek campaign; this is our reading of the verse, set beside the king's own record.

corrections: Old entry said the inscriptions give 'a detailed account of the king's military campaigns and administrative policies': the texts are building and religious statements with a fixed titulary; they contain no campaign narrative (not even of the Greek war).
Old entry said the inscriptions describe 'the roles of various officials' and 'cultural practices' matching Esther: the texts name no officials and no court events.

Old entry said they 'validate the accounts found in the biblical text' of Esther: no Xerxes inscription mentions Esther, Mordecai, Haman, Vashti or Jews; the link is the king's name and the imperial setting.

Old entry said 'Material: Stone and clay inscriptions': the royal texts are on stone (rock faces, building elements, stone tablets); dated clay and papyrus documents from his reign are separate administrative records.

Old entry listed 'Daniel 6 (lions' den)' and 'Ezra 6 (temple reconstruction)': Daniel 6 concerns 'Darius the Mede' and Ezra 6 concerns Darius I; neither relates to Xerxes' inscriptions. The direct Ezra reference is Ezra 4:6.
Old entry dated them 'c. 480 BCE' as one group: Xerxes reigned 486-465 BCE and the inscriptions are not individually dated.

sites.name: Ai Excavations
sites.subtitle: Et-Tell's Early Bronze city, its long gap, and the search for Joshua's Ai
sites.date: Et-Tell: Early Bronze IB-IIIB city (c. 3300-2400 BCE); abandoned; small unwalled Iron Age I village (c. 1220-1050 BCE). Khirbet el-Maqatir (1 km west): Late Bronze I fortress destroyed by fire, dated by its excavators to c. 1400 BCE.
sites.date_basis: Pottery stratigraphy from Marquet-Krause (1933-1935) and Callaway (1964-1972) at et-Tell. At Khirbet el-Maqatir, the excavators date the fortress by LB IB pottery.

discovery.when: 1928 (Garstang soundings); 1933-1935 (Marquet-Krause); 1964-1972 (Callaway, Joint Archaeological Expedition to Ai); 1995-2001 and 2009-2016 (ABR at Khirbet el-Maqatir); 2019 (small et-Tell soundings, Kennedy, unpublished)
discovery.who: John Garstang; Judith Marquet-Krause (Rothschild expedition); Joseph A. Callaway; Bryant G. Wood and Scott Stripling (Associates for Biblical Research); Titus Kennedy
discovery.where: Et-Tell, about 2 km east of Beitin (Bethel), West Bank; Khirbet el-Maqatir, about 1 km west of et-Tell

sites.location: In situ, et-Tell and Khirbet el-Maqatir, West Bank

physical.material: Early Bronze fortifications, citadel, sanctuary and houses at et-Tell; Iron I village houses; Late Bronze I fortress with a two-chambered gate at Khirbet el-Maqatir
physical.dimensions: The Early Bronze IC city at et-Tell measured about 27.5 acres (per the NEAEHL summary). The Maqatir fortress is about 1 ha.

overview: Et-Tell ('the ruin-heap') lies east of Beitin, which is identified with Bethel. It is the usual candidate for the Ai of Joshua 7-8 ('Ai, which is beside Bethaven, on the east side of Bethel', Josh 7:2). John Garstang made soundings there over a few days in 1928. Judith Marquet-Krause excavated it for the Rothschild expedition in 1933-1935, and Joseph Callaway led the Joint Archaeological Expedition in 1964-1972.

Both main excavators found a large walled Early Bronze city, with a citadel, a sanctuary and houses, which ended in the Early Bronze III period. The site then lay empty until a small unwalled village was built on the ruins in Iron Age I. Marquet-Krause wrote that the Middle and Late Bronze Ages were 'nonexistent' and that 'this city had therefore long since been destroyed by the time of Joshua's arrival.' Callaway, whose JBL article of 1968 was titled 'New Evidence on the Conquest of Ai', reached the same gap.

Two responses followed. The Associates for Biblical Research (B. G. Wood, S. Stripling) excavated Khirbet el-Maqatir, 1 km west of et-Tell. They found a small Late Bronze I fortress with a two-chambered gate, destroyed by a 'massive conflagration', and dated it c. 1400 BCE. Others have reopened et-Tell itself: in 2025 J. Kramer publicized Garstang's brief 1928 note of Late Bronze pottery and an unpublished 2019 sounding by T. Kennedy that reportedly yielded Late Bronze pottery and a burned layer.
evidence: Et-Tell: an Early Bronze city (EB IB to EB IIIB, c. 3300-2400 BCE) with walls, citadel and sanctuary, ending in destruction and abandonment (Marquet-Krause 1935; Callaway & Schoonover, BASOR 207, 1972; NEAEHL summary).
Marquet-Krause (1935, as quoted by Eames 2025): 'The Middle and Late Bronze Ages are nonexistent.'
Et-Tell Iron I: a small unwalled village on the acropolis, c. 1220-1050 BCE (NEAEHL summary).
Garstang's 1928 soundings were never fully published. A three-page report mentions Late Bronze material alongside Early Bronze (Eames 2025).
A 2019 sounding at et-Tell (T. Kennedy) reportedly produced Late Bronze pottery and a burned layer. As of Eames (June 2025) the dating of that layer was unpublished.

Khirbet el-Maqatir: a fortress of about 1 ha with a two-chambered gate (socket stones and an upper pivot stone), LB IB pottery throughout, and a 'massive conflagration' with calcined stones and ash, dated by the excavators to c. 1400 BCE (Wood 2012, ABR).
No inscription at either site gives the ancient name.
questions: Is et-Tell Ai? Marquet-Krause (Syria 16, 1935) and Callaway (JBL 87, 1968; BASOR 207, 1972) found no Middle or Late Bronze city at et-Tell. Taken with Josh 8, that yields either no conquest at et-Tell or a wrong identification; L.-H. Vincent (1937, as quoted by Eames 2025) put it as 'Either et-Tell… cannot be identified with Ai, or this identification goes directly against the Bible.' J. Kramer (Expedition Bible video, May 2025) argues that Garstang's note and T. Kennedy's 2019 soundings put Late Bronze material and a burn layer at et-Tell, and that the stone heap over the et-Tell gate fits Josh 8:29. C. Eames (Armstrong Institute, 2025) replies that the destruction layer's date is unpublished, that the gate was already blocked before the stones piled up, and that the stone pile covers a passage only about 1 m wide. The dispute is unresolved until Kennedy's material is published.

Is Khirbet el-Maqatir Ai? B. G. Wood and S. Stripling (ABR, 1995-2016) argue that its Late Bronze I fortress, burned c. 1400 BCE, fits Josh 8 on a 15th-century conquest date. The fortress's small size fits Josh 7:3 ('they are but few'), but Josh 8:25 counts 12,000 dead at Ai. Their case also depends on where Bethel lay relative to Maqatir. That question is argued in their publications and was not re-checked here. The Bronze Age volume of the final report has not been located for this entry; Volume 2 (2023) covers the later periods.

biblical.tie: Ai lies 'beside Bethaven, on the east side of Bethel', with an ambush between Bethel and Ai on the west. Et-Tell lies east of Beitin, and Maqatir lies west of et-Tell. Which site fits depends on where Bethel was.

'Joshua burnt Ai, and made it an heap (tel) for ever, even a desolation unto this day.' The Arabic name et-Tell means 'the heap'. The name corresponds to the text, but the date of the burning at et-Tell (Early Bronze) does not.

The king of Ai is buried under 'a great heap of stones' at the entrance of the city gate. Marquet-Krause found a stone mound over et-Tell's gate. Whether that mound dates to any Late Bronze event has not been established in publication.
'They are but few' versus 12,000 dead. Maqatir's small fortress fits the first. Et-Tell's large Early Bronze city is bigger, but it was not occupied in the Late Bronze Age.
Abram camps between Bethel and Ai. Et-Tell's Early Bronze ruin would have been a landmark heap by any second-millennium date.

corrections: The old entry said 'John Garstang in the 1930s' excavated et-Tell and 'initially interpreted' a destruction there as Joshua's. Garstang made only brief soundings in 1928 and published a three-page note. The 1933-1935 excavation was Judith Marquet-Krause's.
The old entry said 'Kathleen Kenyon in the 1950s' challenged Ai's dating. Kenyon excavated Jericho, not Ai. The long-term excavator of et-Tell was Joseph Callaway (1964-1972).
The old entry cited 'Kathleen Bimson'. No such scholar exists; the confusion may be with John J. Bimson (Redating the Exodus and Conquest, reviewed by Callaway in BA 44, 1981).

The old entry dated et-Tell to 'c. 2500-2000 BCE' with the city destroyed 'around 2500 BCE'. The city's end is Early Bronze IIIB, c. 2400 BCE on the conventional chronology, and the only later occupation is an Iron I village (c. 1220-1050 BCE).

The old entry said the destruction is 'part of a broader regional abandonment rather than a targeted conquest' and gave the size as 'approximately 5 hectares'. Neither claim was found in the sources. The EB IC city measured about 27.5 acres (≈11 ha).
The old entry omitted Khirbet el-Maqatir, the main alternative candidate for Ai, with its burned Late Bronze I fortress (ABR 1995-2016).
The old entry listed 'Judges 1 (Ai's location)'. Judges 1 does not mention Ai. The relevant texts are Josh 7-8 and Gen 12:8; 13:3.

updates.what: J. Kramer (Expedition Bible) publicizes Garstang's 1928 Late Bronze note and T. Kennedy's unpublished 2019 soundings at et-Tell (Late Bronze pottery and a burned layer), arguing that et-Tell is Joshua's Ai after all. Eames (June 2025) responds that the layer's date is unpublished and that the gate and stone-heap arguments do not hold.

sites.name: Amarna Letters
sites.subtitle: Cuneiform diplomatic archive of Amenhotep III and Akhenaten, with letters from Jerusalem's ruler · 14th century BCE
sites.date: Reigns of Amenhotep III and Amenhotep IV / Akhenaten, 14th century BCE (Barton 1916: Abdi-Heba's letters c. 1375-1357 BCE)
sites.date_basis: The letters are addressed to named pharaohs (Amenophis III and IV in Barton's terms) and were found at Akhetaten, the city Akhenaten founded and which was abandoned soon after his reign. BCE figures depend on Egyptian chronology.

discovery.when: Winter 1887-1888
discovery.who: Local villagers (Barton 1916 repeats the account of 'a native Egyptian woman'); tablets then dispersed through the antiquities market
discovery.where: Tell el-Amarna (ancient Akhetaten), east bank of the Nile, Middle Egypt

sites.location: Dispersed. Abdi-Heba's Jerusalem letters EA 285-290 are in the Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin (EA 285 = VAT 1601; EA 286 = VAT 1642; EA 287 = VAT 1644; EA 288 = VAT 1643; EA 289 = VAT 1645 + VAT 2709; EA 290 = VAT 1646). Others are in the British Museum (e.g., EA 252 = BM 29844), Cairo and elsewhere.

physical.material: Clay tablets
physical.language: Akkadian (the diplomatic language), with heavy Canaanite features in letters from the Levant

overview: In 1887-88 villagers at Tell el-Amarna found clay tablets inscribed in cuneiform. They turned out to be the foreign correspondence of Amenhotep III and Akhenaten. Barton (1916, p. 35) describes 'nearly four hundred' tablets. The archive includes letters from the great kings of Babylon, Assyria, Mitanni and Hatti, and from vassal rulers in Canaan and Phoenicia: Rib-Adda of Byblos, Lab'ayu of Shechem, and the rulers of Gezer, Lachish, Megiddo and others.

Six letters (EA 285-290) come from Abdi-Heba (older reading Ebed-Hepa), ruler of Urusalim, Jerusalem. He protests his loyalty, complains that the pharaoh's officials slander him, and begs for archers. He warns that the 'Habiru/'Apiru' are plundering the king's lands and that towns such as Gezer, Ashkelon and Lachish are aiding his enemies. His letters mention Keilah and Aijalon, which also appear in Joshua.

A complete re-edition based on collation of every extant tablet was published by A. F. Rainey (ed. W. M. Schniedewind and Z. Cochavi-Rainey, Brill 2015). A new translation by J. Lauinger and T. Yoder appeared in 2025.

text.quote: There are no lands left to the king, my lord. The Habiri plunder all the countries of the king. If there are mercenaries in this year, then there will be left countries of the king, my lord. If there are no mercenaries, the countries of the king will be lost.
text.translation: Ebed-Hepa (Abdi-Heba) of Jerusalem, EA 286 (Knudtzon 286 = Winckler-Abel 102), trans. G. A. Barton, Archaeology and the Bible (Philadelphia, 1916), Part II ch. XV, p. 346

evidence: Found 1887-88 at Tell el-Amarna; Barton (1916, p. 35) gives 'nearly four hundred' tablets 'inscribed in the Babylonian language and characters'.

EA 285-290 each open 'um-ma ARAD-hi/he-ba', 'thus Abdi-Heba' (CDLI transliterations checked for all six); CDLI places all six in the Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin (VAT 1601, 1642, 1644, 1643, 1645+2709, 1646).
EA 286 opens (CDLI transliteration): a-na LUGAL EN-ia qi-bi-ma um-ma ARAD-he-ba ARAD-ka-ma, 'To the king my lord, say: thus Abdi-Heba your servant'.
In EA 286 Abdi-Heba says neither his father nor his mother set him in his place but 'the arm of the mighty king' (Barton 1916 p. 346).

In EA 287 Abdi-Heba names Gezer, Ashkelon and Lachish as having given food and oil (to his enemies), the 'sons of Labaya' as giving the land to the Habiri, and 'the land of the city of Jerusalem' as granted to him by the king (Barton p. 346-347).
EA 287 mentions a caravan captured 'in the fields near the city Aijalon' and a matter involving Keilah (Barton p. 346-347).
Rainey's 2015 edition is based on collation of all extant tablets (Brill, HdO 110).
questions: Are the Habiru the Hebrews? Barton (1916, Part I p. 188) held that the Habiri 'may have been the first wave of the Hebrew conquest', and elsewhere that they 'were probably the Hebrews'. In the letters themselves the Habiru are a force that local rulers can side with: Abdi-Heba accuses Malkiel and the sons of Labaya of having 'given the land of the king to the Habiri' (EA 287, Barton p. 347). That is, the texts describe the Habiru by what they do, not by descent. The linguistic link 'apiru / 'ibri and the social-category reading were not settled from the primary sources cited here.

When relative to Joshua? Barton (1916, Part II p. 344) records that some readers took the letters as patriarchal-age and others as contemporary with the conquest. Which of these holds depends on the date assigned to the Exodus and conquest (1 Kgs 6:1, Judg 11:26 versus Exod 1:11). The letters themselves name no Israelite leader or tribe.

How big was Abdi-Heba's Jerusalem? Barton (1916, p. 187-188) reads the letters as describing a walled city and a sizeable kingdom reaching Keilah and Aijalon. The excavated Late Bronze remains on the Southeastern Ridge are sparse. The texts show a ruler with a scribe and diplomatic reach; they do not measure the town.

biblical.tie: Jerusalem is a city-state with its own king before Israel holds it. In the 14th century BCE, EA 285-290 show Urusalim ruled by Abdi-Heba as an Egyptian vassal.
Aijalon and Keilah appear in Abdi-Heba's letters (EA 287 in Barton's translation) as places in Jerusalem's sphere, and in the Bible as towns of the Shephelah and hill-country border.
Some readers equate the Habiru who 'plunder all the countries of the king' with the Hebrews. That equation is a reading, not a statement of the text.
Lab'ayu and his sons at Shechem (mentioned by Abdi-Heba) show Shechem as a regional power in the 14th century, the city where Joshua 24 and Judges 9 are set.

sites.name: Mordot Arnona royal administrative center
aka: Jerusalem lmlk storage complex near the US Embassy
sites.subtitle: Judahite administrative site with lmlk and 'private' stamped jar handles · late 8th - mid 7th century BCE
sites.date: Administrative phase: late 8th to first half of the 7th century BCE; the site overall runs from the Late Iron IIA (9th century BCE) to the Late Roman period (4th century CE)
sites.date_basis: Stratigraphy (nine building and construction phases, per Sapir et al., Tel Aviv 2022) and the stamped jar handles: lmlk ('belonging to the king') stamps, 'private' name stamps and incised concentric circles, all types dated by their occurrence in destruction layers of Sennacherib's 701 BCE campaign elsewhere in Judah and in 7th-century contexts. The link of the destroyed first building to 701 BCE is the excavators' interpretation.

discovery.when: Salvage excavations announced July 2020 (IAA); results published 2022 and 2024
discovery.who: Israel Antiquities Authority salvage excavation directed by Neria Sapir and Nathan Ben-Ari (with Benyamin Storchan per Times of Israel 2024); finds studied with Oded Lipschits (Tel Aviv University), Liora Freud and Ido Koch
discovery.where: Mordot Arnona, on the eastern edge of the Arnona neighbourhood of Jerusalem, c. 750 m northeast of Ramat Rahel, near the US Embassy; excavated ahead of a residential development

sites.location: Site excavated in salvage work ahead of construction (now the Mordot Arnona residential neighbourhood); finds held by the Israel Antiquities Authority. Whether any architecture was preserved in place was not stated in the sources located.
overview: Mordot Arnona is a hill c. 750 m northeast of Ramat Rahel on the southern edge of modern Jerusalem, excavated by the Israel Antiquities Authority as a salvage dig. In July 2020 the IAA announced a large structure with ashlar walls, covered by an artificial stone mound, and more than 120 jar handles bearing seal impressions in Hebrew script, including lmlk ('to the king') stamps naming Hebron, Ziph, Socoh and Mmst, and stamps with personal names.

The excavators' 2022 site report (Tel Aviv 49) describes nine building and construction phases from the 9th century BCE to the 4th century CE, with the site functioning as an administrative hub, marked by monumental architecture and many stamped handles, from the late 8th to the mid 7th century BCE, and afterwards as a farming settlement. Their 2024 article in 'Atiqot 110 publishes 17 handles with 'private' stamp impressions, alongside 124 lmlk-stamped handles and 33 handles incised with concentric circles.

As reported by the Times of Israel (Oct 2024), the excavators found an earlier administrative building destroyed down to its foundations and a second one built over it, with stones of the first reused in a platform; the 17 private-name stamps come only from the earlier, destroyed building. They read the destroyed building as belonging to Hezekiah's preparations before Sennacherib's 701 BCE campaign and the rebuilt one as serving the tax/tribute system after it.
evidence: Location: c. 750 m northeast of Ramat Rahel, eastern outskirts of Arnona, Jerusalem ('Atiqot 110 abstract; Tel Aviv 49 abstract).
Nine building and construction phases from the Late Iron IIA (9th c. BCE) to the Late Roman period (4th c. CE) (Sapir et al. 2022).
Administrative phase late 8th - first half of 7th c. BCE, shown by monumental structures and dozens of stamped handles (Sapir et al. 2024 abstract).
Published handle corpus: 17 'private' stamp impressions, 124 lmlk stamps, 33 incised concentric circles (Sapir, Ben-Ari, Koch and Lipschits 2024).

Private-name stamps reported in 2020 include Naham Abdi, Naham Hatzlihu, Meshalem Elnatan, Zafan Abmetz, Shaneah Azaria, Shalem Acha and Shivna Shachar (IAA/Friends of the IAA transliterations, 22 July 2020); the 2024 press adds Menachem Yubna, Peqach Tavra and Tzophen Azaryahu (Times of Israel).
lmlk stamps name the four places Hebron, Ziph, Socoh and Mmst (IAA 2020).
Two superimposed administrative buildings; the first destroyed to its foundations, the second built on its ruins reusing its stones (excavators via Times of Israel, 10 Oct 2024).
The 17 private-name handles were found only in the earlier, destroyed building (excavators via Times of Israel, 10 Oct 2024).
In 2020 the IAA described a structure with ashlar walls covered by an artificial stone mound c. 20 m high over some seven dunams (Friends of the IAA release).
questions: What destroyed the first building, and when? The excavators (Sapir, Ben-Ari and colleagues, as reported by Times of Israel, Oct 2024) tie the destruction and rebuilding to Sennacherib's 701 BCE campaign and read the rebuilding as an Assyrian-era statement of 'who is really in charge'. The evidence cited is the sequence (destroyed building, rebuilt one) and the restriction of private-name stamps to the earlier phase. The published abstracts located here do not state an absolute date (e.g. radiocarbon) for the destruction; the 701 link is an interpretation from the stamp typology and regional history.

Function of the private-name stamps. Sapir, Ben-Ari, Koch and Lipschits ('Atiqot 110, 2024) discuss their role 'on the eve of Sennacherib's campaign'; Ben-Ari (Times of Israel 2024) reads the named men as officials receiving produce, 'likely olive oil or wine', later diverted to Assyria. The stamps themselves carry only personal names (and patronymics); what office these men held is not written on them.

Relationship to Ramat Rahel, 750 m away. Sapir, Ben-Ari, Freud and Lipschits (Tel Aviv 49, 2022) examine how Mordot Arnona and Ramat Rahel together contributed to the political and economic organization of Judah's last 150 years. How the two sites divided the work of collection and storage is not settled in the sources located.

biblical.tie: Hezekiah rebels against Assyria; Sennacherib takes the fortified cities of Judah; Hezekiah pays tribute of silver and gold. The excavators read the destroyed first building and the rebuilt second as the before-and-after of this event. Kings speaks of silver and gold tribute; the Arnona handles are jars for agricultural produce, so the correspondence is to the administrative system, not to the tribute payment described.

Hezekiah builds 'storehouses also for the increase of corn, and wine, and oil' (KJV v. 28). Arnona is a storage/administrative site of his era with stamped storage-jar handles; no text names this site.

Manasseh reigns 55 years after Hezekiah; the rebuilt phase of the first half of the 7th century BCE falls in his reign by the conventional chronology. The Bible says nothing about his administration of produce.

corrections: The widely repeated 2020 figure of '120 stamped handles' is superseded: the 2024 'Atiqot publication gives 17 private-stamped and 124 lmlk-stamped handles (141 stamped) plus 33 handles with incised concentric circles (Sapir et al. 2024 abstract).

The Oct 2024 press figure of '180 handles' does not match the published count; the 'Atiqot 2024 totals come to 174 handles of the three types, of which the 33 concentric-circle handles are incised, not stamped (Sapir et al. 2024 abstract). The source of the 180 figure was not given.

Descriptions of 'two monumental 8th-century buildings' (Times of Israel 2024 wording) blur the sequence: the site's administrative phase runs from the late 8th into the first half of the 7th century BCE (Sapir et al. 2022, 2024), and on the excavators' own reading the second building was built after the 701 BCE destruction, i.e. at the very end of the 8th century or in the 7th.

Headlines calling it proof of the 'tribute system after biblical revolt' present an interpretation as a finding: what the ground shows is a destroyed building, a rebuilt one, and a shift from private-name to lmlk/concentric-circle marking; the link to Assyrian tribute is the excavators' reading (Times of Israel 2024).

sites.name: Assyrian Cuneiform Sealing Fragment from the Western Wall Area
aka: Assyrian letter to the king of Judah
Akkadian inscription near the Temple Mount
sites.subtitle: Akkadian cuneiform fragment of Assyrian clay · late 8th-mid 7th century BCE · announced October 2025
sites.date: Late 8th to mid-7th century BCE (the excavators' date on script and language); found in fill containing First Temple-period debris
sites.date_basis: Paleography and language of the cuneiform (Neo-Assyrian), per the IAA/City of David announcement. The findspot is secondary: fill from a Second Temple-period drainage channel mixed with debris from a First Temple-period building, so the ground gives no independent date.

discovery.when: Announced 22-23 October 2025; the date of recovery was not stated
discovery.who: Recovered by Moriah Cohen in wet-sifting at the Emek Tzurim sifting facility; IAA excavation directed by Ayala Zilberstein with the City of David Foundation; read by Filip Vukosavovic (IAA) and Peter Zilberg (Bar-Ilan); petrography by Anat Cohen-Weinberger (IAA)
discovery.where: Davidson Archaeological Park, less than 100 ft from the Western Wall, north of the City of David, Jerusalem

sites.location: Israel Antiquities Authority, Jerusalem (no inventory number published)

physical.material: Fired clay; petrography matches the Tigris basin (Nineveh / Ashur / Nimrud region), not Jerusalem
physical.dimensions: c. 2.5 cm (about one inch) wide

overview: In October 2025 the Israel Antiquities Authority and the City of David Foundation announced a small clay fragment inscribed in Akkadian cuneiform. It was recovered by wet-sifting soil from the Davidson Archaeological Park beside the Western Wall. The soil came from a Second Temple-period drainage channel and contained debris from a First Temple-period building. It was first presented at the New Discoveries in Jerusalem and Environs conference on 23 October 2025.

Petrographic analysis by Anat Cohen-Weinberger found the clay matches the geology of the Tigris basin, so the object was made in Assyria and carried to Jerusalem. The back carries a cord impression. Peter Zilberg describes it as 'probably a fragment of a bulla, an inscribed royal sealing.'

The readers report that the roughly 20 surviving signs mention a delay in payment, a due date on the first of the month Av, and an officer titled 'holder of the reins', a chariot post connected with the Assyrian court. They propose Hezekiah's reign, possibly his tribute revolt against Sennacherib, but also allow Manasseh or Josiah. As of September 2026 no peer-reviewed edition with a transliteration has been found.

text.quote: Reported content only: a delay in payment (from Judah), a due date on the 1st of the month Av, and the title of an Assyrian officer, the 'holder of the reins' (a chariot officer connected with the royal court).
text.translation: Summary of the decipherers' statements to the City of David Foundation and Times of Israel (22-23 Oct 2025). No transliteration has been published.

evidence: Fragment c. 2.5 cm, with about 20 cuneiform signs preserved and a cord impression on the back (City of David; BAS).
The clay's mineralogy matches the Tigris basin (Nineveh, Ashur, Nimrud/Kalhu region), not local Jerusalem clay (Cohen-Weinberger, IAA).
Found in wet-sifted fill from a Second Temple drainage channel, mixed with debris from a First Temple-period building. This is a secondary context.
The readers report a delay in payment, the 1st of Av as a due date, and the title 'holder of the reins' (a chariot officer).
Date on paleography and language: late 8th to mid-7th century BCE.
Zilberg says other, still unpublished sealings exist (Times of Israel).
questions: Which Judahite king? The IAA/City of David readers propose Hezekiah and his tribute revolt against Sennacherib (2 Kgs 18:7, 13-16). BAS (Steinmeyer, 24 Oct 2025) reports the same team allowing Manasseh or Josiah. The fragment names no king, as reported, so the choice rests on the script date plus the biblical narrative.

Tax notice or royal letter? The City of David page calls it a sherd concerning 'a delay in payment'; Zilberg calls it 'probably a fragment of a bulla, an inscribed royal sealing that served as a short summary'; BAS headlines it 'An Assyrian Letter to the King of Judah'. With about 20 signs and no published edition, the genre cannot be checked independently.

Is it the first cuneiform from Iron Age Jerusalem? The City of David Foundation presents it as the first Akkadian inscription from First Temple Jerusalem. BAS calls it the second cuneiform inscription from the First Temple period found nearby. Which earlier object BAS means is not stated in the published BAS text.

biblical.tie: Ahaz becomes Tiglath-pileser III's vassal and sends silver and gold. The fragment shows Assyrian administrative writing reaching Jerusalem in the vassal period. Which king it concerns is a reading.

Hezekiah rebels against Assyria, then pays Sennacherib 300 talents of silver and 30 of gold. A payment overdue to Assyria is what the fragment reportedly concerns. The link to Hezekiah specifically is the decipherers' proposal.
Manasseh is taken to Babylon by Assyrian commanders. It is listed only because BAS reports Manasseh as a possible date for the fragment.

sites.name: Babylonian Chronicles
sites.subtitle: Year-by-year cuneiform chronicles, including Nebuchadnezzar's capture of Jerusalem on 2 Adar 597 BCE
sites.date: Events: ABC 1 covers c. 747-668 BCE; the Neo-Babylonian series (ABC 2-7) covers 626-539 BCE, with BM 21946 covering 605-594 BCE. Tablets: undated by script (Wiseman 1956); the ABC 1 copy (BM 92502) is dated by its colophon to the 22nd year of Darius (500/499 BCE if Darius I). Levavi (2025) argues ABC 3-5 were composed in the late 590s BCE.
sites.date_basis: Each entry is dated by the Babylonian king's regnal year and month, e.g. 'the seventh year, the month Kislev ... the second day of the month Adar'. Converting to the Julian calendar (2 Adar, year 7 of Nebuchadnezzar = 15/16 March 597 BCE) follows Wiseman (1956). The tablets' own date of writing: Wiseman notes the script 'does not of itself allow any precise dating' and could fall anywhere from nearly contemporary with the events to the end of Achaemenid rule; BM 92502 has a Darius-year-22 colophon.

discovery.when: Acquired by the British Museum in the 19th century; BM 92502 published 1887 (Pinches; Winckler and Strassmaier); BM 21901 published 1923 (C. J. Gadd); BM 21946 and the other Nabopolassar-Nebuchadnezzar tablets published 1956 (D. J. Wiseman)
discovery.who: British Museum collection (not excavated in a recorded context)
discovery.where: Babylon 'so far as can be judged from the internal evidence' (Wiseman 1956); part of ABC 1 or its sources was copied at Sippar

sites.location: British Museum, London: BM 21946 (Jerusalem/Nebuchadnezzar chronicle), BM 21901 (Fall of Nineveh), BM 22047, BM 25127, BM 25124, BM 92502 (ABC 1), BM 35382 (Nabonidus Chronicle)

physical.material: Clay tablets

overview: The Babylonian Chronicles are clay tablets that record Babylonian and neighbouring history year by year in a terse, standard format: regnal year, month, what the king did. The tablets relevant to the Bible are in the British Museum. D. J. Wiseman published four of the Neo-Babylonian ones in Chronicles of Chaldaean Kings (1956), BM 21946 among them. A. K. Grayson's Assyrian and Babylonian Chronicles (1975) numbered the corpus ABC 1-25.

BM 21946 (ABC 5) covers Nebuchadnezzar's first eleven years. It records the defeat of the Egyptian army at Carchemish (605), Nebuchadnezzar's accession, the western campaigns, a drawn battle with Egypt (601), and in year 7 a march to the Hatti-land, a siege of 'the city of Judah', its capture on the 2nd of Adar, the capture of its king, and the installation of 'a king of his own choice'. BM 21901 (ABC 3) records the fall of Nineveh (612) and, in 609, Aššur-uballiṭ and 'a great army of Egypt' crossing the Euphrates against Harran. ABC 1 (BM 92502) records Shalmaneser V's accession and the destruction of a city read Šamara'in/Shabara'in.

The chronicles do not mention the 587/586 destruction of Jerusalem. BM 21946 stops after Nebuchadnezzar's 11th year (594/593), and the next Neo-Babylonian chronicle tablet in Wiseman's set (BM 25124) deals with Neriglissar's campaign of 557/556.

text.quote: He encamped against the city of Judah, and in the month of Adar, on the second day, he seized the city and captured the king. A king of his own choosing he appointed in it; its heavy tribute he took and brought into Babylon.
text.translation: Our literal translation of BM 21946 rev. 12-13 as transliterated by D. J. Wiseman, Chronicles of Chaldaean Kings (1956), p. 72 (ina muḫḫi āl Iaḫudu iddi-ma ina araḫ Addari ūmu 2-KAM āla iṣṣabat šarra iktašad / šarra ša libbišu ina libbi ipteqid bilassa kabittu ilqâm-ma ana Bābili ultērib)

evidence: BM 21946 rev. 11-13 (Wiseman's transliteration): 'Year 7, month Kislev: the king of Akkad mustered his troops, marched to the Hatti-land, encamped against the city of Judah (āl ia-a-ḫu-du), and on day 2 of Adar seized the city and captured the king; he appointed there a king of his own heart, took its heavy tribute and brought it to Babylon.'
The chronicle names neither Jerusalem nor Jehoiachin nor Zedekiah: 'city of Judah', 'the king', 'a king of his own choice'.
Wiseman (1956) converts 2 Adar of Nebuchadnezzar's year 7 to 15/16 March 597 BCE.
BM 21946 obv. 1-8: in Nabopolassar's 21st year (605), crown prince Nebuchadnezzar defeats the Egyptian army at Carchemish.
BM 21946 rev. 5-7: in year 4 (601) the king marches to Egypt; 'in open battle they smote the breast of each other and inflicted great havoc on each other'; the king of Akkad returns to Babylon.

BM 21901 l. 66-67: 'In the month of Tammuz Aššur-uballiṭ, king of Assyria, a great army of Egypt ... crossed the river [and] marched against the city of Harran to conquer it' (Wiseman 1956 translation, 609 BCE).
ABC 1 (BM 92502) i 27-28: 'On the twenty-fifth day of Tebet Shalmaneser took his seat on the throne in Assyria, and the city of Shabarain was destroyed' (Rogers 1912 translation).
BM 92502 is 'a copy made in the twenty-second year of Darius from an older and damaged text' (Wiseman 1956, p. 2).
Tablet provenance: Babylon on internal evidence; no recorded excavation context (Wiseman 1956, pp. 4-5).
questions: Seventh year or eighth? The chronicle dates the capture of the 'city of Judah' to Nebuchadnezzar's 7th year, Adar. Jeremiah 52:28 counts 3,023 Judeans deported 'in the seventh year'; 2 Kings 24:12 says Jehoiachin was taken 'in the eighth year of his reign'. One explanation is different year-counting (accession-year vs. non-accession-year reckoning, or a spring-versus-autumn new year); the texts themselves state only the numbers.

When were the chronicles written? Wiseman (1956) held that the script allows anything from near-contemporary to late Achaemenid. Yuval Levavi (JAOS 145, 2025) argues ABC 3-5 form a complete trilogy composed soon after the last events in ABC 5, around the late 590s BCE. A late-590s composition would make the Jerusalem entry close to contemporary.

Why no 587/586? The destruction of Jerusalem in Zedekiah's 11th year falls after the last year on BM 21946. Levavi (2025) argues ABC 3-5 are complete as they stand, which would make the gap the end of that composition. The Livius.org introduction to ABC 5 instead assumes a 'lost sequel of this chronicle'. Neither position has a surviving tablet behind it.

biblical.tie: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem, takes King Jehoiachin, carries off the treasures, and makes Mattaniah/Zedekiah king. The chronicle: siege of 'the city of Judah', capture of 'the king', appointment of 'a king of his own choice', heavy tribute to Babylon. The events match; the chronicle supplies the day (2 Adar).
'In the seventh year, three thousand Jews and three and twenty' deported. The chronicle also dates the capture to Nebuchadnezzar's 7th year.

'The army of Pharaoh-necho ... by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim.' BM 21946 obv. 1-8 records Nebuchadnezzar's defeat of the Egyptian army at Carchemish in Nabopolassar's 21st year (605).

Necho goes up 'against/to the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates' and Josiah dies at Megiddo. BM 21901 has Aššur-uballiṭ with 'a great army of Egypt' crossing the river against Harran in 609. The chronicle does not mention Josiah.

Jehoiakim's three years of vassalage and the note that the king of Egypt 'came not again any more out of his land'. The chronicle's 601 clash with Egypt ('great havoc on each other') and Nebuchadnezzar's year at home rebuilding his chariotry are the Babylonian side of that period (our reading).

corrections: Old entry's quoted inscription 'In the month of Adar, the enemy captured the city' is not the chronicle's wording. The chronicle says the king of Akkad 'encamped against the city of Judah and on the second day of the month of Adar seized the city and captured the king'.

Old entry says they were 'discovered during excavations' and are housed in 'the British Museum and the Iraq Museum'. The chronicle tablets discussed here are British Museum acquisitions without recorded excavation context; no Iraq Museum holding of them was found.

Old entry says the tablets detail the conquest of Jerusalem 'in vivid detail' and cites Jeremiah 39-52 generally. The chronicle gives three lines on 597 and says nothing about 587/586, the Temple, or Zedekiah's revolt; Jer 39 and 52:4-27 (the 587/586 fall) have no chronicle parallel.

Old entry: 'Confirms 597 BCE Jerusalem conquest'. The chronicle gives the regnal date (year 7, 2 Adar). '597 BCE' is the modern conversion (Wiseman 1956: 15/16 March 597), and the name 'Jerusalem' does not appear; the text says 'the city of Judah'.

updates.what: Yuval Levavi (JAOS 145) argues that chronicles ABC 3-5 form a complete trilogy with no missing sections, with ABC 5 (the Jerusalem chronicle) as its centerpiece, composed around the late 590s BCE, shortly after the last events it records.

sites.name: Baruch ben Neriah Bullae (Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the Scribe)
aka: Bulla of Baruch son of Neriah
sites.subtitle: Two unprovenanced clay seal impressions naming 'Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe' · authenticity contested
sites.date: Claimed late 7th-early 6th century BCE by palaeography. No archaeological context. Laboratory analysis published in 2014 points to modern manufacture (see questions).
sites.date_basis: Neither bulla comes from a recorded excavation; both appeared through the antiquities market. The proposed Iron Age date rests only on letter forms and on the match with the biblical Baruch son of Neriah. Goren and Arie (BASOR 372, 2014) compared the two bullae with more than 180 bullae, most of them from Jerusalem, and concluded their results point 'to the production of the two Berekhyahu bullae in modern times'.

discovery.when: First bulla: antiquities market, published by Nahman Avigad (BA 1979) as 'recently discovered'; second bulla: published by Hershel Shanks (BAR, March/April 1996)
discovery.who: Antiquities market; no excavator
discovery.where: Unknown. No findspot is documented for either bulla.

sites.location: Not confirmed in a published museum record. The first bulla is widely reported as being in the Israel Museum and the second as in a private collection; no museum record was located.

physical.material: Unbaked clay seal impressions (bullae)

overview: Two small clay bullae carry the same three-line seal impression, published as reading 'belonging to Berekhyahu, son of Neriyahu, the scribe'. Berekhyahu is the full, theophoric form of the name Baruch, and the Bible's Baruch son of Neriah is Jeremiah's scribe (Jer 36:4, 32; 45:1).

Nahman Avigad published the first in 1979 ('Baruch the Scribe and Jerahmeel the King's Son', Biblical Archaeologist 42). He wrote that 'two persons mentioned in the Bible are positively identified with the persons named on two recently discovered seal-impressions'. A second impression of the same seal, bearing a fingerprint, was announced by Hershel Shanks in BAR in 1996.

Neither object has an excavated context. In 2014 Yuval Goren and Eran Arie (BASOR 372) published laboratory analyses of both bullae, compared them with more than 180 bullae, most of them from Jerusalem, and concluded the results point to modern production of both.

text.quote: (Belonging) to Berekhyahu / son of Neriyahu / the scribe
text.translation: Our literal rendering of the reading usually given as lbrkyhw / bn nryhw / hspr. The names and title are confirmed by the titles of Avigad 1979 and Goren and Arie 2014; the Hebrew letter-by-letter reading is not confirmed from a primary publication.

evidence: Inscription as published: 'to Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe' (names and title as given in Goren and Arie's 2014 title; Avigad's 1979 title renders it 'Baruch the Scribe').
Two bullae impressed by the same seal design are known; the second carries a fingerprint (Shanks, BAR 1996).
No recorded findspot for either; both came through the antiquities market.

Goren and Arie (BASOR 372, 2014) analysed both bullae and compared them with more than 180 bullae, most from Jerusalem; their abstract states the results point 'to the production of the two Berekhyahu bullae in modern times'.
Avigad (BA 42, 1979) presented the first bulla together with a bulla of 'Jerahmeel the king's son' (cf. Jer 36:26) as positive identifications of biblical persons.
questions: Authentic or forged? For: Avigad (Biblical Archaeologist 42, 1979) presented the first bulla as genuine and identified the owner with Jeremiah's scribe; Shanks (BAR 1996) presented the fingerprinted second bulla as a further impression. Against: Goren and Arie (BASOR 372, 2014) found, by laboratory comparison with more than 180 bullae, that the two Berekhyahu bullae were produced in modern times. Andrew Vaughn and Christopher Rollston (Near Eastern Archaeology 68, 2005) had already set out the case that market inscriptions with sensational biblical names need special scrutiny for forgery. No excavated Berekhyahu bulla exists to settle it.

Is 'Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe' the biblical Baruch? If genuine, name, patronym and title all match Jer 36:4, 32. But a forger would copy exactly those three features from the Bible, so on an unprovenanced object the match cannot count as evidence of authenticity.

biblical.tie: 'Baruch the son of Neriah' writes Jeremiah's scroll; 'Baruch the scribe'. The bulla names Berekhyahu (full form of Baruch) son of Neriyahu (full form of Neriah), the scribe. Exact correspondence of name, father and title, on an object whose authenticity is contested.
Jeremiah gives the sealed deed of purchase to 'Baruch the son of Neriah', who stores it in an earthen vessel. That text describes sealed documents of exactly the kind bullae closed.
Oracle to Baruch son of Neriah. Named person only; no further correspondence.
'Seraiah the son of Neriah', apparently Baruch's brother. Not on the bulla; noted for the family name only.

sources.cite: Nahman Avigad, 'Baruch the Scribe and Jerahmeel the King's Son', Biblical Archaeologist 42/2 (1979): 114-118, doi:10.2307/3209372
sources.verified: Crossref record gives author, title, BA 42:2, pp. 114-118, April 1979; OpenAlex abstract: 'two persons mentioned in the Bible are positively identified with the persons named on two recently discovered seal-impressions'

sources.cite: Hershel Shanks, 'Fingerprint of Jeremiah's Scribe', Biblical Archaeology Review (March/April 1996)
sources.verified: BAS Library page shows title, author Hershel Shanks, BAR March/April 1996 (article body paywalled)

sources.cite: Yuval Goren and Eran Arie, 'The Authenticity of the Bullae of Berekhyahu Son of Neriyahu the Scribe', BASOR 372 (2014): 147-158, doi:10.5615/bullamerschoorie.372.0147
sources.verified: Crossref record gives authors, title, BASOR 372, pp. 147-158, Nov 2014; OpenAlex abstract read: analyses compared with >180 bullae point 'to the production of the two Berekhyahu bullae in modern times'

sources.cite: Andrew G. Vaughn and Christopher A. Rollston, 'The Antiquities Market, Sensationalized Textual Data, and Modern Forgeries', Near Eastern Archaeology 68/1-2 (2005): 61-65, doi:10.1086/nea25067594
sources.verified: Crossref record gives authors, title, NEA 68:1-2, pp. 61-65, March 2005

corrections: Old entry says the bulla was 'authenticated in 1996'. Nothing was authenticated in 1996; a second, fingerprinted bulla was published by Shanks in BAR that year. The only published laboratory study (Goren and Arie, BASOR 2014) concluded both bullae are modern productions.

Old entry gives the inscription as 'Belonging to Baruch, son of Neriah'. The published reading uses the full theophoric forms: 'to Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe', and the title 'the scribe' is part of the text.

Old entry treats the bulla as 'tangible evidence of the existence of Baruch' and 'Authentic'. With no findspot and a published forensic study pointing to modern manufacture, it cannot serve as evidence for Baruch; the biblical text stands on its own.

Old entry gives 'Dimensions: Approximately 1.2 cm diameter' and 'Current Location: Private collection' (while the overview says the same). Neither the measurement nor the current holder could be confirmed in a published record, and the two bullae are reported as held separately.
Old entry links '2 Kings 25 (Babylonian records)'. 2 Kings 25 is the fall of Jerusalem and does not mention Baruch; the Baruch texts are Jer 32, 36, 43 and 45.

sites.name: Beni Hasan: the Aamu Procession in the Tomb of Khnumhotep II
sites.subtitle: Painted procession of 37 Asiatics in a Middle Kingdom rock-cut tomb · Year 6 of Senusret II
sites.date: Year 6 of Senusret II (Usertsen II), 12th Dynasty; early 19th century BCE on conventional chronologies
sites.date_basis: The scene itself carries a date: the royal scribe Neferhotep holds a document headed 'Year 6 under the majesty of ... Usertsen II' (Newberry, Beni Hasan I, p. 69, pl. XXXVIII). Breasted notes this is the latest date in the tomb (ARE I §620 n.). The BCE figure depends on the 12th-Dynasty chronology chosen.

discovery.when: Tomb described by Jomard in 1798; copied by Burton (1825), Champollion, Rosellini and Hay (1828), Lepsius (1842); full survey 1890-1891
discovery.who: Survey published by Percy E. Newberry for the Egypt Exploration Fund's Archaeological Survey of Egypt (1893)
discovery.where: Tomb No. 3 (northern group), rock-cut cemetery of Beni Hasan, east bank of the Nile, Middle Egypt

sites.location: In situ, Tomb No. 3 (BH 3), Beni Hasan, Egypt; north wall of the main chamber, row 3

physical.material: Paint on plaster over rock-cut tomb walls

overview: Beni Hasan is a Middle Kingdom cemetery of rock-cut tombs of the governors of the Oryx nome. Tomb No. 3 belongs to Khnumhotep II, 'Administrator of the Eastern Desert'. The north wall of its main chamber is painted in six rows showing produce and people being brought to him. Row 3 is a procession of foreigners.

The procession is introduced by the royal scribe Neferhotep, holding a document dated Year 6 of Senusret II that counts '37 Aamu of Shu' brought on account of mesdemet (black eye-paint/kohl). The leader is labelled hqꜣ ḫꜣst Ibshꜣ, 'ruler of the desert/foreign land, Abesha'. A line over the group reads 'arrival bringing kohl, which 37 Aamu bring to him.'
The tomb was known and copied long before photography; Newberry (1893) records that the Great Inscription was vandalised in 1888 or 1889 and that the colours had faded since the 1828 copies.

text.quote: The arrival, bringing eye-paint, which 37 Asiatics bring to him. ... Sheik of the highlands, Ibshe.
text.translation: J. H. Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt I (1906) §620 note d, p. 281 (citing Newberry, Beni Hasan I, pl. XXX); cf. Newberry (1893) p. 69: 'arrival bringing kohl which 37 Aamu bring to him'

evidence: Number: 37 Aamu, written twice (the scribe's document and the caption over the group) (Newberry 1893 p. 69).
Group label: 'Aamu of Shu' (ꜥꜣmw n Šw); Breasted renders 'Asiatics of the desert' (ARE I §620 n.).
Leader's title and name: hqꜣ ḫꜣst Ibshꜣ - Newberry 'hak-prince of the desert, Abesha'; Breasted 'Sheik of the highlands, Ibshe'.
Stated purpose: they come 'on account of mesdemet' (eye-paint, stibium or kohl) (Newberry p. 69).
Dated document: Year 6 of Usertsen (Senusret) II, carried by the royal scribe Neferhotep (Newberry p. 69, pl. XXXVIII).
Scene position: Tomb No. 3, north wall, row 3, pls. XXVIII, XXX, XXXI (Newberry 1893).
questions: Who were the Aamu of Shu? J. Kamrin (JAEI 1/3, 2009) treats the group in detail; Breasted (1906, §620 n.) called the leader's name 'a good Hebrew name' while rejecting the old link to Abraham as having 'nothing to do' with it. The captions give only a group label, a place-word (Šw) and a personal name; nothing in the tomb states their homeland beyond that.

The leader's title hqꜣ ḫꜣst is the same phrase later used for the Hyksos rulers ('rulers of foreign lands'). Whether that is just the ordinary Egyptian title for any foreign chief in the 12th Dynasty, or an early instance of the same group, is an inference either way; the tomb only shows the title in use by c. Year 6 of Senusret II.

biblical.tie: The tomb shows a party of 37 West Asians, with a named chief, being received and registered by an Egyptian official in the 12th Dynasty. That matches the biblical picture of small groups of Asiatics coming down to Egypt and being handled by officials. It does not show famine, and the group is not named as any biblical family.

Old entry claimed an exact match. The Ishmaelite caravan carries gum, balm and myrrh and buys Joseph; the Beni Hasan group brings eye-paint and is registered as a party of 37 visitors. The correspondence is general (Asiatics trading goods into Egypt), not specific.

sources.cite: P. E. Newberry, with G. W. Fraser, ed. F. Ll. Griffith, Beni Hasan, Part I (Archaeological Survey of Egypt 1; London: Kegan Paul for the Egypt Exploration Fund, 1893) (Tomb No. 3, frontispiece and pls. II, XXII-XXXVIII; the Aamu scene p. 69, pls. XXVIII, XXX, XXXI, XXXVIII)
sources.verified: Downloaded the archive.org full text of the 1893 volumes; read the Tomb No. 3 history of copying (Jomard 1798 to Lepsius 1842), and p. 69 with the Year 6 document, 'Aamu of Shu, number amounting to 37' and 'hak-prince of the desert, Abesha'. Second scan: https://archive.org/details/india.history.resource.84579 (metadata confirms Newberry, Fraser, Griffith ed., 1893).

sources.cite: J. H. Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt I: The First to the Seventeenth Dynasties (Chicago, 1906), §620 and note d
sources.verified: Downloaded archive.org full text; read §620 (Khnumhotep II's career, visit of 'thirty-seven Bedwin' in Year 6 of Sesostris II) and note d with the quoted caption.

sources.cite: J. Kamrin, 'The Aamu of Shu in the Tomb of Khnumhotep II at Beni Hassan,' Journal of Ancient Egyptian Interconnections 1/3 (2009), DOI 10.2458/azu_jaei_v01i3_kamrin
sources.verified: DOI resolves to JAEI article id 892 (University of Arizona); Crossref record gives title, author Janice Kamrin (ARCE Cairo), JAEI vol. 1 no. 3. Article page itself blocked my fetch, so I have not read her conclusions.

corrections: Old entry: 'discovered in 1902 during excavations ... by Egyptian archaeologists.' The tomb was described by Jomard in 1798, copied by Champollion, Rosellini and Hay in 1828 and Lepsius in 1842, and fully published by Newberry in 1893 (Beni Hasan I, Tomb No. 3).
Old entry: tombs of 'high officials of the 19th nome.' The owner is Khnumhotep II, whose own inscriptions refer to the Oryx nome; the scene is in Tomb No. 3 (Newberry 1893).

Old entry: 'necropolis south of Cairo' is vague to the point of misleading; Beni Hasan is in Middle Egypt, on the east bank of the Nile (Newberry notes Tehneh 14 miles north and Sheikh Said 15 miles south).
Old entry: 'carrying goods such as oils, resins.' The captions state the purpose as mesdemet (eye-paint/kohl) - no oils or resins are named.

Old entry: 'earliest known visual representation of Semitic peoples engaging in trade.' Not established by any source consulted here; removed.
Old entry: 'Script: N/A.' The scene has hieroglyphic captions, including a dated document.

sites.name: Berlin Pedestal Relief
sites.subtitle: Granite statue-base fragment with three bound Asiatic captives and name rings · Egyptian, date disputed
sites.date: Disputed: 18th Dynasty (Giveon; Görg's early view, Thutmose III or Amenhotep II as reported by Hoffmeier 2007) or 19th Dynasty, possibly Ramesses II (Görg 2001 as reported by van der Veen, Theis & Görg 2010), perhaps copied from an older list
sites.date_basis: The date rests on style and spelling alone. The block has no provenance and no text naming a king. The Ashkelon and Canaan spellings are consonantal and match 18th-Dynasty forms (Amenhotep II). The trio of Ashkelon, Canaan and a third name resembles the sequence on Merenptah's stele.

discovery.when: Bought 1913
discovery.who: Ludwig Borchardt, from the dealer M. Nachman (per the Berlin museum's archival notes as reported by van der Veen et al. 2010)
discovery.where: Unknown. It was bought on the antiquities market and never excavated.

sites.location: Ägyptisches Museum und Papyrussammlung, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, inv. ÄM 21687

physical.material: Grey granite
physical.dimensions: 46 cm high × 39.5 cm wide; 7.5 cm thick as sawn (probably cut from a larger block in modern times); name rings 18 × 9 cm (van der Veen et al. 2010, p. 15 and n. 7, n. 10)

overview: A slab of grey granite, probably from the base of a royal statue. It shows three bound Western Asiatic captives, each with an oval 'name ring' on his body naming a conquered place, and above them a band of hieroglyphs reading '[...] one who is falling on his feet'. Ludwig Borchardt bought it for Berlin in 1913 from the dealer M. Nachman, together with a companion slab (ÄM 21688) of about the same size, which shows two Asiatic captives and one Nubian captive.

The left name ring reads ʿ-s-q-l-n, Ashkelon. The middle reads k-y-n-ʿ-nw, Canaan. The right ring is damaged, apparently by modern hacking. It reads i-[?]-šȝ-i-r, and the second sign is almost entirely lost. In 2001 Manfred Görg restored the missing sign as a vulture (ȝ). He read the whole as an archaic writing of 'Israel' and argued that the three names mirror Merenptah's stele (Canaan, Ashkelon, ... Israel). In 2010 P. van der Veen, C. Theis and Görg published photographs taken under raking light and an aluminium-foil impression. They say these show the vulture's leg and claw.

The reading matters because if the third ring does name Israel in the 18th Dynasty (or in a list copied from one), it would put an entity called Israel in Canaan before Merenptah's Year 5 (c. 1208 BCE). J. K. Hoffmeier rejected the reading on the grounds of its sibilant and its orthography. The stone itself cannot settle the question, because its key sign is damaged.

text.quote: Left ring: ʿ-s-q-l-n (Ashkelon). Middle ring: k-y-n-ʿ-nw (Canaan). Right ring: i-[ȝ?]-šȝ-i-r, damaged, restored by Görg as 'Israel'. Band above the captives: '[...] ḫtb.w ḥr rd.wi=f', 'one who is falling on his feet...'.
text.translation: Transliterations and the band translation from P. van der Veen, C. Theis & M. Görg, JAEI 2:4 (2010), pp. 15-17. No public-domain translation exists.

evidence: Grey granite slab, 46 × 39.5 cm, sawn to 7.5 cm thick, bearing three bound Asiatic captives with name rings (van der Veen et al. 2010, p. 15).

Bought in 1913 by Borchardt from M. Nachman, with no findspot (museum archival notes as reported in van der Veen et al. 2010). The companion slab ÄM 21688 (50 × 38 cm, also grey granite) shows two Asiatic captives and one Nubian captive and names Retenu.
Ring 1, Ashkelon, is written consonantally without group-writing. The closest parallel is pLeningrad 1116A from the reign of Amenhotep II.
Ring 2, Canaan (k-y-n-ʿ-nw), has close parallels in Amenhotep II's Memphis and Karnak stelae. It differs from the usual Ramesside form pȝ-Knʿn.

Ring 3 is damaged along its right edge, probably by modern hacking. The first sign is the reed-leaf (i). The second is almost lost; van der Veen and Theis report traces of a vulture's leg and claw from raking-light photography and a foil impression. The remaining signs are the pool-sign šȝ, the reed-leaf i, and r.
Van der Veen et al. report that measuring the ring shows no room for any further sign after šȝ, i and r.
No king's name survives on the fragment.
questions: Does ring 3 read 'Israel'? M. Görg (Biblische Notizen 106, 2001, 21-27) restored the second sign as a vulture (ȝ). He read the name as iȝ-šr-il / yȝ-šr-il, taking the ȝ of šȝ as r, as in Middle Kingdom spellings such as Rw-šȝ-mm for Jerusalem in the Execration Texts. Van der Veen, Theis & Görg (JAEI 2:4, 2010) say that raking-light photographs and a foil impression show the vulture's leg and claw. J. K. Hoffmeier (JETS 50/2, 2007, 241-242) answers that the name is 'plagued by serious linguistic and orthographic problems'. His points: Israel needs ś, not š (Merenptah's stele writes it with s); šȝ is a group-writing for šā, as in Sharuhen; a restored ȝ would stand for Semitic lamed; and the final r is not the l-sign used in 'Ashkelon' on the same block. Van der Veen et al. reply that Egyptian scribes varied their signs for foreign names, for example in the Egyptian spelling of Kurigalzu. The dispute turns on one damaged sign and on the rules for rendering sibilants.

Date. Hoffmeier (2007, p. 241) reports that Görg dated the block on style to Thutmose III or Amenhotep II. Van der Veen et al. (2010, p. 15) report Görg's tentative 19th-Dynasty date (Ramesses II), based on the resemblance to Merenptah's stele, while granting that the spellings copy an earlier 18th-Dynasty source. R. Giveon (Eretz-Israel 15, 1981, as cited by van der Veen et al.) dated it to the 18th Dynasty. With no provenance or royal name, the date floats with the spellings.
Unknown: whether ÄM 21687 and ÄM 21688 came from the same monument, where the statue stood, and which king it portrayed. The sources are silent.

biblical.tie: If ring 3 is Israel, the block would place a group or land called Israel beside Ashkelon and Canaan in an Egyptian list, possibly two centuries before Merenptah. That would bear on the date of Israel's presence in Canaan implied by the settlement accounts.

Advocates of a 15th-century Exodus (B. G. Wood, JETS 48, 2005) cite the block as support for Israel in Canaan under the 18th Dynasty, and so for the 480-year figure. That depends on both the 'Israel' reading and the 18th-Dynasty date, and both are disputed.
Ashkelon appears in the same ring sequence. The biblical texts place Ashkelon among the Philistine and Canaanite coastal cities, and here it stands beside Canaan.

sources.cite: P. van der Veen, C. Theis & M. Görg, 'Israel in Canaan (Long) Before Pharaoh Merenptah? A Fresh Look at Berlin Statue Pedestal Relief 21687', Journal of Ancient Egyptian Interconnections 2:4 (2010): 15-25. doi:10.2458/azu_jaei_v02i4_van_der_veen
sources.verified: The DOI resolves to the JAEI article (article id 937). I read the full PDF from the Wayback Machine capture of the journal's download link: granite, 46 × 39.5 cm, Borchardt/Nachman 1913, the ring readings, the reply to Hoffmeier, and n. 2 citing Görg, BN 106 (2001) 21-27.

sources.cite: J. K. Hoffmeier, 'What Is the Biblical Date for the Exodus? A Response to Bryant Wood', Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 50/2 (June 2007): 225-247, esp. 241-242
sources.verified: Downloaded the PDF and read p. 241: the four objections, the words 'plagued by serious linguistic and orthographic problems', and the report of Görg's Thutmose III / Amenhotep II date.

sources.cite: P. van der Veen, 'Berlin Statue Pedestal Reliefs 21687 and 21688: Ongoing Research', Journal of Ancient Egyptian Interconnections 4:4 (2012). doi:10.2458/azu_jaei_v04i4_van_der_veen
sources.verified: The Crossref and OpenAlex records give the title, JAEI 4:4, and 2012, and OpenAlex describes it as a 'Research report'. The text was not read.

sources.cite: M. Görg, 'Israel in Hieroglyphen', Biblische Notizen 106 (2001): 21-27
sources.verified: Not seen directly. The citation appears identically in Hoffmeier 2007 n. 88 and van der Veen et al. 2010 n. 2, both read this session; the URL is Hoffmeier's article.

corrections: The old entry said it was 'discovered within the museum's archives, where it had been stored since the late 19th century'. It was bought in 1913 by Ludwig Borchardt from the dealer M. Nachman (van der Veen et al. 2010, p. 15).
The old entry described it as 'approximately 30 cm tall'. It measures 46 × 39.5 cm.
The old entry gave 'Material: Stone relief fragment'. It is grey granite, from a statue pedestal.

The old entry said the scene is only interpreted as 'potentially referencing the land of Israel' and called the imagery 'too ambiguous'. The claim is specific: one damaged name ring, read i-[ȝ]-šȝ-i-r and restored as Israel, beside legible name rings for Ashkelon and Canaan. The dispute is over one sign and the sibilant, not over the imagery.

The old entry gave the date as 'c. 13th century BCE'. The proposed dates run from the 18th Dynasty (15th-14th century BCE) to Ramesses II. The spellings point to an 18th-Dynasty source even on the late view.

The old entry said it could be 'one of the earliest known artistic depictions' of Israelites. The captives are generic bound Asiatics with name rings, a standard Egyptian convention, and no figure is individually identified as an Israelite.
The old entry listed Exodus 1, Genesis 47 and Numbers 1. The relief concerns places in Canaan, not Israelites in Egypt, so those ties do not correspond to anything on the object.

sites.name: Bethesda Pool
sites.subtitle: Twin rock-cut pools beside St. Anne's Church, Jerusalem · Second Temple period and later
sites.date: Rock-cut pools in use in the Second Temple period; later Roman and Byzantine/Crusader structures built over them. The precise construction dates are not confirmed from the excavation report.
sites.date_basis: The 1888 report dates only the church above the pool (built after about 10 ft of earth had accumulated over the rock). Dating of the pools themselves rests on the later White Fathers / École Biblique excavations, which have not been reviewed for this entry.

discovery.when: Cistern exposed during clearing of the St. Anne's property after the Crimean War and opened to visitors by 1888; published by Conrad Schick in the PEF Quarterly Statement, July 1888, with a second, western pool reported the same year
discovery.who: The 'Algerian monks' (White Fathers) at St. Anne's; the architect 'Mons. Maux' (as spelled in the report); recorded by Conrad Schick
discovery.where: Grounds of St. Anne's Church, north of the Temple Mount (Haram), near St. Stephen's (Lions') Gate, Jerusalem

sites.location: In situ, St. Anne's (Sainte-Anne) compound, Old City of Jerusalem

physical.material: Rock-cut basins with masonry; later vaults and church remains above
physical.dimensions: 1888 measurement of the first-found pool: 55 ft E-W x 12.5 ft N-S, cut 30 ft deep, reached by a flight of 24 steps from the east scarp; the building above it c. 70 x 25 ft with an eastern apse (PEF QS 1888)

overview: After the Crimean War the Ottoman Sultan presented the ruined church of St. Anne (then the 'Salahieh' school) near St. Stephen's Gate to the Emperor Napoleon. While the French-appointed monks cleared the grounds they found a deep rock-cut 'cistern' with steps. Conrad Schick planned and published it in the Palestine Exploration Fund's Quarterly Statement for July 1888.

Schick's report describes a pool cut 30 ft into rock, 55 by 12.5 ft, with a flight of 24 steps down from the east, lying beneath a later apsed building (read as a church) whose floor was carried on vaults. The PEF editors added that Schick had found 'a second pool to the west of this, forming what is called a twin pool'.

The editors then argued from John 5:2: 'the only possible way for a pool to have five porticoes (unless it is a pentagon) is to be a double or twin pool, so that there may be one portico along each side and one for the wall of separation.' That is an argument from the text to the plan; the 1888 report does not describe standing porticoes.
evidence: Rock-cut pool 55 ft E-W x 12.5 ft N-S, 30 ft deep, 24 steps from the east (Schick, PEF QS 1888).
North wall of masonry with four piers on rock bases carrying arches, spaces later filled in (PEF QS 1888).
A second pool west of the first ('twin pool') reported by Schick in 1888.
A later apsed building (c. 70 x 25 ft) built over the pool after c. 10 ft of earth had accumulated (PEF QS 1888).
Pilgrim testimony forms 'a continuous chain of evidence from the 4th to the 12th century' for the site, per the PEF editors citing Sir Charles Wilson (1888).
Before 1888 the name 'Bethesda' had been attached to the Birket Israil pool north of the Haram (PEF QS 1888).
questions: What the five porticoes were: the PEF editors (1888) proposed one portico on each of four sides of a double pool and a fifth on the dividing wall. U. C. von Wahlde ('The Puzzling Pool of Bethesda', BAR Sept/Oct 2011, as summarized by BAS) describes 'a rectangular pool with two basins separated by a wall' and reads the southern basin, with 'broad steps with landings', as a mikveh and the northern as its reservoir (otzar). The mikveh function is a reading of the stepped design, not an inscription.
Healing cult: whether the site was also, or later, a healing sanctuary (a reading in some later literature) was not documented in the sources cited here and is left open.
Exact dates of construction of each basin and of the dividing wall are not available from a primary excavation report cited here; they stay open here rather than being filled with secondary figures.

biblical.tie: 'There is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches' (KJV). The site is north of the Temple Mount near the traditional Sheep Gate area; a double pool gives a plan that could carry five porticoes, as the 1888 editors argued.

Many sick lie in the porticoes; Jesus heals a man who had been ill 38 years, telling him to take up his bed and walk. The man was lame/infirm, not blind. The find shows the pools; it carries no evidence of the event.
The Sheep Gate of Jerusalem, north of the Temple, which John's 'by the sheep [gate/market]' echoes. Topographic correspondence only.

sites.name: Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III
sites.subtitle: Assyrian four-sided tribute monument from Nimrud · erected c. 825 BCE
sites.date: Main text runs through Shalmaneser III's 31st regnal year (828 BCE); monument dated c. 825 BCE; the Jehu tribute belongs to his 18th regnal year (841 BCE)
sites.date_basis: Regnal-year formula in the text itself: the annals on the obelisk end with 'In my thirty-first regnal year' (RIMA 3 A.0.102.14 l. 174b). The 18th-year date for Jehu's payment comes from parallel annals (RIMA 3 A.0.102.8 and A.0.102.10), which place 'the payment of ... Jehu (Iāūa) of (Bīt-)Ḫumrî' in the 18th-year campaign against Hazael; Assyrian regnal years are tied to absolute dates through the eponym list.

discovery.who: Austen Henry Layard's excavation team (found by the workmen's superintendent as Layard was leaving the trench)
discovery.where: Nimrud (ancient Kalhu), centre of the citadel mound, Layard's Trench J, in a courtyard beside the so-called Central Building

sites.location: British Museum, London, BM 118885 (registration 1848,1104.1)

physical.material: Black limestone
physical.dimensions: Just under 2 m high (Layard: 'about six feet six inches'); four faces, each c. 45 cm wide; stepped (ziggurat-like) top

overview: A four-sided black limestone monument, just under two metres tall, set up in a courtyard at Kalhu (Nimrud), Assyria's capital, near the end of Shalmaneser III's reign. It carries a long annalistic inscription covering his campaigns year by year down to his 31st regnal year, and five horizontal registers of relief that wrap around all four faces. Each register shows a named vassal delivering payment, with a short cuneiform caption (epigraph) above it.

The five payers are Sua of Gilzanu, Iaua (Jehu) 'son of Omri', the land of Muṣri (exotic animals: camels, buffalo, rhinoceros, elephants, monkeys), Marduk-apla-uṣur of Suhu, and Qarparunda of Patina. In the second register a man crouches 'in a pose of tribute' (Oracc Nimrud project) at the king's feet; the caption names the payer as Iaua of Bīt-Ḫumrî, whom the texts pair with Tyre and Sidon in the year of the campaign against Hazael of Damascus.

Layard's crew found the obelisk lying on its side about ten feet down in 1846, and it was shipped to London the same year. Its later campaigns are credited heavily to the field marshal Dayyān-Aššur rather than the king, which the Oracc Nimrud project links to the civil war at the end of Shalmaneser's reign.

text.quote: Tribute of Iaua (Jehu), son of Omri (mâr Humri). Silver, gold, a golden bowl, a golden beaker, golden goblets, pitchers of gold, lead, staves for the hand of the king, javelins, I received from him.
text.translation: D. D. Luckenbill, Ancient Records of Assyria and Babylonia I (Chicago, 1926), §590, p. 211 (epigraph II)

evidence: Epigraph over register 2, transliterated: ma-da-tu šá mia-ú-a DUMU mḫu-um-ri-i ... am-ḫur-šu, literally 'payment of Iāūa son (DUMU) of Ḫumrî ... I received from him' (RIMA 3 A.0.102.88).
Items listed for Iaua: silver, gold, a gold bowl (saplu), a gold tureen (zuqūtu), gold vessels (qabuātu), gold pails (dalāni), tin, staffs of the king's hand, spears.
Register 2 relief: one figure crouched at the feet of the king, who stands under a parasol; tribute-bearers carrying vessels continue around the other three faces of the same register.

The long annal text on the obelisk (A.0.102.14) records the 18th-year battle with Hazael of Damascus (1,121 chariots and 470 cavalry captured) but does not itself name Jehu in that passage; the Jehu name appears only in the epigraph.

Parallel annals name the same payer: 'the payment of the people of Tyre (and) Sidon, (as well as of) Jehu (Iāūa) of (Bīt-)Ḫumrî' after the king set up a statue at Mount Ba'ali-ra'asi (A.0.102.8); A.0.102.10 pairs him with Ba'al-manzer of Tyre.

Layard's account: 'The corner was part of an obelisk, about six feet six inches in height, lying on its side, ten feet below the surface' (Nineveh and its Remains, quoted by the Oracc Nimrud project).
Findspot: Layard's Trench J, centre of the Nimrud citadel; Rassam found a second (broken) obelisk in the same area the following year.

Schneider's notes list the other published texts naming 'Jehu son of Omri' in the 841 BCE campaign: the Aleppo fragment (Michel, WO 1/4, 1949), the Kurba'il statue (Kinnier Wilson, Iraq 24, 1962) and the Safar annals (Safar, Sumer 7, 1951).
questions: Who is 'Iaua son of Omri'? P. Kyle McCarter (BASOR 216, 1974) argued the name could render Joram (Yaw-) rather than Jehu, since Jehu was not of Omri's line; Edwin R. Thiele (BASOR 222, 1976) answered on chronological grounds and Manfred Weippert (Vetus Testamentum 28, 1978) re-examined the spelling and kept Jehu. The Assyrian parallels put the payment in the 18th year (841 BCE), which on the biblical reckoning is Jehu's accession year.

Why 'son of Omri'? One reading takes DUMU Ḫumrî as the Assyrian name for the state (Bīt-Ḫumrî, 'House of Omri'), not a genealogy; that is how the RIAo translation renders it. Tammi Schneider (BAR 21:1, Jan/Feb 1995, 'Did King Jehu Kill His Own Family?') instead took the phrase at face value as possible descent from Omri, noting that four Assyrian texts (the obelisk caption, the Aleppo fragment, the Kurba'il statue and the Safar annals) all call him 'son of Omri'. The inscription itself says only DUMU Ḫumrî.

Is the prostrate figure Jehu himself or an envoy? The caption names Iaua as the payer but does not say he was present in person; the Oracc Nimrud project describes the scene as Jehu's own gesture, and the old entry's 'Israelite servants' are not identified as such in the text.

biblical.tie: The epigraph names a ruler Iaua of the House of Omri paying tribute; 2 Kings names Jehu as the king who ended Omri's dynasty. Our reading: same man. The Bible does not mention this tribute.
Hazael pressing Israel in Jehu's reign; the obelisk annals record Shalmaneser fighting Hazael of Damascus in the same 18th-year campaign.
Hazael as king of Damascus: the obelisk text names Hazael (ḫa-za-aʾ-DINGIR) as Shalmaneser's opponent.

sources.cite: A. Kirk Grayson, Assyrian Rulers of the Early First Millennium BC II (858-745 BC), RIMA 3 (Toronto, 1996), A.0.102.14 (Black Obelisk annals) and A.0.102.87-91 (epigraphs); online as RIAo Shalmaneser III 014 and 088
