corrections: Old entry says the epigraph calls Jehu 'son of Omri' and then that Jehu 'was actually the successor of Omri'. Jehu was not Omri's successor: by 2 Kings he overthrew Joram, Omri's grandson. The epigraph's DUMU Ḫumrî is best read as 'of the House of Omri' (the Assyrian state name).
Old entry says the figure is accompanied by 'Israelite servants'. The relief shows tribute-bearers; the captions say nothing about servants.

Old entry says the obelisk 'confirms the historical existence of Jehu'. The obelisk names Iaua of Bīt-Ḫumrî; the identification with biblical Jehu is a reading (see questions), strongly supported by the 841 BCE date but not written out on the stone.

Old entry dates the obelisk 'c. 825 BCE' with no basis and gives Jehu 841-814 as fact. The obelisk's own text runs to the 31st regnal year (828 BCE); the Jehu payment is the 18th year (841 BCE) per parallel annals; Jehu's reign-length comes from the Bible, not this monument.

Old entry's quoted text ('a golden vase with pointed bottom, golden tumblers, golden buckets... a staff for a king, and wooden staffs') is a loose modern paraphrase; the RIMA 3 rendering is 'a gold bowl, a gold tureen, gold vessels, gold pails, tin, the staffs of the king's hand, (and) spears'.
'Only contemporary image of a biblical Hebrew king' is stated as fact; the only thing the stone shows is a payer captioned as Iaua, who may be the king or his envoy.

sites.name: Papyrus Brooklyn 35.1446
sites.subtitle: Late Middle Kingdom hieratic register; the verso lists a Theban household's servants, many labelled 'Asiatic' · 13th Dynasty
sites.date: Verso (the servant list): Year 1 of Sobekhotep III, 13th Dynasty. Recto and inserted texts: late 12th to early 13th Dynasty (an inserted letter is dated Year 36, assigned to Amenemhat III; another names the vizier Ankhu).
sites.date_basis: The verso is dated in its text to Year 1 of Sobekhotep III (Sekhemre-Sewadjtawy), as recorded in the Mainz 'Persons and Names of the Middle Kingdom' edition (citing Hayes 1955). A BCE figure depends on the 13th-Dynasty chronology, which is loose; the document gives only the regnal year.

discovery.when: Acquired in Egypt before entering the Brooklyn Museum; published 1955
discovery.who: Published by William C. Hayes
discovery.where: Unexcavated (bought, not dug); provenance recorded as Thebes

sites.location: Brooklyn Museum, New York, 35.1446

physical.material: Papyrus, inscribed on both sides
physical.language: Middle Egyptian; the verso records many Northwest Semitic personal names in Egyptian writing

overview: Papyrus Brooklyn 35.1446 is a late Middle Kingdom administrative papyrus written on both sides, published by W. C. Hayes in 1955 and recorded as coming from Thebes. It is not the only 'Brooklyn papyrus': the museum holds other famous papyri (e.g. the medical/snake papyrus), so the accession number matters.

The recto is an administrative register (Hayes 1955 pp. 19-66, pls. I-VII) with inserted documents: a letter dated Year 36 (assigned to Amenemhat III) and a text naming the vizier Ankhu. The verso, dated Year 1 of Sobekhotep III, is a legal list of dependents (Hayes pp. 87-125, pls. VIII-XIV). Each person is listed with a status word, often a work designation, and one or two names.

A large share of the verso's entries are labelled ꜥꜣm (Asiatic man) or ꜥꜣmt (Asiatic woman). Many carry a foreign (Northwest Semitic) name followed by an Egyptian name, e.g. 'ꜥꜣmt ... špr / snb-ḥnwt⸗s'. The list shows Asiatic men, women and children as household servants and textile workers in a Theban household of the 13th Dynasty.

text.quote: ꜥꜣmt, sḫt ḥꜣtjw, mnḥmj - 'Asiatic woman, weaver (?), Menahemi'; ꜥꜣmt, sḫt ḥꜣtjw, špr / snb-ḥnwt⸗s - 'Asiatic woman, weaver (?), Shipra, [Egyptian name] Seneb-henutes'
text.translation: Literal rendering (this encyclopedia) of entries 11 and 21 of the verso as transliterated in the Mainz PNM online edition (Ilin-Tomich), which follows Hayes 1955 pls. VIII-XIV. The work-title sḫt ḥꜣtjw is a textile-worker designation; its exact meaning is uncertain.

evidence: Verso date: Year 1 of Sobekhotep III (PNM record, citing Hayes 1955 pp. 87-125, pls. VIII-XIV).
Provenance: Thebes (PNM record).

Recto: administrative text, late 12th-early 13th Dynasty (Hayes 1955 pp. 19-66, pls. I-VII); inserted letter dated Year 36 (Amenemhat III) and a text naming the vizier Ankhu (PNM records 17754, 3892).
In the PNM edition, at least 36 preserved verso entries carry the label ꜥꜣm or ꜥꜣmt (Asiatic); many other entries are broken at that point.
Foreign names in the list include ꜥpr-ršpw (a name built on the god Reshef), mnḥmj, špr, jšr, ꜥqbj, ꜥqbtw, sk-r-tw, šmštw, bꜥꜣtwjj and hjjbjrw (PNM transliterations).
Many Asiatics carry double names: foreign name / Egyptian name (e.g. špr / snb-ḥnwt⸗s; ꜥpr-ršpw / [broken]).
Status words beside the Asiatic entries are household and textile-work designations (e.g. sḫt ḥꜣtjw, ḏꜣ šsr, ḥrj-pr 'house-servant/domestic'); none is a building or quarry designation.
Children are recorded with their mothers, e.g. an Asiatic woman's son named ꜥnḫw / pꜣ-ꜥꜣm ('the Asiatic') (PNM entries 56-58).
questions: How to read the names: W. F. Albright ('Northwest-Semitic Names in a List of Egyptian Slaves from the Eighteenth Century B.C.', JAOS 74, 1954) treated the foreign names as Northwest Semitic; S. H. Horn reviewed Hayes's edition in JNES 16 (1957). Individual equations with Hebrew names (e.g. špr = Shiphrah, mnḥmj = Menahem, ꜥqb- = the root of Jacob) are readings of consonants, not proven identities; I have not read Albright's article to state which equations he made.

Date in BCE: the text fixes a regnal year of Sobekhotep III; 13th-Dynasty absolute dates are poorly fixed, so any BCE figure (often given as 18th century BCE, as in Albright's title) is an estimate outside the document.

biblical.tie: The papyrus shows people labelled Asiatic, with Northwest Semitic names, serving in an Egyptian household at Thebes in the 13th Dynasty, some given Egyptian names, and bearing children there. That matches the biblical picture of Semites living and serving in Egypt (compare Joseph's renaming, Gen 41:45). It does not name any Israelite, and the verso is not a list of construction labour.
One Asiatic woman is named špr, the same consonants as Shiphrah, one of the two Hebrew midwives. That is a correspondence of name form only (our observation), in a document from a different setting.

sites.name: Bubastite Portal (Shoshenq I Campaign Relief, Karnak)
sites.subtitle: Egyptian triumph relief and town list of Shoshenq I (biblical Shishak) · c. 925 BCE · Karnak
sites.date: Carved in or after Shoshenq I's year 21 (Breasted: about 924 BCE); the campaign it commemorates came earlier (Breasted: about 926 BCE, Rehoboam's 5th year)
sites.date_basis: Breasted (ARE IV §709) dates the building of the Bubastite gate and first court to Shoshenq's year 21 from the Silsila quarry inscription (ARE IV §§701-708). The BCE figures depend on synchronising Shoshenq with Rehoboam's 5th year (1 Kgs 14:25); the relief itself carries no regnal date for the campaign.

discovery.when: Always visible; published in the 19th century
discovery.who: Published by Champollion, Rosellini, Lepsius and Mariette (Breasted ARE IV §709 n.); full facsimile by the Epigraphic Survey (Oriental Institute, Chicago) 1954
discovery.where: South wall of the Great Temple of Amun, Karnak, beside the Bubastite gate (south entrance of the First Court), between the Second Pylon and the temple of Ramesses III

sites.location: In situ, Karnak Temple, Luxor, Egypt. Four name rings (Nos. 105-108) are in Berlin (Breasted, ARE IV §709 n.)

physical.material: Sandstone temple wall, sunk relief

overview: Shoshenq I, founder of Egypt's 22nd Dynasty, added a gateway and the great First Court to the Amun temple at Karnak. On the outer south wall beside that gate (the 'Bubastite Portal') is a triumph scene. Amun and the goddess of Thebes lead rows of bound captives to the king, and each captive's body is a crenellated oval holding a place name. Breasted (1906) counted 156 ovals; about 75 names were still legible, and the fourth and tenth rows were almost entirely lost.

The legible names include towns in the Jezreel and Beth-Shean valleys and the central hills: Taanach, Shunem, Beth-Shean, Rehob, Hapharaim, Mahanaim, Gibeon, Beth-Horon, Aijalon, Megiddo. There is also a long series of Negev names, many of them compounds built with 'field' and similar words. Breasted read Nos. 71-72 as 'the Field of Abram'. Jerusalem does not appear among the surviving names. Breasted wrote that it 'must have been lost in one of the lacunae'.

A fragment of a large Shoshenq I stela was picked out of Schumacher's spoil at Megiddo by the Oriental Institute team in the 1920s. Breasted, in Fisher's 1929 report, took it as evidence that Shoshenq set up a victory monument in one of the towns on his list.

text.quote: Thou wentest forth in victory, and thou hast returned in might; thou hast united [...]; I have [...] for thee the countries that knew not Egypt, that had begun to invade [thy] boundaries, in order to cut off their heads.
text.translation: Amun's speech to Shoshenq I, J. H. Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt IV (Chicago, 1906) §720, p. 356

evidence: Triumph scene: 156 captive-ovals in ten rows (65 led by Amun, 91 by the goddess of Thebes); about 75 names legible in 1906 (Breasted ARE IV §718).
Legible names include Taanach (14), Shunem (15), Beth-Shean (16), Rehob (17), Hapharaim (18), Mahanaim (22), Gibeon (23), Beth-Horon (24), Aijalon (26) and Megiddo (27) (Breasted §712-713).
Nos. 71-72 read by Breasted as p3 hqr 'brm, 'the Field of Abram' (§715).
No. 29, Yw-d-h-m-rw-k, had been rendered 'the king or kingdom of Judah'; Breasted (§713) says it 'is, of course, not to be rendered' so.
Jerusalem is not among the preserved names (Breasted §717; Breasted in Fisher 1929 p. xii: 'Shishak's list ... does not mention it').
The accompanying inscriptions are 'made up of stereotyped phrases drawn from earlier monuments' (Breasted §709).
A fragment of a round-topped Shoshenq I stela, about 20 inches thick and restorable to about 5 ft wide, was recovered from Schumacher's dump at Megiddo (Breasted foreword to Fisher, OIC 4, 1929).
questions: Where is Jerusalem? 1 Kgs 14:25-26 says Shishak 'came up against Jerusalem' and took the temple and palace treasures. Breasted (ARE IV §717, 1906) held that the name 'must have been lost in one of the lacunae', since 31 names in rows 4 and 10 and 12 others are destroyed. In Fisher 1929 he states simply that the Karnak list 'does not mention it'. The wall itself shows only that Jerusalem is not among the surviving names; whether it was ever carved cannot be read from the damaged rows.

Is the list a route or a composite? Breasted (1906, §711-712) read the list by geographic clusters and noted that it seems to mix towns of Israel and Judah (e.g., No. 19 possibly Adoraim). K. A. Wilson's monograph The Campaign of Pharaoh Shoshenq I into Palestine (FAT II/9, 2005; reviewed by Hoffmeier, BASOR 349, and Kitchen, JSS 54) and A. Dodson's 'The Palestinian Campaign(s) of Shoshenq I' (2023) take up how far the relief records one historical route. Their arguments have not been reviewed for this entry.

Does No. 29 name Judah? Nineteenth-century readers rendered Yw-d-h-m-rw-k as 'the king or kingdom of Judah'. Breasted (1906 §713) rejected this, calling it the 'much-discussed' name. The wall supports only the consonantal sequence; what the name means was not settled from a primary source cited here.

biblical.tie: 'Shishak king of Egypt' attacks in Rehoboam's 5th year. The Karnak relief is the Egyptian record of a Shoshenq I campaign against towns in the same land. The equation Shishak = Shoshenq is by name and period. The relief does not name Rehoboam, Judah (see No. 29) or Jerusalem.

The Chronicler says Shishak 'took the fortified cities which belonged to Judah'. The relief's Negev and southern names fit a southern operation; Breasted identifies Arad and possibly Sharuhen among them.
Breasted's reading 'the Field of Abram' (Nos. 71-72) would be a 10th-century place name containing the name Abram. It is a toponym, not a mention of the patriarch.

sites.name: Caiaphas Ossuary
aka: Ossuary of Joseph son of Caiaphas
sites.subtitle: Inscribed limestone bone box from a family tomb in Jerusalem · 1st century CE
sites.date: 1st century CE (Second Temple period, before 70 CE)
sites.date_basis: Secondary burial in ossuaries is a Jerusalem practice of roughly the last century before the Roman destruction (Greenhut, BAR 1992). In the same cave a bronze coin of Herod Agrippa I dated 42/43 CE was found in the skull of a woman in the ossuary inscribed 'Miriam daughter of Simon' (Greenhut 1992), giving a fixed point for use of the tomb. No inscription on the Joseph ossuary carries a date.

discovery.when: Late November / December 1990
discovery.who: Found by workmen building a water park; excavated for the Israel Antiquities Authority by Zvi Greenhut
discovery.where: Burial cave in the Peace Forest below the Haas Promenade (North Talpiyot), south Jerusalem

sites.location: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (Israel Antiquities Authority collection); the bones were reburied on the Mount of Olives

physical.material: Limestone, chip-carved decoration
physical.language: Aramaic personal name formula ('X son of Y')

overview: In late November 1990 workmen landscaping a water park in Jerusalem's Peace Forest broke into a rock-cut burial cave with four loculi (kokhim). Zvi Greenhut of the Israel Antiquities Authority excavated it. The cave held twelve ossuaries; four had been pulled out by the workmen, two lay in situ in loculus IV and six were scattered in the chamber. Five ossuaries carried names.

Two ossuaries carry a form of the family name Qafa' / Qayafa', the first time the name had turned up in an archaeological context. One is inscribed simply 'Qafa''. The other, the most elaborately decorated box in the cave (two circles, each holding a central rosette ringed by five whorl rosettes), found undisturbed in loculus IV, is inscribed 'Yehosef bar Qayafa'' on the back of a long side and 'Yehosef bar Qafa'' on a narrow side.

The Joseph ossuary held bones of six people: two infants, a child of 2-5, a youth of 13-18, an adult woman and a man of about 60 (anthropology by Joseph Zias). Whether that man is the high priest Joseph Caiaphas of Josephus and the Gospels is the open question; Greenhut himself framed it as a question, not a finding.

text.quote: Yehosef bar Qayafa' (long side) / Yehosef bar Qafa' (narrow side) = 'Joseph son of Caiaphas'
text.translation: Literal rendering (this encyclopedia) of the transliteration printed by Z. Greenhut, BAR 18:5 (1992)

evidence: Twelve ossuaries in one small family kokhim cave; five inscribed with names.
Two inscriptions spell the name differently on the same box: QYP' (Qayafa') and QP' (Qafa').
A second ossuary is inscribed only 'Qafa''.
The Joseph box is the most elaborately carved in the cave (double rosette circles).
Bones of six individuals in the Joseph box, including a male of about 60; the other 'Qafa'' box held five individuals and no elderly male.
Bronze coin of Agrippa I (42/43 CE) in a woman's skull in the 'Miriam daughter of Simon' ossuary.
Two iron nails were recorded in the 1990 excavation (one inside an ossuary, one on the floor of a kokh); the IAA later stated they had been misplaced (as reported in Shimron et al. 2020).
No title (priest, high priest) appears on either Caiaphas ossuary.
questions: Identity of the 60-year-old man: Greenhut (BAR 18:5, 1992) asks whether the ornate box and the name make him the high priest, but states it is 'another question'; the inscriptions carry no priestly title, and the box contained six people.

Reading of the name: the two spellings QYP' and QP' on one box are published by Greenhut and Reich (1992). W. Horbury, 'The Caiaphas Ossuaries and Joseph Caiaphas', PEQ 126 (1994) 32-48, re-examined the inscriptions and their relation to the Josephus name; the full argument is not accessible for this entry, so its specific reading is not reported here.

The nails: Shimron, Deutsch, Schoch and Gutkin (Archaeological Discovery 8, 2020) argue from matching sediment, flowstone and microbial signatures that two unprovenanced nails in the Tel Aviv University anthropology collection are the lost Caiaphas-tomb nails and bear crucifixion-related bone and wood; the IAA (as quoted in that paper) says the university nails have a different provenance and the tomb nails are simply misplaced.

Z. Lewy (Archaeology & Anthropology: Open Access 4:2, 2021) reads the carved motifs of ossuary IAA 1991-465 in the same tomb as a messianic palm-scion symbol for Jesus; that is iconographic interpretation with no inscriptional support.

biblical.tie: Names 'Caiaphas' as high priest at whose house Jesus was examined. The ossuary gives the same family name; it does not carry the title.
Caiaphas as high priest 'that year', son-in-law of Annas. The ossuary adds nothing about office or kinship to Annas.
Caiaphas named with Annas in the priestly leadership.

Josephus gives the personal name: 'Joseph, who was also called Caiaphas'. The ossuary's 'Yehosef bar Qayafa'' matches the pair Joseph + Caiaphas; note it reads 'son of Caiaphas', i.e. Caiaphas as a family name.

sources.cite: Zvi Greenhut, 'Burial Cave of the Caiaphas Family', Biblical Archaeology Review 18:5 (Sept/Oct 1992)
sources.verified: BAS Library landing page shows author and issue; full text read from the PDF copy at jamestabor.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/Burial-Cave-of-the-Caiaphas-Family.pdf (twelve ossuaries, five inscribed, Yehosef bar Qayafa'/Qafa' spellings, six individuals incl. male c. 60, Agrippa I coin 42/43 CE)

Old entry gives the inscription only as 'Joseph son of Caiaphas'. There are two inscriptions on the box with different spellings (Yehosef bar Qayafa' and Yehosef bar Qafa'), plus a second ossuary reading 'Qafa'' (Greenhut 1992).

sites.name: Capernaum Synagogue
sites.subtitle: White limestone synagogue over earlier basalt remains · Late Roman / Byzantine
sites.date: Prayer hall built in the late 4th century CE; east court completed after the mid-5th century; abandoned in the 7th century (Loffreda). Earlier basalt pavement beneath the nave dated by the excavators to the 1st century CE.
sites.date_basis: Stratified excavation by the Studium Biblicum Franciscanum since 1969: 'more than 30,000 Late Roman coins' and pottery sealed in the fills under the floors (Loffreda). The 1st-century date of the basalt pavement under the nave rests on pottery and coins in and beneath it (Loffreda reports Hellenistic pottery and coins in the layer below it). The older late-2nd/early-3rd-century date (following Watzinger) was based on architectural style.

discovery.when: Ruins described in the 19th century (E. Robinson); partly restored by G. Orfali 1922-1925; stratigraphic excavation by V. Corbo and S. Loffreda from 1969
discovery.who: Studium Biblicum Franciscanum (Franciscan Custody of the Holy Land)
discovery.where: Capernaum (Kfar Nahum), NW shore of the Sea of Galilee

sites.location: In situ, Capernaum

physical.material: White limestone superstructure on foundations/walls of black basalt; basalt side room
physical.dimensions: Prayer hall interior 23 m N-S x 17.28 m E-W (Loffreda)

overview: The standing white-limestone synagogue has a rectangular prayer hall, its facade facing south toward Jerusalem, with a U-shaped stylobate dividing the nave from east, west and north aisles, stone benches along the east and west aisles, a trapezoidal eastern courtyard with porticoes, a southern porch and a basalt side room at the NW corner. Two small platforms (aediculae/bemas) flanked the central entrance in the first phase, later replaced by one platform across the nave.

Stratigraphic excavation since 1969 dated the prayer hall to the late 4th century CE on the basis of more than 30,000 Late Roman coins and pottery; the east court was finished after the mid-5th century and the building was abandoned in the 7th. Earlier scholars (Wilson, Orfali) had thought it the 1st-century synagogue itself, and Watzinger's school dated it to the late 2nd-early 3rd century by style.

Beneath the nave the excavators found a large basalt-stone pavement they date to the 1st century CE, over a layer with Hellenistic pottery and coins, and a 'basalt stone wall' under the limestone walls that the white synagogue reused as footing. Corbo identified pavement and wall as the 1st-century synagogue; Loffreda identifies the pavement as the 1st-century synagogue and considers the wall possibly an intermediate phase.
evidence: Prayer hall interior 23 x 17.28 m, facade to the south (Loffreda).
Over 30,000 Late Roman coins plus pottery from sealed contexts under the white synagogue (Loffreda).
Basalt pavement under the central nave, dated 1st century CE by the excavators; beneath it Hellenistic pottery and coins.
Basalt wall under the peripheral walls, continuous under the outer walls but broken or missing under the stylobates; axis shifted relative to the limestone walls; tops levelled with pebbles.
East-court foundations are separate, better-built, and abut the basalt wall.
Private houses (pavements, walls, fireplaces) under the aisles, porch and east court.
Nothing found names the 1st-century builder; the pavement is uninscribed.
questions: Date of the white synagogue: S. Loffreda and V. Corbo (SBF excavations from 1969) date the prayer hall to the late 4th century from 30,000+ coins and pottery beneath it. J. Magness ('Capernaum', in Ancient Synagogues in Palestine, British Academy 2024) evaluates 'a recent claim' that the white synagogue was built in the 3rd century and rebuilt after the earthquake of 363 CE and served Jews called minim, and gives a 'fine-grained analysis' of the dating evidence for the synagogue, the domus ecclesia and the octagonal church; her detailed conclusions are not accessible for this entry.

What lies beneath: Corbo reads both the 1st-century basalt pavement and the basalt wall as the 1st-century synagogue; Loffreda agrees on the pavement but suggests the wall may be an intermediate building between the 1st-century synagogue and the late-4th-century one. The argument for 'synagogue' is inferential: the pavement is too large for a house, sacred buildings are often rebuilt on the same spot, and pilgrims such as Egeria placed the synagogue there (Loffreda).

Why a lavish synagogue beside a Christian shrine in the 4th-5th century: W. V. Cirafesi, Capernaum: Jews and Christians in the Ancient Village (Fortress 2024) treats the building in chapters on Jewish Christ-followers before the 4th century and 'Architecturalizing Jesus in the Fourth Century'; S. Tarkhanova (2020) re-dates the 'peopled scroll' friezes by stylistic method. Their specific arguments have not been reviewed for this entry.

biblical.tie: Jesus teaches and exorcises in the synagogue at Capernaum on the Sabbath. The standing limestone building is 300+ years later; only the basalt pavement under it is of 1st-century date, and its identification as that synagogue is the excavators' inference.

Jewish elders say the centurion 'built us our synagogue'. Loffreda explicitly links the 1st-century pavement to 'the long-looked for synagogue built by the Roman centurion'; the pavement carries no builder's name.
The bread-of-life discourse is set 'in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum'.
Capernaum as Jesus' base ('his own city'); the site has 1st-century houses under the later synagogue.

sources.verified: Archived page read: text by the excavator; hall 23 x 17.28 m; late-4th-century date from 30,000+ Late Roman coins and pottery; E court after mid-5th c.; abandoned 7th c.; Watzinger's 2nd-3rd c. dating rejected

sources.verified: Crossref record confirmed (Greek Orthodox side of the site); text not read

corrections: Old entry: 'Discovery: 1905+'. The ruins were already described by E. Robinson in the 19th century; restoration began under Orfali in 1922-1925 and the stratigraphic excavations that dated it began in 1969 (Loffreda). The 1905 German work is not documented in the sources cited here.
Old entry: 'Material: Stone and mosaic'. The synagogue is white limestone on basalt; no mosaic floor is reported in the excavator's description (limestone slab pavements).
Old entry: 'Dimensions: Approximately 20 meters long'. Prayer hall interior is 23 x 17.28 m, plus an east court and south porch (Loffreda).
Old entry: 'beautifully decorated ark'. The excavator reports two small platforms flanking the entrance, later replaced by a single platform; no preserved ark.

Old entry: 'Luke 7:5 (Jesus taught in Capernaum)'. Luke 7:5 says the centurion built the synagogue; Jesus' teaching there is Mark 1:21 / Luke 4:31.
Old entry: 'testament to the enduring legacy of ancient Jerusalem'. Capernaum is in Galilee, not Jerusalem.

sites.name: Rock-cut cult complex on the eastern slope of the City of David
sites.subtitle: Eight rock-hewn rooms with altar, standing stone and sealed favissa · cut in the Middle Bronze Age, out of use in the 8th century BCE
sites.date: Probably cut at the end of the Middle Bronze Age (c. 1550 BCE); last cultic phase Iron Age IIB, ending in the 8th century BCE
sites.date_basis: The excavators' dating (Shukron et al., 'Atiqot 116, 2025) of the construction and final stage, based on the finds, including an 8th-century favissa assemblage. The article's abstract gives 'likely constructed in the Middle Bronze Age, with its final stage in Iron Age IIB'. The c. 1550 BCE figure and the 8th-century end are from the BAS summary (Jan 2026).

discovery.when: Excavated by Eli Shukron; final publication January 2025 (years of excavation not stated in the sources read)
discovery.who: Eli Shukron, with report co-authors Liora Freud, Helena Roth, Reli Avisar and Efrat Bocher
discovery.where: Eastern slope of the City of David, Jerusalem, about 300 yards from the Temple Mount

sites.location: In situ (rock-cut rooms)

physical.material: Rooms cut into bedrock
physical.dimensions: Eight rooms covering over 2,300 sq ft (BAS 2026 summary)

overview: A series of eight rooms cut into the bedrock of the City of David's eastern slope, about 300 yards from the Temple Mount, were published in 'Atiqot 116 (January 2025) by Eli Shukron and co-authors. They interpret the rooms as a cultic complex, 'likely constructed in the Middle Bronze Age, with its final stage in Iron Age IIB'.

According to the Biblical Archaeology Society's summary (21 January 2026), the features include an altar with a drainage channel, a standing stone (massebah) left upright, an oil press, a winepress, V-shaped floor carvings of unclear use, and a sealed cave (favissa). The favissa held 8th-century BCE cooking pots and storage jars, Hebrew inscriptions, loom weights, scarabs, stamp seals and grinding stones.

Shukron states that the complex 'ceased to function during the eighth century, possibly as part of King Hezekiah's religious reform'. Helena Roth notes that it is built in rock-cut chambers rather than as a stone-built temple, and that a missing eastern wall may mean it was 'open to the valley'.
evidence: Eight rock-hewn rooms on the eastern slope, over 2,300 sq ft in total, about 300 yards from the Temple Mount (BAS 2026).
Features: an altar with a drainage channel, an upright massebah, an oil press, a winepress, and V-shaped floor cuttings (BAS 2026).

A sealed favissa (a storage pit or cave for retired cult objects) held an 8th-century assemblage: cooking pots, storage jars, Hebrew inscriptions, loom weights, scarabs, stamp seals and grinding stones (BAS 2026).
The excavators' phasing: 'likely constructed in the Middle Bronze Age, with its final stage in Iron Age IIB' ('Atiqot 116 abstract).
No eastern wall survives (Roth, as reported by BAS 2026).
questions: Temple or cult installation? The 'Atiqot authors (Shukron, Freud, Roth, Avisar and Bocher 2025) call it a 'cultic complex'. The BAS headline calls it 'A Second Temple in First Temple Jerusalem'. BAS notes that the deity is not identified and that two temples to the same deity so close together would be unusual. Roth contrasts the rock-cut plan with stone-built Iron Age temples such as Arad, Beersheba, Lachish and Moza. No published counter-reading by a named scholar is cited here.

Did it close because of Hezekiah? Shukron says the complex went out of use in the 8th century, 'possibly' because of Hezekiah's reform. The evidence is the 8th-century favissa and the deliberate sealing. Linking the closure to a specific king is his inference.

How are the Hebrew inscriptions read? BAS reports inscriptions of possible magical or religious significance in the favissa, but the readings are not available in the sources cited here (the 'Atiqot PDF was not openly accessible).

biblical.tie: Hezekiah removes the high places, breaks the pillars (matsevot) and cuts down the asherah, and the Rabshakeh taunts him for it. An upright massebah in a cult complex a few hundred yards from the Temple, with its last phase in the 8th century, fits this. The link is the excavator's 'possibly'.
'You shall not set up a pillar (massebah)'. The complex has one, left standing.

Josiah defiles the high places 'before Jerusalem' and breaks their pillars. This is a later reform aimed at shrines outside the Temple; the eastern-slope complex had already gone out of use by then, on the excavators' dating.

sources.cite: Shukron, E., Freud, L., Roth, H., Avisar, R. and Bocher, E. 2025. "Evidence of Worship in the Rock-Cut Rooms on the Eastern Slope of the City of David, Jerusalem." 'Atiqot 116, article 5. doi:10.70967/2948-040X.1126

Crossref confirms the DOI, authors and date (12 Jan 2025). Full PDF blocked by a Cloudflare check and not read.

updates.what: Final publication of the complex in 'Atiqot 116 by Shukron and colleagues.
BAS popular report brings the 'Atiqot results to wide attention and reports Shukron's suggestion of closure under Hezekiah.

corrections: Headlines calling this a 'second temple' in Jerusalem go further than the excavators' own words. The report calls it a 'cultic complex', and the deity is not identified.
Statements that it was 'closed by Hezekiah' present a possibility as fact. The excavator says the complex ceased in the 8th century, 'possibly as part of King Hezekiah's religious reform'.

second temple in First Temple Jerusalem

sites.name: Rock-cut moat between the City of David and the Ophel
sites.subtitle: Rock-cut ditch dividing the lower city from the acropolis · in use by the Late Iron IIA, backfilled in the Late Hellenistic period
sites.date: Cutting date unknown. In use as a moat by the Late Iron IIA (the excavators' press statement: 9th century BCE) and until the Late Hellenistic period, when it was backfilled
sites.date_basis: Stratigraphy and pottery in the fills against the scarps, as summarized in the Tel Aviv 50 (2023) abstract: 'Although the initial cutting of the ditch cannot be determined, it is clear that by the Late Iron IIA, the ditch served as a moat.' A Middle Bronze Age cutting is a suggestion by analogy with other large quarrying works in Jerusalem, not a dated observation (Shalev, quoted by the City of David Foundation).

discovery.when: Givati Parking Lot excavations; first published 2023, announced to the press July 2024
discovery.who: Israel Antiquities Authority and Tel Aviv University; directors Yuval Gadot (TAU) and Yiftah Shalev (IAA); funded by the City of David Foundation
discovery.where: Givati Parking Lot, north-western part of the City of David (Southeastern Ridge), Jerusalem Walls National Park; linked to a sloping rock surface exposed farther east by Kathleen Kenyon in the 1960s

sites.location: In situ, Givati Parking Lot excavation, City of David, Jerusalem

physical.dimensions: Tel Aviv 2023 paper: about 30 m wide, at least 6 m deep. 2024 press release: at least 9 m deep, at least 30 m wide, traced at least 70 m west-east when joined to Kenyon's section
physical.material: Cut in bedrock, with vertical rock scarps on north and south

overview: Excavations in the Givati Parking Lot, on the ridge south of the Ophel and Temple Mount, exposed a man-made rock-cut ditch close to the summit of the hill, bounded on both north and south by near-vertical scarps, with an installation of intertwined channels in it. Yuval Gadot, Efrat Bocher, Liora Freud and Yiftah Shalev published it in Tel Aviv 50 (2023) as 'An Early Iron Age Moat in Jerusalem between the Ophel and the Southeastern Ridge/City of David.'

By comparing it with Kathleen Kenyon's 1960s excavation slightly to the east, where she had recorded bedrock dropping to the north where it should rise, the team concluded that one ditch crossed the whole width of the ridge and cut the residential lower city off from the acropolis to the north. The July 2024 announcement gave the joined length as at least 70 m west-east.

The date when the ditch was first cut is not established. The published abstract states it served as a moat by the Late Iron IIA and stayed open until Late Hellenistic construction filled it in. Shalev's 2024 statement adds that Middle Bronze Age cutting is possible because major quarrying in Jerusalem is usually of that date, and that the excavators are 'confident that it was used at the time of the First Temple and the Kingdom of Judah (ninth century BCE)'.
evidence: Man-made ditch about 30 m wide and at least 6 m deep near the summit of the Southeastern Ridge, with rock scarps on its north and south sides (Gadot et al., Tel Aviv 50, 2023, abstract).
An installation of intertwined channels lies in the ditch; its function is described as 'enigmatic' (Gadot et al. 2023, abstract).

Joined with Kenyon's sloping-bedrock observation farther east, the ditch crosses the full width of the ridge, separating the Southeastern Ridge from the Ophel (Gadot et al. 2023, abstract; City of David Foundation release).
Press figures: at least 9 m deep, at least 30 m wide, at least 70 m west-east (City of David Foundation release; Times of Israel, 21 July 2024).
The ditch served as a moat by the Late Iron IIA and was backfilled by Late Hellenistic construction (Gadot et al. 2023, abstract).
The date of first cutting 'cannot be determined' (Gadot et al. 2023) / 'is unknown' (Shalev, 2024 release).
questions: When it was cut. Gadot, Bocher, Freud and Shalev (Tel Aviv 50, 2023) title the paper 'An Early Iron Age Moat' but state that 'the initial cutting of the ditch cannot be determined'; the fixed point is its use by the Late Iron IIA. Shalev (IAA/City of David release, 2024) raises a Middle Bronze Age cutting because, in his words, such large construction and quarrying works in Jerusalem 'are usually dated to the Middle Bronze Age'. No MB material from the cut itself is reported in the sources read. The full paper is not openly accessible (publisher access restriction), so the ceramic basis of 'Late Iron IIA' is known here only from the abstract.

Whether this is the Millo or part of it. Gadot (2024 release) says the find 'opens up a renewed discussion' of the terms Ophel and Millo; the release quotes 1 Kgs 11:27. Neither the paper abstract nor the release identifies the moat as the Millo. 'Millo' comes from the root 'fill', and the moat was a cut, later filled only in the Hellenistic period; our reading is that a direct equation needs an argument the sources read here do not make.

Depth: the 2023 paper gives 'at least 6 m', the 2024 release 'at least nine meters'. Whether this reflects further excavation after the paper went to press or a different measuring point is not stated in either source.

biblical.tie: David takes the stronghold of Zion, calls it the City of David, and 'built round about from Millo and inward' (KJV). The moat marks a physical northern edge of the lower city in the Iron Age; whether it existed in David's day is not established, since the cutting date is unknown.

Solomon builds the Millo and 'repaired the breaches of the city of David his father' (KJV, 11:27). The excavators cite this verse as the kind of topographic reshaping the moat represents; they do not identify the moat as the Millo.

Jotham and Manasseh build on 'the wall of Ophel'; Nehemiah's builders repair toward 'the wall of Ophel'. The find physically separates the Ophel from the ridge to the south, giving a concrete boundary to the term; the texts do not mention a moat.

Popular reports that date the moat to the Middle Bronze Age, or to David or Solomon, go past the evidence. The excavators' paper says the initial cutting 'cannot be determined'; the MB date is offered only as a possibility by analogy, and the dated use starts in the Late Iron IIA.

Reports that equate the moat with the biblical Millo overstate the source: the excavators say it 'opens up a renewed discussion' about the Millo and Ophel and quote 1 Kgs 11:27, but make no identification.

sites.name: Cyrus Cylinder
sites.subtitle: Babylonian foundation cylinder of Cyrus II · after 539 BCE
sites.date: After the capture of Babylon by Cyrus in 539 BCE (British Museum record: production date '539 BC (after)')
sites.date_basis: Internal: the text narrates Cyrus's entry into Babylon and the handing over of Nabonidus, then speaks in Cyrus's voice as king of Babylon; the object was a foundation deposit for the rebuilding of Babylon's wall Imgur-Enlil described at the end of the text. No regnal-year date is preserved.

discovery.who: Hormuzd Rassam (British Museum excavations)
discovery.where: Babylon (Amran mound), Iraq; findspot evidence discussed by C. B. F. Walker 1972

sites.location: British Museum, London, BM 90920 (reg. no. 1880,0617.1941), Room 52; joined fragment NBC 2504 on loan from the Yale Babylonian Collection

physical.material: Fired clay (coarse core with large stone inclusions, finer surface slip), wheel-made
physical.dimensions: Length 21.9-22.8 cm; diameter 7.8-8.2 cm (end A), 7.9 cm (end B), 10 cm maximum

overview: A barrel-shaped clay foundation cylinder found in several pieces by Hormuzd Rassam at Babylon in 1879. The text, written in Babylonian script and language, first describes (in the third person) how Nabonidus, the last Neo-Babylonian king, disrupted the cult of Marduk and burdened Babylon's population with labour-service; how Marduk searched for a righteous ruler, called Cyrus king of Anshan by name, and let him enter Babylon without battle. From line 20 the text switches to Cyrus's own voice: 'I am Cyrus, king of the world...'.

Cyrus claims to have ended the forced labour at Babylon, received tribute from kings 'from the Upper to the Lower sea', returned the gods of a named list of cities (Ashur, Susa, Agade, Eshnunna, Zamban, Me-Turnu, Der, the land of the Gutians, the cities across the Tigris) to their shrines, and gathered their inhabitants back to their dwellings. The gods Nabonidus had brought into Babylon were returned 'by command of Marduk'. The text closes with food offerings and the rebuilding of Babylon's wall Imgur-Enlil, during which an older foundation inscription of Ashurbanipal was found.

The cylinder does not mention Judah, Jerusalem, the Jews, or YHWH. Its connection to the biblical return from exile is one of policy and phrasing (a king returning deported peoples and their cult objects on a god's command), not a direct reference. A fragment in Yale (NBC 2504) restoring lines 36-45 was identified and joined in the 1970s, and in 2009-2010 two fragments of a clay tablet carrying a copy of the same text were identified in the British Museum by W. G. Lambert and Irving Finkel, showing the text also circulated outside the foundation deposit.

text.quote: (32) the gods, who dwelt in them, I brought them back to their places, and caused them to dwell in a habitation for all time. All their inhabitants I collected and restored them to their dwelling places.
text.translation: R. W. Rogers, Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament (New York, 1912), p. 383, line 32

evidence: Museum record: fired clay cylinder, length 21.9-22.8 cm, BM 90920 / 1880,0617.1941, excavated by Hormuzd Rassam at Babylon (Amran).
The cylinder broke into several pieces in antiquity; it was refired in 1961; plaster fills were removed in 2007.
Lines 1-19 are in the third person (Marduk chooses Cyrus); lines 20 onward are in the first person of Cyrus.
Line 12 (Rogers 1912): Marduk 'sought a righteous prince... Cyrus, king of Anshan, he called by name'.
Line 17: Babylon entered 'without battle and conflict'; Nabonidus delivered into Cyrus's hand.
Lines 30-32 list the places whose gods and people were returned: all are in Mesopotamia and the lands east of the Tigris; no western (Syro-Palestinian) place is named.
Line 33: the gods of Sumer and Akkad that Nabonidus had brought into Babylon were returned to their shrines 'by command of Marduk'.
Closing lines (with the Yale fragment NBC 2504, lines 36-45) describe rebuilding the wall Imgur-Enlil and finding an inscription of Ashurbanipal.

Two fragments of a clay tablet carrying a copy of the cylinder's text were identified in the British Museum's collections in 2009-2010 (W. G. Lambert, I. Finkel); one clarifies a passage illegible on the cylinder, the other supplies part of its missing text.
questions: Scope of the 'repatriation': the text itself names only Mesopotamian and trans-Tigridian cult centres (lines 30-32). A. Kuhrt (JSOT 25, 1983) reads the cylinder as a Babylonian building inscription in the Mesopotamian royal tradition, praising Cyrus in terms used of earlier kings, and argues it cannot be taken as evidence of an empire-wide policy of freeing deportees. Readers who connect it with Ezra 1 point to the same clause: the pattern 'return the gods, gather the people' is the same kind of act Ezra 1:2-4 and 6:3-5 attribute to Cyrus for Jerusalem. The cylinder is silent on Judah; any link is our inference from the parallel.

Genre: the British Museum curatorial note records the suggestion (Harmatta 1971; see BM bibliography) that the author used Ashurbanipal's foundation inscription found in the wall as a literary model. The 2009-2010 tablet copies show the text also circulated on tablets; whether that means it was 'distributed throughout the empire' (British Museum statement reported in The Art Newspaper, Feb 2010) or only copied within Babylonia is not settled by two fragments of unknown findspot.

'Human rights charter': the text contains no statement of rights; the British Museum record says the concept 'would have been quite alien to Cyrus's contemporaries'. UNESCO's General Conference in November 2025 nevertheless adopted a resolution calling it 'an early charter of human rights and cultural diversity'. That is a modern political reading, not something the cuneiform says.

biblical.tie: Both texts present Cyrus as acting on a god's command to return a deported people and restore a temple. The cylinder does the same for Mesopotamian cults under Marduk. The type of act corresponds; the named people and god do not.
Return of the Jerusalem temple vessels corresponds in kind to line 32-33's return of cult images to their shrines (Israel had no cult image; the vessels are the parallel object).

YHWH 'calls Cyrus by name' and takes him by the right hand; the cylinder line 12 has Marduk calling Cyrus by name and taking his hand. Same royal-election language, different god. This is a verbal parallel, stated as our observation.

sites.name: Deir 'Alla Plaster Inscription (Balaam son of Beor)
aka: Book of Balaam son of Beor
sites.subtitle: Ink-on-plaster text naming 'Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods' · c. 800 BCE · Tell Deir 'Alla, Jordan
sites.date: c. 800 BCE (script and archaeological context)
sites.date_basis: Script type and the destruction of the building in which the plaster wall stood (Livius summary, citing Hoftijzer and van der Kooij 1976). No radiocarbon dates are confirmed in the sources cited here.

discovery.who: Dutch expedition under H. J. Franken
discovery.where: Tell Deir 'Alla, east Jordan Valley, about 8 km east of the Jordan and 1 km north of the Jabbok (Zarqa)

sites.location: Amman, Jordan. A Wikipedia pointer says the Jordan Archaeological Museum; this is not confirmed in a published museum record.

physical.material: Ink on wall plaster, recovered in many fragments
physical.script: Northwest Semitic alphabetic script, ink written; red ink used for emphasis (Wikipedia pointer, not confirmed)
physical.language: Disputed: the editio princeps is titled 'Aramaic Texts'; later studies classify it differently (see questions)

overview: In 1967 the Dutch expedition under H. J. Franken found fragments of an ink text painted on the plastered wall of a building at Tell Deir 'Alla, in the Jordan Valley near the Jabbok. J. Hoftijzer and G. van der Kooij published the editio princeps in 1976 as Aramaic Texts from Deir 'Alla (Brill), with chapters on the conservation, the plaster and the script. The same editors later published The Balaam Text from Deir 'Alla Re-Evaluated (1991).

The fragments are grouped into 'combinations'. Combination I opens with a title naming 'Balaam son of Beor', 'a seer of the gods'. The gods come to him at night, and he sees a vision 'in accordance with El's utterance'. The vision reports a decree of the gods (the Shaddai-gods): the heavens are to be sewn shut with dense cloud, and there is to be darkness and no light. The goddess named with this decree is read Shagar-and-Ishtar in the Livius translation.
The text names Balaam son of Beor, El, and the Shaddai-gods. As translated on Livius, it does not name Israel, Moab, Balak, YHWH, or a donkey.

text.quote: The title line names 'the book of Balaam son of Beor', described as a seer of the gods. The next line says the gods came to him at night and he saw a vision according to the utterance of El.
text.translation: Paraphrase of Combination I, lines 1-2, after the published editions (Hoftijzer and van der Kooij 1976; Levine's translation via Livius). No public-domain translation exists, since the text was found in 1967.

evidence: Found in 1967 by the Dutch expedition under H. J. Franken; editio princeps Hoftijzer and van der Kooij 1976.
Written in ink on wall plaster and recovered as fragments grouped into combinations; two main combinations (I and II) plus smaller groups.
Combination I, line 1 names bl'm br b'r, 'Balaam son of Beor', and calls him a seer of the gods.
Deities named: El, the Shaddai-gods (šdyn), and a goddess read Shagar-and-Ishtar.
Content of the vision: the heavens closed with cloud, darkness instead of light.
Date c. 800 BCE on script and context.
questions: Language: the 1976 editio princeps presents the texts as Aramaic. The Livius summary calls it 'a language between Aramaic and Canaanite'. The 1991 re-evaluation volume has separate chapters by P. K. McCarter ('The Dialect of the Deir 'Alla Texts') and D. Pardee ('The Linguistic Classification of the Deir 'Alla Text Written on Plaster') on this question. Their specific arguments have not been reviewed for this entry, so their positions are not stated here.

Genre and meaning of Combination I: Hoftijzer's 1991 chapter 'What Did the Gods Say?' addresses the divine decree. Tsolin and Oriekhova (The World of the Orient, 2025) read the texts as an example of the prophetic genre massa'. The texts of both were not read.

Relation to Numbers 22-24: Deir 'Alla preserves a non-Israelite tradition about Balaam son of Beor as a seer receiving night visions, about 800 BCE, east of the Jordan. Whether Numbers draws on such a tradition, or the two share a common older figure, is interpretation. The plaster text itself gives no information on the direction of borrowing.

biblical.tie: Same name and patronymic, 'Balaam son of Beor'. Same role: a seer who receives visions from the divine, including at night (Num 22:8-9, 19-20: God comes to Balaam at night). Num 24:4, 16 also uses 'Shaddai' ('who sees the vision of Shaddai'), and the plaster text has the Shaddai-gods (šdyn).
Other biblical mentions of Balaam son of Beor. The plaster text confirms that a Balaam tradition existed east of the Jordan around 800 BCE. It says nothing about Balak, Moab or Israel.

sources.cite: J. Hoftijzer and G. van der Kooij (eds.), Aramaic Texts from Deir 'Alla (Documenta et Monumenta Orientis Antiqui 19; Leiden: Brill, 1976), DOI 10.1163/9789004670327
sources.verified: Crossref record: title, editors Hoftijzer and van der Kooij, Brill, 1976. Chapter records include 'The Script of the Deir 'Alla Plaster Text' pp. 42-96 and 'Conservation and Analysis' pp. 17-22.

sources.verified: Crossref record: author Hackett, Brill DOI with ISBN 9780891307235, chapters 'The Script' 9-19 and 'The Text' 21-89. Content not read.

sources.verified: Crossref record: title, authors, journal, 30 Mar 2025. Content not read.

corrections: Claims that the inscription 'mentions Balak' or 'Moab' or 'Israel': the translated text names Balaam son of Beor, El, the Shaddai-gods and Shagar-and-Ishtar. Balak, Moab and Israel do not appear.
Claims that it is a Hebrew inscription: its language classification is disputed, and the editio princeps presents it as Aramaic.
Claims that it proves the events of Numbers 22-24: it shows a Balaam son of Beor tradition, as a seer of divine night visions, in the Jordan Valley c. 800 BCE. It does not narrate the Balak episode.

sites.name: Durupınar Formation
aka: Nuh'un Gemisi (Noah's Ark) natural site, Doğubayazıt
sites.subtitle: Boat-shaped landform near Doğubayazıt, Ağrı, Turkey · proposed as Noah's Ark · first permitted deep core drilling 2026
sites.date: Undated as an object. No radiometric date on the formation itself has been published. Geological readings assign its rocks to Eocene–Miocene strata (Avcı 2007) or to flood-plain sediments and volcanics shaped by later landslides (Collins 2016); advocates assign it to the Genesis flood.
sites.date_basis: The '3500–5000 years' figure circulating since Oct 2023 comes from a press statement (Hürriyet, 26 Oct 2023) about ~30 rock/soil samples tested at Istanbul Technical University; no dating method, lab number, or material dated was stated, and no paper has been located. The same statement also gives 'human activity from the Chalcolithic, 5500–3000 BC'. The two ranges do not match: 3,500–5,000 years before present is c. 3000–1500 BCE. The 2026 cores and ~1,000 soil samples are in lab (Ankara); radiocarbon results were promised for winter 2026–27, not yet released as of 27 Sep 2026.

discovery.when: 11 September 1959 (aerial photo review); site visit 1960
discovery.who: Turkish Army mapping captain Durupınar (named 'İhsan' on the Doğubayazıt district governorate page; 'İlhan' in most English sources); 1960 visit by George Vandeman and photogrammetrist Arthur Brandenberger per secondary accounts (not checked against the 1960 LIFE article itself)
discovery.where: Telçeker/Üzengili area, c. 27–30 km south(-west) of the summit of Greater Ararat, c. 3.5 km from the Turkey–Iran transit road, Doğubayazıt district, Ağrı province

sites.location: In situ. Collins (2016) gives Google Earth centre 39°26'26"N, 44°14'0.5"E, elevation 6,625 ft (c. 2,020 m); Collins & Fasold (1996) said c. 7,000 ft. Protected by decision no. 3657 (17 Sep 1987) of Turkey's High Council for Immovable Cultural and Natural Property as a natural site and open-air museum; visitor centre on the adjacent slope.

physical.material: Disputed by drill core and thin section: 1988 cores reached mudflow material and, at c. 5 m, layered bedrock (Baumgardner); Collins's 12 thin sections were basalt/andesite; Avcı (2007) reads Miocene limestone on Eocene clays; the 1988 team leader reported the drilled bedrock as ophiolite
physical.dimensions: Length 157 m / 515 ft (Wyatt; Collins 2016; Noah's Ark Scans); 538 ft in an earlier Wyatt measurement; 165 m × 50 m × 13 m (Doğubayazıt district governorate); 150 m × 50 m × 4 m high (Avcı 2007)

overview: The Durupınar formation is a pointed-oval, hull-shaped ridge of rock and mud lying in the Telçeker earthflow valley south of Mount Ararat in eastern Turkey. A Turkish army mapping captain named Durupınar spotted its outline on aerial survey photographs in September 1959. LIFE magazine printed a photo in its 5 September 1960 issue, pp. 112–114, as cited by Collins & Fasold 1996. Ron Wyatt took it up from 1977 on, and David Fasold, John Baumgardner (then at Los Alamos) and Atatürk University geologist Salih Bayraktutan surveyed it through the 1980s. Wyatt measured it as 515 ft (157 m), which he equated to 300 'Royal Egyptian cubits' of 20.6 in. On 17 September 1987 Turkey's Ministry of Culture and Tourism council (decision 3657) protected it as a natural site and open-air museum.

The claim that it is an ark rests on its shape and length, on metal-detector lines (13 longitudinal lines and 9 transverse lines, taken as walls), on iron-rich 'brackets', and on 'petrified wood' samples. Since 2014 it also rests on geophysics by Noah's Ark Scans (Andrew Jones et al.). Their 100 MHz GPR in 2019 showed right-angled and linear reflectors down to about 7 m, and ERT and LiDAR were added later. In 2024 they sampled soil at 22 points inside and outside the outline. A separate Turkish-American team (Istanbul Technical University, Ağrı İbrahim Çeçen University, Andrews University) reported first lab results on about 30 samples in October 2023.

The case against it rests on rock evidence. In 1988 four core holes went down as far as 10 m and recovered no wood, petrified or otherwise (Baumgardner, 1988). They met a ridge of layered bedrock along the centreline, and Baumgardner said it matched a roadcut about 0.5 mi away. Collins's thin sections showed the 'iron bracket' is limonite granules in a clay–quartz–calcite matrix, not smelted iron, and the 'wood' samples are basalt and andesite. In 2026 the first permitted deep coring programme (Sivas Cumhuriyet University, directed by Cenker Atila, with Noah's Ark Scans) cored to 18 m inside and outside the formation from June to September. On 23 Sep 2026 the team announced a drill bit broke on a hard layer at 4–5 m. They suggested petrified wood but have no lab result yet. Samples went to Ankara, and results are promised for winter 2026–27 into 2027.
evidence: Outline: pointed-oval ridge; length measured 157 m (515 ft) by Wyatt and later workers; width given as 50 m maximum (district governorate; Avcı 2007); relief given as 4 m (Avcı 2007) to 13 m (governorate).
Metal-detector survey (Wyatt, Fasold, Baumgardner, 1980s): 13 longitudinal lines of iron response converging at the pointed end, 9 transverse lines; Fasold reported >5,000 buried iron targets.

The 'iron bracket' in thin section and SEM (Collins & Fasold 1996) is limonite granules shaped like ilmenitic-magnetite crystals, in a matrix of calcite, clay, quartz and anthophyllite. Five SEM spots gave variable composition with high, variable TiO2, which smelted iron would not show.
Collins made 12 thin sections of 'petrified wood' samples collected by Fasold along the length and width of the formation; all were basalt or andesite (Collins 2016).

1988 coring (Bayraktutan & Baumgardner, 28 Jul–7 Aug 1988): hole 1 to 10 m, all mudflow material; holes 2–3 to about 6 m, changing abruptly at 5 m from pea-gravel mudflow to layered bedrock; hole 4 met bedrock at the surface. Baumgardner wrote in 1988 that there was 'no evidence for wood, petrified or otherwise'. Limonite nodules turned up at 3 points in the mudflow.

White fossiliferous limestone crops out at the formation's midpoint. Collins (2016) reports that drilling shows it continues through and beyond the formation rather than ending at a point. Atabey (2025) dates the region's fossiliferous limestones as Eocene, 55–33 million years old.
A stream channel 1.5 m wide and 1.5 m deep, filled with cobbles, cuts one dark sedimentary layer near the rounded end. The layers dip about 5° from the limestone toward the lower end (Collins 2016).

GPR, 2019 (Noah's Ark Scans / ToPa 3D, 100 MHz): right-angled and linear reflectors to about 7 m on the NW side. A 234-ft 'central corridor' is a later reinterpretation of the same data (as reported by Fox News, 2025). No raw radargrams have been peer-reviewed.

Soil chemistry, 2024 (Noah's Ark Scans, soil scientist William Crabtree): 22 points inside and outside the outline, collected in September and analysed over winter. Reported ratios vary by outlet: organic matter 2x, 2.72x ('carbon') or 3x inside vs outside; potassium about 38–40% higher inside; a pH difference. The lab is not named and no dataset has been published.

ITU / AİÇÜ / Andrews University samples (press release, Oct 2023): about 30 rock and soil samples tested at ITU. Reported contents are clayey material, marine material and 'sea products' (mollusc remains), stated to be '3500 to 5000 years' old. The method, the material dated and the lab IDs were not given.

Ceramic sherds exposed by road construction near the formation (reported Dec 2025 – Jan 2026) were assigned to the Chalcolithic, 5500–3000 BC, by Faruk Kaya (AİÇÜ). Typology is the implied basis. No excavation context has been published.

2026 season (29 Jun – 11 Sep 2026, under Sivas Cumhuriyet University with Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change approval): about 20 researchers from 5 countries. Work included GPS/3D modelling, GPR, cores to 18 m inside and outside the formation, and about 1,000 soil samples from 100–150 points. Arkeonews (23 Sep 2026) reported carbon about 40% higher inside, and a drill bit broke at 4–5 m inside the outline.
questions: What is the formation made of? Collins & Fasold (J. Geoscience Education 44, 1996) read it as a doubly plunging syncline, from converging limonite lines at the pointed end and fossiliferous limestone cutting the fold. Collins later withdrew the syncline reading in a postscript to his reprint. Collins (PSCF 68:4, 2016) instead reads flat-lying flood-plain sediments shaped by landslide debris flowing around a resistant basalt mass at the pointed end. Avcı (Bull. Eng. Geol. Environ. 66, 2007) reads a slumped, joint-bounded block of Miocene limestone creeping on Eocene clays, noting an axial displacement of about 20° from the valley trend. Güner (Jeomorfoloji Dergisi 14, 1986; summarised by Avcı) read a residual hill of ophiolitic bedrock. Atabey (MTA geologist, ResearchGate upload June 2025, after a site visit on 30 May 2025) returns to a syncline shaped by landslide. The naturalistic readings disagree with each other on mechanism, even though all agree the rock is bedrock.

Wood or rock? Wyatt (1994 video; Wyatt Archaeological Research) identified black layered rock as petrified wood and deck beams, citing Galbraith Laboratory chemistry (Fe, Mg, Al, Ca, Ti). Collins (2016) answers that those element ratios match basalt, not silicified wood, which is nearly pure SiO2, and his 12 thin sections are all volcanic rock. The 1988 cores found no wood (Baumgardner). The 2026 claim of a hard layer at 4–5 m that broke a bit (Jones, press release 23 Sep 2026) is untested until the core is sectioned; basalt and limestone were both already logged in this formation.

Do the GPR 'rooms' show structure or bedding? Noah's Ark Scans (Jones 2023, 7th Int. Noah's Ark Symposium; 2019 ToPa 3D survey) read 100 MHz right-angle reflectors at about 7 m as walls and corridors. Collins (2020, 'Discussion of the Subsurface Images Project') reads the same patterns as joint sets, alteration of feldspar to clay along fractures, and dense basalt masses. He notes that the joint system on the surface is where the metal-detector 'wall' ribbons were laid. Neither side has published radargrams with ground truth from cores; the 2026 cores are the first test able to settle it.

Is the inside/outside soil difference meaningful? Crabtree (Noah's Ark Scans, 2024–25) reads higher organic matter, potassium and carbon inside the outline as decayed wood. No lab, method or data table has been published, and the reported ratios differ between outlets (2x, 2.72x, 3x). The ridge holds a different substrate from the surrounding mudflow (bedrock near the surface vs colluvium, per the 1988 cores), which is itself a possible cause of different soil and vegetation. That reading is ours, and it is untested.

What was dated in 2023? The Hürriyet report (26 Oct 2023) quotes Kaya: samples were found in the dating study to be '3500 ile 5000 yıl öncesine ait' (3,500–5,000 years old). The same report says there was human activity 'milattan önce 5500 ve 3000 yılları arasındaki' (5500–3000 BC). Material, method and lab report are all unstated, and no publication was found. Kaya himself said (Hürriyet 2023; Christian Daily, 8 Jan 2026) that the dating cannot show the ark was there and that 'no satisfactory information or evidence has been reached.'

biblical.tie: The text gives 300 × 50 × 30 cubits (KJV: 'The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, the breadth of it fifty cubits, and the height of it thirty cubits'). At an 18-in (0.457 m) cubit that is 137 × 23 × 13.7 m. At the 20.6-in (0.5236 m) 'Egyptian royal' cubit chosen by Wyatt and Fasold it is 157 × 26 × 15.7 m. The formation's length of 157 m matches only if the 20.6-in cubit is chosen. Its maximum width of 50 m (governorate, Avcı) is about double 50 cubits; Fasold argued the *average* width matches. Its relief of 4 m (Avcı) to 13 m (governorate) is a landform height, not a hull depth. The cubit choice is an interpretive step, not something the text gives.

'The ark rested ... upon the mountains of Ararat' (plural). The text names a mountain region, not a peak. The site lies in the Ararat range about 27–30 km from Greater Ararat's summit, so it falls within the text's wording, as do other candidate locations in the same region; the verse does not single out this spot.
'Gopher wood' and pitch: the 1988 cores and Collins's 12 thin sections found no wood. The 2026 cores are the next test of this claim; results are pending.

sites.name: Ebla Tablets (Royal Archives of Palace G)
sites.subtitle: Third-millennium cuneiform archive from the royal palace at Tell Mardikh, Syria
sites.date: Early Bronze Age, the generations before the destruction of Palace G (third millennium BCE; commonly placed in the 24th century BCE)
sites.date_basis: Stratigraphy of Palace G at Tell Mardikh (the tablets lay in the palace's destruction level) and synchronisms in the texts with Mesopotamian rulers. Exact BCE figures depend on the Mesopotamian chronology used and on which king destroyed the palace, which the Ebla texts themselves do not record.

discovery.when: 1974-1975 (first tablets 1974; main archive 1975)
discovery.who: Italian Archaeological Expedition to Syria, Sapienza University of Rome, directed by Paolo Matthiae; epigraphist Giovanni Pettinato (later Alfonso Archi)
discovery.where: Palace G, acropolis of Tell Mardikh (ancient Ebla), northern Syria

sites.location: Syria (Syrian national collections). The specific museums holding the tablets are not confirmed from a primary source.

physical.material: Clay tablets

overview: In 1974-1975 the Italian mission led by Paolo Matthiae found thousands of cuneiform tablets and fragments in the royal Palace G at Tell Mardikh, identifying the site as the city of Ebla. The epigraphist Giovanni Pettinato reported on them in The Biblical Archaeologist in 1976, and Alfonso Archi later took over much of the publication (see Archi 2015). Matthiae published a new account of how the tablets were found, distributed and shelved in Studia Eblaitica 11 (2025).

The texts are overwhelmingly administrative: records of textiles, metals and livestock, with letters, treaties, ritual texts and school lexical lists, some bilingual Sumerian-Eblaite. They document Ebla's dealings with dozens of Syrian and Mesopotamian cities in the Early Bronze Age.

In the late 1970s Pettinato and D. N. Freedman announced links to Genesis - names like the patriarchs', and the five 'Cities of the Plain'. Archi and others disputed these readings in print (Biblical Archaeologist 1980-1981). The disputes are about individual readings of cuneiform signs, and are recorded here as disputes, not as findings.
evidence: Find-spot: Palace G on the acropolis of Tell Mardikh; the archives' finding and arrangement are the subject of Matthiae, Studia Eblaitica 11 (2025) 1-20.
Discovery in the mid-1970s: Sapienza University (Sept. 2024) dates the discovery of 'the cuneiform tablets from the royal archives' to almost 50 years earlier.
Language and script: cuneiform used for Sumerian and for the local Semitic language, Eblaite (the subject of Archi 2015; details not re-reviewed for this entry).
Since 2011 the site was damaged: Sapienza (2024) reports that it was 'turned into a military base' with 'clandestine excavation and destruction' in 2014-2019, followed by a 2024 recovery mission.
questions: Cities of the Plain: D. N. Freedman ('The Real Story of the Ebla Tablets: Ebla and the Cities of the Plain,' BA 41, 1978, 143-164) presented Pettinato's readings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela in an Ebla tablet. A. Archi ('Further Concerning Ebla and the Bible,' BA 44, 1981, 145-154) and Pettinato himself ('Ebla and the Bible,' BA 43, 1980, 203-216) returned to the question; Freedman summarised the state of the epigraphic evidence in BA 43 (1980) 200-203. The texts of these articles were not available for this entry, so which readings each finally held cannot be stated here from the sources. The tablet sign-readings are the evidence; the published editions (ARET) are where they must be checked.

Personal names: early announcements compared Ebla names with Abraham, Ishmael, Eber, Saul, David and names ending in -ya (read as Yah). Whether -ya is a divine name or a hypocoristic ending is a question of Eblaite grammar; the same BA exchange (1978-1981) is the place the argument was made. Not resolved from sources read here.
'Canaan': the old entry says the tablets contain an early reference to Canaan. No primary source cited here confirms a reading of Canaan in the Ebla texts; left open.

biblical.tie: Ebla shows a literate Semitic-speaking kingdom in Syria with wide trade and treaty relations, centuries before the patriarchal setting. Specific links to Genesis (names, the Cities of the Plain) depend on disputed sign readings and are not established by any source read here.

corrections: Old entry: 'over 17,000 clay tablets.' That figure comes from early announcements counting fragments and chips; no source cited here supports 17,000 tablets, and published counts are of fragments. Figure removed pending a primary count (Archi 2015 ch. 5 or Matthiae 2025).

Old entry: 'unique syllabic cuneiform script that predates Akkadian cuneiform.' Nothing in the sources consulted supports a separate script; the tablets are in Mesopotamian cuneiform used for Sumerian and Eblaite.

Old entry: 'references to ... Haran, and possibly Sodom and Gomorrah, ... names ... Abraham, Eber, and Saul' as findings. These were proposals from 1976-1978 and were contested in print (Pettinato BA 1980; Archi BA 1981); they are disputes, not results.

Old entry: 'demonstrated that the patriarchal world described in Genesis was not a later literary construction.' No Ebla text mentions any biblical person or event; the claim goes beyond the evidence.
Old entry: tablets 'housed in ... the University of Rome.' The tablets are Syrian state property; the University of Rome (Sapienza) is the excavating institution.
Old entry: 'excavations ... between 1974 and 1976.' The Italian excavation at Tell Mardikh began in 1964 (Sapienza 2024: 'sixty years'); the archive was found in 1974-1975.

sites.name: Ekron Royal Dedicatory Inscription
sites.subtitle: Limestone temple dedication naming Ekron and five of its rulers · first half of the 7th century BCE
sites.date: First half of the 7th century BCE, during the reign of Ikausu (Achish), son of Padi
sites.date_basis: The builder 'kysh son of Padi matches two kings of Ekron in Assyrian records. Padi appears in Sennacherib's annals for the 701 BCE campaign, and Assyrian records call both Padi and Ikausu kings of Ekron (Gitin, Dothan and Naveh, Archaeology 51/1, 1998). The Assyrian texts naming Ikausu were not re-read for this entry. The stone was found in the destruction debris the excavators attribute to Nebuchadnezzar's sack of 603 BCE.

discovery.who: Tel Miqne-Ekron excavation directed by Seymour Gitin (W. F. Albright Institute) and Trude Dothan (Hebrew University); text read by Joseph Naveh
discovery.where: Temple Complex 650, elite zone of the lower city, Tel Miqne (Ekron), in the Babylonian destruction debris

sites.location: The Israel Museum, Jerusalem (on public display by 1997, per Demsky, JANES 25, 1997); plaster copy at the Tel Ekron Museum, Kibbutz Revadim

physical.material: Porous local limestone block, probably from the temple wall (Demsky 1997)
physical.script: Alphabetic script close to Phoenician; five lines within a drawn frame, with word dividers
physical.language: A Canaanite dialect close to Phoenician, used at Ekron (Demsky calls it South Canaanite and links it to the 'Ashdodite' of Neh 13:24)

overview: In 1996 the Tel Miqne-Ekron excavation found a limestone block with a five-line inscription in the destruction debris of Temple Complex 650, a large building (186 by 124 ft) in the elite zone of the lower city. The excavators attribute the destruction to the Babylonian sack of 603 BCE. Seymour Gitin, Trude Dothan and Joseph Naveh published it in Israel Exploration Journal 47 (1997) and summarized it for a general audience in Archaeology (1998).

The text records a temple built by 'kysh (Achish; in Assyrian, Ikausu), son of Padi, son of Ysd, son of Ada, son of Ya'ir, ruler of Ekron, for his lady, a goddess whose name is read Ptgyh. It asks her to bless him, protect him, prolong his days, and bless his land.

Because the inscription names both the city (Ekron) and two rulers known as kings of Ekron from Assyrian records, it settles that Tel Miqne is Ekron. In the same complex a storage jar was found inscribed 'for Baal and for Padi' (Archaeology 1998).

text.quote: The house that 'kysh son of Padi, son of Ysd, son of Ada, son of Ya'ir, ruler of Ekron, built for Ptgyh his lady. May she bless him and guard him and lengthen his days and bless his land.
text.translation: Literal translation (this encyclopedia) of the published transliteration (Gitin, Dothan and Naveh, IEJ 47, 1997). Compare the editors' English in Archaeology 51/1 (1998). No public-domain translation exists.

evidence: Found in the Babylonian destruction debris of Temple Complex 650, a 186 x 124 ft structure in the elite zone of the lower tel (Gitin, Dothan and Naveh 1998).
The text runs five lines, 72 letters by the editors' count in Archaeology (1998).
It names the city Ekron ('qrn) and five generations of its rulers: 'kysh, Padi, Ysd, Ada, Ya'ir (same).
Padi and Ikausu are named as kings of Ekron in Assyrian royal records. The other three rulers are otherwise unknown (same).
A storage jar in a side room of the same temple complex is inscribed 'for Baal and for Padi' (same).

The block is porous local limestone, the text is set in a drawn frame, and the engraver added the final he of the goddess's name above a word-divider, apparently as an afterthought (Demsky 1997, from autopsy at the Albright Institute and the Israel Museum).
questions: The goddess's name. Naveh (IEJ 1997) read Ptgyh, marking the third letter as uncertain, and took it as a non-Semitic (Greek) name. Demsky (JANES 25, 1997), after examining the stone under different lighting, says the supposed small gimel is 'no more than a wedged shaped chip in the porous stone' and reads ptyh. Schaefer-Lichtenberger (1998) proposed Pythogaia (Gaia), and Press (BASOR 365, 2012) argues that identification lacks supporting evidence and rests on the idea of an Aegean 'Great Goddess', which he rejects.

The king's name. The editors vocalize 'kysh as Achish, following the Bible, and give Ikausu from Assyrian texts. Naveh derives it from Achaios, 'Achaean/Greek'. Demsky prefers a link with Anchises (Iliad). Both are etymological proposals; the stone gives only the consonants 'kysh.

Language. The editors note that a 7th-century Philistine city wrote in a dialect close to Phoenician. Demsky reads it as the local South Canaanite dialect, a forerunner of Nehemiah's 'Ashdodite'. The inscription does not show what language the early Philistines spoke.

biblical.tie: Ekron is one of the five Philistine cities. The stone names 'qrn and its ruler, fixing Ekron at Tel Miqne.
Achish, king of Gath in David's time. The Ekron king 'kysh has the same name in a different city about three centuries later. This is a name parallel, not the same person.

Hezekiah strikes the Philistines, and Sennacherib's 701 BCE campaign follows. Padi, the Ekron builder's father, is the king of Ekron in Sennacherib's account of that campaign (Archaeology 1998); the Bible does not name him.
Prophetic oracles against Ekron. The Babylonian destruction layer in which the stone was found fits the 7th-6th century horizon of Jeremiah and Zephaniah (our reading).
'Half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod'. Demsky (1997) links the inscription's dialect to this Philistine-city speech.

corrections: The inscription is sometimes said to name 'Achish king of Gath' from 1 Samuel. The stone names 'kysh as ruler of Ekron, son of Padi, in the 7th century BCE. The biblical Achish ruled Gath about three centuries earlier.

It is often called 'Philistine language'. The dialect is close to Phoenician (the editors) or local South Canaanite (Demsky 1997). It does not preserve the early Philistines' own non-Semitic language.
The goddess's name is sometimes given as a settled 'Ptgyh = Pythogaia'. The third letter is contested (Demsky 1997 reads ptyh), and the Gaia identification is disputed (Press 2012).
