sites.name: El-Araj (Bethsaida-Julias candidate)
aka: Church of St. Peter at el-Araj
sites.subtitle: Roman-period village and Byzantine basilica on the NE shore of the Sea of Galilee · 1st c. BCE - 3rd c. CE; basilica 5th/6th c. CE
sites.date: Roman-period occupation 1st century BCE - 3rd century CE; after a gap of about two centuries, a Byzantine basilica (dated 5th century by the Times of Israel report, 6th century by Notley 2022)
sites.date_basis: Excavators' pottery, coins and lamp typology (including Herodian lamps they describe as made only in Jerusalem before 70 CE) and the stratigraphy beneath the church floor (Di Segni et al., Liber Annuus 73, 2023; project season reports 2025-2026). The date of the basilica differs between the published abstracts and press reports (5th vs 6th century); no radiocarbon dates were seen for this entry.

discovery.when: Multi-season excavation; the tenth season ran July-August 2026; basilica found 2021
discovery.who: El-Araj Excavation Project (Bethsaida-Julias), archaeological director Mordechai Aviam (Kinneret College), academic director and co-director R. Steven Notley (Pillar College, New Jersey)
discovery.where: El-Araj, on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee, about 2 km from et-Tell

sites.location: In situ (northern shore of the Sea of Galilee)
overview: El-Araj is a low site on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee that R. Steven Notley and Mordechai Aviam have excavated over ten seasons (to 2026) as the most likely location of Bethsaida, the fishing village the Gospels name as home of Peter, Andrew and Philip, which Josephus says Herod Philip raised to a city called Julias. Their excavation has exposed Roman-period houses with finds running from the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE, and, above them after a gap of about two centuries, a Byzantine basilica found in 2021.

Three Greek inscriptions were set in the basilica's mosaic floor. One names 'the chief of the apostles and the keeper of the keys of the heavenly spheres', titles the editors (Di Segni, Ashkenazi, Aviam and Notley 2023) take as referring to Peter. They identify the building with the church that the pilgrim Willibald saw in 725 CE at 'Bethsaida, whence came Peter and Andrew', built where their house had stood, and argue that the Byzantine church therefore marks where Byzantine Christians placed Bethsaida.

In July 2025 a wildfire burned across the site for three days and cleared the vegetation, exposing Roman-period architectural pieces (column drums, Corinthian and Doric capitals, cornices). The tenth season (July-August 2026) worked the Roman level (2nd-3rd century CE) in Areas D, F and G and reported coin hoards (150+ coins), Herodian lamps, chalk/stone vessels, fishing weights, frescoed walls, fine glass and a half Doric capital. The rival candidate, et-Tell about 2 km away, has been excavated as Bethsaida since 1987 by Rami Arav.

text.quote: The basilica's mosaic floor carried three Greek inscriptions. The one reported in the editors' abstract names 'the chief of the apostles and the keeper of the keys of the heavenly spheres' (titles of Peter). It does not name Peter or Bethsaida. The other two inscriptions' contents were not seen for this entry.
text.translation: English phrase from the abstract of Di Segni, Ashkenazi, Aviam and Notley, Liber Annuus 73 (2023) 365-384; no public-domain translation exists (found 2021).

evidence: Josephus, Ant. 18.2.1 (18.28), Whiston trans.: Philip 'advanced the village Bethsaida, situate at the lake of Gennesareth, unto the dignity of a city ... and called it by the name of Julias, the same name with Caesar's daughter.'

Willibald, Hodoeporicon ch. XIV (725 CE), Brownlow trans., PPTS 3 p. 16: 'And thence they proceeded to Bethsaida, whence came Peter and Andrew. There is now a church where their house was formerly. They stayed there one night.'
Byzantine basilica with mosaic floor found at el-Araj in 2021 (Di Segni et al. 2023 abstract).

Three Greek inscriptions in the mosaic; one mentions 'The chief of the apostles and the keeper of the keys of the heavenly spheres' (Di Segni et al. 2023 abstract). The project's 2026 post quotes it as 'the chief of the Apostles and the keeper of the keys of heaven'.
The inscription does not contain the name Bethsaida or Peter; the link to Peter rests on the titles.

Roman-period remains beneath the church and elsewhere span the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE, followed by an occupation gap of about two centuries before the church (Di Segni et al. 2023 abstract).
The July 2025 wildfire exposed column drums, two Corinthian and two Doric capitals, cornices and house foundations (Times of Israel, 30 Aug 2025).

Season 10 (2026) finds: 150+ coins in several hoards, three intact Herodian lamps, a discus lamp (2nd-3rd c. CE), chalk/stone vessels, fishing weights, frescoed walls, fine glassware, a half Doric capital (project season reports, 1 and 8 Aug 2026).
No inscription found at el-Araj names the settlement.
questions: Which site is Bethsaida. Notley (Near Eastern Archaeology 70:4, 2007: 220-230) argued in 'Et-Tell Is Not Bethsaida'; Arav (Near Eastern Archaeology 74:2, 2011: 92-100) answered in 'Bethsaida - A Response to Steven Notley'. The specific arguments in those two papers were not read for this entry (titles and pagination confirmed via Crossref only). What the el-Araj team puts forward (Di Segni et al. 2023): Roman-period occupation 1st c. BCE - 3rd c. CE at el-Araj plus a Byzantine church with Petrine titles matching Willibald's church. What stands against a simple equation on their own evidence: the two-century gap between the Roman and Byzantine phases, so the church shows where Byzantine Christians placed Bethsaida, not directly where the 1st-century village was.

Is the Roman town Julias as well as Bethsaida? Josephus (Ant. 18.28) says Philip made the village a city named Julias. The excavators read the architectural pieces (Corinthian/Doric capitals, cornices) and site size as fitting a polis and the stone vessels as marking a Jewish population (season 10 reports, 2026). No inscription or civic building naming Julias has been reported.

Date of the basilica: Notley (Novum Testamentum 64:4, 2022) calls it a 6th-century basilica; the Times of Israel report (2025) calls it fifth-century. The published sources seen do not state the dating evidence.

Capernaum vs el-Araj as the house of Peter: Notley (NovT 2022) argues the el-Araj finds challenge the 1921 identification (by Orfali) of the octagonal church at Capernaum as built over Peter's house. The Gospels place Peter's house at Capernaum (Mark 1:21, 29) while John 1:44 calls Bethsaida his town; both traditions sit in the text.

biblical.tie: Bethsaida named as the town of Philip, Andrew and Peter. The el-Araj church inscription uses Petrine titles, and Willibald located Peter and Andrew's house at Bethsaida.
Healing of a blind man at Bethsaida, which Mark calls a village (kome). The excavators hold that the Roman-period remains are the village later made into Julias (their reading).
Jesus withdraws to 'a city called Bethsaida' before the feeding of the five thousand.
Woe pronounced on Chorazin and Bethsaida. Nothing in the finds bears on this beyond the location question.

corrections: Circulating press (Times of Israel 2025) renders the inscription as 'Head and Leader of the Heavenly Messengers' and 'Keeper of the Keys'. The editors' own abstract (Di Segni et al. 2023) gives 'The chief of the apostles and the keeper of the keys of the heavenly spheres'.

sites.name: Elephantine Papyri
sites.subtitle: Aramaic archives of the Judean garrison at Yeb (Elephantine), Egypt · 5th century BCE
sites.date: 5th century BCE, mostly the reigns of Artaxerxes I and Darius II; the dated temple petition (Cowley 30) is year 17 of Darius II (Cowley: 408 BCE); the festival letter (Cowley 21) is year 5 of Darius II (Cowley: 419 BCE)
sites.date_basis: Regnal-year dates written in the documents themselves (often double-dated by Babylonian/Jewish and Egyptian months). Cowley identifies the Darius of nos. 21 and 30 as Darius II because the same community leader, Yedoniah, appears in both.

discovery.when: Papyri surfaced on the antiquities market from the 1890s; the Sayce-Cowley group was published 1906; German excavations on Elephantine in 1906-1908 recovered the papyri published by Sachau (1911)
discovery.who: Groups acquired or excavated by various parties; editions by A. H. Sayce and A. E. Cowley (1906), E. Sachau (1911), A. E. Cowley (collected edition, 1923), E. G. Kraeling (Brooklyn papyri, 1953)
discovery.where: Elephantine island (ancient Yeb) at Aswan (Syene), southern Egypt

sites.location: Dispersed. Cowley (1923) names Cairo and Berlin as holding the originals of the major groups; the Brooklyn Museum holds the papyri published by Kraeling in 1953; other pieces are in other collections. Individual inventory numbers were Not confirmed in a published museum record.

physical.material: Papyrus (letters, contracts, lists, literary texts such as Ahiqar)
physical.script: Aramaic (square-type cursive of the Achaemenid chancery)

overview: Elephantine, an island in the Nile at the first cataract opposite Syene (Aswan), held a Persian-period military colony that included a Judean garrison. Its members wrote in Aramaic, the administrative language of the Persian empire. Their surviving papyri include marriage contracts, property deeds, loans, lists of contributions, private and official letters, and copies of literary works such as the Words of Ahiqar and a version of Darius I's Behistun inscription.

The best-known letter (Cowley 30) is a petition from Yedoniah and the priests of Yeb to Bigvai (Bagohi), 'governor of Judaea', dated the 20th of Marheshwan, year 17 of Darius. It reports that in year 14, while the satrap Arsames was away, the priests of the Egyptian god Khnum conspired with the local Persian official Waidrang (Vidranga), whose son Nephayan led troops who destroyed 'the temple of Ya'u the God' (YHW) in the fortress, burnt its cedar roof and took its gold and silver bowls. It says the temple already stood when Cambyses conquered Egypt (525 BCE), and that an earlier letter to Johanan the high priest in Jerusalem went unanswered. It also mentions a letter to Delaiah and Shelemiah, sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria.

A short memorandum (Cowley 32) records the reply of Bigvai and Delaiah: the altar-house of the God of Heaven should be rebuilt 'as it was before', with meal-offering and incense offered on it. Burnt offering is not mentioned. Another letter (Cowley 21), from one Hananiah in year 5 of Darius, passes on a royal instruction about the festival of Unleavened Bread in Nisan (14th-21st). The word 'Passover' in it falls in a damaged part of the papyrus and is Cowley's restoration.

text.quote: To our lord Bigvai, governor of Judaea, your servants Yedoniah and his colleagues, the priests who are in Yeb the fortress... Already in the days of the kings of Egypt our fathers had built that temple in the fortress of Yeb, and when Cambyses came into Egypt he found that temple built.
text.translation: A. Cowley, Aramaic Papyri of the Fifth Century B.C. (Oxford, 1923), no. 30, lines 1 and 13-14, pp. 113-114

evidence: Cowley 30 (petition): dated '20th of Marheshwan, the 17th year of Darius the king'; recto lines 1-17, verso 18-30; Cowley calls it in excellent condition.
Names the god of the Yeb temple as Ya'u (YHW) and calls him 'God of Heaven'.
Temple destroyed in Tammuz, year 14 of Darius, by troops led by Nephayan on the order of his father Waidrang, at the urging of the priests of Khnum.
Temple details: stone pillars, five gateways of hewn stone, doors with bronze hinges, cedar roof, gold and silver basins.
Claims the temple existed before Cambyses entered Egypt and was spared when Egyptian temples were overthrown.
Names Johanan the high priest in Jerusalem, Ostanes brother of Anani, and Delaiah and Shelemiah, sons of Sanballat governor of Samaria.
Cowley 32: memorandum of Bigvai and Delaiah authorizing rebuilding 'as it was before' with meal-offering and incense; animal burnt offering is not listed.

Cowley 22 (contribution list), lines 123-125: the temple fund is divided between Ya'u and 'Anathbethel in nearly equal shares, with a smaller share to Ishumbethel; Cowley 44 records an oath 'by the temple and by 'Anathya'u' (Cowley 1923, Introduction).
Cowley 21: in year 5 of Darius, Hananiah conveys a royal instruction to keep days 15-21 of Nisan as Unleavened Bread; 'Passover' is restored in a lacuna.
Cowley 1923 notes that early critics (Belleli 1909, Jahn 1913) questioned authenticity over the double dates; Cowley rejected this after the astronomical studies of Knobel, Fotheringham and Smyly.
questions: How 'Jewish' was the Yeb community's religion? The texts show a YHW temple with sacrifice outside Jerusalem, contrary to Deut 12's single-sanctuary law. The archive's own contribution list (Cowley 22) divides the temple fund between Ya'u, 'Anathbethel and Ishumbethel, and an oath is sworn 'by 'Anathya'u' (Cowley 44); Cowley (1923) concluded they recognized 'Anath, Bethel, Ishum and Herem besides Ya'u, while admitting 'the evidence does not show' how these related. J. D. Moore ('A Supposed Diaspora Community at Elephantine or How the Persians Reinvented Judean-ness', in Judeans in the Land of the Nile, Zaphon 2026) questions the 'diaspora' label itself. G. Granerød in the same volume weighs Papyrus Amherst 63 as evidence for the community's background. What the papyri do not say is where or when the community's ancestors left Judah. Moore's 2026 monograph goes further, treating the colony as 'colonial state dependents' of the Persian administration rather than mercenaries.

Language of the community: M. A. Cunningham ('A Case for Hebrew at Yeb: The Vidranga Passage and Judean Diglossia', JNES 84/1, 2025) argues from the wording of the Vidranga passage in the temple petition that Hebrew was still in use alongside Aramaic. The documents themselves are all Aramaic.

Was the 'Passover Papyrus' about Passover? Cowley (1923, no. 21) restores 'Passover' in damaged lines. The surviving text clearly concerns the seven days of Unleavened Bread, Nisan 15-21, by royal instruction. How far the restoration can be trusted is a question about the gap, not something the preserved text settles.

Why was burnt offering left out of the rebuilding memorandum (Cowley 32)? The document gives no reason. Cowley and later writers connect it to Egyptian (Khnum-priest) hostility to animal sacrifice or to Jerusalem's claims; that is inference from silence.

biblical.tie: Sanballat appears in Nehemiah as Nehemiah's opponent. Cowley 30 names 'Delaiah and Shelemiah the sons of Sanballat governor of Samaria' in the 17th year of Darius II: an outside document naming Sanballat as governor of Samaria and giving his sons' names. Cowley uses this and Bigvai's office in 408 to put Nehemiah's 32nd year of Artaxerxes (Neh 13:6) under Artaxerxes I, 433 BCE.
Lists Johanan among high priests of the Persian period. Cowley 30 names 'Johanan the high priest' in Jerusalem in Darius II's reign.

Aramaic chancery letters in Ezra use the same forms and title 'God of Heaven' as the papyri. The petition's pattern (appeal to Persian officials to rebuild a YHW temple, with a written authorization in reply) is the same process Ezra 5-6 describes for Jerusalem.
Cowley 21's Nisan 14 / Nisan 15-21 dates, no leaven seen in dwellings, and no work on the 15th and 21st correspond to the Torah's festival rules.

Jeremiah addresses Judeans living in Egypt 'at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph and Pathros'. Elephantine is in the far south (Pathros); the papyri show a Judean community there a century later. Any direct link between the two groups is not in the sources.

discovery.when: 1928 (left part of second slab, east parados of the theatre); 1929 (complete slab in situ); 1947 (remaining fragment, in a late vaulted building SW of the theatre)
discovery.who: American School of Classical Studies at Athens excavations; the 1929 find published by T. Leslie Shear
discovery.where: Paved square (c. 19 x 19 m) east of the stage building of the theatre, Corinth, at its entrance from the street along the theatre's east side

sites.location: The complete slab was found in situ in the square east of the theatre at ancient Corinth (Gill 1989); current storage of the 1928/1947 fragments Not confirmed in a published museum record

physical.material: Grey Acrocorinthian limestone paving slabs; letters originally inlaid bronze, now only the cuttings survive
physical.dimensions: Each slab c. 0.66 x 2.27 x 0.15 m; three adjoining slabs, total width 6.81 m; letters 0.18 m high (Gill 1989, after Kent)
physical.script: Latin capitals (letter cuttings for bronze inlay)

overview: Three fragments of two inscribed paving slabs, originally one of three adjoining slabs, from the paved square east of the stage building of Corinth's theatre. The Latin letters were bronze inlays set into cuttings; the bronze is gone and only the cuttings and two punctuation marks remain.

The text reads: [praenomen nomen] Erastus pro aedilit[at]e s(ua) p(ecunia) stravit - '[...] Erastus, in return for his aedileship, laid (this pavement) at his own expense.' The left slab carrying the first part of his name is lost; about seven letters stood before 'Erastus'.

The first published report (Shear, AJA 1929) called Erastus a procurator because the text was incomplete; the full reading as aedile came only after the 1947 fragment. Whether this aedile is the Erastus 'oikonomos of the city' of Romans 16:23 is the live question.

text.quote: [...] Erastus pro aedilit[at]e s(ua) p(ecunia) stravit - '[...] Erastus, for his aedileship, laid (the pavement) at his own expense'
text.translation: Latin text and translation as printed in D. W. J. Gill, Tyndale Bulletin 40 (1989) 293, after J. H. Kent, Corinth VIII.3 (1966) no. 232 (modern scholarly translation, quoted briefly)

evidence: Language is Latin, not Greek; office named is aedile (aedilitas), not treasurer.
Letters were bronze inlay; only the cuttings survive, 0.18 m high.
Name preserved: the cognomen Erastus only; praenomen and nomen lost on the missing left slab.
Found in three campaigns: 1928, 1929, 1947; studies before 1947 lacked the full text (Gill 1989, n. 1).
The inscription carries no date formula.
Romans 16:23 calls Erastus ὁ οἰκονόμος τῆς πόλεως; the stone's title is aedile. The equation of the two titles is itself disputed.
questions: Same man as Rom 16:23? J. H. Kent (Corinth VIII.3, 1966, p. 99) held the identification 'still seems sound' because he dated the pavement to the mid-1st century, the cognomen Erastus was uncommon at Corinth, and oikonomos could render aedile (as summarized by Gill 1989). H. J. Cadbury (JBL 50, 1931) and A. G. Roos (Mnemosyne 1930) objected that a Christian holding a pagan-linked magistracy was unlikely (Gill 1989, n. 29).

Title equivalence: J. K. Goodrich (NTS 56, 2010, 90-115), relying on a new inscription from the Achaean colony of Patras, argues oikonomos tes poleos = quaestor, a post held by the economic elite, and rebuts the arcarius (slave treasurer) and aedile equations.

Date and publication record: S. J. Friesen ('The Wrong Erastus', in Corinth in Context, Brill 2010, 231-256) states 'the inscription was incorrectly published and the identification of the two Erastus references is wrong'; per Goodrich (NTS 57, 2011, 583-593) Friesen argues the Romans Erastus was an unbelieving public slave. Goodrich 2011 replies, and also answers A. Weiss's claim that Corinth had no municipal quaestorship. Friesen's specific re-dating evidence is not accessible for this entry.

biblical.tie: 'Erastus the oikonomos of the city greets you' - written from Corinth. Same cognomen, same city; the stone says aedile, the letter says oikonomos. Identity is a reading, not a statement of either text.
An Erastus sent by Paul with Timothy into Macedonia; no office given.
'Erastus remained at Corinth'; no office given.

sites.name: Egyptian Execration Texts
sites.subtitle: Middle Kingdom ritual curse lists naming foreign rulers and places, written on pots and prisoner figurines
sites.kind: Inscription (ritual texts on pottery and clay figurines)
sites.date: Middle Kingdom. Berlin bowls: earlier group; Brussels/Saqqara figurines: end of the 12th Dynasty (possibly early 13th), about one generation after the bowls (Posener 1940)
sites.date_basis: Posener (1940, §6) dated the figurines by palaeography (later than the Illahun papyri of Senusret III-Amenemhat III, earlier than Papyrus Boulaq 18) and by Egyptian personal names on the companion figurines built on 12th-Dynasty royal names, including Senusret III, giving a terminus post quem. He found cases where a Nubian prince's father appears on the bowls and the son on the figurines, putting a generation between the two groups.

discovery.when: Berlin bowls: published by Kurt Sethe in 1926. Saqqara figurines: found 1922; Brussels figurines: bought 1938
discovery.who: Sethe (Berlin); C. M. Firth's excavation (Saqqara, 1921-1922 season); Jean Capart / Musées Royaux, Brussels (purchase); published by Georges Posener (1940)
discovery.where: Saqqara group: at the entrance of the 'Street of Tombs', along the north enclosure wall of the pyramid temple of Teti, in a small mudbrick chapel with five stelae. Brussels group: bought from a dealer; Posener judged it to share an origin with the Saqqara finds.

sites.location: Ägyptisches Museum, Berlin (bowls); Egyptian Museum, Cairo (Saqqara figurines, moved there in 1938); Musées Royaux d'Art et d'Histoire, Brussels (figurines)

physical.material: Pottery bowls/sherds (Berlin); unbaked clay figurines of bound captives about 30 cm high (Brussels/Cairo); five alabaster figurines in Cairo
physical.language: Middle Egyptian, with foreign (Semitic and Nubian) names in Egyptian writing

overview: The Execration Texts are ritual curse lists. Egyptian priests wrote the names of hostile rulers, peoples and places - Nubian, Libyan, Asiatic and even Egyptian - on pots or on clay figurines of bound prisoners, which were then broken or buried to disable the enemies named. Two big groups are known: the bowls published by Kurt Sethe in 1926 (Berlin), and the figurines published by Georges Posener in 1940 (Brussels and Cairo).

The Asiatic section names Levantine rulers with their towns, in a fixed formula: 'The ruler of [place], (called) [name].' Posener's list includes ꜣwšꜣmm (E 45), which Sethe had identified with Jerusalem, and Skmimi (Posener p. 68), which Posener equates with the Skmm of the Sebek-khu stela and 'the biblical Shechem'. ꜣskn (E 2) is identified with Ashkelon.
The texts are magic, not administration. They name the places the Egyptians feared or claimed; they say nothing about tribute.

text.quote: The ruler of Skmimi, (called) Ibsh-Hadad. ... The ruler of Iskn, (called) Muri.
text.translation: Literal translation (this encyclopedia) of Posener's transliterations and French renderings, Princes et pays d'Asie et de Nubie (1940), p. 68 (Shechem) and E 2 (Ashkelon). No pre-1930 English translation of these texts exists.

evidence: Asiatic princes list formula: 'Le prince de [pays] (appelé) [nom]' (Posener 1940, section E).
E 45: ꜣwšꜣmm, with two princes in the Berlin texts (Sethe e 27-28, f 18); Sethe identified it with Jerusalem (Posener 1940).
Shechem: Skmimi / Skmmi, ruler 'Ibš-Hadad', a name compounded with Hadad (Posener 1940, p. 68).
E 2: ꜣskn, ruler Mwri; the Berlin texts spell it with -nw (Sethe e 23-25, f 15); identified with Ashkelon (Posener 1940).

Saqqara figurines found in 1922 in a mudbrick chapel with five private stelae north of Teti's temple enclosure; rediscovered by Posener in a Saqqara storeroom in spring 1938 and moved to Cairo (Posener 1940, §2).
Brussels figurines: unbaked clay, c. 30 cm high, bound captives, hieratic texts; bought in Paris in summer 1938 (Capart's foreword to Posener 1940).
questions: Is ꜣwšꜣmm Jerusalem? Sethe (1926) proposed it and Posener (1940, E 45) reports it without objection. The equation rests on the consonants (Egyptian ꜣ can render l/r: ꜣ-w-š-ꜣ-m-m ~ Rushalimum). No text states the place's location.

Two Jerusalem rulers vs one: the Berlin bowls give ꜣwšꜣmm two princes; the figurine list gives one (name mostly effaced). Whether this reflects a change of ruler across one generation, as Posener argued for the Nubian princes, is his inference from the two series.

biblical.tie: Shechem is attested as a ruled town in Middle Kingdom Egypt's list of Asiatic enemies, i.e. it existed as a political centre in the Middle Bronze Age, the setting Genesis gives Abram and Jacob there. The text says nothing about its people beyond the ruler's name.
If ꜣwšꜣmm is Jerusalem (Sethe's reading), the city had rulers by the late 12th Dynasty - the earliest mention of the name outside the Bible. The Execration Texts do not mention Salem or Melchizedek.
Ashkelon (ꜣskn) appears as a ruled city in the same lists.

sources.cite: G. Posener, Princes et pays d'Asie et de Nubie: textes hiératiques sur des figurines d'envoûtement du Moyen Empire, suivis de Remarques paléographiques sur les textes similaires de Berlin par B. van de Walle (Brussels: Fondation Égyptologique Reine Élisabeth, 1940)

Old entry: 'Written in Egyptian hieroglyphs.' They are written in hieratic (Posener 1940; Capart's foreword).

sites.name: Ezion-geber and Tell el-Kheleifeh
sites.subtitle: Iron Age casemate fortress at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, identified with Ezion-geber · 8th–6th centuries BCE
sites.date: 8th to 6th centuries BCE, with a later postscript of uncertain length (Pratico 1985). Glueck had dated five periods from the 10th to the 5th century BCE.
sites.date_basis: Pottery horizons re-studied by Pratico (BASOR 259, 1985) from Glueck's unpublished excavation records. Glueck's 10th-century start rested on the assumed biblical identification, not on the pottery. Ben-Ami et al. (Levant 58, 2026) date the twin fortress at 'En Hazeva to the first half of the 8th century BCE by radiocarbon and argue Tell el-Kheleifeh was built alongside it.

discovery.when: Surveyed 1933 (Fritz Frank); excavated 1938–1940
discovery.who: Fritz Frank (identification); Nelson Glueck (three seasons, American Schools of Oriental Research)
discovery.where: Low mudbrick mound c. 500 m north of the Gulf of Aqaba shore, between modern Eilat and Aqaba (Jordanian side)

sites.location: In situ, Aqaba region, Jordan

physical.material: Mudbrick (casemate walls)

overview: Tell el-Kheleifeh is a low mudbrick mound about 500 m inland from the northern tip of the Gulf of Aqaba, about halfway between Eilat and Aqaba. Fritz Frank surveyed it in 1933 and identified it with biblical Ezion-geber. Nelson Glueck accepted that identification and excavated three seasons in 1938–1940. He announced it as Solomon's port and a great copper smelter.

Glueck never published a technical final report. Gary Pratico went back to his records and pottery (BASOR 259, 1985). He found two main building phases, a casemate fortress and then a fortified settlement, and pottery from the 8th to 6th centuries BCE with a later postscript. On that evidence nothing at the site belongs to the 10th century.

Glueck returned to the site's interpretation in 'Ezion-Geber' (Biblical Archaeologist 28, 1965); that article's text is not quoted here. In January 2026 Ben-Ami, Weiss, Erickson-Gini and Boaretto (Levant 58) paired Kheleifeh with the 'En Hazeva fortress at the Arabah's northern outlet. They dated 'En Hazeva by radiocarbon to the first half of the 8th century BCE, before Assyrian dominance, and attributed both forts to the northern Kingdom of Israel.
evidence: A casemate fortress, later expanded into a fortified settlement (Pratico 1985).
Pottery horizons from the 8th to the 6th centuries BCE; no securely 10th-century assemblage (Pratico 1985).
The site stands about 500 m from the present shoreline. No harbour installations are reported in the published abstracts.
Glueck's 'smelter' reading of the main building is not supported by Pratico's 1985 reappraisal of the excavation records, which assigns the pottery to the 8th–6th centuries BCE.
'En Hazeva, the matching fortress at the Arabah's other outlet, is radiocarbon-dated to the first half of the 8th century BCE (Ben-Ami et al. 2026).
questions: Is Tell el-Kheleifeh Ezion-geber at all? Frank (1933) and Glueck (BASOR 71, 1938; BASOR 75, 1939; BASOR 79, 1940) identified it as Ezion-geber, and Glueck's dating followed from that identification. Pratico (1985) says the identification 'is both an archaeological and an historical problem'. His pottery gives 8th–6th centuries BCE, while 1 Kings 9:26 places Solomon's fleet at Ezion-geber in the 10th. Either Solomon's Ezion-geber lies elsewhere, or it left no remains at this mound.

Who built the fortress? Ben-Ami et al. (Levant 2026) argue the 8th-century date of 'En Hazeva and the scale of both forts point to the northern Kingdom of Israel, before Assyrian hegemony. An 8th-century date also overlaps Judah's Uzziah/Azariah, who 'built Elath and restored it to Judah' (2 Kgs 14:22). That reading of the text is mine; the Levant abstract does not discuss it.

Glueck's 5 periods from the 10th to 5th century (BASOR 1938–40) against Pratico's two phases from the 8th to 6th century (BASOR 1985). The difference comes from Glueck fitting the pottery to the biblical date, which Pratico sets aside.

biblical.tie: 'King Solomon made a fleet of ships in Ezion-geber, which is beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom.' Pratico's re-study of Kheleifeh found no 10th-century occupation, so the mound does not show Solomon's port.
Jehoshaphat's ships 'were broken at Ezion-geber' (9th century BCE). Pratico's 8th-century start is also later than this.
Azariah builds Elath (8th century), and later Edom takes it. This is the period in which the Kheleifeh fortress was actually standing (Pratico; Ben-Ami et al.).
Ezion-geber as a wilderness station. The mound has no remains of that period.

sites.name: Galilee Boat (Jesus Boat)
sites.subtitle: Wooden hull of a Lake Kinneret boat recovered from the shore mud · Early Roman period
sites.date: Roughly 2,000 years old (Cohen 2005); the report's radiocarbon range was not confirmed in the sources cited here
sites.date_basis: The excavation report includes a radiocarbon study (I. Carmi, 'Radiocarbon Dating of the Boat', in Wachsmann et al., 'Atiqot [ES] 19, 1990, pp. 127-128). Its figures, and any pottery or construction-typology arguments in that report, have not been reviewed for this entry and are not repeated here. The IAA conservation report states only that the boat was found 'after about 2000 years' (Cohen, 'Atiqot 50, 2005).

discovery.when: 1986 (exposed by the drop in lake level; excavated the same year)
discovery.who: Excavation directed by Shelley Wachsmann with Kurt Raveh for the Israel Department of Antiquities and Museums; conservation by Orna Cohen
discovery.where: NW shore of the Sea of Galilee, about 500 m south of Kibbutz Ginnosar

sites.location: Yigal Allon Centre ('Man in the Galilee Museum'), Kibbutz Ginnosar, in a purpose-built exhibition hall with environmental control (Cohen 2005)

physical.material: Wood of twelve plant genera; 105 of 113 strakes cedar (Cedrus), one pine; 45 of 60 frames unworked oak branches; also carob, redbud, hawthorn, laurel, Atlantic pistachio, plane, sycamore fig, willow, Christ-thorn; iron nails and staples; mortise-and-tenon joined planking

overview: In 1986, with the lake level low, the hull of an ancient boat was exposed in the mud of the Kinneret shore near Kibbutz Ginnosar. The Israel Department of Antiquities and Museums excavated it in a rescue operation directed by Shelley Wachsmann and Kurt Raveh; the excavation report is 'Atiqot (English Series) 19 (1990).

The team kept the hull intact rather than dismantling it, because the tenon joints and the corroded iron nails formed an 'iron-wood continuum' that dismantling would have broken. The boat was moved about 500 m north to Kibbutz Ginnosar and conserved in a pool with a two-step polyethylene glycol treatment (PEG 600, then PEG 4000). Eleven years passed from excavation to the end of conservation, and three more to build its exhibition hall (Cohen 2005).

It is a working boat with a long life: many repairs, timbers reused from older boats, some parts removed in antiquity, and finally abandoned on the shore (Cohen 2005; Werker 2005). Nothing on or in it names an owner or links it to any person.
evidence: Hull built of 12 plant genera; strakes 92% cedar, frames 75% unworked oak branches (Werker, 'Atiqot 50, 2005).
Cedar is the one wood not local to the lake; it was brought from further north (Werker 2005).
Several timbers are repairs or reused from older boats; some parts were removed in antiquity (Cohen 2005).
Iron nails and staples survive, corroded into the wood (Cohen & Roman 1990; Cohen 2005).
The boat was found abandoned on the shore, not wrecked in deep water (Cohen 2005).
No inscription, no personal objects tied to an owner are reported in the sources read.
questions: Exact date: the 1990 report contains a radiocarbon study (Carmi 1990); the individual C-14 determinations and any supporting pottery evidence are not accessible for this entry, so no narrower date is asserted here.

Original vs. repair timbers: Werker (2005) states it is 'difficult to decide, based on anatomical structure, which of the timbers differing from the main scheme of conifer/oak wood was originally used ... and which was added later as a replacement' - the boat's building history is only partly recoverable.

Link to the Gospels: Wachsmann (The Sea of Galilee Boat, 1995, ch. 'Galilean Seafaring in the Gospels') compares the hull with Gospel boat scenes; the boat itself carries no evidence connecting it to Jesus or the disciples. The 'Jesus Boat' name is a media label (Cohen 2005: 'dubbed the "Jesus Boat" by the media').

biblical.tie: Fishermen on this lake working from boats with hired men (Mark 1:20). The find shows what one lake boat of the period was built of and how it was repaired; it is a type-specimen, not a boat named in the text.
A boat on the lake large enough for Jesus and the disciples, with a stern where Jesus slept 'on the cushion'. The hull size is what makes the comparison; the text gives no dimensions.
Fishing from boats near the shore of the lake; same setting and vessel class, nothing more specific.

sites.name: Gallio Inscription, Delphi
sites.subtitle: Fragmentary Greek letter of the emperor Claudius naming the proconsul Gallio · 52 CE
sites.date: Between the end of 51 / beginning of 52 CE and 1 August 52 CE (Claudius' 26th imperial acclamation)
sites.date_basis: Line 2 gives Claudius as acclaimed imperator for the 26th time (numeral KS). He is already 'imperator XXVII' on the Aqua Claudia arch dedicated 1 August 52 (CIL VI 1256), so the letter falls before that; Deissmann (1912, App. I pp. 248-250), using data compiled by H. Dessau, puts it 'between (the end of 51 or more probably) the beginning of 52 and 1 August 52'. The tribunician-power numeral (12th) is restored, not read.

discovery.when: Fragments recovered in the French excavations at Delphi before 1905; first published by Émile Bourguet in 1905; more fragments identified later (Deissmann 1912 reports three 'new' fragments, Delphi nos. 728, 500 and 2311)
discovery.who: École française d'Athènes excavations; edited by É. Bourguet (1905), A. Plassart (1970)
discovery.where: Sanctuary of Apollo, Delphi; H. Pomtow held that it was set on an outer wall of the south side of the temple of Apollo

sites.location: Delphi Archaeological Museum; the four 'old' fragments bear Delphi collection numbers 3883, 2178, 2271 (old no. 59), 4001 (Deissmann 1912, App. I p. 244)

physical.material: Whitish-grey limestone from the Hagios Elias quarries near Delphi
physical.dimensions: Letter height 18-20 mm; original line length estimated at c. 1.40 m (Deissmann 1912)

overview: A letter of the emperor Claudius to Delphi (or, on another reading, to Gallio's successor), cut on limestone and set up at the sanctuary of Apollo. It survives as a set of fragments; Plassart's 1970 edition (Fouilles de Delphes III.4, no. 286) combines nine of them, and Oliver (Hesperia 1971) printed a revised text.

The prescript gives Claudius' titles including his 26th acclamation as imperator. The body refers to what 'L. Junius Gallio, my friend and proconsul' reported, and, on Plassart's reading of line 5, concerns Delphi's depopulation: Claudius wants new, well-born settlers invited to keep up the city.

Gallio is the Roman governor before whom the Jews of Corinth brought Paul (Acts 18:12-17). Because Achaia's proconsuls normally served one year, the letter's date pins Gallio's term to 51/52 or 52/53 and gives the one external fixed point in the chronology of Paul's Corinthian stay.

text.quote: Tiberius Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus ... acclaimed imperator for the 26th time, father of the fatherland ... as Lucius Junius Gallio, my friend and proconsul [of Achaia, wrote] ...
text.translation: Literal translation (this encyclopedia) of the Greek of lines 1-2 and 5-6 as printed by A. Deissmann, St. Paul (Eng. tr. 1912), Appendix I p. 246 (names, 'my friend' and 'proconsul' partly restored; 'of Achaia' wholly restored)

evidence: The numeral 26 for Claudius' imperial acclamations is legible; Deissmann calls it 'above all doubt' (1912, p. 248).
Gallio's name survives as Γαλλίων with [Ἰού]νιος partly restored; φ[ίλος] and [ἀνθύπ]ατος are partly restored; the province name 'Achaia' is a restoration.
The addressee's name in the prescript is lost.
Four 'old' fragments (Delphi 3883, 2178, 2271, 4001) plus further fragments; Plassart's 1970 edition uses nine.
Letter height 18-20 mm; limestone from the local Hagios Elias quarries.
Seneca, Ep. Mor. 104.1: Gallio, taking a fever in Achaia, took ship at once, saying the illness was of the place, not the body (quoted in a footnote by Deissmann 1912, App. I).
questions: Who received the letter: A. Plassart (FD III.4, 1970) divides line 17 so it contains a second-person singular pronoun and concludes the recipient was an individual, probably Gallio's successor as proconsul. J. H. Oliver (Hesperia 40, 1971, 239-240) rejects this because the letters can be the end of a verb and because Gallio is still called proconsul in the text; he reads the recipient as a community, Delphi or the Amphictyonic Council.

Imperial titles in line 1: Deissmann (1912) restored 'pontifex maximus' (ἀρχιερεὺς μέγιστος), making a 71-letter line; Plassart (1970) omitted it; Oliver (1971) accepts the omission, citing a Claudian letter from Miletus (Milet III no. 156) that also lacks the title.

Start of Gallio's year: Deissmann (1912, pp. 252-255) argues proconsuls took office in early summer and puts Gallio's entry around mid-summer 51, giving Paul's arrival at Corinth in early 50; this rests on the one-year-term rule and the acclamation range, not on a date stated in the inscription. If the letter was written after Gallio's successor arrived (Plassart's reading), the term shifts; the inscription alone does not decide between 51/52 and 52/53.

Whether the 'new' fragments belong to the same letter: Pomtow (in Deissmann 1912, p. 243) held they were cut by the same mason but belonged to another rescript, on line spacing and letter height; Deissmann left it open; Plassart (1970) included them.

biblical.tie: 'When Gallio was proconsul (ἀνθυπατεύοντος) of Achaia' the Jews brought Paul before the tribunal at Corinth. The inscription attests a Gallio holding the proconsulship in Claudius' 26th acclamation. It says nothing about Paul, Corinth or the Jews.
Paul stayed 18 months in Corinth; combining this with Gallio's dated term is the basis of the 50-51/52 CE reconstruction. That combination is an inference, not a statement in the stone.
Aquila and Priscilla came from Italy 'because Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome' - the same emperor who issued this letter.

sites.name: Gezer Calendar
sites.subtitle: Inscribed limestone tablet listing the farming year · Gezer · Iron Age (date by script only)
sites.date: Iron Age; late 10th or early 9th century BCE is the usual palaeographic date. Macalister, the excavator, dated it to the 6th century BCE.
sites.date_basis: Letter shapes only. Macalister (1912, II p. 24) found it in 'Fourth Semitic debris' in trench 8 with associated pottery he calls 'unfortunately scanty'; he dated it by that pottery to the 6th century BCE, while the palaeographers he cites put it two centuries earlier. No independent stratigraphic or radiocarbon date exists for the tablet itself.

discovery.who: R. A. Stewart Macalister (Palestine Exploration Fund excavation)
discovery.where: Tell Gezer, trench 8, northern end, in 'Fourth Semitic debris'

sites.location: Istanbul Archaeology Museums (Gezer lay in Ottoman territory in 1908)

physical.material: Limestone tablet (not a potsherd), lower part lost along an oblique break through a square peg-hole
physical.dimensions: Macalister gives the height as 4¼ in (about 11 cm); his width and thickness figures do not come through legibly in the scan used
physical.script: Early alphabetic linear script: Phoenician or early Hebrew, which is disputed (see questions)
physical.language: Northwest Semitic: Hebrew or Phoenician, which is disputed

overview: A small limestone tablet found in 1908 during R. A. S. Macalister's excavation of Gezer for the Palestine Exploration Fund. According to Macalister's final report, it came from the northern end of trench 8, in debris of his 'Fourth Semitic' period, with little datable material around it. The inscription is scratched into the stone. It has seven lines of writing, plus the remains of an eighth line written vertically and cut off at the break. The back is plain, and the left edge carries a diagonal fret pattern. A peg-hole suggests it was fixed to a wall.

The text lists farming tasks in order, each tied to one month or two: ingathering, sowing, late sowing, the flax harvest, the barley harvest, the harvest of all the rest (or 'harvest and measuring'), pruning or vine-tending, and summer fruit. Read with the 'two months' forms, the list covers twelve months. The vertical line at the edge is usually read as a personal name beginning 'Abi-', and some restore it as 'Abiyah'.

Right after the find, Lidzbarski, Gray, Pilcher, Ronzevalle, Dalman, Vincent, Marti and Cook each published competing readings in the Palestine Exploration Fund Quarterly Statement and the Revue Biblique. Macalister collected them in 1912. The main disagreement was whether a repeated sign was the conjunction 'and' or a dual ending meaning 'two months'. Later work split over whether the script and language are Hebrew or Phoenician.

text.quote: (1) Month of the fruit-harvest—Month of (2) the sowing—Month of the after-grass— (3) Month of the flax-harvest— (4) Month of the barley-harvest— (5) Month of the harvest of all [the rest]— (6) Month of the pruning of vine-plants— (7) Month of the fig-harvest—
text.translation: M. Lidzbarski's rendering as printed in R. A. S. Macalister, The Excavation of Gezer 1902-1905 and 1907-1909 (London: PEF / John Murray, 1912), vol. II p. 25. On pp. 25-26 Macalister also prints Vincent's alternative: '(1) Two months, late crops—Two months, (2) sowing—Two months, spring crops— (3) One month, cutting of flax— (4) One month, harvest of barley— (5) One month, all the harvest— (6) Two months, fruits [vines]— (7) One month, summer fruits'.

evidence: Material: limestone tablet with the text scratched in. It is not an ostracon.
Seven horizontal lines survive, plus the start of a vertical eighth line interrupted by the fracture (Macalister 1912, II p. 24).
The lower part of the tablet is lost along an oblique break through a square peg-hole. A second hole on the back connects to it.
The back is plain except for one or two tool marks. The left edge has a diagonal fret of about five or six lines to the inch.
Findspot: trench 8, north end, 'Fourth Semitic debris', with scanty associated pottery (Macalister 1912, II p. 24). This is not a closed, well-stratified context.
Farming vocabulary on the tablet: ingathering (ʾsp), sowing (zrʿ), late sowing (lqš), flax (pšt), barley (śʿrm), harvest (qṣr), pruning (zmr), summer fruit (qṣ).

Macalister reports that within a year of the find, opinion on its date was split between the 8th century and earlier (Lidzbarski, Gray and Ronzevalle for the 8th; Vincent and Marti otherwise). Macalister himself put it in the 6th century BCE.
questions: Script and language. W. F. Albright (1943, as quoted by Rollston) called it 'perfect classical Hebrew'. C. Rollston (Biblical Archaeology Review, May/June 2012) argues that 'there is no lexeme or linguistic feature in the Gezer Calendar that can be considered distinctively Hebrew' and that the script is Phoenician, citing J. Naveh's judgment that 'no specifically Hebrew characters can be distinguished.' A. Koller (JNES 72, 2013) works from the Hebrew lexicon, reading mʿṣd / ʿṣd as the Hebrew term for the flax-harvesting tool and task. D. Sivan (IEJ 48, 1998) sets out the Northwest Semitic linguistic features. The disputed evidence is a handful of word forms and letter shapes. No single feature settles it.

'And' or 'two months'. Lidzbarski and Gray (PEFQS 1909) read a recurring sign after 'month' as the conjunction w- ('a month and ingathering'). Vincent (Revue Biblique 1909) read it as a dual or suffix ending, giving 'two months'. His reading turns eight items into twelve months. Ronzevalle reached twelve months another way and argued the text is a rotation of work, not a calendar (all summarized by Macalister 1912, II pp. 25-26).

Date. Macalister (1912) dated it to the 6th century BCE from associated pottery. The palaeographers he reports put it about two centuries earlier. Today's late 10th or early 9th century BCE date rests entirely on letter shapes, because the findspot does not fix it. Whether it belongs to Solomon's Gezer (1 Kgs 9:15-17) therefore depends on the palaeographic sequence, not on stratigraphy.

Purpose. Scholars have proposed a school exercise, a tax or administrative schedule (Ronzevalle, via Macalister 1912), or a farmer's mnemonic. The tablet itself says nothing about its purpose. The peg-hole suggests it was displayed or hung up, and that is the only physical clue.

biblical.tie: The first item is ʾsp, 'ingathering'. The same root names the Feast of Ingathering (ḥag hāʾāsip), which the text places 'at the end of the year' or 'at the turn of the year'. The two sources share the word and a year that turns at the autumn harvest.

The tablet's 'barley harvest' (qṣr śʿrm) uses the same two words as 'the beginning of barley harvest' in these verses. On the tablet it comes before the harvest of everything else, which matches Ruth's barley-then-wheat order.
Rahab hides the spies under 'stalks of flax' (pištê hāʿēṣ) laid on the roof. The tablet has a month for flax (pšt), which confirms flax was a scheduled crop in the region's farming year.
Gezer is named as a city Solomon rebuilt. The tablet comes from Gezer, but its tie to Solomon's reign is only as good as the palaeographic date, because its findspot does not date it.

corrections: The old entry called it a 'limestone ostracon'. It is a limestone tablet. An ostracon is a potsherd or flake used as a writing surface, and Macalister describes a shaped tablet with a peg-hole (1912, II p. 24).

The old entry called it 'the earliest known example of an Ancient Hebrew inscription' as settled fact. Whether it is Hebrew at all is disputed (Rollston 2012, citing Naveh, argues Phoenician), and Macalister's own first report dated it to the 6th century BCE.

The old entry dated it to 'c. 950 BCE' without qualification. The only basis for any 10th-century date is palaeography, because the findspot was 'Fourth Semitic debris' with scanty associated pottery (Macalister 1912, II p. 24).

The old entry linked it to 1 Kings 4:7 (Solomon's twelve district officers, each supplying one month's provisions). The tablet names no king, district, official or tax. The link is an interpretation the object does not show.

The old entry listed Numbers 13 and 1 Chronicles 27. Nothing in the text corresponds to either. The real verbal ties are ʾsp in Exod 23:16 and 34:22, barley harvest in Ruth 2:23, and flax in Josh 2:6.
The old entry described it as showing 'administrative organization'. The text is a bare list of farming tasks by month and says nothing about administration.

sites.name: Gezer Six-Chambered Gate
sites.subtitle: Iron Age city gate, Field III, Tel Gezer · Stratum 8/VIII
sites.date: Built with Gezer Stratum 8 (Tandy numbering) / VIII (HUC numbering); 14C model for Stratum 8 construction: 998-957 BCE (68.3%), 1023-942 BCE (95.4%). The gate itself has not been radiocarbon-dated.
sites.date_basis: Stratigraphy and ceramics (Dever's HUC excavations 1967-1971, 1984, 1990) plus a Bayesian 14C model on short-lived samples from the administrative building adjoining the gate (Webster et al. 2023). Finkelstein & Piasetzky (2024) contest the reliability of that dataset.

discovery.when: First exposed 1902-1909 (misidentified); recognised as a gate 1958 (on paper); cleared 1967-1971
discovery.who: R. A. S. Macalister (Palestine Exploration Fund) exposed half of it and called it a 'Maccabaean castle'; Yigael Yadin identified it from Macalister's plan (1958); William G. Dever and the HUC-JIR/Harvard Semitic Museum expedition excavated it
discovery.where: South side of Tel Gezer (Field III), Israel

sites.location: In situ, Tel Gezer National Park, Israel

physical.material: Stone masonry; ashlar tower recorded beside it (Dever 1985 plan)

overview: A monumental city gate on the south side of Tel Gezer with three chambers on each side of a central passage, tied into a casemate wall. Macalister exposed half of it in 1902-1909 and published it as the 'Maccabaean castle' (Excavation of Gezer I, plan p. 217). In 1958 Yigael Yadin, reading Macalister's plan without seeing the buried remains, argued that it was half of an Iron Age gate matching gates he knew at Hazor (Stratum X) and Megiddo (Stratum VA/IVB), and tied all three to 1 Kings 9:15.

The Hebrew Union College / Harvard Semitic Museum excavations under William G. Dever cleared the structure in 1967-1971 and confirmed the gate. Dever later excavated 'Palace 10,000', a large administrative complex immediately west of the gate and in use with it.

Renewed work by the Tandy Institute (Ortiz and Wolff, 2006-2017) produced the first 14C series for the Iron Age city. The gate's own stones were not sampled; the dates come from the adjacent administrative building of the same stratum.
evidence: Plan: central passage flanked by three chambers per side (a 'four-entryway' gate in Dever's wording), joined to a casemate wall.
Macalister's volume I lists a 'Plan of the Maccabaean castle' and 'Eastern jamb of the gate of the Maccabaean castle' (figs. at pp. 217-218): he dug the structure and misdated it.

Dever's stratigraphic grounds (JJAR 1, 2021, p. 107): Stratum VIII lies above a late Philistine Decorated Ware stage and a destruction; hand burnish only, no wheel burnish; a heavy destruction after the third street level of VIII; 9th-8th c. administrative structures overlie it.
Webster et al. 2023: Stratum 8 built 998-957 BCE (68.3% hpd) and destroyed 969-940 BCE (68.3%); the authors state the model 'rule[s] out a 9th century BC date' for the stratum.
The dated samples are from the administrative building next to the gate, not from the gate foundations.
questions: Date of the gate: Dever (JJAR 1, 2021) assigns it to the 10th c. BCE on stratigraphy (Stratum VIII above late Philistine ware, hand-burnish-only ceramics, destruction he attributes to Shoshenq I) and cites the new 14C dates; Webster, Wolff and Ortiz (PLOS ONE 2023; JEMAHS 12.4, 2024) model Stratum 8 construction at 998-957 BCE. Finkelstein and Piasetzky ('The Gezer Discrepancy', JEMAHS 12.4, 2024) object that the contexts' stratigraphic attribution is not secure and that the Gezer dates disagree with other Shephelah 14C sequences.

Whether the gate belongs to the same plan as Hazor and Megiddo: Yadin (IEJ 8, 1958) argued one royal design; at Megiddo, Finkelstein et al. (Tel Aviv 46, 2019) place six-chambered Gate 2156 in Strata VA-IVB, which they date to the Omride 9th century, so the three gates would not be contemporary on their reading. At Gezer the 14C model (Webster et al. 2023) puts the stratum in the early 10th century.
Sampling gap: no sample comes from the gate's construction fill; the link rests on the gate and Palace 10,000 being in the same stratum (Dever 2021; Webster et al. 2023).

biblical.tie: The text names Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer among Solomon's building works and says Pharaoh had taken and burned Gezer and given it to his daughter, Solomon's wife, after which Solomon rebuilt it. The find is a gate in the stratum the excavators date to the early 10th c.; no inscription names a builder. Reading the gate as Solomon's is an inference from date and plan.

Dever (2021) links the destruction beneath Stratum VIII to an Egyptian campaign (he names Siamun); the Tandy team's 14C work is framed against the same verse. This is the excavators' reading, not a written record at the site.

Old entry: 'Dimensions: approximately 15 meters wide'. No measurement is given in a verified source cited here; removed.
Old entry: 'Date c. 1000 BCE' stated as fact. The 14C model for Stratum 8 (not the gate) is 998-957 BCE at 68.3%, and it is contested (Finkelstein & Piasetzky 2024).
Old entry cites 1 Kings 4:19 and 2 Chronicles 8:1 as connections; neither names Gezer. The relevant text is 1 Kgs 9:15-17.
Old summary box claim 'Evidence of Solomonic building program' removed as a fact: it is an interpretation, now stated as a reading in `biblical`.

updates.what: JEMAHS 12.4 published a forum on the Gezer 14C dates: summary by Webster, Wolff and Ortiz, a critique by Finkelstein & Piasetzky ('The Gezer Discrepancy'), and responses by Dever, A. Mazar, Ben-Yosef, Garfinkel, Maeir, Levy and Ben-Dor Evian, with the authors' closing remarks.

sites.name: Gezer Water System
sites.subtitle: Rock-cut stepped tunnel to a spring cave · Middle Bronze Age
sites.date: Middle Bronze Age IIB, c. 1750-1650 BCE for its construction per the 2010-2018 excavators; Macalister (1912) had already dated it to c. 2000 BCE 'at the latest'. Not Solomonic.
sites.date_basis: Pottery in the fill: the 2015 season found Late Bronze pottery above Middle Bronze pottery of 1800-1500 BCE (Warner, reported by BAS 2015); the final publication (Tsuk et al., 2025) dates the tunnel to MB IIB. Macalister reasoned from 'Third Semitic' (Late Bronze) silt closing the entrance plus wear on the steps.

discovery.when: 1907-1909 (cleared); re-excavated 2010-2018
discovery.who: R. A. S. Macalister (PEF); re-excavated by Dan Warner, Eli Yannai and Tsvika Tsuk with Dennis Cole and Jim Parker (NOBTS with the Israel Nature and Parks Authority and IAA)
discovery.where: Trench 29, inside the city near the 'First Semitic Palace' court, Tel Gezer

sites.location: In situ, Tel Gezer National Park, Israel

physical.material: Cut into bedrock limestone
physical.dimensions: Macalister: entrance pit 34 ft 6 in long; entrance arch 23 ft high x 12 ft 10 in wide; tunnel slopes at 38-39 degrees from vertical; water level 94 ft 6 in vertically below rock surface; terminal natural cave c. 80 x 28 ft. BAS (2015) summary: shaft c. 138 ft long at 38 degrees.

overview: A keyhole-shaped shaft cut into the bedrock opens into a broad, barrel-vaulted stepped tunnel that descends steeply to a natural cave holding groundwater. Macalister cleared it over more than a month and published it as the 'Water-passage' (Excavation of Gezer I, 1912, pp. 256-265).

Macalister found only a few stray objects in the silt, noted flint-tool marks on the upper walls, and found no inscription. From the Late Bronze ('Third Semitic') material that closed the entrance and the worn state of the steps, he dated the cutting to about 2000 BCE at the latest and attributed it to the Canaanite city.

The tunnel was re-exposed and dug deeper in 2010-2018. The excavators date it to Middle Bronze IIB (c. 1750-1650 BCE), state that there was no exit from the system, and report finds they read as cultic and calendrical; their final report is The Canaanite Water System at Gezer (2025).
evidence: Keyhole-shaped entrance pit, 34 ft 6 in long, 7 ft 5 in wide at north end and 14 ft 6 in at south; steps cut in its floor (Macalister I, p. 258).
Tunnel entrance 'an imposing archway, 23' high and 12' 10" broad'; steps across the full width; barrel-vaulted roof (Macalister I, p. 259).
Water stood 94 ft 6 in vertically below the rock surface, about 130 ft below the ground surface at the time of excavation; 200 gallons drawn off did not lower it (Macalister I, p. 261).
The tunnel ends in a natural cave c. 80 x 28 ft; Macalister found no second opening (pp. 261-262).
'No trace of an inscription of any sort was observed' (Macalister I, p. 262).
2015 season: pottery showed 'a clear transition from Late Bronze Age pottery to Middle Bronze Age pottery dating between 1800 and 1500 B.C.' (Warner, quoted by BAS).
questions: Date: Macalister (1912) placed it c. 2000 BCE at the latest because Late Bronze silt sealed it and the steps were heavily worn; Dever (as reported by BAS 2015) had suggested Late Bronze or Iron Age; Warner, Yannai and Tsuk (2010-2018 excavations; final report 2025) date it to MB IIB from the ceramic sequence in the fill. The fill dates the tunnel's disuse; the construction date is inferred from what lies beneath it.

Purpose: Macalister thought it was begun as a siege exit and struck the spring by accident, because a vertical well would have been shorter by about 3 to 5; Père Vincent (in Macalister's note) held it was cut for water from the start. The 2025 report adds a cultic/calendrical reading of finds (reported by Pathway, Oct 2025); the finds themselves have not been examined for this entry.

biblical.tie: Names Gezer among Solomon's works. On every date proposed by the excavators (c. 2000 BCE; MB IIB), the water system predates Solomon by many centuries and is not part of that building work.
The 2025 report's authors connect finds they read as solar/lunar cultic to the Aijalon Valley episode (quoted in Pathway, 2025). This is their reading; no text at the site names it.

Press coverage of the book, quoting Parker on the MB IIB date and the Josh 10 connection.

sites.name: Hazor Six-Chambered Gate
sites.subtitle: Iron Age gate and casemate wall, upper city of Tel Hazor · Stratum X
sites.date: Hazor Stratum X. Excavators (Yadin; Ben-Tor) date it to the 10th c. BCE; Finkelstein dates Stratum X to the 9th c. BCE (Omride). No radiocarbon date for the gate is cited in the sources here.
sites.date_basis: Stratigraphy and pottery, and comparison with Megiddo VA-IVB and Gezer VIII. Ben-Tor & Ben-Ami (IEJ 48, 1998) and Ben-Tor (BASOR 317, 2000; NEA 76, 2013) argue 10th c.; Finkelstein (BASOR 314, 1999; Tel Aviv 27, 2000) argues a low (9th c.) date.

discovery.when: 1957-1958 (third and fourth seasons)
discovery.who: Yigael Yadin, James A. de Rothschild Expedition (Hebrew University)
discovery.where: Upper city (acropolis) of Tel Hazor (Tell el-Qedah), Upper Galilee, Israel

sites.location: In situ, Tel Hazor National Park, Israel

physical.material: Stone masonry

overview: A city gate with three chambers on each side of the passage, set in a casemate wall around the western part of Hazor's upper city. Yigael Yadin exposed it in the 1957-1958 seasons of the James A. de Rothschild Expedition; the final report for those seasons is Hazor III-IV (1989).

Yadin assigned the gate and casemate wall to Stratum X and, noticing the same plan at Megiddo and (from Macalister's plan) Gezer, tied the three to the list in 1 Kings 9:15 (IEJ 8, 1958). That comparison is the origin of the 'Solomonic gates' label.
Whether Stratum X is 10th-century (Solomon) or 9th-century (Omrides) has been argued in print since 1999 between Finkelstein and the Hazor excavators Ben-Tor and Ben-Ami.
evidence: Six-chamber plan (three chambers each side of the passage) joined to a casemate wall (Yadin; summarised by Madain Project from the excavation reports).
Stratum X: the stratum Yadin gave the gate; Dever (JJAR 1, 2021, n. 33) cites Zarzecki-Peleg 1997 and Ben-Tor & Ben-Ami 1998 for its 10th-c. date.
No inscription or datable object naming a builder is associated with the gate in any source checked.
questions: Date of Stratum X: Ben-Tor and Ben-Ami ('Hazor and the Archaeology of the Tenth Century B.C.E.', IEJ 48, 1998) and Ben-Tor (BASOR 317, 2000; NEA 76.2, 2013) keep it in the 10th c.; Finkelstein ('Hazor and the North in the Iron Age: A Low Chronology Perspective', BASOR 314, 1999; Tel Aviv 27, 2000) lowers it to the 9th c. The ceramic arguments in these papers have not been reviewed for this entry; only titles, venues and the positions they take were verified.

Link to Megiddo: Finkelstein et al. (Tel Aviv 46, 2019) date Megiddo's six-chambered Gate 2156 to Strata VA-IVB in the Omride period; if the Hazor and Megiddo gates are one design, the Megiddo date bears directly on Hazor's.

Sameness of the three gates: Yadin (1958) described the Gezer gate as matching Hazor and Megiddo; Dever (2021) reports this as 'almost identical in plan'. A measured side-by-side comparison has not been located for this entry.

biblical.tie: Lists 'Hazor, and Megiddo, and Gezer' among Solomon's building works. The find is a fortification of the plan Yadin linked to that verse; its builder is not named on site. The Solomonic attribution depends on Stratum X being 10th-century.
Records Tiglath-pileser III taking Hazor. Not directly tied to the gate in any source verified here.

sites.name: Hazor Destruction Layer
sites.subtitle: Fiery end of the largest Late Bronze Age city in Canaan · 13th century BCE
sites.date: 13th century BCE. The precise date within the century is disputed; Yadin put it c. 1230 BCE. Bechar et al. (2021) offer two radiocarbon-based scenarios.
sites.date_basis: Pottery and imported Aegean-type and Egyptian objects in the burned levels, and a radiocarbon series from the renewed excavations (Bechar, Ben-Tor, Wachtel, Ben-Tor et al., Ägypten und Levante 31, 2021). No text found at the site dates the destruction.

discovery.when: 1955-1958 and 1968 (Yadin); 1990-present (Selz Foundation Hazor Excavations in Memory of Yigael Yadin); 2023-present (renewed work in the lower city)
discovery.who: Yigael Yadin (Hebrew University); Amnon Ben-Tor, later Shlomit Bechar and Igor Kreimerman (Selz excavations); Univ. of Haifa lower-city team
discovery.where: Tel Hazor (Tell el-Qedah), north of the Sea of Galilee, Upper Galilee, Israel

sites.location: In situ, Tel Hazor National Park, Israel

physical.material: Burned mudbrick and basalt architecture, ash layers, smashed and mutilated statuary
physical.dimensions: Upper city (acropolis) plus lower city: about 200 acres (≈80 ha) in all, per the excavation project

overview: Hazor is the largest Bronze Age tell in the southern Levant. It has a high upper city and a vast enclosed lower city. Yigael Yadin excavated it in 1955-1958 and 1968. Amnon Ben-Tor renewed the work in 1990 as the Selz Foundation Hazor Excavations in Memory of Yigael Yadin, which continues today, and new teams re-opened the lower city in 2023.

The last Canaanite city, of the 13th century BCE, ended in a fire. J. Ebeling describes it as 'so intense that it cracked the basalt architectural elements' and says it left ash up to about three feet deep. It destroyed the ceremonial palace (Building 7050) on the acropolis and the gate shrine. Statues of Canaanite and Egyptian rulers and deities were found deliberately mutilated.

Who burned Hazor is argued from those remains. Yadin and Ben-Tor argue for the Israelites of Joshua 11. S. Zuckerman argues for an internal social and ideological crisis. Egyptian and Sea Peoples scenarios have also been weighed. Bechar et al. (2021) combined stratigraphy, radiocarbon and imported objects and proposed two possible scenarios for the date and process of the end.
evidence: A destruction by fire at the end of the Late Bronze Age affected both the upper and lower cities (Selz excavation project; Ebeling 2003).
The fire was hot enough to crack basalt architectural elements, and ash layers reach about three feet (Ebeling 2003).
Statues of Canaanite and Egyptian rulers and deities were deliberately mutilated (Ebeling 2003, summarizing the Ben-Tor excavations).
The ceremonial palace (Building 7050) on the acropolis burned with its contents in place: bronze statues, ivory, jewellery, seals and a lion-headed rhyton (BAS summary of Ben-Tor 2013).

Radiocarbon from the renewed excavations, together with Aegean-type and Egyptian objects, did not produce a single agreed date. Bechar et al. (2021) present 'two different possible scenarios' for when and how the city ended.

The 2023-present renewed excavation of Area H in the northern lower city found much of that sector uninhabited in the Late Bronze Age. This contradicts the earlier view of a continuously occupied lower city (Shalvi & Bechar, Tel Aviv 52, 2025).
There is no inscription naming a destroyer. Cuneiform fragments from Hazor exist, but none describes the fall.
questions: Who destroyed Hazor? A. Ben-Tor (BAR 39:4, 2013; see Ebeling 2003) argues for the Israelites. The statues of Egyptian kings and Canaanite gods were mutilated, which he says neither Egyptians nor Canaanites would do to their own icons, and Sea Peoples material is absent at Hazor. S. Zuckerman (Journal of Mediterranean Archaeology 20/1, 2007) reads the same destruction as the product of 'social, political, cultural and ideological circumstances' inside a city already in decline, including termination rituals. In both cases the evidence is the pattern of burning and mutilation, and no text names the attacker.

Which century, and which stratum? I. Finkelstein re-interpreted the Late Bronze sequence. Ben-Tor & Zuckerman (BASOR 350, 2008) defended a scheme close to Yadin's against him, using Yadin's published data and the renewed excavations. Bechar et al. (2021) keep two scenarios open for the date and process. How Joshua 11 lines up in time with the burning depends on which scenario holds.

How big was the Late Bronze city? Shalvi & Bechar (2025) found much of the northern lower city empty in the LB, so the size of the city at the moment of destruction is being revised downward in at least that sector.

biblical.tie: 'Hazor beforetime was the head of all those kingdoms… and he burnt Hazor with fire… save Hazor only; that did Joshua burn.' The text says Hazor was burned, and was singled out as burned, and the site has a massive fire ending the Late Bronze city. The text does not give a date, and the site does not name the attacker.

The command to hew down the graven images of the gods. Ben-Tor points to the mutilated statues as the behaviour of an iconoclastic attacker. The mutilation is the finding; its link to these commands is his reading.

'Jabin king of Canaan, that reigned in Hazor', destroyed by Israel. This is a second biblical account of a king of Hazor being overthrown. If both accounts refer to the same 13th-century destruction, only one burning is visible in the Late Bronze strata. How to reconcile Joshua 11 with Judges 4 is an interpretive question the stratigraphy does not answer.
Solomon builds Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer. The Iron Age city with its six-chambered gate and casemate wall (attributed by the project to the 10th century BCE) is built over the burned Canaanite city.
Tiglath-pileser III takes Hazor in 732 BCE. The project reports the destruction of the Iron Age city in that campaign.

corrections: The old entry described a city 'covering approximately 10 hectares'. Hazor's upper and lower cities together cover about 200 acres, roughly 80 ha (excavation project). It is the largest Bronze Age site in the country, not a 10 ha town.

The old entry gave the destruction as 'c. 1200 BCE'. The project and Ebeling place it in the 13th century BCE (Yadin c. 1230 BCE), and Bechar et al. (2021) leave two scenarios open. '1200' is not the excavators' date.

The old entry claimed Hazor is 'the only major Canaanite city in the region that exhibits evidence of such a systematic destruction'. No source consulted makes that claim, and it is not a finding of the excavations.

The old entry listed 'scattered weaponry' as destruction evidence. The reported evidence is intense fire, cracked basalt, deep ash and mutilated statues. No weapon scatter is reported in the sources consulted.

The old entry listed 'a sophisticated water system' among the features of the destroyed Canaanite city. None of the sources consulted describes a water system in the Late Bronze city. Hazor's well-known water shaft belongs to the Iron Age (Israelite) city built over it; that dating has not been re-checked for this entry.

The old entry said the evidence 'confirms violent conquest'. The violence is confirmed. The identity of the attacker is argued from indirect evidence (statue mutilation) and remains disputed (Ben-Tor vs. Zuckerman).
The old entry gave the dig dates as '1955-1958, Yadin' only. Yadin also dug in 1968, and the Selz excavations have run annually since 1990, with renewed lower-city work from 2023.

updates.what: Ebeling & Mazow publish a reconstruction of the cult niche in ceremonial palace Building 7050, the building that burned in the final Canaanite destruction.

Shalvi & Bechar report the first results of the renewed (2023-) lower-city excavations in Area H: much of the northern lower city was uninhabited in the Late Bronze Age, and the Orthostat Temple shows previously unrecognised modifications.
Bechar & Yasur-Landau publish the Middle Bronze I foundation of Hazor (PEQ, online first), revising the city's beginnings rather than its end.

sites.name: The Broad Wall
aka: Israelite wall in the Jewish Quarter
sites.subtitle: Iron Age city wall on Jerusalem's Western Hill · 8th c. BCE
sites.date: 8th century BCE; long assigned to Hezekiah (late 8th c.), but a 2024 radiocarbon programme moves Jerusalem's big 8th-century fortification works earlier, to Uzziah
sites.date_basis: Avigad's excavations placed it in the 8th century BCE (final report ed. Geva 2000, not read by me); it was built over demolished Iron Age houses. The 2024 radiocarbon study (Regev et al., PNAS 121/19) dated fortifications on the City of David's eastern slope and buildings in the Givati Parking Lot, not this wall directly.

discovery.when: Early 1970s
discovery.who: Nahman Avigad, Hebrew University Jewish Quarter excavations (1969-1982)
discovery.where: Jewish Quarter of the Old City, Jerusalem (Western Hill)

sites.location: In situ, Jewish Quarter, Old City of Jerusalem (open-air display below street level)

physical.material: Unworked and roughly worked fieldstones
physical.dimensions: About 7 m thick; c. 65 m exposed length; preserved up to c. 3.3 m high (figures as reported in summaries of the final report)

overview: A stretch of massive Iron Age city wall uncovered by Nahman Avigad in the early 1970s in the Jewish Quarter, on the hill west of the Temple Mount. Its width - about seven metres - earned it the name 'Broad Wall' after Nehemiah 3:8 and 12:38, which mention a 'broad wall' in Jerusalem.

The find showed that by the 8th century BCE the fortified city had spread from the narrow City of David ridge onto the Western Hill. The wall was built across the remains of earlier houses, which were cleared to make room for it; Avigad connected that with Isaiah 22:10, 'the houses have ye broken down to fortify the wall'.

Avigad attributed the wall to Hezekiah's preparations against Assyria (2 Chr 32:5). In 2024 a radiocarbon study of Iron Age Jerusalem argued that the westward spread of the city had begun by the 9th century BCE and that the major 8th-century fortification works it dated belong to the late reign of Uzziah rather than Hezekiah. That study dated other structures; it did not publish dates from the Broad Wall itself.
evidence: Stone wall about 7 m wide, c. 65 m of unbroken length exposed, preserved up to c. 3.3 m high.
Located on the Western Hill (today's Jewish Quarter), west of the Temple Mount - outside the older City of David ridge.
Built over and through earlier domestic structures that were razed along its line (Hebrew University 'Jerusalem Mosaic' text on the Jewish Virtual Library).
Excavated as part of Areas A, W and X-2, published in the Jewish Quarter final report vol. I (Geva ed. 2000).
No inscription; no dated object in the wall itself was published in the sources cited here.

Regev et al. (PNAS 2024), 103 radiocarbon dates from five Jerusalem areas: westward expansion under way by the 9th c. BCE (Building 100, Givati Parking Lot); a new eastern-slope fortification after the mid-8th-century earthquake, attributed to late Uzziah.
questions: Hezekiah or Uzziah? Avigad attributed the wall to Hezekiah's preparations before the 701 BCE Assyrian campaign (as reported in the Hebrew University's Jerusalem Mosaic text); the attribution leans on the late-8th-century context and on the match between the demolished houses and Isa 22:10 / 2 Chr 32:5. Avigad 1983 and the 2000 final report were not available for this entry, so the pottery argument has not been checked against them directly. Regev, Gadot, Uziel, Boaretto et al. (PNAS 121/19, 2024) write that 'the major building project of Jerusalem's 8th-century BC fortifications was previously assigned to King Hezekiah ... based on our chronology, these activities can now be associated with the latter years of King Uzziah' - but their samples come from the City of David and the Givati Parking Lot. The Times of Israel (30 Apr 2024) reported the study as redating 'the wall' to Uzziah; the published paper text does not mention the Broad Wall. Whether the Western Hill wall moves with the eastern-slope wall is not settled by direct dates.
Israel Finkelstein circulated 'Observations on the article Regev et al.' in May 2024 challenging parts of the radiocarbon interpretation (seen as a listing only; not read).

Who lived inside it? Summaries of Avigad's work tie the Western Hill's growth to refugees after Assyria took the northern kingdom (720s BCE). The 2024 dates for 9th-century building on the western side push the start of expansion earlier; the refugee explanation remains an inference about why the city grew, not something the wall itself shows.

biblical.tie: The only verses that use the phrase 'the broad wall' (ha-homah ha-rehavah) - in Nehemiah's time. The modern name comes from here; there is no inscription linking this wall to that name.
'Ye have numbered the houses of Jerusalem, and the houses have ye broken down to fortify the wall.' The wall is built over razed houses - a physical match to the verse's action.

Hezekiah 'built up all the wall that was broken, and raised it up to the towers, and another wall without'. This is the basis for the Hezekiah attribution; the verse does not use the name 'broad wall'.

Uzziah 'built towers in Jerusalem at the corner gate, and at the valley gate' and fortified them - relevant if the 2024 redating of Jerusalem's 8th-century works to Uzziah is extended to this wall (our reading).
