sites.name: Hezekiah Bulla
sites.subtitle: Royal seal impression from the Ophel, Jerusalem · late 8th c. BCE
sites.date: Reign of Hezekiah of Judah (the Hebrew University release gives 727-698 BCE; other chronologies give 716-686 BCE)
sites.date_basis: The inscription names Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah; the refuse dump it came from is dated by its pottery to the time of Hezekiah or shortly after (Hebrew University release, 2 Dec 2015).

discovery.when: Excavated in the 2009 season; identified as Hezekiah's in wet-sifting and announced 2 December 2015
discovery.who: Eilat Mazar's Ophel excavations (Hebrew University Institute of Archaeology); found in sifting by Efrat Greenwald, identified by Reut Ben-Aryeh
discovery.where: Ophel, Area A, south of the Temple Mount, Jerusalem - an Iron Age refuse dump beside the 'Royal Building'

sites.location: Not established from a museum record; no published source confirms where it is kept today.

physical.material: Clay bulla
physical.dimensions: Bulla 13 x 12 mm, 3 mm thick; oval seal impression 9.7 x 8.6 mm, with the mark of the seal-ring's frame around it

overview: A small lump of clay that once sealed a document or container, stamped with the personal seal of King Hezekiah. It came from wet-sifted soil of a refuse dump excavated in 2009 in the Ophel, just south of the Temple Mount, and was recognised as a royal seal impression during sifting; it was announced by the Hebrew University in December 2015 and published in the first volume of the Ophel final reports.

The impression reads, in Old Hebrew, 'Belonging to Hezekiah [son of] Ahaz, king of Judah'. The word 'son' is not written. The centre shows a two-winged sun with its wings turned downward, flanked by two ankh signs.

According to the excavators the dump dates to the time of Hezekiah or shortly after and came from an adjacent 'Royal Building' used for storing foodstuffs. It was the first seal impression of a Judahite or Israelite king recovered in a controlled excavation (as opposed to the antiquities market).

text.quote: lḥzqyhw ʾḥz mlk yhdh - 'Belonging to Hezekiah [son of] Ahaz, king of Judah'
text.translation: English as issued in the Hebrew University release (2 Dec 2015); transliteration as reproduced in secondary listings of Mazar 2015 (the final report chapter itself not read)

evidence: Clay bulla 13 x 12 x 3 mm; oval seal impression 9.7 x 8.6 mm with the frame of the seal ring visible around it (Hebrew University release, 2015).
Legend: 'of Hezekiah (son of) Ahaz, king of Judah'; no word for 'son' is present.
Iconography: two-winged sun with downturned wings, flanked by two ankh (life) symbols.
Findspot: refuse dump in Ophel Area A, dated to Hezekiah's time or shortly after; found in 2009 season material, identified in wet-sifting at Emek Tzurim.
Published in E. Mazar (ed.), The Ophel Excavations to the South of the Temple Mount 2009-2013, Final Reports Vol. I (2015), whose final chapter presents the Hezekiah find.
questions: Hezekiah's regnal dates are themselves disputed from the biblical numbers: 2 Kgs 18:1 puts his accession in the 3rd year of Hoshea of Israel (implying c. 727/726), while 2 Kgs 18:13 puts Sennacherib's invasion (701 BCE on the Assyrian record) in his 14th year (implying c. 715). The Hebrew University release uses 727-698 BCE; others use 716/715-687/686. The bulla confirms the person and title, not the dates.

What the winged-sun motif means. LeMon (Hebrew Bible and Ancient Israel 13, 2024) reads the Hezekiah bulla's winged sun within Judahite royal iconography and uses it to argue that the voice of Psalms 61 and 63 (sheltering under God's wings) is the king's; that is his interpretation of the image, not something written on it.
The wording without 'son' (ben) is unusual but also known from other Hebrew seals; a published parallel list has not been confirmed for this entry.

biblical.tie: Hezekiah is 'son of Ahaz' and king of Judah - exactly the name, patronym and title on the bulla.
The narratives of Hezekiah's reign; the bulla shows a Judahite king of that name using a personal seal in Jerusalem, but records no event.
Lists Hezekiah as king of Judah in Isaiah's time; the 'Isaiah bulla' was found about 3 m away in the same context (see isaiah-bulla).

sites.name: Siloam Tunnel Inscription
sites.subtitle: Hebrew rock inscription from the Gihon-Siloam tunnel · late 8th c. BCE (debated)
sites.date: Undated text; placed c. 700 BCE by the radiometric dates for the tunnel and by letter-forms; other workers argue for earlier (early 8th c.) or much later dates
sites.date_basis: The inscription names no king and no year. Its date is inferred (1) from the tunnel it was cut into: radiocarbon on plant material in the tunnel plaster and U-Th on speleothems (Frumkin, Shimron & Rosenbaum, Nature 2003) point to c. 700 BCE; (2) from Old Hebrew letter-forms; (3) from pottery in fills near the Gihon Spring, which Reich & Shukron (2011) read as pushing completion back to the early 8th century.

discovery.who: A local youth exploring the tunnel (commonly identified as a pupil of Conrad Schick); first published by A. H. Sayce, 1881
discovery.where: Right (east) wall of the tunnel near its southern (Siloam Pool) end, City of David, Jerusalem

sites.location: Istanbul Archaeology Museums (cut out of the tunnel wall in 1890 and taken to the Imperial Ottoman Museum, Constantinople). Inventory number reported in secondary listings as 2195 T; not checked against a museum record.

physical.material: Limestone bedrock of the tunnel wall (now a cut-out, broken slab)
physical.script: Old Hebrew (Paleo-Hebrew), words divided by dots

overview: A six-line Hebrew inscription carved into the wall of the rock-cut water channel that carries the Gihon Spring's water under the City of David to the Siloam Pool. It was noticed in 1880 a few metres in from the tunnel's southern end and published by A. H. Sayce in the Palestine Exploration Fund Quarterly Statement in 1881.

The text is a builders' record, not a royal dedication: it describes the last moments of cutting, when two crews tunnelling toward each other could hear each other's voices through the rock, then broke through 'axe against axe', after which the water flowed 1,200 cubits from the spring to the pool, under 100 cubits of rock. No king, date or god is named.

The inscription was hacked out of the wall in 1890, broke into pieces, was recovered by the Ottoman authorities and taken to Constantinople, where it remains in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums. In September 2025 Turkey's president publicly refused Israel's renewed request for its return.

text.quote: The boring through [is completed]. And this is the story of the boring through: while yet [they plied] the drill, each toward his fellow, and while yet there were three cubits to be bored through, there was heard the voice of one calling unto another ... and the waters flowed from the source to the pool for a thousand and two hundred cubits.
text.translation: G. A. Barton, Archaeology and the Bible (Philadelphia: American Sunday-School Union, 1916; 2nd ed. 1917), Part II, ch. 12, p. 377

evidence: Six lines of Old Hebrew carved on a smoothed patch of the tunnel wall near the Siloam end.

Content: two crews cutting toward each other; 3 cubits left when voices were heard; a 'crevice'/fissure in the rock on the right; breakthrough 'axe against axe'; water flowed 1,200 cubits from spring (motsa) to pool (berekah); 100 cubits of rock overhead (Barton 1917, p. 377).
No king, regnal year, deity or patron is named in the text.
Barton (1917) records the tunnel as 'about 1,700 feet long' after the Parker expedition cleared it (1909-11); the inscription's own figure is 1,200 cubits.
Radiocarbon dates on plant remains in the channel plaster and U-Th dates on speleothems put the tunnel's construction around 700 BCE (Frumkin, Shimron & Rosenbaum 2003).
The stone was cut out of the wall in 1890, breaking it; it has been in Constantinople/Istanbul since (Barton 1917: 'now in the Imperial Ottoman Museum at Constantinople').
questions: Who dug it and when. Frumkin, Shimron & Rosenbaum (Nature 425, 2003) date the tunnel to c. 700 BCE from 14C on organic material in the original plaster and U-Th on stalactites, which fits Hezekiah. Reich & Shukron (Tel Aviv 38, 2011) argue completion was at least several decades earlier, in the early 8th century, from pottery in the fills they excavated beside the Gihon Spring, which would mean the tunnel predates Hezekiah. Finkelstein republished a response on 'The Finds from the Rock-Cut Pool in Jerusalem and the Date of the Siloam Tunnel' (2024 collected essays); the chapter's existence is confirmed, but its argument is not summarized here.

Paleography vs. a Hasmonean date. Rogerson & Davies (Biblical Archaeologist 59, 1996) proposed the tunnel and inscription could be 2nd-century BCE; Hendel (Biblical Archaeologist 59, 1996) and Cahill (1997) replied that the letter-forms are Iron Age Hebrew. The later radiometric dates (2003) are consistent with the Iron Age side.

Is 2 Kings 20:20 describing THIS tunnel? The verse credits Hezekiah with 'a pool, and a conduit' bringing water into the city; 2 Chr 32:30 says he 'stopped the upper watercourse of Gihon, and brought it straight down to the west side of the city'. The tunnel runs from the Gihon to a pool on the west side of the City of David, which matches the description; the inscription itself does not name Hezekiah, so the identification rests on the correspondence, not on the text.

The 2025 Siloam Dam dates (805-795 BCE, Regev et al., PNAS 122/35) show that major Gihon-Siloam waterworks already existed c. 800 BCE; they date the dam, not the tunnel, so they do not settle the tunnel's date either way.

biblical.tie: Credits Hezekiah with making 'a pool, and a conduit' and bringing water into the city; the tunnel is a conduit delivering Gihon water to a pool. The inscription itself names no king.
Hezekiah stops the springs outside the city before the Assyrian siege and brings the Gihon water 'straight down to the west side of the city of David' - the course of this tunnel.

Speaks of gathering 'the waters of the lower pool' and making 'a ditch between the two walls for the water of the old pool' in a siege context; our reading: a general fit with Jerusalem waterworks, not a specific reference to the inscription.

sites.name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre excavations (Sapienza University of Rome, 2022-2025)
sites.subtitle: Excavation beneath the church floor: quarry, cultivated soil, tombs, Roman and Constantinian phases · 2022-2025
sites.date: Sequence from quarrying (Iron Age onward, exploitation 'prolonged in time') through cultivation, Roman, Constantinian (4th century CE) and later phases. The cultivation layer has not yet been radiocarbon-dated.
sites.date_basis: Stratigraphy and finds in the preliminary reports, including 4th-century coins of Constantius II and Valens in Constantinian construction contexts (HA-ESI). Stasolla said in March 2025 that radiocarbon testing of the cultivation evidence 'has not yet been carried out' (Times of Israel).

discovery.when: Excavation campaign May-November 2022 (IAA licence G-20/2022), continued 2023 and 2024, completed inside the church in 2025
discovery.who: Francesca Romana Stasolla, Sapienza University of Rome, as part of the floor-restoration project agreed by the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate, the Custody of the Holy Land and the Armenian Patriarchate
discovery.where: Beneath the floor of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (Anastasis rotunda, aisles, ambulatories, entrance), Old City of Jerusalem

sites.location: In situ (Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem)
overview: From 2022 to 2025 a Sapienza University of Rome team under Francesca Romana Stasolla excavated beneath the floor of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre while the floor was being restored. The project was approved by the three main communities that hold the church. The first season (May-November 2022, IAA licence G-20/2022) opened five areas in the north aisle and the northwest of the Rotunda. The 2023 season worked in the southeast Rotunda, in front of the Aedicule, and in the northeast ambulatory. The 2024 season covered the entrance, the southeast ambulatory and the Franciscan area. The 2025 report states that the excavations inside the church are complete.

The lowest levels are an ancient limestone quarry. The 2024 report says it 'extends over the entire area of the current church' and that its use was 'prolonged in time'. Above the quarry the 2022 report records a cultivation phase with remains of 'cereals, grapes, figs and gramineous plants', and damaged funerary structures on the bedrock. Later levels include the Constantinian church's northern wall and triporticus, the apse of the early Christian church with a Roman street beneath it, 4th-century coins, an 11th-century mosaic, and Crusader pillar foundations.

Public reports in 2025 (Times of Israel, March; Latin Patriarchate, July) highlighted olive and grapevine evidence from pollen and plant remains, and linked it to John 19:41's 'garden'. Stasolla also said that radiocarbon dating of that evidence had not yet been done.
evidence: Quarrying traces are 'visible all along the exposed rock surfaces', with varied depths and unfinished stones (HA-ESI 2022 season report).
A cultivation phase above the quarry with remains of cereals, grapes, figs and grasses, and evidence of olive and grape cultivation (HA-ESI 2022 season report).
Damaged funerary structures on the bedrock, below the Christian phases (HA-ESI).
Constantinian phase: the northern enclosing wall and triporticus of the 4th-century church, water channels and cisterns, and coins of Constantius II (337-361 CE) and Valens (r. 364-378 CE) (HA-ESI).
2023: the apse of the early Christian church, with a Roman street running beneath it (Liber Annuus 73 abstract).
2024: the quarry underlies the entire church and was worked over a long period (Liber Annuus 74 abstract).
As of March 2025, the plant evidence had been identified by pollen and archaeobotanical analysis, but radiocarbon testing 'has not yet been carried out' (Stasolla, quoted by Times of Israel).
questions: Is the cultivated soil a 1st-century garden? Stasolla (Times of Israel, March 2025; Latin Patriarchate, July 2025) links the olive and grapevine evidence to John 19:41. The published season report (HA-ESI) lists a cultivation phase with cereals, grapes, figs and grasses, and, as of March 2025, no radiocarbon date. So the layer is shown to be later than the quarry and earlier than the Christian construction, and nothing tighter yet.

Inside or outside the city? Stasolla: 'at the time of Jesus, the area was not part of the city yet', but it was inside the city by Hadrian's time (Times of Israel, March 2025). This fits John 19:20 and Heb 13:12 only if the relevant wall line is fixed. The Holy Sepulchre reports read here do not themselves fix the course of the 1st-century wall.

Which tomb? The Latin Patriarchate (July 2025) reports several rock-cut tombs and says one is 'possibly' the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea. The HA-ESI report records damaged funerary structures. Nothing inscribed ties any tomb to a named person.

biblical.tie: 'In the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb'. The excavation shows cultivation (vines, figs, cereals; olive per the 2025 statements) and rock-cut burials over an old quarry. Neither is yet dated closely enough to put it in the 1st century.
The crucifixion is outside the city gate but near the city. Stasolla says the area was outside the city in Jesus' time and inside it by Hadrian's time.
A tomb 'hewn out in the rock'. Tombs cut into the old quarry face are attested beneath the church (Latin Patriarchate 2025; HA-ESI).

sources.cite: Stasolla, F. R. 2024. "Jerusalem, Church of the Holy Sepulchre" (Preliminary Report). Hadashot Arkheologiyot - Excavations and Surveys in Israel (online report, 2024). doi:10.69704/jhaesi.116.2004.26542

sites.name: Ipuwer Papyrus
aka: Dialogue of Ipuwer and the Lord of All
sites.subtitle: Egyptian lament of a land turned upside down · New Kingdom copy of an older poem
sites.date: Copy: 19th Dynasty (Gardiner 1909: handwriting 'impossible' to put earlier than the beginning of the 19th Dynasty), i.e. 13th century BCE on the conventional chronology. Composition: disputed, somewhere between the First Intermediate Period and the Second Intermediate Period.
sites.date_basis: Palaeography dates the copy: Gardiner (1909, Introduction §1) puts the hand of the recto no earlier than the start of the 19th Dynasty and notes signs of an older exemplar. Language and content are the only evidence for the date of composition, and the text has no internal regnal date.

discovery.when: Before 1828 (bought at the Anastasi sale in 1828)
discovery.who: Giovanni Anastasi (collector); purchased for the Leiden museum
discovery.where: Memphis according to Anastasi, which Gardiner understood as Saqqara. The exact findspot is unrecorded.

sites.location: Rijksmuseum van Oudheden, Leiden, Netherlands: Papyrus Leiden I 344 (recto = Ipuwer; verso = hymns to a sun god)

physical.material: Papyrus, inscribed on both sides; now mounted in book form under varnish, which darkened it
physical.dimensions: 378 cm long in its present damaged state; 18 cm high (Gardiner 1909, Introduction §1)
physical.script: Hieratic, in a 'small and crabbed literary hand' (Gardiner)

overview: A long hieratic papyrus in Leiden, bought in 1828 from the collection of Giovanni Anastasi, who said it came from Memphis. The front (recto) holds a literary poem in seventeen pages, with the beginning lost and pages 8-17 badly damaged. The back holds sun hymns in a different, later hand. Alan H. Gardiner published the text and translation in 1909. He measured the roll at 378 cm long and 18 cm high.

The speaker is a sage named Ipuwer. He laments a land in collapse: civil strife, plundered tombs and offices, servants taking their masters' place, foreigners ('Asiatics') in the Delta, trade with Byblos and Keftiu cut off, famine, death, and a river that 'is blood'. The latter part addresses a 'Lord of All', and the final pages are fragmentary. Most of the poem is built from refrains repeated line after line ('Forsooth...', 'Behold...', 'Destroyed is...').

Modern readers who connect it with the Exodus point to the blood-river line and the general picture of catastrophe. Egyptologists connect it with a period of internal breakdown in Egypt, or read it as a literary lament. The manuscript itself names no king, no Hebrews and no Moses, has no plague sequence, and carries no internal date.

text.quote: Forsooth, (men's) hearts are violent. Plague is throughout the land. Blood is everywhere. … Forsooth, the river is blood, and (yet) men drink of it. Men shrink from (?) (tasting) human beings, and thirst after water.
text.translation: A. H. Gardiner, The Admonitions of an Egyptian Sage from a Hieratic Papyrus in Leiden (Pap. Leiden 344 recto) (Leipzig: Hinrichs, 1909), translation of Admonitions 2,5-6 and 2,10 (page.line of the papyrus). Gardiner notes that the word he renders 'plague' in 2,5 is the word the first Sallier papyrus uses of the Hyksos.

evidence: Object: Papyrus Leiden I 344, 378 cm × 18 cm, inscribed on both sides. The recto has 17 pages of about 14 lines each (Gardiner 1909, Introduction §1).
The recto's hand is dated no earlier than the start of the 19th Dynasty. Unfilled spaces and omissions suggest the scribe was copying from a damaged older manuscript (Gardiner 1909, Introduction §1).
Acquired at the 1828 Anastasi sale. Anastasi reported Memphis as the source, and there is no excavated context.
The text says 'the river is blood, and (yet) men drink of it' (2,10) and 'Plague is throughout the land. Blood is everywhere' (2,5-6).
Asiatics are in the Delta: 'A foreign tribe from abroad has come to Egypt' (3,1) and 'The Asiatics are skilled in the arts of the Marshlands' (4,5-8) (Gardiner's summary translation).
Social reversal: gold, lapis lazuli, silver and malachite 'are fastened on the necks of female slaves' (3,2-3), and 'He who had no grain is (now) the possessor of granaries' (9,4-5).
Cattle: 'Cattle moan because of the state of the land' (5,5), and 'cattle are left to stray, and there is none to gather them together' (9,2-3).
The text names no pharaoh, no Israelites and no event that can be dated. The beginning of the poem is lost.
questions: When was it composed? A. H. Gardiner (1909, Appendix) weighed two backgrounds: the First Intermediate Period (6th-11th Dynasties) and the Hyksos period (K. Sethe). He came down for the 12th Dynasty, citing the language and administrative details such as the six 'Great Houses' (6,12), 'but … we have no means of attaining anything more than a strong presumptive probability.' J. Van Seters (JEA 50, 1964) dated it to the late Middle Kingdom and Second Intermediate Period from its vocabulary, its administrative titles and its references to Asiatics. R. Enmarch (2009) treats it as a Middle Kingdom literary composition (c. 1980-1630 BCE) and reads it as literature rather than reportage.

Is it an Egyptian account of the Exodus plagues? I. Velikovsky (Ages in Chaos, 1952) read it as an Egyptian witness to the plagues and moved the Exodus to the end of the Middle Kingdom, starting from parallels such as the blood-river line. (His chapter has not been opened for this entry; this summary of his claim comes from secondary accounts.) Against that reading, from the text itself: it has no sequence of plagues, no Hebrews, and no slave people leaving. The foreign Asiatics it names are entering Egypt, not leaving it. Gardiner tied the 'plague' word in 2,5 to the Hyksos by way of the Sallier papyrus. Any correspondence with Exodus is a reading brought to the text from outside.

History or literature? A reading of the text as a record of real conditions (Gardiner 1909, who thought it described a real collapse) competes with a reading of it as a literary lament using stock 'world turned upside-down' themes (Enmarch 2009). The papyrus contains no dated event that could decide between them.

biblical.tie: The river turned to blood: the Nile's water 'shall be turned to blood … and the Egyptians shall lothe to drink of the water of the river' (KJV v.18). Ipuwer 2,10: 'the river is blood, and (yet) men drink of it … thirst after water'. Both passages share the image of a blood-river people cannot drink. Ipuwer attaches it to no plague sequence, no staff and no Moses.
Livestock afflicted. Ipuwer has cattle straying and moaning, but it does not have them dying by a stroke from God.

Jewellery of gold and silver passing to servants. Ipuwer 3,2-3 has gold, silver and lapis lazuli 'on the necks of female slaves'. The direction differs: in Exodus Egyptians give to departing Israelites; in Ipuwer Egyptian servants take their masters' wealth.
Later retellings of the rivers turned to blood. They share the same single image only.

corrections: The old entry dated the papyrus to 'the Middle Kingdom period' and called it a 'copy of a text originally composed during the 13th Dynasty' surviving in 'a later copy from the 12th century BCE'. The surviving manuscript is a New Kingdom copy whose hand Gardiner (1909) dates to no earlier than the start of the 19th Dynasty. The date of composition is disputed (12th Dynasty per Gardiner; Second Intermediate Period per Van Seters 1964) and is not fixed at the 13th Dynasty.
The old entry gave the length as 'approximately 3 meters'. Gardiner measured it at 378 cm long and 18 cm high.
The old entry gave the discovery as 'Early 19th century, Egypt'. The papyrus was bought at the Anastasi sale in 1828. Anastasi gave Memphis (Saqqara) as its source, and it has no excavated findspot.

The old entry said the text describes 'the suffering of the poor, the plundering of the wealthy'. It mostly describes the reverse: the poor become rich and servants take their masters' places (Gardiner's section on the social order reversed).

The old entry said the papyrus reveals conditions 'that may have contributed to... the Israelites' enslavement and subsequent liberation'. The text never mentions Israelites, slaves leaving Egypt or any plague sequence. The foreigners it names are Asiatics entering the Delta.
The old entry said 'many scholars draw parallels'. The specific parallel reading is Velikovsky's (1952). The shared material is one image, a blood-river, plus general disaster themes.

sites.name: Isaiah Bulla
sites.subtitle: Damaged seal impression from the Ophel, Jerusalem · late 8th - early 7th c. BCE
sites.date: Iron Age IIB context, late 8th - early 7th century BCE
sites.date_basis: Stratigraphic: found in undisturbed Iron Age debris beside the 'royal bakery' in the Ophel, in the same soil assemblage as the Hezekiah bulla (about 3 m / under 10 ft away). The text carries no date.

discovery.when: Excavated 2009; published February 2018
discovery.who: Eilat Mazar's Ophel excavations (Hebrew University); recognised in wet-sifting
discovery.where: Ophel, south of the Temple Mount, Jerusalem - outside the south-eastern wall of the building Mazar calls the royal bakery

sites.location: Not established; not confirmed in a published museum record.

physical.material: Clay bulla (reverse bears a cloth/sack impression per the excavation team's account)
physical.dimensions: About half an inch (c. 1.3 cm) across, oval (BAS report)

overview: A small, damaged clay seal impression found in 2009 in the same Ophel refuse context as the Hezekiah bulla and published by Eilat Mazar in Biblical Archaeology Review in 2018. It has three registers: at the top a largely lost image (read by the team as a grazing doe), in the middle the name lyšʿyh[w] - '(belonging) to Yesha'yah[u]' (Isaiah) - and at the bottom the letters nby.

The bottom word breaks off at the damaged edge. If an aleph followed, nbyʾ would be navi, 'prophet', and the seal would read 'Isaiah the prophet' - but that also needs a restored 'the' (h) or a different syntax, and the final aleph is not preserved. Mazar herself stated that because of the damage 'it is not known' whether the word ended in aleph.

The identification with the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz therefore rests on (a) the name Isaiah, (b) the possible reading 'prophet', and (c) the find context next to King Hezekiah's bulla. No patronymic is present.

text.quote: Registers 2-3 as read by Mazar (2018): l-yšʿyh[w] / nby[ʾ] - '(Belonging) to Yesha'yah[u] / nby[...]' - with the letters in brackets restored, not preserved.
text.translation: Reading as reported by the Biblical Archaeology Society from Mazar, BAR 44.2 (2018); English literal rendering by this encyclopedia

evidence: Clay bulla about half an inch across, oval; upper portion and left side damaged (BAS report, 2018).
Middle register: the name Yesha'yah (Isaiah), with the final letters partly restored.
Bottom register: the letters n-b-y; the break comes right where an aleph would be needed to spell 'prophet'.
Top register: traces of an image, read by the excavation team as a grazing doe.
No patronymic ('son of ...') is present.
Found in 2009 in Iron Age debris less than 10 ft (about 3 m) from the Hezekiah bulla; announced in February 2018.
questions: Does nby mean 'prophet'? Mazar (BAR 44.2, 2018) proposes restoring nbyʾ, 'prophet', and connects the bulla with Isaiah son of Amoz, pointing to the find next to Hezekiah's bulla and to the frequent pairing of the two in Kings and Isaiah. Rollston (in Biblical and Ancient Near Eastern Studies in Honor of P. Kyle McCarter Jr., SBL Press, pp. 409-426) argues the broken final letter could equally be restored as other letters giving a personal name or gentilic (e.g. 'son of Nby', 'the Nobite'), that 'prophet' is spelled without yod in Lachish Letter 3 line 20, and that without a patronymic the owner cannot be tied to the biblical Isaiah son of Amoz.

Would a prophet's title appear on a seal used on goods? Haggai Misgav (quoted in The Times of Israel, 22 Feb 2018) doubted that 'prophet' would be used on such a seal; the excavation team notes the reverse shows a sack impression, i.e. it sealed a commodity rather than a papyrus document.

The name itself was not rare: Rollston's point is that other men named Yesha'yahu are known from Iron Age inscriptions, so the name alone does not identify the prophet. The findspot next to the royal bulla is the strongest contextual argument on Mazar's side; the damaged letter is the weakest point.

biblical.tie: Isaiah son of Amoz, 'the prophet' (2 Kgs 19:2; 20:1), active under Hezekiah. The bulla preserves the name Isaiah and possibly nby[ʾ]; it does NOT preserve 'son of Amoz'.
Isaiah and Hezekiah interact repeatedly; the physical proximity of the two bullae in one Ophel deposit is the contextual link. Our reading: suggestive, not proof of identity.

sources.cite: E. Mazar, 'Is This the Prophet Isaiah's Signature?' Biblical Archaeology Review 44.2 (March/April-May/June 2018)
sources.verified: BAS news page (originally 22 Feb 2018) names this BAR article and double issue, and gives the registers, the damaged nvy, the missing aleph, the half-inch size and the <10 ft distance from the Hezekiah bulla; BAR article itself not read.

sources.verified: Crossref record gives title, author, volume title, SBL Press, pp. 409-426 (Crossref's date field is wrong; the volume is 2022 per the publisher listing seen in search). Arguments summarised from search listings of Rollston's posts; chapter not read in full.

sources.cite: A. Borschel-Dan, 'In find of biblical proportions, seal of Prophet Isaiah said found in Jerusalem,' The Times of Israel, 22 February 2018
sources.verified: Read: quotes Rollston on the missing aleph and Haggai Misgav doubting 'prophet' on such a seal; gives findspot near the royal bakery.

corrections: Old entry says it was 'discovered in 2018'. It was excavated in 2009; 2018 is the publication/announcement.

Old entry says the bulla 'bears an inscription that reads "Belonging to Isaiah the Prophet"'. The preserved letters are lyšʿyh[...] / nby; the aleph needed for 'prophet' is lost at the break, as Mazar herself stated.
Old entry says it 'is housed in the Israel Museum'. No published museum record confirms this.

Old entry: 'suggests that the seal may have been used to authenticate documents or messages attributed to the prophet'. The excavation team's own description of a sack impression on the reverse points to sealing goods, not documents.

The old summary box ('Authentic', 'Debated authenticity'): authenticity of the object is not the dispute - it came from a controlled dig. The dispute is the READING of the damaged last word and the identity of the owner.
Old biblical list 'Isaiah 1-66 (Prophetic writings)' is too broad; the tie is to the person Isaiah son of Amoz (Isa 1:1; 2 Kgs 19:2; 20:1).

sites.name: Isaiah Scroll (Great Isaiah Scroll)
sites.subtitle: Complete parchment scroll of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 1 · 2nd century BCE
sites.date: 2nd century BCE: radiocarbon 335-122 BCE (calibrated, 1 sigma); palaeography c. 150-125 BCE; AI style model 180-100 BCE
sites.date_basis: Two independent AMS radiocarbon measurements on the same area (column XXXIX): 2128 +/- 38 BP (ETH-6651, Bonani et al. 1991/92) and 2141 +/- 32 BP (AA-14984, Jull et al. 1995); Jull et al. give the calibrated range 335-122 BC (1 sigma), 2 sigma 356-291 BC (24%) / 250-103 BC (76%). Palaeographic date cited by Jull et al. from F. M. Cross: 'c. 150-125 B.C.E.' The Israel Museum record says 'ca. 125 BCE'. The 2025 'Enoch' model (Popovic et al.) dates both halves 180-100 BCE.

discovery.who: Among the first seven scrolls found by Bedouin in Qumran Cave 1 (finders' names not confirmed in the sources cited here)
discovery.where: Qumran Cave 1, NW shore of the Dead Sea

sites.location: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (Shrine of the Book), accession no. HU 95.57/27, Government of Israel

physical.material: Parchment, sheets sewn together (a sheet join between columns 27 and 28 is noted by Popovic et al. 2021)
physical.dimensions: L 734 cm; H 22-25 cm (Israel Museum record); Popovic et al. 2021 give 7.34 m, averaging 26 cm high
physical.script: Jewish square script of the Hasmonaean type

overview: 1QIsa-a is one of the seven scrolls found in Qumran Cave 1 in 1947. It contains the whole Book of Isaiah, chapters 1-66, in 54 columns written on parchment, 7.34 m long. The Israel Museum lists it as HU 95.57/27, property of the Government of Israel, displayed in the Shrine of the Book.

Its text is 'generally in agreement with the Masoretic or traditional version codified in medieval codices, such as the Aleppo Codex, but it contains many variant readings, alternative spellings, scribal errors, and corrections' (Israel Museum record). Its spelling is very full (many vowel letters), and in the second half the orthography and morphology differ from the first.

There is a physical break in the middle: a three-line blank at the bottom of column 27 and a sheet join between columns 27 and 28. Popovic, Dhali and Schomaker (2021) found by computer analysis of letter shapes that two main scribes wrote the two halves, with the switch at columns 27-29.

text.quote: Contains the entire Book of Isaiah (chs. 1-66) in 54 columns; the text follows the same book and order as the medieval Masoretic codices, with many variant readings, fuller spellings, scribal errors and corrections (Israel Museum record).
text.translation: No public-domain translation of the scroll's own variant text has been located for this entry

evidence: 54 columns, all 66 chapters of Isaiah (Israel Museum record).
Length 734 cm; height 22-25 cm per museum, c. 26 cm average per Popovic et al. 2021.
Radiocarbon: 2128 +/- 38 BP (ETH-6651) and 2141 +/- 32 BP (AA-14984), both from column XXXIX.
Three-line blank at the foot of column 27 and a sheet join between columns 27 and 28.
Orthography and morphology change in the second half; blank spaces left in the second half (Popovic et al. 2021).
Handwriting analysis: two main scribes, transition at columns 27-29 (Popovic et al. 2021).
Many variant readings, spelling differences, errors and corrections relative to the medieval Masoretic codices (Israel Museum record).
questions: One scribe or two: older palaeographic debate asked whether differences between the halves are normal variation of one hand; Popovic, Dhali and Schomaker (PLOS ONE 16, 2021) report statistically significant writer difference with a phase transition in columns 27-29 and conclude two main scribes who closely mirrored one another's style.

Absolute date: Jull et al. (Radiocarbon 37, 1995) give a 2-sigma radiocarbon range whose larger probability block is 250-103 BC but which also allows 356-291 BC (24%); the palaeographic date (Cross: c. 150-125 BCE) sits inside the later block. Popovic et al. (PLOS ONE 20, 2025) find their style model dates both halves to the same period, 180-100 BCE, i.e. neither half is significantly later.

How close to the Masoretic Text: the Israel Museum record describes the text as 'generally in agreement' with the medieval Masoretic codices 'but' with 'many variant readings'. The critical edition (Ulrich & Flint, DJD XXXII, 2010) lists the variants; whether they are 'minor' is an evaluation, not a measurement, and is left to the variant lists.

biblical.tie: The scroll is a copy of the whole book in one scroll, including both chs. 1-39 and 40-66 continuously; it is direct manuscript evidence that the book circulated in its 66-chapter form by the 2nd century BCE.

Jesus is handed 'the scroll (biblion) of the prophet Isaiah' in the Nazareth synagogue and unrolls it to Isa 61. The Great Isaiah Scroll shows what a complete Isaiah scroll of the period physically was: one continuous parchment roll.
The Ethiopian official reads Isaiah 53 aloud from a scroll; same book, same format.
The Gospels quote Isa 40:3 for John the Baptist; the scroll contains that verse in a pre-Christian copy.

sites.name: Ishtar Gate
sites.subtitle: Glazed-brick city gate of Nebuchadnezzar II, Babylon · early 6th c. BCE
sites.date: Reign of Nebuchadnezzar II (604-562 BCE); archaeomagnetic best fit 569 BCE (Di Chiara et al. 2024)
sites.date_basis: Bricks of the earliest phase are stamped with Nebuchadnezzar II's name and the gate carried his consecration inscription (Koldewey 1914, p. 45). Di Chiara et al. (PLOS ONE 2024) measured geomagnetic intensity in bricks from all three building phases: the average fits the Levantine archaeomagnetic curve best at 569 BCE; they assign the data point an age of 583 +/- 22 BCE from the reign itself, and conclude the phases were built in quick succession.

discovery.when: Excavated February-November 1902 (Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft excavations at Babylon, 1899-1917)
discovery.who: Robert Koldewey
discovery.where: North side of the Kasr mound, Babylon (Iraq), at the end of the Procession Street

sites.location: Foundations and lower walls in situ at Babylon, Iraq. The front gate and part of the Procession Street were rebuilt from excavated glazed-brick fragments in the Pergamonmuseum / Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin (on display from 1930); that wing has been closed since 23 Oct 2023. Other glazed-brick fragments went to Istanbul in the 1903 find division and to Baghdad in 1926 (SMB); single animals from the Procession Street and gate are in several other museums.

physical.material: Baked brick in bitumen; relief bricks both unglazed-moulded and coloured-glazed
physical.dimensions: Surviving walls stood 12 m high at excavation (Koldewey); animal reliefs each 13 brick courses tall, rows 24 courses (c. 2 m) apart; 9 rows of animals visible

overview: The Ishtar Gate was the main northern gate of Nebuchadnezzar II's Babylon, a double gateway through the city's inner walls at the end of the Procession Street. Koldewey excavated it in 1902 and called it 'the largest and most striking ruin of Babylon', its walls still standing 12 metres high.

Its walls carried rows of bulls and dragons (the sirrush, Marduk's animal) in moulded brick relief - first unglazed, then in flat and relief glazed brick as the road level was repeatedly raised. The famous striding lions belong to the walls of the Procession Street leading to the gate, not to the gate itself. A limestone block found between the two doorways bears Nebuchadnezzar's consecration text for the gate.

German excavators shipped glazed-brick fragments to Berlin under the 1903 and 1926 find divisions; conservators reassembled 72 animal reliefs and the front gate, shown in the Pergamonmuseum from 1930. The Berlin building is under renovation: Staatliche Museen zu Berlin say the South Wing closed on 23 October 2023, the museum partly reopens on 4 June 2027, and the Vorderasiatisches Museum's full collection returns with the South Wing, expected in 2037.

text.quote: (Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon, son of) Nabopolassar (King of Babylon am I). The gate of Nana (Ishtar... I built) with (blue) enamelled bricks . . . for Marduk my lord. Lusty bulls of bronze and mighty figures of serpents I placed at their thresholds
text.translation: Consecration inscription of the Ishtar Gate, trans. L. Messerschmidt, in R. Koldewey, The Excavations at Babylon (1914), p. 45

evidence: Double gateway: two doorways one behind the other joined into one block, through the paired inner walls (Imgur-Bel and Nimitti-Bel) (Koldewey 1914, pp. 32-34).
Decoration: alternating horizontal rows of bulls and sirrush dragons; each animal 13 courses high, repeating every 24 courses (c. 2 m); 9 rows visible from top to bottom (Koldewey 1914, pp. 39-41).
The road level was raised at least twice; traces of successive pavements between the animal rows (Koldewey 1914, p. 42).
Consecration inscription on a limestone block found between the two doorways at the level of the topmost pavement (Koldewey 1914, p. 45).
Lions in glazed relief lined the defensive walls of the Procession Street approaching the gate (Koldewey 1914, p. 26).

Nebuchadnezzar's East India House Inscription describes rebuilding the gates of Imgur-Bel and Nimitti-Bel with burnt brick and 'brilliant stones on which bulls and serpents were engraved' and placing bronze bulls and upright serpents at their thresholds (Langdon 1905, p. 131).

Archaeomagnetic intensity from five brick specimens across three phases: 136 +/- 2.1 ZAm2, best fit 569 BCE on the Levantine curve; significantly different from the value for the 586 BCE Jerusalem destruction layer (148.9 +/- 3.9 ZAm2) (Di Chiara et al. 2024).
Berlin reconstruction built from fragments allotted in the 1903 (Istanbul) and 1926 (Baghdad) find divisions; 72 animal reliefs assembled in two years; displayed from 1930 (SMB).
questions: Before or after the fall of Jerusalem? Di Chiara, Tauxe, Gries, Helwing, Howland & Ben-Yosef (PLOS ONE 19/1, 2024) find the gate's magnetic intensity differs significantly from that recorded in Jerusalem's 586 BCE destruction layer and fits the curve best at 569 BCE, so they conclude the gate was built after 586 'although probably not immediately after'. The 583 +/- 22 BCE figure sometimes quoted is the age they assigned from Nebuchadnezzar's reign, not an independent measurement. Our note: an intensity-only match on a regional curve can cross the curve at more than one date, so the 569 BCE figure depends on the Levantine curve's shape and resolution for the 6th century.

How much of what Berlin shows is the ancient gate? Koldewey (1914) describes the monument as a double gateway with walls still 12 m high; Berlin shows the smaller front gate rebuilt from sorted fragments with modern bricks (SMB). Anyone quoting a height should say whether it is the ruin at Babylon, the Berlin reconstruction, or a reconstruction drawing.

biblical.tie: Nebuchadnezzar walks on his palace and says 'Is not this great Babylon, that I have built'; the gate is one of his signed building works a few hundred metres from the palace.
Judahite exiles (597 and 586 BCE) were taken to Babylon. If the 2024 archaeomagnetic result holds, the gate standing today was built after the 586 deportation; our reading, not the text's.
'The broad walls of Babylon shall be utterly broken, and her high gates shall be burned with fire' - a prophecy about the walls and gates of this city; the gate is one of those gates.

biblical.ref: Bel and the Dragon (Greek additions to Daniel)
biblical.tie: Koldewey (1914, p. 46) himself compared the sirrush, 'the dragon of Babylon' on the gate, with the dragon story; that comparison is his suggestion.

sources.cite: R. Koldewey, The Excavations at Babylon, trans. A. S. Johns (London: Macmillan, 1914)
sources.verified: Read the archive.org full text: gate excavated Feb-Nov 1902 (p. vii); walls 12 m high (p. 32); bulls and sirrush rows (pp. 39-42); consecration inscription and Messerschmidt translation (p. 45); lions of the Procession Street (p. 26).

sites.name: Samaria Ivories (the 'Ivory House' finds)
sites.subtitle: Carved ivory inlays from the royal quarter of Samaria · Iron Age II (9th-8th c. BCE range)
sites.date: Iron Age II; the range usually given is 9th-8th century BCE. No object carries a date, and the dating is itself disputed (see questions).
sites.date_basis: Not dated by inscription. Dating rests on (a) the find contexts in and around the Israelite palace/acropolis at Samaria, and (b) stylistic comparison with the ivory hoards from Nimrud and Arslan Tash. The 1908-10 Harvard excavators assigned the second palace phase to Ahab by building sequence ('it is the earliest of the three structures' for Omri, the next for Ahab), not by any inscription.

discovery.when: A few pieces 1908-1910 (Harvard Expedition, G. A. Reisner, C. S. Fisher, D. G. Lyon); the main body 1931-1935 (Joint Expedition to Samaria led by J. W. Crowfoot, with K. M. Kenyon and E. L. Sukenik; ivories published by J. W. and G. M. Crowfoot)
discovery.who: Harvard Expedition; then the Joint Expedition (PEF, British Academy, British School of Archaeology in Jerusalem, Hebrew University, Harvard)
discovery.where: Summit (royal acropolis) of Samaria/Sebaste; Harvard pieces in areas S2, S4, S7; Joint Expedition pieces in areas Qc, Qk, Qd, Qh, Z and B (per the 1938 publication's plan, as cited by Pienaar 2008)

sites.location: Not confirmed in a published museum record. The pieces were split between the two expeditions and are not in one collection; no museum inventory numbers were located.

physical.material: Elephant ivory, carved in relief and openwork; some pieces set with coloured glass/stone inlay
physical.dimensions: Mostly small plaques and fragments; about 500 pieces in all (Pienaar 2008, citing Crowfoot & Crowfoot 1938 and Barkay 1992)

overview: Samaria, the northern kingdom's capital, has produced a large body of carved ivory: plaques, panels and fragments that were once inlays on furniture and wall panelling. A few came from the Harvard excavations of 1908-10. The main body came from the Joint Expedition of 1931-35, published by J. W. and G. M. Crowfoot in PEQ (1933) and in Early Ivories from Samaria (Samaria-Sebaste II, 1938). About 500 pieces are counted, and only a small part could be restored.

The motifs are those of the Levantine ivory workshops known from Nimrud and Arslan Tash. One group is Egyptianizing: the child Horus (Harpocrates) on a lotus, Isis and Nephthys, Heh, Horus and Ma'at. The other group has the 'woman at the window', winged sphinxes, winged human figures, lion-and-bull combat and the stylized palmette 'tree'.

'Ivory House' is a modern label taken from 1 Kings 22:39. The Harvard report (1924) already called the second Israelite palace building the 'ivory palace' of Ahab, before the main ivory finds, on the strength of its fine ashlar masonry and its place in the building sequence.
evidence: About 500 carved ivory pieces from the royal quarter; only a small fraction restorable (Pienaar 2008, citing SS II and Kenyon 1960).
Findspots spread across several areas of the summit (Harvard S2, S4, S7; Joint Expedition Qc, Qk, Qd, Qh, Z, B), not a single sealed room.
Egyptianizing iconography (Harpocrates on lotus, Isis/Nephthys, Heh, Horus with Ma'at) alongside Levantine motifs (woman at the window, winged sphinx, lion and bull).
Same motif repertoire as ivories from Nimrud and Arslan Tash, e.g. the 'woman at the window'.

Reisner-Fisher-Lyon (1924): the second palace was 'naturally identified with the "ivory palace" of Ahab, and the smoothly dressed surfaces ... are sufficient justification for this name' - an identification based on masonry and sequence, not on ivory finds.
No ivory from Samaria carries a royal name; nothing on the objects names Ahab.
questions: When were the ivories made and deposited? The Crowfoots (PEQ 1933; Early Ivories from Samaria, 1938) presented them in the context of the Israelite palace and the biblical 'ivory house' of Ahab. Ron E. Tappy (The Archaeology of Israelite Samaria II: The Eighth Century BCE, 2001, ch. 'The Archaeo-Historical Context of the Samaria Ivories', pp. 443-503) re-examined the excavation records and treats the ivories' contexts within the eighth-century material. The objects themselves are not stratigraphically dated; the question turns on which fills and floors they came from.

Whose workshop? Irene J. Winter (Iraq 43, 1981) separated a 'South Syrian' carving style from the Phoenician and North Syrian styles found at Nimrud, which bears on whether the Samaria pieces are imports or local work. D. Barag (Anatolian Studies 33, 1983) proposed using glass inlays to classify and date ninth-eighth century ivories.
Ahab's 'house of ivory' (1 Kgs 22:39) or the later 'houses of ivory' Amos condemns (Amos 3:15; 6:4)? Because the ivories are undated, they fit either text; no find ties them to one king.

biblical.tie: 'The ivory house which he [Ahab] built.' Samaria has produced a large body of ivory inlay from its royal quarter; nothing ties any piece to Ahab by name or by sealed date.

'Houses of ivory' and 'beds of ivory' among Samaria's elite. The ivories are furniture and wall inlays of exactly that kind; Amos is set in the 8th century, within the date range proposed for the ivories.
'Palaces of ivory' as a royal luxury; a general parallel only.

corrections: Old entry says the ivories were uncovered 'in the early 1930s by the American archaeologist J.H.H. St. John'. No such excavator appears in the reports. The Joint Expedition of 1931-35 was directed by J. W. Crowfoot (British), with Kathleen Kenyon and E. L. Sukenik; the ivories were published by J. W. and G. M. (Grace) Crowfoot. A few pieces had already come from the Harvard excavation of 1908-10.

Old entry states the palace 'is believed to have been the residence of King Ahab' and that the ivories 'directly correlate' with 1 Kgs 22:39. No inscription names Ahab; the 'ivory palace' label was given by the Harvard team in 1924 on architectural grounds.

Old entry cites '1 Kings 22:42' and '2 Chronicles 18:10' for the ivory house. Neither verse mentions ivory: 1 Kgs 22:42 is Jehoshaphat's accession, and 2 Chr 18:10 is Zedekiah's iron horns. The ivory texts are 1 Kgs 22:39, Amos 3:15, Amos 6:4 and Ps 45:8.
Old entry gives a firm date 'c. 850 BCE'. The objects are undated; the range discussed runs across the 9th-8th centuries.

sites.name: Jehohanan Crucifixion Remains
sites.subtitle: Heel bone pierced by an iron nail, from an ossuary in a Jerusalem tomb · 1st century CE
sites.date: 1st century CE, before 70 CE
sites.date_basis: Context: secondary burial in an inscribed ossuary in a Jewish rock-cut tomb of the Second Temple period at Giv'at ha-Mivtar; Tzaferis (BAR 1985) places the man 'shortly after the turn of the era and sometime before the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in 70 A.D.' No absolute date on the bone itself was located.

discovery.who: Found by building contractors; excavated by Vassilios Tzaferis for the Israel Department of Antiquities; bones studied by Nicu Haas (1970), re-examined by Joseph Zias and Eliezer Sekeles (1985)
discovery.where: Giv'at ha-Mivtar, a suburb north of Jerusalem

sites.location: Not confirmed in a published museum record

physical.material: Human right calcaneus (heel bone) with an iron nail, olive-wood fragments; limestone ossuary
physical.dimensions: Nail 11.5 cm long (Zias & Sekeles 1985); Haas (1970) had reported 17-18 cm

overview: In 1968 contractors building north of Jerusalem opened Jewish rock-cut tombs at Giv'at ha-Mivtar. Vassilios Tzaferis excavated them (IEJ 20, 1970). In one ossuary, inscribed 'Jehohanan son of HGQWL', were the bones of a man in his twenties whose right heel bone was still transfixed by an iron nail.

The nail had entered the side of the heel and its tip had bent back on itself, which Zias reads as the nail having struck a knot in the upright so that it could not be pulled out when the body was taken down. Olive wood lay between the nail head and the bone, read as a small wooden plaque under the nail head.

Nicu Haas's 1970 anatomical report reported the nail as 17-18 cm and reconstructed both heels as fixed by one nail. Zias and Sekeles's 1985 re-examination measured the nail at 11.5 cm, too short to pass through two feet, and found no traumatic injury to the forearms.

text.quote: Jehohanan the son of HGQWL
text.translation: Ossuary inscription as rendered by J. Zias, 'Crucifixion in Antiquity: The Evidence' (the patronymic left untranslated)

evidence: Right calcaneus penetrated laterally by an iron nail, tip bent back on itself (Zias).
Nail length 11.5 cm (Zias & Sekeles 1985), not 17-18 cm (Haas 1970).
Olive-wood remains between nail head and bone.
No traumatic lesion on the forearms found in the 1985 re-examination.
Skeleton friable, fragmentary, with many post-mortem breaks.
Ossuary inscription gives a personal name and an unexplained patronymic/epithet HGQWL.
The man received normal Jewish secondary burial in a family tomb.
questions: How he was fixed to the cross: N. Haas (IEJ 20, 1970) proposed one 17-18 cm nail through both heels (as reported by Zias); J. Zias and E. Sekeles (IEJ 35, 1985) reject this because the nail is only 11.5 cm and they found no traumatic injury to the forearms, and Zias concludes the arms were bound, the feet nailed separately.

How many crucifixion victims survive: Zias (essay) and Gualdi-Russo et al. (Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences 11, 2019) both treat Giv'at ha-Mivtar as the only well-documented case; Gualdi-Russo et al. propose a second, 'possible' case from an isolated Roman burial at Gavello, northern Italy (excavated 2007), from a lesion on a heel bone, while stating the poor bone preservation complicates the reading. Zias explains the rarity by crucifixion nails being taken as healing amulets (Mishnah Shabbat 6:10) and by victims often being tied.
Meaning of HGQWL: the sources read give it untranslated; its reading (patronymic, place or nickname) is not settled in them.

biblical.tie: Thomas speaks of 'the print of the nails' in Jesus' hands. The find shows nailing of the feet in 1st-century Judea; it gives no evidence about hands, and Zias's reading of this victim is that the arms were tied.
'See my hands and my feet' - the Gospel implies wounds in the feet; this is the one physical example of a Judean crucifixion victim's foot being nailed.

Joseph of Arimathea obtains the body and gives it Jewish burial in a rock tomb. Jehohanan too, though crucified, was released for burial in a family tomb and later placed in an ossuary - showing a crucified man could receive regular Jewish burial.
Anyone hanged on a tree must be buried the same day; cited by Zias as background to Jewish handling of executed bodies.

sites.name: Jehoiachin Ration Tablets
sites.subtitle: Oil-ration lists from Nebuchadnezzar's palace at Babylon naming the exiled king of Judah · c. 595-570 BCE
sites.date: Dated archive texts run from Nebuchadnezzar II's 10th to 35th years (c. 595-570 BCE); the one Jehoiachin tablet with its date preserved is from year 13 (592/591 BCE)
sites.date_basis: Regnal-year dates written on the tablets (Babylonian dating by year of Nebuchadnezzar); converted with the standard Neo-Babylonian chronology.

discovery.when: Excavated 1902-1903 (Koldewey's work on the north-east corner of the Southern Citadel, Dec 1902 - Jan 1904); the Jehoiachin entries were identified in Berlin by E. F. Weidner and published in 1939
discovery.who: Robert Koldewey (Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft); read by Ernst F. Weidner
discovery.where: The 'Vaulted Building' at the north-east corner of the Southern Palace (Kasr), Babylon - tablets from its stairway chamber

sites.location: Vorderasiatisches Museum, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin (secondary listings cite VAT 16378 and excavation numbers Babylon 28122, 28178, 28186; not checked against a museum record). The museum's South Wing has been closed since 23 Oct 2023.

physical.material: Clay tablets
physical.dimensions: The dated year-13 tablet is about three inches tall (CoJS)

overview: Administrative tablets from the storerooms of Nebuchadnezzar II's palace at Babylon record monthly issues of sesame oil and other staples to people held or maintained at court. Four of them list rations for 'Ya'u-kinu (also written Ya'ukin), king of the land of Yahudu' - Jehoiachin, king of Judah, deported in 597 BCE - together with his five sons and other Judahites.

Koldewey found the tablets in the vaulted substructure at the north-east corner of the Southern Palace, noting in 1914 that 'the large number of tablets found in the stairway chamber on the south side' related to food supplies, which led him to read the building as a storehouse. Ernst Weidner recognised Jehoiachin's name in the Berlin tablets and published the key texts in 1939. In 2025 Olof Pedersén published the whole archive of 527 texts.

The same lists issue oil to craftsmen and dignitaries from many lands (secondary transcriptions mention carpenters from Arvad, woodworkers from Byblos and Greek craftsmen). Pedersén's summary notes that the largest single quantity of oil in the archive went to Jehoiachin.

text.quote: One tablet lists 10 sila of oil for 'Ya'ukin, king of Yahudu', 2 1/2 sila for 'the sons of the king of Yahudu' (another tablet: 'the 5 sons of the king of Yahudu'), and 4 sila for eight men of Yahudu.
text.translation: Summary of the published readings (Weidner 1939, as reproduced in secondary sources; full edition Pedersén 2025); no public-domain translation exists

evidence: About three hundred ration texts dated between Nebuchadnezzar's 10th and 35th years (CoJS); Pedersén (2025) publishes 527 texts and fragments from the palace archives.
Four texts name Jehoiachin with the title 'king of the land of Yahudu'; one is dated year 13 of Nebuchadnezzar (592/591 BCE) (CoJS).
Five sons of the king of Judah receive oil alongside him (secondary transcriptions of Weidner's texts).

The archive records barley, dates and sesame oil shipped mostly by boat, stored in silos and issued to foreigners and guests; the largest single oil allocation goes to Jehoiachin (Pedersén 2025 abstract).

Findspot: the Vaulted Building of the Southern Palace; Koldewey (1914, p. 100) records many tablets in its southern stairway chamber and reads the building as a storehouse (he also proposed it as the Hanging Gardens, an identification CoJS reports as since abandoned).
questions: Prisoner or pensioner? 2 Kgs 25:27-29 says Evil-Merodach 'did lift up the head of Jehoiachin ... out of prison' in the 37th year of the exile (c. 561 BCE). The tablets show him drawing large rations with his household in 592/591 BCE. CoJS reads the size of the ration as evidence that he was not imprisoned for the whole exile; another reading (ours) is that a period of confinement came later than 592. The tablets themselves say nothing about prison.

Five sons in 592 BCE: 1 Chr 3:17-18 lists seven sons of Jeconiah (Shealtiel, Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jecamiah, Hoshama, Nedabiah). The tablet count (five) is a snapshot of one year and does not contradict a later total; it does bear on Jer 22:30 ('write ye this man childless'), which the text itself explains in the same verse as 'no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David'.

Weidner's 1939 first edition ('Jojachin, König von Juda, in babylonischen Keilschrifttexten', Mélanges syriens offerts à M. René Dussaud II) is the standard reference in secondary literature; it was not available for this entry, so it is not listed as a verified source.

biblical.tie: Jehoiachin surrenders to Nebuchadnezzar and is carried to Babylon with his mother, wives and officials - the tablets show him in Babylon, at the royal storehouse's expense, by 592 BCE.

'His allowance was a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day' - a royal food allowance of exactly the kind these lists record, though these tablets date some 30 years before the release described there.
Sons of Jeconiah the captive; the tablets record five unnamed sons of the king of Judah receiving oil.

corrections: Old entry: 'discovered during excavations in the ancient city of Babylon in the 1930s' / 'Discovery: 1930s, Iraq'. They were excavated 1902-1903 by Koldewey's German expedition; the 1930s is when Weidner identified them in Berlin (published 1939).

Old entry: 'date to approximately 560 BCE'. The archive runs from Nebuchadnezzar's year 10 to 35 (c. 595-570 BCE); the dated Jehoiachin tablet is year 13 (592/591 BCE) - about 30 years before the release in 2 Kgs 25:27 (c. 561).
Old entry: the tablets 'confirm' 2 Kgs 25:27-30. They record rations decades earlier; they match 2 Kgs 24:15 (deportation to Babylon) and the kind of allowance in 25:30, not the release event itself.
Old entry omits the five sons and the other foreign recipients recorded on the same lists.
Old 'Ezra 2 (Return from exile)' tie removed; the tablets have no connection to the return lists.
Old location 'Pergamon Museum, Berlin' - they belong to the Vorderasiatisches Museum (in the Pergamonmuseum building), whose galleries have been closed since October 2023.

sites.name: Bullae of Jeremiah's officials: Jehucal son of Shelemiah, Gedaliah son of Pashhur, Gemariah son of Shaphan
sites.subtitle: Three excavated clay seal impressions from the City of David naming men who appear in Jeremiah 36-38 · late 7th to early 6th century BCE
sites.date: Late 7th to early 6th century BCE (palaeographic dating)
sites.date_basis: Letter forms. Mykytiuk (Maarav 16/1, 2009) dates the Gedaliah bulla by the form of its he and the Gemariah bulla by its first nun to the late 7th to early 6th century. The findspots of the Jehucal and Gedaliah bullae lie in contexts whose date is disputed, so he relies on palaeography rather than stratigraphy.

discovery.when: Gemariah: Yigal Shiloh's City of David excavations (1978-1985). Jehucal: announced 4 Aug 2005. Gedaliah: announced 31 July 2008.
discovery.who: Gemariah: Yigal Shiloh. Jehucal and Gedaliah: Eilat Mazar; the Jehucal bulla was found by Area A supervisor Yoav Farhi.
discovery.where: Gemariah: Locus 967, the 'House of the Bullae', Area G. Jehucal: between two large stones in the Large Stone Structure, Mazar's Area A. Gedaliah: Mazar's excavation at the summit of the City of David (findspot map in Mazar 2009: 69).

sites.location: Current repository not stated in the sources cited here

physical.material: Unfired clay seal impressions (bullae)
physical.dimensions: Jehucal: about 0.4 inch (1 cm) wide per the BAR caption; Gedaliah: about 1 cm long per news reports (both as reported by Mykytiuk 2009)

overview: Three bullae (clay lumps stamped by a seal to close a document) from the City of David carry names that also appear in Jeremiah 36-38. The Gemariah bulla came from the hoard of 51 bullae in the 'House of the Bullae' (Locus 967) in Area G of Yigal Shiloh's excavations. Eilat Mazar announced the Jehucal bulla on 4 August 2005 and the Gedaliah bulla on 31 July 2008, both from her excavation at the summit of the City of David.

The readings, as transcribed by Mykytiuk (2009), are lyhwkl bn shlmyhw bn shby, 'belonging to Yehukal son of Shelemyahu son of Shobi'; lgdlyhw bn pshhwr, 'belonging to Gedalyahu son of [P]ashhur'; and lgmryhw [b]n shpn, 'belonging to Gemaryahu son of Shaphan'. The Bible names Jehucal son of Shelemiah and Gedaliah son of Pashhur together among the officials who heard Jeremiah and had him put in the cistern (Jer 37:3; 38:1-6). It places Gemariah son of Shaphan the scribe in a chamber of the temple under Jehoiakim (Jer 36:10-12, 25).

Mykytiuk grades the Jehucal and Gedaliah matches 'grade 2 or higher' (reasonable, with a third identifying mark lacking) and the Gemariah match 'grade 3' (reliable). He notes that the stratigraphic context of Mazar's two bullae is disputed and that her final publication was still awaited in 2009.

text.quote: (1) Belonging to Yehukal, son of Shelemyahu, son of Shobi. (2) Belonging to Gedalyahu, son of [P]ashhur. (3) Belonging to Gemaryahu, [so]n of Shaphan.
text.translation: Literal translation (this encyclopedia) of the transliterations lyhwkl b[n] shlmyhw bn shby; lgdlyhw. bn [p]shhwr.; lgmryhw [b]n shpn, as published in Mykytiuk, Maarav 16/1 (2009): 86, 92, 110. No public-domain translation exists.

evidence: Jehucal bulla: a horizontal oval from a nearly circular seal. There is no border line, and three lines hold five words without dividers. A chip removes the top of the first letter of line 2, the nun of bn (Mykytiuk 2009: 86).
Jehucal bulla: found by Area A supervisor Yoav Farhi 'between two large stones' in the Large Stone Structure; discovery announced 4 Aug 2005 (Mykytiuk 2009: 87).
Jehucal's patronyms: Mykytiuk reads shin, Shelemyahu and Shobi, because those spellings match known biblical names (2 Sam 17:27 has Shobi), rather than sin (Mykytiuk 2009: 86-87).

Gedaliah bulla: aniconic horizontal ellipse. A single line surrounds the face and a double line divides two registers. Diagonal scratches cross the centre, and the pe of Pashhur is partly scraped off, so it is 'very uncertain at first sight' (Mykytiuk 2009: 92-93).
Gedaliah bulla: discovery announced 31 July 2008. Photos are in Mazar, Palace of King David (2009): 66, 68, and the findspot is mapped on p. 69 (Mykytiuk 2009: 92-93).

Gemariah bulla: from Locus 967 ('House of the Bullae'), Area G, Shiloh's excavations, in a hoard of 51 bullae. Its first nun (lower register), documented in an early photograph before it broke off, has parallel shafts and a perpendicular crossbar, a late-7th-century form (Mykytiuk 2009: 90, 110-111).
questions: Same men or namesakes? Mykytiuk (Maarav 2009) accepts all three matches. Jehucal and Gedaliah are grade 2 or higher: the name and patronym match, and the date and setting fit. Gemariah is grade 3. He notes that another father-and-son pair Shelemyahu/Yehukal could have lived in Jerusalem, and that a royal-palace findspot would be a third identifying mark if the Large Stone Structure could be shown to be royal.

Stratigraphic context. Eilat Mazar (Palace of King David, 2009) takes the Large Stone Structure to be a royal building used until 586 BCE. Finkelstein, Herzog, Singer-Avitz and Ussishkin ('Has King David's Palace in Jerusalem Been Found?', Tel Aviv 34, 2007) dispute her dating of the building's elements. Mykytiuk (2009: 94) states that the Gedaliah and Jehucal findspots 'lie in an archaeological context whose date is disputed' and relies on palaeography.

The first letter of Gedaliah's patronym. Mykytiuk argues for pe, ruling out kaph and mem on letter shape and space; nun 'perhaps cannot be ruled out completely'. The identification with Pashhur depends on this reading.

biblical.tie: Zedekiah sends 'Jehucal the son of Shelemiah' to Jeremiah. The bulla reads Yehukal son of Shelemyahu (and adds a grandfather, Shobi).
'Gedaliah the son of Pashhur' and 'Jucal the son of Shelemiah' hear Jeremiah and urge his death, and he is put into the cistern. Both names appear on bullae from the same excavation.
Baruch reads the scroll 'in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the scribe'; Gemariah later pleads with Jehoiakim not to burn it. The Area G bulla reads Gemaryahu son of Shaphan.
Shaphan the scribe under Josiah, father of Ahikam, Gemariah and others. The bulla names Gemariah's father Shaphan, but gives no title for him.

updates.what: Mykytiuk's BAS list of biblical persons identified in inscriptions was updated (now '53 People'); it still includes Gemariah, Jehucal and Gedaliah.

corrections: A claim circulating with this find (including in the sister project's catalogue) says the Jehucal and Gedaliah bullae were found 'in the 586 BCE destruction layer'. Mykytiuk (2009: 94) states that their findspots lie in a context whose date is disputed and that stratigraphy may not match the bullae's date, so they are dated by palaeography.

Calling the bullae 'Jeremiah's captors' own seals' is a step too far. They are clay impressions of seals, and the identification with the biblical officials rests on matching name plus patronym plus date, graded 'grade 2 or higher', not certain, for Jehucal and Gedaliah (Mykytiuk 2009).

The sister project cited the madainproject.com list for these bullae. That is not a primary source; the primary publications are Shiloh and Tarler (1986), Mazar (2009), and the analysis in Mykytiuk (2009).
Gedaliah's patronym is sometimes printed as certain. The first letter of Pashhur is damaged and uncertain (Mykytiuk 2009: 92-93).

sites.name: Jericho Excavations
sites.subtitle: Tell es-Sultan · the burned Bronze Age city and the dispute over its date
sites.date: The site spans the Natufian and Neolithic through the Iron Age. The key layer for Joshua 6 is the fiery destruction of the last Middle Bronze city (Garstang's City IV; Sultan IVc). Its date is disputed between c. 1550-1525 BCE (Kenyon; Nigro & Yasine 2024 radiocarbon) and c. 1400 BCE (Garstang 1935; Wood 1990).
sites.date_basis: Pottery typology, Egyptian scarabs from the tombs, and radiocarbon. Bruins & van der Plicht (Radiocarbon 37, 1995) measured charred grain from Kenyon's destruction layer at a weighted average of 3306 ± 7 BP, which they calibrated to 'the late 17th or the 16th century BC'. Nigro & Yasine (2024) report new 14C samples dating the final destruction of the MB city to 1550-1525 BCE and the 'Hyksos Palace' fire to about 1530 BCE. Wood (1990) relied on a single charcoal date (BM-1790) of 1410 ± 40 BCE, together with LB I pottery and scarabs.

discovery.when: 1868 (Warren); 1907-1909 and 1911 (Sellin & Watzinger); 1930-1936 (Garstang); 1952-1958 (Kenyon); 1997-2000 and 2009-present (Italian-Palestinian Expedition, Sapienza University of Rome with the Palestinian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities)
discovery.who: Charles Warren; Ernst Sellin and Carl Watzinger; John Garstang; Kathleen M. Kenyon; Lorenzo Nigro, Nicolò Marchetti, Hamdan Taha, Jehad Yasine
discovery.where: Tell es-Sultan, beside the spring of ʿEin es-Sultan, Jericho (Ariha), West Bank

sites.location: In situ, Tell es-Sultan, Jericho. The site was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List on 17 September 2023 (Nigro & Yasine 2024).

physical.material: Mudbrick city walls on a stone revetment (Middle Bronze rampart), destruction debris, burned houses with storage jars of grain

overview: Tell es-Sultan is the mound of ancient Jericho beside a perennial spring. Excavators since 1868 have reached levels from the Neolithic tower to the Iron Age. The layer at issue for Joshua 6 is the violent end of the last Middle Bronze Age city. Its rampart had a stone revetment wall at the base topped by mudbrick. The city was burned, its walls collapsed, and houses were left with jars full of grain.

John Garstang (1930-1936) called this burned city 'City IV'. In 'The Fall of Bronze Age Jericho' (PEQ 1935) he dated its fall to about 1400 BCE. Kathleen Kenyon (1952-1958) showed that the collapsed 'double wall' Garstang had tied to the conquest belonged to the Early Bronze Age. Bryant Wood, who argued for the later date, grants this point. Kenyon dated City IV's destruction to the end of the Middle Bronze Age, about 1550 BCE, and allowed only a small, short-lived 14th-century occupation afterwards. In 1990 Bryant Wood (BAR 16:2) argued from Garstang's and Kenyon's pottery, the tomb scarabs and one radiocarbon date that the destruction came about 1400 BCE. Piotr Bienkowski answered him in the same magazine (BAR 16:5).

The Italian-Palestinian expedition has worked at the site since 1997. Its 2019-2023 report (Nigro & Yasine, Vicino Oriente 29, 2024) dates the MB city's final destruction by radiocarbon to 1550-1525 BCE. The same report documents Late Bronze Age reoccupation, with 15th-century pottery in rooms by Garstang's 'Middle Building', and reuse of the old wall line. It also documents Iron Age I-II houses and an Iron Age II ostracon.
evidence: The last MB city (Sultan IVc / City IV) was destroyed by fire. Walls and floors were burned and mudbrick collapsed against the stone revetment (Garstang; Kenyon; Nigro & Yasine 2024 §§5-6).

Storage jars full of grain lay in the destruction. Wood (1990) reports that Kenyon recovered 'six bushels of grain in one season'. The Sapienza team found an array of grain jars in destruction layer F.2331/2332 (Nigro & Yasine 2024 §6.2).
Radiocarbon on short-lived cereal grains from Kenyon's final MB destruction gave a weighted average of 3306 ± 7 BP (Bruins & van der Plicht 1995), calibrated to the late 17th or 16th century BCE.

New 14C: final destruction of the MB city at 1550-1525 BCE (House A341). The 'Hyksos Palace' fire is dated to about 1530 BCE and the earlier Sultan IVb palace destruction to 1635 BCE (Nigro & Yasine 2024, §§5.1, 6.2-6.3).
The collapsed 'double wall' on the summit that Garstang tied to the conquest is Early Bronze Age. Kenyon established this, and Wood (1990) accepts it: 'In this she was right and Garstang wrong.'

Late Bronze reoccupation (Sultan V): rooms by Garstang's 'Middle Building' yielded 15th-century BCE pottery, including a Cypriot White Slip II bowl. The same horizon produced the cuneiform tablet Garstang found (Nigro & Yasine 2024, §6.4). Windle (2026) cites Nigro (2023) for an LB II mudbrick wall, 2 m wide, set on top of the old Cyclopean wall.

Wood (1990) reports one charcoal sample from the final Bronze Age destruction dated '1410 B.C.E., plus or minus 40 years' (BM-1790). The ABR repost now adds an editorial note flagging an update on this C-14 datum.

Iron Age: houses of Sultan VIa (Iron I, radiocarbon 977 ± 45 BCE) sit on the Spring Hill. An ostracon (TS.19.P.1404/2) was found in 2019 in an Iron IIB surface layer. It is incised on an older EB IV sherd and reads ʾš wʾšt, 'man and woman' (Puech 2024).
questions: When did City IV fall? J. Garstang (PEQ 67, 1935) put it about 1400 BCE, from destruction-level pottery, tomb scarabs and the absence of Mycenaean ware. K. Kenyon (Digging Up Jericho, 1957) put it about 1550 BCE. As Wood (1990) characterizes her case, it rested mainly on the absence of imported Cypriot pottery diagnostic of LB I. B. G. Wood (BAR 16:2, 1990, 44-58) answered with local LB I pottery forms, Garstang's Cypriot bichrome, a continuous scarab series (Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Amenhotep III), 20 architectural phases that he said cannot fit in Kenyon's timespan, and C-14 BM-1790 at 1410 ± 40 BCE. P. Bienkowski (BAR 16:5, 1990) rejected Wood's pottery and stratigraphic arguments as flawed. The later radiocarbon on short-lived grain supports a 16th-century end: Bruins & van der Plicht (1995) at 3306 ± 7 BP, and Nigro & Yasine (2024) at 1550-1525 BCE. The pottery-and-scarab case for c. 1400 is Wood's.

Was Jericho a walled city in the Late Bronze Age? Kenyon found only scant 14th-century occupation. Nigro & Yasine (2024) report 15th-century pottery and LB buildings over the burned palace. Windle (2026), citing Nigro (2023), reports an LB II mudbrick wall set on the old Cyclopean wall. What remains open is whether that wall existed in LB I or only later, and how large the LB town was.

What was Iron Age Jericho? Nigro & Yasine (2024) hold that in Iron IIA (960-840 BCE) Jericho was 'in all likelihood a city of the Kingdom of Moab', and they tentatively identify it with Qeriho in the Mesha Stele. É. Puech (2024), publishing the ostracon from the same excavation, reads its ʾšt ('woman') as a form attested only in Phoenician and its Canaanite ancestor. He judges that the spelling 'is not in favour of a Benjaminite, Hebrew-speaking occupation' but points to a Canaanite one. He dates it by palaeography to about 900-730 BCE. The ostracon itself is not Moabite by Puech's reading.
Unknown: the cause of the MB wall collapse (earthquake, assault, or fire damage). The excavation reports describe the collapse but do not settle its cause.

biblical.tie: 'The wall fell down flat… And they burnt the city with fire.' Tell es-Sultan's last MB city has collapsed mudbrick at the foot of its revetment and a burn layer. Correspondence in kind is clear. Correspondence in date depends on the dispute above: c. 1550-1525 BCE by radiocarbon, c. 1400 BCE on Wood's reading.

Rahab's house on the wall and flax on the roof. Wood (1990, via ABR) points to houses built against the lower city wall on the north side, which Sellin & Watzinger found still standing. That is his reading, not a find labelled as Rahab's.

The city was 'devoted' and its goods not taken. Full grain jars left in the burn layer fit a city that was not plundered for food and fell after harvest. Wood draws this inference; the jars themselves are the evidence.
The curse on rebuilding and Hiel's refounding in Ahab's day. Iron II occupation is attested (Sultan VIb-c, Nigro & Yasine 2024). That is consistent with a 9th-century town, but nothing names Hiel.

Eglon of Moab takes 'the city of palm trees'. Nigro & Yasine (2024) cite this passage for a Moabite Jericho in Iron IIA. That is their reading of the site; Puech reads the ostracon's language as Canaanite.
Elisha heals Jericho's spring. The tell sits beside ʿEin es-Sultan, the spring that has always made settlement here possible.
