corrections: The old entry named 'Kathleen Bimson' as a 1990s-present excavator. No such excavator exists. The 1990 case for a c. 1400 BCE destruction was Bryant G. Wood's (BAR 16:2). John J. Bimson argued for re-dating the Exodus in print but did not dig at Jericho. The 1997-present excavations are the Italian-Palestinian expedition (Nigro, Marchetti, Taha, Yasine).
The old entry said Garstang excavated in the 'early 20th century'. Garstang dug in 1930-1936. The early-20th-century excavation was Sellin & Watzinger's (1907-1909, 1911).

The old entry said Kenyon saw the destruction as 'part of a broader regional collapse rather than a specific conquest'. Kenyon's specific claims were a date (end of MB, c. 1550 BCE) and that Garstang's 'double wall' was Early Bronze Age. She did not document a 'regional collapse' as the cause.

The old entry said 'recent excavations... suggest [the destruction] may align more closely with the biblical narrative'. The latest excavators' radiocarbon puts the final MB destruction at 1550-1525 BCE (Nigro & Yasine 2024), which supports Kenyon's date. The c. 1400 BCE case rests on Wood's 1990 reading of the pottery, scarabs and one BM date.

The old entry gave the layer thickness as 'up to 5 meters thick' and said walls were 'systematically dismantled'. Neither claim was found in the reports consulted. Wood describes the destruction debris as 'a yard or more thick'.

The old entry listed Judges 6-7 (Midianites) and Genesis 13 (Lot's separation). Neither passage concerns Jericho: Judges 6-7 is set in the Jezreel valley, and Genesis 13 speaks of the Jordan plain without naming Jericho. The relevant texts are Joshua 2 and 6, Judges 3:13, 1 Kings 16:34 and 2 Kings 2:19-22.

The old entry described Jericho as 'one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities'. The tell was not continuously inhabited. The reports record gaps, for example after the MB destruction and between LB and Iron occupation phases.

updates.what: Nigro & Yasine publish the 2019-2023 interim report. New 14C dates put the final Middle Bronze destruction at 1550-1525 BCE and the 'Hyksos Palace' fire at about 1530 BCE. The report documents 15th-century LB rooms and argues for Moabite control of Jericho in Iron IIA (960-840 BCE).

Puech publishes the ostracon found in 2019 (TS.19.P.1404/2), ʾš wʾšt, 'man and woman'. It comes from an Iron IIB layer and is dated palaeographically to about 900-730 BCE. Puech reads the language as Canaanite (Phoenician-type ʾšt), not Hebrew, and does not call it Moabite.
20th campaign (May and September 2024), mainly conservation and sampling across Areas A-G and the Neolithic tower.
Windle's 'Latest Research' series summarizes Nigro's case for a Late Bronze II mudbrick wall on the old Cyclopean wall and City V resettlement c. 1450 BCE.

sites.name: Jerubba'al inscription, Khirbet al-Ra'i
sites.subtitle: Proto-Canaanite ink inscription on a small jug · late 12th - early 11th century BCE
sites.date: Late 12th or first half of the 11th century BCE (c. 1150-1050 BCE)
sites.date_basis: Archaeological context: fill of stone-lined Silo A310 in an earlier Iron Age I phase of Area A, dated by its pottery (bell-shaped bowls absent from Lachish Level VI; CP-5 cooking pot rim) to the second half of the 12th and the 11th century BCE, and lying stratigraphically below the upper Iron Age I level radiometrically dated to c. 1050 BCE. The editors state the palaeographic date agrees (Rollston et al. 2021: 6-8, 12).

discovery.when: Two sherds on the last day of the 2019 season; a third sherd in the 2020 season
discovery.who: Khirbet al-Ra'i expedition (Yosef Garfinkel, Hebrew University; Saar Ganor, Israel Antiquities Authority; Kyle H. Keimer and Gil Davis, Macquarie University); read by Christopher Rollston
discovery.where: Khirbet al-Ra'i, 4 km west of Tel Lachish, Judean Shephelah: Area A, probe in the south-eastern side, sifted fill of Silo A310

sites.location: Israel Antiquities Authority (photographed by Dafna Gazit, IAA); no museum or inventory number located

physical.material: Brown ink on pottery: three sherds of one small closed vessel, perhaps a jug, painted, burnished and kiln-fired

overview: Three small sherds of one painted and burnished closed vessel, perhaps a jug, carry letters written in brown ink in Proto-Canaanite (early alphabetic) script. Two were found on the last day of the 2019 season in the sifted fill of a stone-lined silo (A310) in Area A at Khirbet al-Ra'i, a 1.7-hectare site 4 km west of Lachish; the third turned up when the whole silo was emptied and sifted in 2020. The silo had become a dump for household rubbish in an earlier Iron Age I phase.

Two sherds join exactly and preserve five letters. The editors read the second to fifth as resh, bet, ayin (with the dot 'pupil' of the old eye-sign) and lamed; the first is only partly preserved and is 'most consistent' with a yod. Read right to left this gives Yrb'l, the personal name Jerubba'al. Traces of a sixth letter on the joined sherds and of two letters on the third sherd cannot be read.

The editio princeps (Rollston, Garfinkel, Keimer, Davis and Ganor, Jerusalem Journal of Archaeology 2, 2021) notes that Jerubba'al is the name given to Gideon in Judges 6:32, but states that no patronymic is present and that an identification with the biblical figure would need a patronymic, title or epithet. They date the context to the late 12th or early 11th century BCE and present it as the first Iron Age I inscription from the Shephelah, bridging the Late Bronze Age Lachish texts and the 10th-century Qeiyafa and Beth-Shemesh texts.

text.quote: [y]rb'l -- 'Jerubba'al' (the first letter partly preserved, read as yod)
text.translation: Our transliteration and rendering of the reading in Rollston et al., Jerusalem Journal of Archaeology 2 (2021): 8, 12. No public-domain translation exists (found 2019).

evidence: Found in Silo A310, Area A, Khirbet al-Ra'i: two sherds on the last day of the 2019 season, a third in 2020 when the whole silo was sifted (Rollston et al. 2021: 3-4).
All three sherds belong to one small closed vessel, perhaps a jug, painted, burnished and fired; no other joining sherds were found in the probe (Rollston et al. 2021: 4).
Brown ink; eight letters or traces in total on the three sherds; five decipherable on the two joined sherds (Rollston et al. 2021: 8).
Letters 2-5 are clear: resh, bet, ayin, lamed. Letter 1 is incomplete; the editors prefer yod but name aleph and ed (dh) as possible alternatives (Rollston et al. 2021: 8, 12).

The ayin retains its internal dot, and the bet stands rotated 90 degrees from its Phoenician stance, features the editors use to classify the script as Proto-Canaanite rather than Phoenician or Old Hebrew (Rollston et al. 2021: 11).
Direction of writing is argued, not given: read left to right the letters could yield l- plus 'bry; the editors prefer right to left because of the stance of the resh (Rollston et al. 2021: 11-12).
No patronymic is present (Rollston et al. 2021: 9).
Context date: pottery of the second half of the 12th and the 11th century BCE, stratigraphically below a level radiocarbon-dated to c. 1050 BCE, giving c. 1150-1050 BCE (Rollston et al. 2021: 6-7).
The silo fill was domestic rubbish of a few hundred sherds, no complete vessels (Rollston et al. 2021: 4, 6).
questions: Is the first letter a yod? Rollston et al. (JJAR 2, 2021: 12) read the partly preserved first sign as yod, comparing the Lachish ewer, but state the traces could be aleph (giving a Ba'al name with the root nwr, 'light') or ed (dh). The reading Jerubba'al depends on this one incomplete letter.

Which direction does it read? The editors (2021: 11-12) prefer right to left because of the stance of the resh; they allow that left to right could read as a lamed plus 'bry, a name or ethnic term. Proto-Canaanite of this period was not fixed in direction (they compare the left-to-right Qubur Walaydah lamed).

Is this Gideon? The editors (2021: 9) say it 'would be tempting' but, following Mykytiuk (2004: 32), an identification needs a patronymic, title or epithet, and none is present; they note Gideon is placed at Ophrah of Manasseh (Judg 6:11), 'not the same region' though 'not that distant'. Keimer, Davis, Ganor and Garfinkel (Biblical Archaeology Review, Winter 2025, as summarised by BAS, Feb 2026) again treat it as evidence of the name in the period, not of the biblical man. No publication located argues the vessel was Gideon's.

What does the name mean? The editors (2021: 9-10) follow Noth (1928) in deriving it from rby/rbb with Ba'al, 'May Ba'al be great', and note that Judges 6:32 gives a folk etymology from ryb, 'let Ba'al contend'. They add that ba'al ('lord') could early on refer to Yahweh (e.g. the name Bealiah, 1 Chr 12:5/6). This is the editors' reading of the name, not something the three sherds decide.

biblical.tie: Joash says 'Let Baal plead against him'; 'Therefore on that day he called him Jerubbaal' (KJV). The sherds carry the same consonants, yrb'l, from the same general period (12th-11th c. BCE). The inscription has no patronymic, so it attests the name, not the man.

Further uses of Jerubbaal as Gideon's name. The inscription shows the name was in real use in southern Canaan in Iron Age I; its findspot is in the Shephelah, while Gideon's Ophrah is in Manasseh (Judg 6:11).
The name altered to Jerubbesheth, with 'shame' replacing Ba'al. The editors cite this as the later pejorative treatment of Ba'al names; the inscription preserves the unaltered form.

sources.cite: Rollston, C., Garfinkel, Y., Keimer, K. H., Davis, G. and Ganor, S. 2021. "The Jerubba'al Inscription from Khirbet al-Ra'i: A Proto-Canaanite (Early Alphabetic) Inscription." Jerusalem Journal of Archaeology 2: 1-15. doi:10.52486/01.00002.1
sources.verified: Downloaded and read the full PDF text (pp. 1-13): context in Silo A310, 2019/2020 finds, pottery and radiometric date, reading yrb'l with alternatives, direction, patronymic caveat citing Mykytiuk 2004: 32. Note: the printed DOI 10.52486/01.00002.1 returned 404 at doi.org and was not found in the Crossref API on 2026-09-27 (prefix 10.52486 is registered with Crossref), so it is given as printed on the article.

sources.verified: Fetched: joint IAA/Hebrew University announcement; Garfinkel quote 'we cannot tell whether he owned the vessel'; 'first hard evidence' claim; small liter-sized locally produced jug, c. 1100 BCE.

updates.what: Biblical Archaeology Society re-issued its 2021 report; no new data.
Excavators' Biblical Archaeology Review (Winter 2025) overview of Khirbet al-Ra'i, discussing a possible Ziklag identification and mentioning the Jerubbaal sherd; no change to the reading.

corrections: Headlines presenting it as 'evidence of Gideon' (e.g. CBN 'Israeli Archaeologists Uncover Evidence of Gideon', Dec 2022, seen in search results) go beyond the editors, who state no patronymic is present and an identification cannot be made (Rollston et al. 2021: 9; Garfinkel: 'we cannot tell whether he owned the vessel', Times of Israel 2021).

Press describing a 'five-letter inscription' on 'three sherds' (Times of Israel 2021) conflates two things: the five letters are on the two joined sherds; the three sherds together carry eight letters or traces, three of them unreadable (Rollston et al. 2021: 8).
The name is often given as fully legible. The first letter is only partly preserved; yod is the editors' preferred reading over aleph or ed (Rollston et al. 2021: 12).

Claims that it is 'the first inscription to be found from the time of the Judges' (e.g. ABR, Wood 2022; ynet 2021 'first-ever inscription from time of biblical judges', seen in search results) are broader than the editio princeps, which says only that no Iron Age I inscription had previously been found in the Shephelah, and itself cites the Qubur Walaydah inscription for comparison (Rollston et al. 2021: 11-12).
The meaning is often given as 'let Baal contend'. That is the folk etymology in Judges 6:32; the editors derive the name, with Noth, from rby/rbb, 'May Ba'al be great' (Rollston et al. 2021: 9-10).

sites.name: Radiocarbon Chronology of Iron Age Jerusalem (Regev et al., PNAS 2024)
sites.subtitle: 103 radiocarbon dates from the City of David and the Giv'ati Parking Lot · published April 2024
sites.date: Samples span the 12th century BCE to the Babylonian destruction of 586 BCE; published online 29 April 2024 (PNAS 121/19)
sites.date_basis: 103 AMS radiocarbon measurements on short-lived single items (about two-thirds seeds) from stratified contexts, measured at the Weizmann Institute (lab codes RTD...). Wiggle-matched against the calibration curve and checked against 100 single tree-ring measurements from calendar-dated Irish oak.

discovery.when: Sampling during excavations of the 2010s-2020s; published 2024
discovery.who: J. Regev, Y. Gadot, J. Uziel, O. Chalaf, Y. Shalev, H. Roth, N. Shalom, N. Szanton, E. Bocher, C. L. Pearson, D. M. Brown, E. Mintz, L. Regev, E. Boaretto (Weizmann Institute, Tel Aviv University, Israel Antiquities Authority)
discovery.where: Southeastern Ridge ('City of David') Areas C and U (Spring Tower, Fortified Passage, Mid-Slope fortification), Area E (Shiloh's area, section T5), and Giv'ati Parking Lot Areas 10 and 70-south (Building 100)

sites.location: Data and supplementary appendix published with PNAS 121(19) e2321024121; the excavation areas are in situ in Jerusalem
overview: Until this study, the absolute dates for Iron Age Jerusalem rested on pottery typology, stratigraphy and the biblical text. Regev and colleagues took single charred items (mostly seeds) from tightly controlled contexts in five excavation areas and dated 103 of them. They also dated 100 individual tree rings from calendar-dated Irish oak to test the calibration curve across the 'Hallstatt plateau' (c. 800-400 BCE), where radiocarbon normally loses resolution.

The paper reports four results. Occupation in the 12th-10th centuries BCE is shown by 18 dates, which the authors call 'widespread occupation of yet undetermined character'. There was extensive building and westward expansion in the 9th century BCE, including Building 100 in the Giv'ati Parking Lot and the Spring Tower area. An earthquake destruction is dated to c. 766-750 BCE, which the authors link to Amos 1:1. Fortifications that had been credited to Hezekiah are reassigned to the later years of Uzziah.

The study also found that measured radiocarbon ages depart from the calibration curve around 730-710 BCE and around 586 BCE. The authors present this as a correction others must apply when dating late Iron Age sites in the region.
evidence: 103 archaeological radiocarbon measurements plus 100 single-ring measurements from dated Irish oak (PNAS 2024).

18 of the 103 dates (almost 20%) fall in the 12th-10th centuries BCE. Only three of them (RTD10780, 9598, 9585) come from contexts with clearly associated early Iron Age pottery; the rest are charred remains in building materials.
A twig in Room 17049 (Area U), 'perhaps representing roofing material', dated to the 10th century BCE (RTD11182).
Dates from beneath the Spring Tower at the Gihon Spring span the 10th-9th centuries BCE.
A 9th-century BCE date was obtained for construction in Area U (Room 19040) and for the start of Building 100 in the Giv'ati Parking Lot, which the authors say stayed in use until 586 BCE.
Earthquake horizon: combined 2507 ± 8 uncal BP, calibrated c. 766-750 BCE.
In Area 70-south, two of three OSL (luminescence) dates were older than the radiocarbon dates from the same spots, with non-overlapping ranges.
Neither the Stepped Stone Structure nor the Large Stone Structure was sampled; the paper does not mention them.
The paper names neither David nor Solomon; the biblical references it makes are Amos 1:1 (earthquake) and 2 Kgs 15-16 (Uzziah / Syro-Ephraimite war).
questions: What kind of 10th-century Jerusalem? Regev et al. (PNAS 2024) show 12th-10th century occupation but call it 'of yet undetermined character', because only 3 of the 18 early dates have diagnostic pottery. Y. Garfinkel (JEMAHS 12/4, 2024) sets these dates beside Khirbet Qeiyafa (c. 30 dates, 1000-970 BCE) and the Gezer six-chambered gate dates (Webster et al. 2023) and reads them as a flourishing early kingdom of Judah; he cites Regev et al. for monumental building in 9th-century Jerusalem. The Jerusalem dates alone do not decide whether the 10th-century settlement was a capital.

Who built the 8th-century fortifications? Regev et al. (2024) date the Mid-Slope fortification to after the c. 760 BCE earthquake and credit it to Uzziah in the Syro-Ephraimite war period. The attribution they revise credited these works to Hezekiah in the late 8th century (their ref. 59); readers who keep Hezekiah usually cite 2 Chr 32:5 and Isa 22:10, but in Regev et al.'s reading the dated sequence puts construction soon after the c. 760 BCE earthquake, earlier than Hezekiah. Vukosavovic, Shalev, Roth, Chalaf and Uziel (Tel Aviv, July 2026, 'In the Wake of the Amos Quake') return to the mid-8th-century fortifications; that article's argument has not been reviewed for this entry.

Does radiocarbon agree with luminescence? In Area 70-south, two of three OSL dates came out older than radiocarbon from the same spots (PNAS 2024 SI Figs. S39, S41). The paper reports this and leaves it unresolved.
I. Finkelstein circulated a response in May 2024 ('Observations on the article Regev et al.', academia.edu). The page was not accessible for this entry, so its arguments are not stated here.

biblical.tie: Radiocarbon shows people living and building on the Southeastern Ridge in the 12th-10th centuries BCE, the time the Bible gives for the Jebusite city, David's capture and Solomon's reign. The dates show occupation. They do not show who ruled, how large the town was, or any particular building the Bible describes.
The authors link a destruction layer dated c. 766-750 BCE (2507 ± 8 BP) to 'the earthquake' by which Amos dates his book. That link is their reading.

The authors credit the post-earthquake Mid-Slope fortification to Uzziah. 2 Chr 26:9 does say Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem and fortified them. The date is the paper's evidence; the name Uzziah is its reading.
Building 100 and other structures end in the conflagration the paper dates to 586 BCE, which is also the anchor for the second calibration offset.

corrections: Headlines that the study 'proves David and Solomon's kingdom': the paper names neither king. It reports 12th-10th century occupation 'of yet undetermined character' and says only 3 of 18 early dates have diagnostic pottery.
Claims that the study dated the Stepped Stone Structure or the Large Stone Structure ('David's palace'): neither was sampled or mentioned.
Claims that Hezekiah's wall was re-dated to Uzziah as a fact: the date (after the c. 760 BCE earthquake) is measured; the attribution to Uzziah is the authors' reading of that date.

Claims that radiocarbon 'cannot date the Iron Age II' because of the Hallstatt plateau: the study reached decadal resolution in parts of the plateau by wiggle-matching sequences and checking against 100 dated tree rings.

updates.what: PNAS publishes a follow-on piece by Levy, Smith, Najjar, Vaknin and Ben-Yosef, 'Absolute dating, the Bible, and World cultural heritage'.
Garfinkel (JEMAHS 12/4) uses the Jerusalem dates alongside Qeiyafa and Gezer to argue for a 10th-century kingdom of Judah.
The same Weizmann/IAA team dates the Siloam Pool dam to c. 800 BCE (PNAS 122/35), extending the 9th-century waterworks picture.
Vukosavovic et al. publish on the mid-8th-century fortifications after the 'Amos quake' in Tel Aviv.

sites.name: Khirbet Qeiyafa Fortifications
sites.subtitle: Casemate wall and two four-chambered gates · late 11th-early 10th c. BCE
sites.date: Single Iron Age phase; olive pits from the destruction layer give c. 1000 BCE (Garfinkel et al. 2015). Finkelstein & Piasetzky's regional model places the site later, in the 10th c. BCE.
sites.date_basis: AMS 14C on short-lived samples (burnt olive pits) from the destruction layer (Radiocarbon 54, 2012; 57, 2015), plus Iron I/IIA pottery; disputed by a regional Bayesian model (Finkelstein & Piasetzky, Radiocarbon 57, 2015).

discovery.when: Excavated 2007-2013 (five seasons)
discovery.who: Yosef Garfinkel (Hebrew University of Jerusalem) and Saar Ganor (Israel Antiquities Authority)
discovery.where: Hilltop on the north side of the Elah Valley, between Azekah and Socoh, Judean Shephelah, Israel

sites.location: In situ, Khirbet Qeiyafa, Elah Valley, Israel

physical.material: Casemate wall of large (megalithic) stones; Hellenistic additions in smaller stones on top
physical.dimensions: Enclosed area 2.3 ha; c. 200 m of the casemate wall exposed

overview: Khirbet Qeiyafa is a 2.3-hectare hilltop town above the Elah Valley enclosed by a casemate wall of very large stones. The Hebrew University and Israel Antiquities Authority excavated about a fifth of it in 2007-2013 under Yosef Garfinkel and Saar Ganor.

The wall has two gates, west and south, each with four chambers. Millard (2011) notes the west gate was 'inserted where a space had been designed for it as the wall was built', and that the casemate rooms served as back rooms of the houses built against the wall. A Hellenistic occupation lies directly on the Iron Age town with nothing in between.
The Iron Age town was short-lived and ended in a sudden destruction that left hundreds of restorable vessels. Burnt olive pits from that destruction were radiocarbon-dated to about 1000 BCE.
evidence: Casemate wall with megalithic stones; small-stone Hellenistic additions at the top (Millard 2011, p. 4).
Two gates, west and south, each with four chambers (project website; Millard 2011).
Casemate chambers integrated into houses as back rooms (Millard 2011, p. 4).
Single Iron Age phase ending in destruction with 'hundreds of restorable pottery vessels, stone utensils and metal objects' (project website).
17 burnt olive-pit samples from a jar in the destruction layer, some split between two laboratories: '~1000 BC' (Garfinkel et al., Radiocarbon 57, 2015).
questions: Date: Garfinkel et al. (Radiocarbon 54, 2012; 57, 2015) date the destruction to c. 1000 BCE from on-site olive pits; Finkelstein & Piasetzky (Radiocarbon 57, 2015) combine 14C from six Shephelah sites in a Bayesian model and push Qeiyafa into the 10th c., later than the excavators' estimate.

Who built it: Garfinkel & Ganor (JHS 8, 2008) treat it as a Judahite stronghold of David's kingdom; Na'aman (JHS 17, 2017) argues nothing in the published finds ties it to Jerusalem or the highlands and that its trade links point to a Shephelah context.

Identification: Garfinkel & Ganor (JHS 8, 2008) identify it as Sha'arayim ('two gates') because it is the only Iron Age site in Judah or Israel with two gates. Other identifications have been proposed (Millard 2011, p. 4, notes this without detail). No name is written at the site.

biblical.tie: Places the Philistine-Israelite confrontation in the Elah Valley between Socoh and Azekah and names Sha'arayim on the Philistine retreat route. The site sits in that valley and has two gates; the name identification is the excavators' reading.
Lists Sha'arayim among Shephelah towns of Judah near Azekah and Socoh.

sources.cite: Khirbet Qeiyafa Archaeological Project, Hebrew University of Jerusalem (project website).
sources.verified: Home page read: 2.3 ha; casemate wall with megalithic stones, c. 200 m exposed; two gates (west and south) 'each with four chambers'; excavations 2007-2013, directors Garfinkel and Ganor; 'the first early Judean city to be dated by 14C'.

sites.name: Khirbet Qeiyafa Ostracon
sites.subtitle: Five-line ink inscription on a jar sherd · c. 1000 BCE
sites.date: Destruction layer of the single Iron Age phase at Khirbet Qeiyafa: c. 1000 BCE by the excavators' 14C (Garfinkel et al. 2015); later 10th c. BCE by Finkelstein & Piasetzky's regional model (2015).
sites.date_basis: Find context (Building 2, Iron Age level) and 14C of olive pits from the same destruction; the script, which Millard (2011) calls 'Canaanite' rather than Phoenician or Hebrew, fits the late 11th-10th c.

discovery.who: Khirbet Qeiyafa excavation (Y. Garfinkel, S. Ganor); first published by Haggai Misgav
discovery.where: Room adjacent to a casemate in Building 2, north of the west gate, Khirbet Qeiyafa

sites.location: Studied at the Institute of Archaeology, Hebrew University of Jerusalem (project site). Current display/inventory number Not confirmed in a published museum record.

physical.material: Pottery sherd from a large jar, black ink
physical.dimensions: Max. 15 x 16.5 cm (Millard 2011)
physical.script: Early alphabetic ('Canaanite' letter forms per Millard; 'Proto-Canaanite/Early Alphabetic' per excavators)
physical.language: Disputed: Hebrew (Misgav, Galil, Puech) or undetermined Canaanite (Millard: could be Hebrew, Canaanite, Phoenician or Moabite)

overview: A sherd from a large storage jar with five lines of black-ink writing, found in 2008 in Building 2 next to the casemate wall north of the west gate at Khirbet Qeiyafa. At about 15 x 16.5 cm it carries more alphabetic text than any other inscription of its date from the region (Millard 2011).

The letters are irregular, some are abraded, the same letter appears in different stances, and the direction of reading was at first uncertain. Haggai Misgav published the editio princeps in Khirbet Qeiyafa Vol. 1 (2009) and read only some words; Ada Yardeni, Aaron Demsky and Shmuel Ahituv also offered partial readings.

Full readings followed from Gershon Galil (Ugarit-Forschungen 41, 2009) and Émile Puech (Revue Biblique 117, 2010), which differ from each other. Alan Millard (2011), following Ed Cook, argued the simplest reading is a list of personal names.

text.quote: Line 1 as transliterated by Millard: ʾ l t ʿ š / w ʿ b d ʾ ... Read as words: 'Do not do [it], and serve/make ...' (Misgav, Galil) or as names: 'Ellat-ʿash and ʿEbed-...' (Cook, Millard). Line 2 opens špṭ: 'judge' / 'he judged', or the name Shaphat.
text.translation: Literal rendering (this encyclopedia) of the transliteration printed in A. Millard, Tyndale Bulletin 62.1 (2011), pp. 8-10; not a published translation.
text.quote_type: own literal translation of published transliteration

evidence: Ink on a jar sherd, max. 15 x 16.5 cm; lines possibly missing above line 1 and at the right edge (Millard 2011, p. 4).
Word divider of three vertical dots appears in line 1 only (Millard, p. 7).
Clearly legible sequences include špṭ at the start of line 2, nqm in the middle of line 4, and bdmlk at the end of line 4 (Millard, pp. 9-11).
Letter forms are inconsistent and 'not the work of an experienced scribe' (Millard, p. 4).
Found in a single-phase Iron Age town dated by 14C to c. 1000 BCE (Garfinkel et al. 2015).
questions: What it says: Misgav (Khirbet Qeiyafa 1, 2009, pp. 255-256) holds the verbs in line 1 are Hebrew and the text is a message with judicial or ethical commands; Galil (UF 41, 2009) reads a social statement ('Judge the slave and the widow...'); Puech (RB 117, 2010) reads a narrative about oppression and the establishing of a king; Demsky and Ahituv (2009 conference, per Millard n. 15) treat it as a writing exercise; Cook and Millard (Tyndale Bulletin 62, 2011) read a list of names (Ellat-ʿash, ʿEbed-..., Shaphat, Bodmilk), noting that nqm-names are Phoenician and ʿlmn ('widow') needs an unseen n.

Language: the reading ʾal taʿaś ('do not do') makes the text Hebrew because ʿśh is otherwise known only in Hebrew and Moabite; Millard (2011) shows the same five letters can be a personal name, which removes that argument.
Date: tied to the site's destruction, c. 1000 BCE (Garfinkel et al., Radiocarbon 57, 2015) or later 10th c. (Finkelstein & Piasetzky, Radiocarbon 57, 2015).

biblical.tie: The sherd comes from the Elah Valley site the excavators connect with the David-Goliath setting; the text itself mentions no person or place known from the Bible.
Galil's reading (judge the slave, widow, orphan, stranger) parallels this legal language; that parallel exists only on his restoration of damaged letters (e.g. ʾlmn).

sites.name: Kuntillet 'Ajrud (Horvat Teman) inscriptions
sites.subtitle: Iron Age way-station in northeastern Sinai with ink and plaster inscriptions naming YHWH of Samaria and YHWH of Teman · c. 800 BCE
sites.date: Late 9th to first half of 8th century BCE. Radiocarbon places construction at c. 820-795 BCE and abandonment after 745 BCE; the date is disputed on pottery grounds.
sites.date_basis: Radiocarbon determinations re-analysed by Finkelstein and Piasetzky (Tel Aviv 35, 2008), plus ceramic comparison (Ayalon 1995; Freud 2008 against Singer-Avitz 2006, 2009). The inscriptions are dated with the site and by palaeography.

discovery.who: Ze'ev Meshel (Tel Aviv University); inscriptions published by Shmuel Ahituv, Esther Eshel and Meshel
discovery.where: Kuntillet 'Ajrud, on the Darb el-Ghazza route in northeastern Sinai (Egypt)

sites.location: Site in northeastern Sinai. The present repository of the pithoi and plaster fragments is not stated in the sources cited here.

physical.material: Ink on two large storage jars (pithoi A and B); ink on wall plaster; incised inscriptions on storage jars and stone vessels
physical.script: Hebrew in a Phoenician-type script (Zevit 2001: 377-378, cited by Smoak and Schniedewind 2019, calls 'Phoenician' anachronistic here)
physical.language: Hebrew with northern (Israelite) features; theophoric names in -yaw

overview: Kuntillet 'Ajrud is a small Iron Age building complex on a hill by wells in northeastern Sinai, on the Darb el-Ghazza route. Ze'ev Meshel excavated it in 1975-1976 and titled his 2012 final report 'An Iron Age II Religious Site on the Judah-Sinai Border'. The 2015 Hebrew edition, 'To YHWH of Teman and His Ashera', dropped the 'religious site' label and replaced Pirhiya Beck's chapter on the drawings with one by Tallay Ornan.

The inscriptions are the reason the site is famous. They are blessing formulas written in ink on two pithoi found in a bench room of the main building. Pithos A (KA 3.1) blesses 'by YHWH of Shomron (Samaria) and by his asherah'. Pithos B (KA 3.6, 3.9) blesses 'by YHWH of Teman and by his asherah'. A plaster text near the bench-room entrance (KA 4.2) describes a theophany in which El shines forth, the mountains melt, and Baal and 'the name of El' appear 'on the day of battle'. Four inscriptions carry the title sr 'r, 'commander of the fortress'.

Painted drawings on Pithos A include two figures that some identify as the Egyptian god Bes, and a lion beneath a tree with gazelles (as described by Smoak and Schniedewind 2019). Whether the figures are deities, and which ones, is disputed.

text.quote: [... I have blessed you] by YHWH of the Teman and by his asherah ... whatever he asks from a man, he (YHWH) will give generously ... and YHW will give to him according to his heart.
text.translation: Literal translation (this encyclopedia) of inscription KA 3.9 (Pithos B) from the transliteration [brktk] lyhwh.htmn wl'shrth ... kl 'shr ysh'l m'sh hnn h' ... wntn lh yhw klbbh, as published by Ahituv, Eshel and Meshel 2012 and quoted in Smoak and Schniedewind, Religions 10(3):211 (2019). No public-domain translation exists.

evidence: KA 3.1, red ink on Pithos A: '... I have [b]lessed you to YHWH of Shomron (Samaria) and to his 'asherah' (Ahituv et al. 2012: 87, as quoted by Smoak and Schniedewind 2019).

KA 3.6, Pithos B: 'Message of Amaryaw: Say to my lord, are you well? I have blessed you to YHWH of Teman and his 'asherah. May he bless you and may he guard you, and may he be with my lord' (Ahituv et al. 2012: 95, as quoted in the same).
KA 3.9, Pithos B: lyhwh.htmn wl'shrth, 'by YHWH of the Teman and by his asherah' (same).
KA 4.2, plaster near the western entrance of the bench room: names El, Baal and YHWH with theophany language ('when El shines forth ... the mountains will melt') (Ahituv et al. 2012: 110).
Four inscriptions carry the military title sr 'r, 'commander of the fortress': three on storage jars and one on plaster (Ahituv et al. 2015: 80-81, 113; Schniedewind 2019).
No temple, altar or conventional cult figurine was found. Schmidt (2016) notes that 'none of the standard diagnostics' of cult were found in the bench room (quoted by Smoak and Schniedewind 2019).
Personal names use the northern theophoric ending -yaw, and the pottery has been read as Israelite-influenced (Ayalon 2012). Singer-Avitz (2006) instead reads the bulk of the pottery as Judahite.
Radiocarbon: built c. 820-795 BCE and abandoned after 745 BCE; historical considerations may narrow this to c. 795-730/720 BCE (Finkelstein and Piasetzky 2008, abstract).
questions: What does 'his asherah' mean? Lemaire (Jerusalem Journal of Archaeology 7, 2024: 58-60) sets out four readings. (1) A goddess, Yahweh's consort: Dever (BASOR 255, 1984) and others, on the basis of Ugaritic Athirat. (2) A sanctuary: Cross (2009), Sass (2014) and Puech (2015), on the basis of Phoenician and Aramaic 'shrt meaning shrine. (3) A wooden pole standing for the goddess: Day (1992). (4) A sacred tree or grove: Na'aman and Lissovsky (Tel Aviv 35, 2008), and Lemaire, citing Deut 16:21, the Septuagint's alsos ('grove'), and Mishnah Avodah Zarah 3:7. Lemaire also notes that Ahituv translated the word as a goddess in 2008 and as 'a sacred cultic object' in 2012.

Was it a religious site? Meshel's 2012 report called it one. Hadley (1993) argued it has no temple, shrine or cult objects. Smoak and Schniedewind (Religions 2019) read it as a fortress and way-station whose texts include scribal practice letters. Na'aman and Lissovsky (2008) propose that the cult took place outside, around a sacred tree, and that the building served as the goddess's storehouse.

When was it occupied? Singer-Avitz (Tel Aviv 33, 2006) compared the pottery with Lachish III and down-dated the site to the end of the 8th century BCE. Freud (Tel Aviv 35, 2008) pointed to forms already present in Iron IIA and kept the late 9th to first half of the 8th century. Finkelstein and Piasetzky (Tel Aviv 35, 2008) used radiocarbon to put construction at c. 820-795 BCE. Singer-Avitz replied in Tel Aviv 36 (2009).

Who is drawn on Pithos A? Beck (1982; 2012) read the figures religiously. Ornan (2015; 2016) finds parallels for the drawings in Neo-Assyrian palace reliefs and reads the building as a royal or state outpost. Identifying the two figures as Bes, or one of them as Asherah, is not settled by the drawings themselves.

biblical.tie: Forbids planting an asherah, 'any tree', beside YHWH's altar and setting up a standing stone. Kuntillet 'Ajrud pairs YHWH with 'his asherah' in blessings, the practice this law bans. The exact nature of the asherah is the open question above.
Asherah in Samaria and later in Jerusalem, condemned by the Kings historian. The 'YHWH of Samaria and his asherah' formula is a firsthand northern example from the Jehu dynasty era.
God comes 'from Teman' or from Seir and Sinai, and the mountains quake or melt. The inscriptions have 'YHWH of Teman', and the plaster text has mountains melting when El shines forth.
'The LORD bless you and keep you'. KA 3.6 has 'may he bless you and may he guard you' in a letter formula, the same pair of verbs.

corrections: The inscriptions are often quoted as 'Yahweh and his Asherah' with a capital A, as if a goddess's personal name were certain. The Hebrew is l'shrth, 'his asherah', with a possessive suffix. Ahituv himself translated it as 'a sacred cultic object' in the 2012 final report (Lemaire 2024: 60).

A 'Kuntillet Ajrud final report' ISBN 978-965-221-088-3 circulates in online references. Open Library resolves that ISBN to a different book (the Hazor 1990-2009 Iron Age report), so it cannot be used for Meshel 2012.

The site is often called a temple. No temple, altar or conventional cult object was found (Hadley 1993; Schmidt 2016, quoted in Smoak and Schniedewind 2019), and the 2015 Hebrew edition dropped the 'religious site' label.

Calling the site 'Judahite' ignores the northern evidence: -yaw names, 'YHWH of Samaria', and pottery with northern ties. Singer-Avitz (2006) is the main dissent, reading the pottery as mostly Judahite.

sites.name: Kurkh Monolith (Stela of Shalmaneser III)
sites.subtitle: Assyrian royal stela naming 'Ahab the Israelite' at Qarqar · c. 852 BCE
sites.date: Text ends with the battle of Qarqar in Shalmaneser III's 6th regnal year (853 BCE); stela probably set up c. 852 BCE
sites.date_basis: Regnal-year sequence in the inscription, whose narrative stops at the 6th-year campaign (Qarqar); Assyrian regnal years are fixed by the eponym list. The British Museum dates the stela c. 852 BC, reasoning that Shalmaneser set it up during his campaign in the Diyarbakır region the following year.

discovery.who: John George Taylor, British consul in Diyarbakır (not Layard)
discovery.where: Kurkh (modern Üçtepe Höyük), Bismil district, Diyarbakır province, south-eastern Turkey

sites.location: British Museum, London, BM 118884 (registration 1863,0619.2); donated by Taylor in 1863. A companion stela of Ashurnasirpal II from the same find is BM 118883.

physical.material: Limestone, round-topped stela
physical.dimensions: c. 221 cm high, 87 cm wide, 23 cm deep
physical.script: Neo-Assyrian cuneiform, carved across the front (over the relief) and the back and sides

overview: A round-topped limestone stela showing Shalmaneser III standing before four divine emblems (winged disk of Aššur, star of Ištar, horned crown of Anu, crescent of Sîn), with an inscription covering his campaigns year by year from his accession to his sixth regnal year. It was found in 1861 at Kurkh on the upper Tigris by J. G. Taylor, together with a stela of Shalmaneser's father Ashurnasirpal II, and both went to the British Museum in 1863.

The last campaign recorded is the sixth-year march into Syria (853 BCE). Shalmaneser takes cities of Irḫulena of Hamath and destroys Qarqar, then lists the forces of a coalition of 'twelve kings' that met him there. The third entry is '2,000 chariots (and) 10,000 troops of Ahab (Aḫ-abbu) the Israelite (Sirʾalāyu)'. The king claims 14,000 enemy dead and a rout 'from Qarqar to Gilzau', and the text breaks off in the middle of the battle description.
The list is the earliest dated extra-biblical text that names a king of Israel. It is also the first cuneiform mention of 'Arabs' (Gindibu' with 1,000 camels).

text.quote: 1,200 chariots, 1,200 cavalry, 20,000 soldiers, of Hadad-ezer, of Aram (? Damascus); 700 chariots, 700 cavalry, 10,000 soldiers of Irhulêni of Hamath, 2,000 chariots, 10,000 soldiers of Ahab, the Israelite ...
text.translation: D. D. Luckenbill, Ancient Records of Assyria and Babylonia I (Chicago, 1926), §611, p. 223

evidence: Line ii 91-92 transliterated: 2 LIM GIŠ.GIGIR.MEŠ 10 LIM ERIM.MEŠ šá ma-ḫa-ab-bu KUR.sir-ʾa-la-a-a: '2,000 chariots, 10,000 troops of Ahab of the land Sir'ala (Israel)' (RIMA 3 A.0.102.2).

Coalition as listed: Hadad-ezer of Damascus 1,200 chariots / 1,200 cavalry / 20,000 troops; Irḫulena of Hamath 700 / 700 / 10,000; Ahab 2,000 chariots / 10,000 troops; plus contingents of Byblos(?), Egypt, Irqanatu, Arwad, Usanatu, Si'annu, Gindibu' the Arab (1,000 camels), and Ba'sa of Bīt-Ruḫubi (Ammon).
The contingent attributed to 'Byblos' is written KUR.gu-<bal>-a-a in the RIAo edition: the sign 'bal' is an editorial restoration, not on the stone; Luckenbill (1926) printed 'Gueans'.
Numbers of two contingents are broken ([N],000 troops of Adunu-ba'al; [N] hundred of Ba'sa), so the coalition total cannot be computed from the stone.
The text says 'these twelve kings' but names eleven rulers/lands (the count depends on how the list is divided).
Claimed Assyrian result: 14,000 enemy killed, pursuit 'from Qarqar to Gilzau'; the text ends at line ii 102 describing captured chariots and horses.
Relief: king before emblems of Aššur, Ištar, Anu and Sîn; inscription runs across the relief surface.
questions: Did Ahab really field 2,000 chariots, more than any other ally? Nadav Na'aman (Tel Aviv 3, 1976, 'Two Notes on the Monolith Inscription of Shalmaneser III from Kurkh') argued the figure is a scribal error and that Ahab's force was 200 chariots, on grounds that 2,000 is out of scale with the other contingents (Damascus 1,200, Hamath 700) and that the stela was carved with other scribal errors (his argument as summarized in later discussions; the article itself is not summarized here). Against emendation: the stone as carved reads 2 LIM (2,000). Shigeo Yamada's collation of the monolith (The Construction of the Assyrian Empire, 2000, pp. 380-383) is the published check on the carved signs.

Was Qarqar an Assyrian victory? The stela claims a rout, but the Black Obelisk annals record Shalmaneser fighting 'Hadad-ezer of Damascus and twelve kings of the land Ḫatti' again in his 11th regnal year and 'twelve kings' again in his 14th (RIMA 3 A.0.102.14 ll. 87-92). The RIAo introduction to Shalmaneser III reads Qarqar as a battle he 'may in fact have been defeated [in] or ... may have been a draw'.

Why is Ahab called 'Sir'ala-ite' here while Jehu is 'of Bīt-Ḫumrî' twelve years later? Brad Kelle (JBL 121, 2002) examined the Neo-Assyrian names for the northern kingdom and what they imply for Israelite history; the stone itself gives only KUR.sir-ʾa-la-a-a.

biblical.tie: Ahab king of Israel in Samaria. The stela names 'Ahab the Israelite' as a coalition member in 853 BCE; the Bible does not mention Qarqar.

Ahab fighting Ben-hadad of Aram, then 'three years without war between Aram and Israel'. On the stela, Ahab fights alongside Damascus (Hadad-ezer) against Assyria. Our reading: a temporary alliance against a common enemy; the text says nothing about relations before or after.
Israelite chariotry. The stela's 2,000-chariot figure (or 200 if Na'aman's emendation is right) is the only external number for Israel's chariot force.

sites.name: Lachish Letters
sites.subtitle: Hebrew military letters on potsherds from the gate of Lachish · c. 588-586 BCE
sites.date: Final years of Judah, just before Lachish fell to Nebuchadnezzar II (c. 588-586 BCE)
sites.date_basis: Found in the burnt destruction debris of the city gate complex of Lachish (Level II), attributed to the Babylonian campaign that ended with Jerusalem's fall in 586 BCE; the letters themselves carry no year.

discovery.when: January-February 1935 (most of the letters); a few more in 1938
discovery.who: James Leslie Starkey's Wellcome-Marston expedition to Tell ed-Duweir (Lachish)
discovery.where: Burnt remains of the gate complex (gate chamber), Tel Lachish

sites.location: Most in the British Museum, London; a smaller group, including Letter 6, in Jerusalem (Rockefeller Museum / Israel Antiquities Authority). Individual museum numbers circulate in secondary listings but were not checked against museum records.

physical.material: Pottery sherds (ostraca) written in ink

overview: Twenty-one inscribed potsherds found in the burnt gate complex of Lachish, most of them in 1935 by J. L. Starkey's expedition. Most are letters from a subordinate named Hoshayahu to his superior Ya'ush, written in ink in Hebrew during the Babylonian invasion that ended Judah's kingdom. They were first published by Harry Torczyner (later Tur-Sinai) in 1938.

Letter 3 reports that 'the commander of the army, Coniah son of Elnathan, has gone down to go to Egypt' and mentions a letter passed on through 'the prophet'. Letter 4 ends with the writer saying that they are watching for the fire-signals of Lachish according to the signs his lord gave, 'for we cannot see Azekah'.

Jeremiah 34:7 names Lachish and Azekah as the last fortified cities of Judah still holding out against Babylon. Letter 4 is read by many as a snapshot of that moment; what it literally says is that the writer's post could not see Azekah.

text.quote: Letter 4 (closing lines): the writer tells his lord that they are watching for the signal-fires of Lachish according to all the signs his lord has given, because they cannot see Azekah.
text.translation: Paraphrase of Lachish Letter 4 (Torczyner 1938 editio princeps; no public-domain English translation exists)

evidence: 21 ostraca, ink on pottery, Old Hebrew cursive; found in the burnt gate complex of Lachish (Windle 2025; CoJS).
Most are addressed to Ya'ush by his servant Hoshayahu (CoJS).
Letter 3 names 'Coniah son of Elnathan', commander of the army, who has 'gone down to go to Egypt', and refers to 'the prophet'.
Letter 4 closes: watching for the signals of Lachish; 'we cannot see Azekah'.
The word 'prophet' in Letter 3 line 20 is spelled without a yod (point made by Rollston in the Isaiah-bulla debate).
Found in the destruction layer of the gate complex, i.e. they were lying there when the city burned.
questions: Where were the letters written, and what are they? The long-standing reading (Torczyner 1938 and most later work, as summarised by CoJS) is that Hoshayahu commanded an outpost between Lachish and Jerusalem and sent these letters to Ya'ush at Lachish. Yigael Yadin argued instead that Hoshayahu was at Lachish itself and that the sherds are drafts or copies of letters sent (on papyrus) to Ya'ush in Jerusalem. Anson Rainey ('Watching Out for the Signal Fires of Lachish', PEQ 119, 1987) defended the outpost reading (as summarised by Windle 2025; Rainey's article itself not read).

Does 'we cannot see Azekah' mean Azekah had already fallen? That is a common inference tied to Jer 34:7. The letter itself only says the post could not see Azekah; it could also mean the line of sight was blocked or the signal was not lit. The text does not say Azekah fell.

Are the letters full texts? Person (Jerusalem Journal of Archaeology 7, 2024) argues that Iron Age Judahite written texts, including the Lachish letters, were metonymic stand-ins for fuller oral messages, so the ostraca 'did not necessarily contain the full' message.
Who is 'the prophet' in Letter 3? The name is not given. Identifications with Jeremiah or Uriah (Jer 26:20-23) are readings, not text.

biblical.tie: 'The king of Babylon's army fought against Jerusalem, and against all the cities of Judah that were left, against Lachish, and against Azekah: for these defenced cities remained.' Letter 4 names exactly Lachish and Azekah in a siege-signalling context.

Elnathan son of Achbor is sent to Egypt to fetch the prophet Uriah; Letter 3 has a 'Coniah son of Elnathan' going down to Egypt. Same patronym and destination; whether the same family is our inference.
The Babylonian siege of Judah's cities under Zedekiah, the setting of the destruction layer the letters were found in.

sites.name: Lachish Reliefs
sites.subtitle: Assyrian palace reliefs of Sennacherib's capture of Lachish (701 BCE) · carved c. 700-681 BCE
sites.date: Event: Sennacherib's 701 BCE campaign in Judah. Carving: for the South-West Palace at Nineveh, c. 700-681 BCE
sites.date_basis: The epigraph names Sennacherib and Lachish; the 701 BCE campaign date comes from Sennacherib's annals (third campaign). The reliefs decorate his South-West Palace, dated by the British Museum to 700-681 BCE (gallery text gives 700-692 BCE for Room 10b).

discovery.when: During Layard's second expedition to Nineveh (published 1853)
discovery.who: Austen Henry Layard
discovery.where: Room XXXVI of Sennacherib's South-West Palace, Kuyunjik (Nineveh), near Mosul, Iraq

sites.location: British Museum, London, Room 10b ('Assyria: Siege of Lachish')

physical.material: Gypsum (alabaster) wall slabs carved in low relief
physical.dimensions: Series of 13 slabs lining a room Layard measured as 38 by 18 feet

overview: A continuous series of carved wall panels from a single room in Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh, showing the Assyrian assault on the Judahite city of Lachish, the surrender of its people, and the king receiving the spoil and captives. Layard found them late in his second expedition and described them in 1853: thirteen slabs, some almost entire though cracked by fire, with the epigraph 'complete'.

The scenes show a hilly country of figs and vines, a city with double walls and towers, ten ramps built against the walls, seven battering rams, massed archers and slingers, defenders throwing torches, impaled prisoners, families leaving with carts, and Sennacherib enthroned before a tent while prisoners and spoil pass before him.

A short cuneiform caption above the king names Sennacherib and Lachish. The same campaign is described in Sennacherib's annals and in 2 Kings 18-19; the Assyrian siege ramp was later excavated at Tel Lachish itself (Ussishkin).

text.quote: Sennacherib, king of the universe, king of Assyria, sat upon a house chair (while) the booty of Lachish passed before him.
text.translation: D. D. Luckenbill, Ancient Records of Assyria and Babylonia, vol. II (Chicago, 1927), §489, p. 198 (epigraph; after Paterson, The Palace of Sennacherib, pls. 74-76)

evidence: 13 carved slabs from one room (Room XXXVI, 38 x 18 ft) of the South-West Palace at Nineveh (Layard 1853, pp. 148-151).
Epigraph above the enthroned king naming Sennacherib and Lachish (Layard 1853, p. 152; Luckenbill 1927, §489).
City shown with double walls, towers and outworks; ten ramps and seven battering rams against it (Layard 1853, p. 149).
Defenders wear a pointed helmet with a fringed lappet over the ears; some captives wear a turban with a hanging end (Layard 1853, p. 149).
Captives and spoil: furniture, arms, shields, chariots, metal vessels, camels, ox-carts carrying women and children; prisoners impaled below the walls (Layard 1853, p. 149).
The series ends with a plan of the Assyrian camp with tents, a fire-altar and two chariots bearing standards (Layard 1853, p. 151).
British Museum dates the South-West Palace panels to 700-681 BCE and displays them in Room 10b with a prism of Sennacherib's campaign account.
questions: What exactly does the epigraph say? Layard (1853, p. 152), using the young decipherment of his day, translated: 'Sennacherib, the mighty king, king of the country of Assyria, sitting on the throne of judgment, before (or at the entrance of) the city of Lachish (Lakhisha). I give permission for its slaughter.' Luckenbill (1927, §489), working from Paterson's plates, reads: 'sat upon a house chair (while) the booty of Lachish passed before him'; Barton (1917, p. 373, from Winckler 1892) likewise has 'sat on his throne, and the spoil of the city of Lachish passed before him'. The later readings contain no permission to slaughter; the 1853 wording should not be quoted as the text.

Is it the biblical Lachish? Henry Rawlinson (Outlines of Assyrian History, p. xxxvi) placed the caption's city on the coast between Gaza and Rhinocolura; Layard (1853, p. 153 n.), 'supported ... by Dr. Hincks', rejected this and placed it among the cities of Judah listed in Josh 15:39. The epigraph's Lakisu and the excavated siege remains at Tel Lachish (Ussishkin, Journal for Semitics 24/2, 2017) now tie the reliefs to Tel Lachish.

How literal is the picture? Ussishkin (2017) treats the reliefs as one of five complementary sources for the siege, alongside the Bible, the annals, the excavated city level and the battle remains; comparing the carved city with the excavated site is his method. Where the relief and the ground disagree in detail is argued in his work; the full article is not summarized here.

biblical.tie: Sennacherib is 'at Lachish' when Hezekiah sends tribute and when the Rabshakeh is sent to Jerusalem; the reliefs show Sennacherib enthroned at Lachish receiving its spoil.
Sennacherib 'himself laid siege against Lachish, and all his power with him' - the reliefs show the massed army and the king present.
The Rabshakeh is sent 'from Lachish to Jerusalem' - the same setting.
'O thou inhabitant of Lachish, bind the chariot to the swift beast' - a prophetic line naming Lachish in this era; our reading of its relevance.

sites.name: Large Stone Structure
aka: Summit of the City of David building
sites.subtitle: Massive walls at the summit of the City of David, Jerusalem · date disputed (Iron I to Hellenistic)
sites.date: Disputed. Mazar: built in the mid-10th c. BCE (Iron IIA) on top of Iron I pottery; Faust (2010): Iron I; Finkelstein et al. (2007): not one building, main walls Hellenistic.
sites.date_basis: Pottery beneath and within the walls (Mazar 2006, 2009). No radiocarbon date for the LSS itself was found; the 2024 City of David radiocarbon study (Regev et al., PNAS) sampled other areas.

discovery.who: Eilat Mazar (Shalem Center / Hebrew University)
discovery.where: Northern summit of the City of David ridge, near Kathleen Kenyon's Area H, above the Stepped Stone Structure, Jerusalem

sites.location: In situ, City of David, Jerusalem

physical.material: Walls of large, mostly undressed stones
physical.dimensions: Wall widths 6-8 ft (c. 1.8-2.4 m) per Mazar (BAR 2006); excavated area over 3,000 sq ft

overview: In 2005 Eilat Mazar opened an area of over 3,000 square feet at the northern summit of the City of David and exposed a set of very wide walls built of large stones. She treated them as one building, named it the Large Stone Structure, and argued it was part of one complex with the Stepped Stone Structure on the slope below.

Mazar dated construction to the 10th c. BCE: worn Iron I (12th-11th c.) pottery lay beneath the walls, and Iron IIA pottery, including a Cypriot Black-on-Red juglet, came from later phases. She proposed that it was the palace built for David by Hiram's craftsmen (2 Sam 5:11). Among later finds she reported a bulla of Yehuchal son of Shelemiyahu, a name that occurs in Jer 37:3.

Three published readings compete: Mazar's 10th-century palace; Finkelstein, Herzog, Singer-Avitz and Ussishkin (2007), who say the walls do not form one building and date the most elaborate ones to the Hellenistic period; and Faust (2010), who dates the structure to Iron I, before David.
evidence: Walls 6-8 ft wide of large stones (Mazar, BAR 32.1, 2006).
Iron I pottery (12th-11th c. BCE) beneath the structure; Iron IIA pottery (10th-9th c.) in later phases; a Cypriot Black-on-Red juglet (Mazar 2006).
Seal impression reading 'Yehuchal son of Shelemiyahu son of Shovi' from the site; the building was still in use in the late Iron Age (Mazar 2006).
Finkelstein et al. (2007): the walls 'do not belong to a single building'; the Stepped Stone Structure has at least two phases (a possible 9th c. BCE phase and a Hellenistic one).
Regev et al. (PNAS 2024) found that 18 of their dates fall in the 12th-10th c. BCE in other City of David areas ('widespread occupation of yet undetermined character'); the LSS was not sampled.
questions: Date and unity: Mazar (BAR 2006; The Palace of King David, 2009) dates a single building to the mid-10th c. from Iron I sherds sealed beneath it and Iron IIA material in it; Finkelstein, Herzog, Singer-Avitz and Ussishkin (Tel Aviv 34, 2007) say the walls belong to different structures and the elaborate ones are Hellenistic; Faust (ZDPV 126, 2010) dates it to Iron I and says 'the building was not the palace built for King David by the Phoenicians.'
Relation to the Stepped Stone Structure: Mazar and Faust treat LSS and SSS as one complex; Finkelstein et al. (2007) separate the SSS into at least two phases.
No radiocarbon date: the 2024 PNAS study that re-dated Iron Age Jerusalem (Regev et al.) did not sample the LSS, so its date still rests on pottery alone.

biblical.tie: Hiram of Tyre sent cedar, carpenters and masons, 'and they built David a house.' Mazar identifies the LSS with this house on location and date; the building carries no inscription naming its owner.
David 'went down to the stronghold' when the Philistines came. Mazar reads this as the palace lying above/outside the fortress; this is her reading.
Name Jehucal son of Shelemiah, a court official under Zedekiah; a bulla with the same name and patronym came from Mazar's excavation (late Iron Age use of the area).

sites.name: Magdala Synagogue
sites.subtitle: Early Roman synagogue with the carved 'Magdala Stone' · 1st century CE
sites.date: Early Roman: a building of the mid-1st century BCE (early phase, probably not yet a synagogue), used as a synagogue in two later phases; abandoned at the time of the Great Revolt (66-70 CE)
sites.date_basis: Excavators' stratigraphy (HA-ESI 125, 2013): Stratum 3 pottery 50 CE to end of 1st century CE; glass early 1st century to 40 CE; Hasmonean and 1st-century CE coins, including a coin of 43 CE in the foundation of the reading-room mosaic, a Year 2 Great Revolt coin in the street, and a coin of 80 CE on the synagogue's ceiling collapse.

discovery.when: 2009 (salvage excavation seasons 2009-2013)
discovery.who: Israel Antiquities Authority, directed by Dina Avshalom-Gorni and Arfan Najar, before construction of a hotel
discovery.where: Northern part of the Migdal antiquities site, NW shore of the Sea of Galilee ('Hawaii Beach'), at the foot of Mount Arbel, c. 4 km north of Tiberias

sites.location: In situ at Migdal (Magdala). The whereabouts of the original carved stone vs. a replica were Not confirmed in a published museum record

physical.material: Roughly hewn basalt walls; basalt column fragments; mosaic and painted plaster (fresco); carved limestone block

overview: Between 2009 and 2013 the Israel Antiquities Authority excavated the northern quarter of Migdal ahead of hotel construction and exposed dwellings, a stone-paved street, an industrial quarter with small pools, and a synagogue north of the road at its western end. The excavators identify the site with Migdal Nunia / Taricheae, the chief town of the western shore before Tiberias was founded in 19 CE.

The latest synagogue phase, preserved as abandoned, had a long vestibule, a reading room surrounded by a raised corridor with stone benches, and a small side room. Two stylobates in the reading room carried basalt columns (E. Netzer suggested six). Walls and columns bore colored fresco panels (dark red, mustard yellow, blue); a mosaic with a rosette flanked by meanders was begun in the corridor and apparently left unfinished.

On a bed of small stones in the reading room lay a four-legged rectangular stone block carved in relief on five sides. One side shows a seven-branched menorah on a triangular base standing on a square structure, flanked by amphorae and columns. The excavators read the stone as representing the Second Temple and used as a prayer table.
evidence: Three construction phases; the earliest, mid-1st century BCE, 'probably not used as a synagogue' (HA-ESI 125).
Coin of 43 CE sealed in the foundation of the reading-room mosaic - a terminus post quem for that floor.
Coin of 80 CE on the ceiling collapse; Year 2 revolt coin in the street.
Carved stone block with a seven-branched menorah flanked by amphorae and columns.
Frescoed walls and columns; mosaic begun but cut off at both ends.
The quarter was abandoned and robbed after the Roman conquest; alluvium covered it; no reoccupation until the 1970s.
No dedicatory inscription naming the building or its builders is reported in the preliminary report.
questions: Function of the carved stone: the excavators (HA-ESI 125, 2013) read it as representing the Second Temple and used as a prayer table; the 2024-25 final volume (Talgam, Avshalom-Gorni, Najar, From the Magdala Stone to the Syriac Bema) treats it at length in relation to later synagogue and church liturgical furniture. Alternative readings have not been reviewed for this entry.

When it became a synagogue: the excavators assign synagogue use to the two later phases of a building first built in the mid-1st century BCE; the 43 CE coin under the mosaic dates only the latest floor. Whether the first synagogue phase predates Jesus' ministry (c. 28-30 CE) is not settled by the preliminary report's evidence.

'Earliest in the Galilee': the excavators state the synagogue 'is the earliest one discovered so far in the Galilee'; this is a claim about present evidence, dependent on the dating of other early synagogues.

biblical.tie: Jesus went 'throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues'. Magdala is a Galilean lakeshore town with a synagogue in use in the 1st century CE; no text places Jesus in this building.
'Mary called Magdalene' - named after Magdala (Migdal). The excavation shows the Jewish town of that name in the Early Roman period.

A synagogue with a scroll read on the Sabbath; the Magdala reading room with benches around a central space and a carved stone table is the physical setting of such a reading, per the excavators' interpretation.

sites.name: Mari Tablets (Royal Archives of Mari)
sites.subtitle: Old Babylonian palace archive from Tell Hariri on the Middle Euphrates, Syria · early 18th century BCE (middle chronology)
sites.date: Old Babylonian period; the palace archive belongs mainly to the kings Yasmah-Addu and Zimri-Lim, ending with the city's fall to Hammurabi of Babylon (18th century BCE on the middle chronology)
sites.date_basis: The letters and administrative texts carry year-names and royal names (Zimri-Lim etc.) and synchronise with Hammurabi of Babylon; absolute dates follow whichever Mesopotamian chronology is used. This reconstruction is standard in the publications cited (e.g. Fleming 2004, ch. 'The Tribal World of Zimri-Lim') but was not re-read in the original reports during this pass.

discovery.when: Site identified 1933-1934 (first campaign, winter 1933-34); palace and archives excavated in the following seasons (second campaign 1934-35 onward)
discovery.who: French expedition directed by André Parrot
discovery.where: Royal palace at Tell Hariri (ancient Mari), Middle Euphrates, eastern Syria near the Iraqi border

sites.location: Syria and France (Louvre) hold Mari material; the present repository of the archive tablets is not confirmed from a primary source

physical.material: Clay tablets
physical.language: Akkadian (Old Babylonian dialect with West Semitic / 'Amorite' vocabulary and names)

overview: Tell Hariri on the Euphrates was identified as ancient Mari by André Parrot's French expedition, whose preliminary reports appeared in the journal Syria from 1935. The royal palace yielded an archive of letters, legal and administrative documents from the Old Babylonian period, published in the series Archives royales de Mari (ARM).

The letters are the main value of the archive: correspondence between the kings of Mari (especially Zimri-Lim), their officials, governors and other rulers, including reports on tribal groups and on messages from prophets and ecstatics delivered in the name of gods. An English translation of a large selection is W. Heimpel, Letters to the King of Mari (2003).

Biblical links drawn from Mari fall into three kinds: (1) prophecy - letters reporting oracles to the king, edited in ARM 26 and compared with biblical prophets by A. Malamat (1998); (2) tribal society - the pastoral tribes of Zimri-Lim's world studied by D. Fleming (2004); (3) places - Mari letters mention Hazor in Canaan (Malamat 1998, chs. on Mari and Hazor).
evidence: Excavation began with Parrot's first campaign, winter 1933-34 (Parrot, Syria 16, 1935, 1-28 and 117-140); second campaign winter 1934-35 (Syria 17, 1936, 1-31).
The archive's letters include reports of prophetic messages: edited in ARM 26 (Malamat 1998 ch. 'New Light from Mari (ARM XXVI) on Biblical Prophecy').
Hazor appears in Mari documents, including trade relations (Malamat 1998, 'Hazor Once Again in New Mari Documents'; 'Mari and Hazor: Trade Relations in the Old Babylonian Period').
Zimri-Lim's kingdom included organised pastoral tribes; Fleming (2004) devotes ch. 1 ('The Tribal World of Zimri-Lim', pp. 24-103) to them.
questions: How close are Mari prophecy and biblical prophecy? A. Malamat (Mari and the Bible, Brill 1998) argues for real parallels (e.g. 'A Mari Prophecy and Nathan's Dynastic Oracle', pp. 106-121; 'Episodes Involving Samuel and Saul and the Prophetic Texts from Mari', pp. 102-105). The evidence is the text of the ARM 26 letters; the parallels are his reading.

Personal and place names compared with Genesis (Laban, Nahor, the 'Benjaminite' tribes, the Hapiru): the old entry asserts these as findings. No primary edition cited here confirms or refutes each; they remain unverified here and should be checked in the ARM volumes before being printed as facts.

Absolute date: 'mid-18th century BCE' depends on the middle chronology; Malamat (1998, 'Mari and Hazor: The Implication for the Middle Bronze Age Chronology', pp. 51-55) uses the Mari-Hazor synchronism in that argument.

biblical.tie: Mari letters report prophets speaking to a king in a god's name, with messages checked and sent on by officials - a documented prophetic institution a millennium before the biblical prophets. The texts do not mention Israel.

Hazor appears in Mari documents as a significant Canaanite city in trade contact with Mari, consistent with Joshua's description of Hazor as 'the head of all those kingdoms' - an independent attestation of Hazor's standing, not of Joshua's events.
Mari shows pastoral tribes moving between towns and grazing land in upper Mesopotamia/Syria in the Old Babylonian period. That is a setting like the patriarchal narratives'; it names no patriarch.

sites.name: Late 7th-Century Egyptian and East Greek Pottery at Megiddo (Level X-3)
sites.subtitle: Egyptian-made and East Greek pottery from Level X-3 at Tel Megiddo · late 7th century BCE · published 2025, disputed 2026
sites.date: Late 7th century BCE (Level X-3, per the Megiddo Expedition)
sites.date_basis: Pottery typology and stratigraphy of post-732 BCE layers in Area X (Finkelstein et al., SJOT 2025). Shalvi et al. (Levant 2026) re-date the same ceramic categories and argue the site was abandoned c. 640 BCE.

discovery.when: Recent Megiddo Expedition seasons; published January 2025
discovery.who: Megiddo Expedition (Tel Aviv University; I. Finkelstein, M. J. Adams, A. Fantalkin, A. Kleiman)
discovery.where: Area X, Tel Megiddo, Jezreel Valley

sites.location: In situ at Tel Megiddo; finds held by the Megiddo Expedition (inventory numbers not published in the sources seen)
overview: The Megiddo Expedition has published several layers from after the Assyrian conquest of 732 BCE from a small area (Area X), with a mudbrick wall and two successive buildings. Level X-3, which they date to the late 7th century BCE, produced what they describe as an exceptional number of Egyptian-made pottery vessels and a significant amount of East Greek pottery. They read this as an Egyptian (26th Dynasty, Saite) presence at Megiddo, with Greek mercenaries in Egyptian service.

Finkelstein, Adams, Fantalkin and Kleiman (Scandinavian Journal of the Old Testament, January 2025) present this as the archaeological background to the meeting of Josiah and Pharaoh Necho at Megiddo in 609 BCE (2 Kgs 23:29).

In August 2026 Shalvi, Gimatzidis, Kahn, Wodzinska, Ownby and Gilboa (Levant) re-examined the stratigraphy and the Phoenician, Greek, Egyptian and Assyrianizing pottery. They argue that Megiddo was abandoned c. 640 BCE, before Assyria collapsed, and not significantly resettled in the Iron Age, so that there was no Saite-period stronghold at Megiddo in 609.
evidence: Area X exposed a mudbrick wall and two successive buildings with layers of the 8th-6th centuries BCE (BAS summary of the SJOT paper).
Level X-3 contains 'an exceptional number of Egyptian-made pottery vessels' and 'a significant number of East Greek pottery' (SJOT 2025 abstract).
BAS reports the excavators' claim that no other site in the region has as much Egyptian pottery, and no inland site as much Greek pottery.
The Levant 2026 response counters that Strata III and II are both phases of Neo-Assyrian Magiddu, with no archaeologically attested Neo-Babylonian occupation and abandonment c. 640 BCE.
No inscription naming Necho or Josiah has been reported from these layers.
questions: Was Megiddo an Egyptian stronghold in 609 BCE? Finkelstein et al. (SJOT 39/1, 2025) date Level X-3 to the late 7th century and read its Egyptian-made vessels and East Greek wares as a Saite garrison with Greek mercenaries. Shalvi et al. (Levant, 2026) re-examine the stratigraphy and the same four ceramic groups and date the end of occupation to c. 640 BCE, before any Saite control, with no significant later Iron Age resettlement. The dispute is over the dating of the Greek and Egyptian pottery types and how the strata connect, not over whether the pottery exists.

Josiah's death: 2 Kgs 23:29 says only that Necho killed Josiah at Megiddo 'when he saw him'. 2 Chr 35:20-24 describes a battle in the valley of Megiddo. BAS notes that the difference between the two accounts is still argued. The pottery could bear on whether an Egyptian post stood at Megiddo; it cannot show which account describes the encounter.

biblical.tie: Necho goes up to the king of Assyria at the Euphrates; Josiah goes to meet him, and Necho kills him at Megiddo. If Finkelstein et al. are right, Megiddo then held an Egyptian presence. If Shalvi et al. are right, the site was largely deserted and the encounter took place at or near a ruin.
The Chronicler describes a battle in the valley of Megiddo with archers and a chariot. The pottery evidence does not address the form of the encounter.
Necho's army at the Euphrates at Carchemish, 605 BCE. This is the same Egyptian push north that the Megiddo excavators use to explain their garrison.

sites.name: Megiddo Stables
sites.subtitle: Pillared buildings with stone troughs, Stratum IV · date disputed (10th-8th c. BCE)
sites.date: Megiddo Stratum IV, labelled 'ca. 1000-800 B.C.' by the excavators (Lamon & Shipton 1939); later phased as IVA and dated by Finkelstein to the 8th c. BCE ('Horse Industry City: Eighth-Century BCE Megiddo', 2025).
sites.date_basis: Stratigraphy of the University of Chicago excavation; the 1939 attribution to Solomon rested on 1 Kings. Later dates rest on re-phasing of Megiddo's strata and radiocarbon from the renewed Tel Aviv University excavations.

discovery.when: University of Chicago seasons 1925-1934 (as covered by Megiddo I)
discovery.who: Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago Megiddo Expedition; published by Robert S. Lamon and Geoffrey M. Shipton (1939), who cite P. L. O. Guy's earlier report (OIC 9) for the stables
discovery.where: Tel Megiddo, Jezreel Valley, Israel: southern compound (Area A) and northern group (Area C)

sites.location: In situ, Tel Megiddo National Park, Israel

physical.material: Stone pillars and stone troughs; lime-plastered central passages, rubble-floored side aisles
physical.dimensions: Southern compound 64 x 85 m with a courtyard 55 m square; each unit a c. 3 m central passage flanked by aisles of similar width; pillars c. 0.5 m square; troughs c. 1.2 x 0.6 m, 0.7 m high (Lamon & Shipton 1939)

overview: Two groups of long tripartite pillared buildings found on Tel Megiddo by the University of Chicago expedition: a southern compound of five units facing a 55 m courtyard with a central water tank, and a northern group. In each unit a central lime-plastered passage is flanked by rubble-floored aisles, separated by rows of stone pillars alternating with stone troughs.

Lamon and Shipton (Megiddo I, 1939) read them as stables for about 450 horses: the pillars had holes cut at the corners just above the troughs, which they took as tethering holes. They assigned them to Stratum IV (ca. 1000-800 BCE) and to Solomon, using the chariot figures in Kings and Chronicles to argue for three-horse chariot teams.
The identification as stables and the Solomonic date have both been questioned. Finkelstein's 2025 treatment frames Megiddo of the 8th century BCE as a 'horse industry city'.
evidence: Southern compound: five units facing a courtyard 55 m on a side, overall 64 x 85 m, with a water tank near the courtyard's centre (Lamon & Shipton 1939, p. 32).

Rows of stone pillars alternating with stone troughs c. 1.2 x 0.6 x 0.7 m; holes cut through pillar corners just above the troughs, 'almost invariably on the side toward the central passage' (Lamon & Shipton, pp. 32-44).
Central passages lime-plastered; side aisles floored with rubble (pp. 32-44).
Excavators' capacity estimate: about 450 horses for both groups; the counts per unit are the excavators' reconstruction (pp. 43-44).
No inscription or text found with the buildings.
questions: Function: Lamon & Shipton (1939) identify stables from troughs, tie-holes and rubble stall floors; Cantrell (The Horsemen of Israel, 2011, ch. 5 'Stables of Israel: The Case of Megiddo') and Finkelstein (NEA 88.3, 2025, 'Horse Industry City') keep the horse interpretation in their titles; Franklin ('Entering the Arena: The Megiddo Stables Reconsidered', 2017) and Davies ('Solomonic Stables at Megiddo After All?', PEQ 1988) re-examined the question. The texts of these later studies, and the storehouse alternative the old entry mentions, have not been reviewed for this entry, so their specific evidence is not reported here.

Date: Lamon & Shipton assign Stratum IV to ca. 1000-800 BCE and to Solomon on the strength of 1 Kings; Finkelstein (2025) places the horse complex in the 8th c. BCE. The stratigraphic arguments of the later studies have not been reviewed for this entry; only titles, venues and dates were verified.

biblical.tie: Solomon built 'cities for his chariots, and cities for his horsemen'. The buildings are horse facilities on the excavators' reading, at a city named in 1 Kgs 9:15; the verse does not name Megiddo as a chariot city.
Kings gives 40,000 stalls, Chronicles 4,000. Lamon & Shipton (1939, p. 44) used the 4,000 figure and 1 Kgs 10:26-29 to argue for three-horse teams. This is their reading.
Solomon's 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, and horse trade prices. Corresponds to large horse facilities only if the buildings are 10th-century stables, which is disputed.

sites.name: Merneptah Stele
sites.subtitle: Egyptian victory hymn naming Israel · Year 5 of Merneptah (c. 1208 BCE)
sites.date: Year 5 of Merneptah, 3rd month of Shemu, day 3 (c. 1208 BCE on the conventional Egyptian chronology)
sites.date_basis: The text is dated internally to Merneptah's regnal year 5 (Breasted, ARE III §607: 'Year 5, third month of the third season, third day'). The BCE figure depends on which absolute chronology is used for the 19th Dynasty; the stone gives only the regnal year.

discovery.who: W. M. Flinders Petrie (text first edited by Wilhelm Spiegelberg)
discovery.where: Ruins of Merneptah's mortuary temple, western Thebes

sites.location: Egyptian Museum, Cairo (JE 31408)

physical.material: Dark grey syenite (granitic stone) 'infiltrated with quartz veins' (Petrie)
physical.dimensions: 10 ft 3 in high, 5 ft 4 in wide, 13 in thick (Petrie 1897, §24) = c. 3.12 x 1.63 x 0.33 m
physical.language: Late Middle / Late Egyptian (Ramesside literary hymn)

overview: A large stone stela reused by Merneptah: the front carries a text and scene of Amenhotep III, which Merneptah's workmen took from Amenhotep's temple; Merneptah's own 28-line inscription is cut on the back. Petrie found it in 1896 in Merneptah's mortuary temple at western Thebes and recorded it as a single block of dark grey syenite over 10 feet tall. A fragmentary duplicate of Merneptah's text stood at Karnak.

Most of the text is a poetic celebration of Merneptah's Year-5 victory over the Libyans. The closing strophe (lines 26-28) turns to the Levant and lists defeated foreigners: Canaan, Ashkelon, Gezer, Yenoam, Israel, and Kharu (Hurru). Israel is the only name in that list written with the classifier for a people rather than the throw-stick-and-hill-country classifier used for Ashkelon, Gezer and Yenoam.

This is the earliest securely read occurrence of the name Israel outside the Bible. Breasted (1906) already noted that the Israel clause is short and built from stock phrases also applied to other defeated peoples.

text.quote: Carried off is Askalon; Seized upon is Gezer; Yenoam is made as a thing not existing. Israel is desolated, his seed is not; Palestine has become a widow for Egypt.
text.translation: J. H. Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt III (1906) §617, pp. 263-264

evidence: Text dated Year 5 of Merneptah, 3rd month of Shemu, day 3 (Breasted ARE III §607).
Stela is a reused Amenhotep III monument; Merneptah's text is on the back (Petrie 1897 §24; Breasted ARE III §602 n.).
Petrie's measurement: 10 ft 3 in x 5 ft 4 in x 13 in, dark grey syenite with quartz veins, 'condition perfect' apart from one chip.
Line 27 spells the name y-s-r-i-a-r (Breasted: 'Israel (Y-s-r-'-r)').
Ashkelon, Gezer and Yenoam carry the foreign-land/city classifier; Israel carries the classifier for a people (man + woman + plural strokes).
The Israel clause 'his seed (pr.t) is not' is a formula also used of other defeated enemies (Breasted ARE III §603-604).
A second, fragmentary copy of the text exists at Karnak (Breasted ARE III §602 n., citing Dümichen and Erman).
questions: Where is Israel and what kind of group is it? M. G. Hasel (BASOR 296, 1994) reads the closing strophe as a structured ring in which Israel sits inside Canaan/Hurru and, from the people-classifier plus the meaning of pr.t, argues Israel was a sedentary/agricultural socio-ethnic group. Readers who stress the scribal inconsistency of classifiers in Ramesside texts treat the people-classifier as weaker evidence of social form; the stone itself proves only that Egyptian scribes classed Israel as a people, not a city-state.

Does Israel appear in pictures too? F. J. Yurco (JARCE 23, 1986) reattributed battle reliefs on the Cour de la Cachette wall at Karnak from Ramesses II to Merneptah and matched them scene-for-scene to Ashkelon, Gezer, Yenoam and Israel, identifying Israel with Canaanite-dressed chariot-less foes. D. B. Redford (IEJ 36, 1986) rejected the reattribution; A. F. Rainey (BAR 17/6, 1991) accepted the Merneptah date but argued Israel is the scene of Shasu-dressed captives. The reliefs carry no captions naming Israel, so every identification is a reading.

Merneptah's own Levantine campaign: some doubt Merneptah campaigned in Canaan at all and read the strophe as conventional boast; Breasted (1906, §605-606) pointed to the Year 3 border journal and the title 'binder of Gezer' as independent indications that he did.
What 'his seed is not' means: Breasted (1906) showed it is a stock phrase for devastation (grain/offspring), not a reference to killing Hebrew boys as some 1890s writers claimed.

biblical.tie: The stela places a people called Israel in the southern Levant by Merneptah's Year 5, alongside Canaanite towns (Ashkelon, Gezer) that the Bible also names. It says nothing about how or when Israel arrived.

Gezer is listed as 'seized'; the Bible reports Gezer remaining Canaanite until an Egyptian pharaoh took it for Solomon. The stela is independent evidence of Egyptian military interest in Gezer, not of the specific biblical event.
Reading, not finding: the stela shows Israel already in Canaan by c. 1208 BCE; anyone placing the Exodus must fit it before that date. The stone does not mention an exodus.
