sites.name: Mesha Stele
sites.subtitle: Victory and building inscription of Mesha king of Moab · 9th c. BCE
sites.date: 9th century BCE. The Louvre record: 'IXe s. av. J.-C. (Epoque de Mesha vers 830-805)' and 'Gravé peu après 842'.
sites.date_basis: No regnal year in the text. Mesha names Omri king of Israel and Omri's son; 2 Kgs 3:4-5 places Mesha's revolt after Ahab's death. Letter forms fit the 9th c.

discovery.when: August 1868
discovery.who: Seen by the missionary F. A. Klein; squeeze taken for Charles Clermont-Ganneau before local people broke the stone; fragments recovered and reassembled by Clermont-Ganneau
discovery.where: Dhiban (ancient Dibon), Jordan

sites.location: Musée du Louvre, Paris, Department of Near Eastern Antiquities, AO 5066 (also MNB 752); Sully wing, room 303 per the collections record

physical.material: Basalt
physical.dimensions: H. 125 cm, W. 69 cm, D. 37 cm (Louvre); round-topped; broken and reassembled with restorations
physical.script: Alphabetic, Phoenician-type letters ('34 lines in Phoenician-type characters' - Louvre)

overview: A round-topped basalt stele, 125 cm high, inscribed in 34 lines in the name of Mesha son of Kemosh-[yat] king of Moab, 'the Dibonite'. The Louvre record says it was engraved shortly after 842 BCE for a sanctuary of the god Kemosh.

Klein saw the complete stone at Dhiban in 1868. A paper squeeze was taken for Clermont-Ganneau; the stone was then broken up by local people, and Clermont-Ganneau recovered fragments that were reassembled with the squeeze as guide. The Louvre bought it from him in 1873.

Mesha says Omri king of Israel oppressed Moab 'many days' because Kemosh was angry with his land, that Omri's son said he too would oppress Moab, and that Kemosh restored the land in Mesha's day. He lists taking Ataroth from the men of Gad, taking Nebo and carrying off 'the vessels of Yahweh' to Kemosh, driving the king of Israel out of Jahaz, and building works at Qarhoh, Aroer, the Arnon road and other towns. The closing lines, damaged, speak of Horonaim.

text.quote: Omri, king of Israel - he oppressed Moab many days, because Chemosh was angry with his land. And his son succeeded him, and he also said I will oppress Moab. ... And I took from there the altar-hearths of Yahweh (Jehovah), and I dragged them before Chemosh.
text.translation: George A. Barton, Archaeology and the Bible (Philadelphia: American Sunday-School Union, 1916), pp. 363-364 (translated from Smend and Socin 1886).

evidence: Basalt, H 125 x W 69 x D 37 cm; incomplete, fragmented, reassembled with restoration (Louvre AO 5066).
34 lines of text in Phoenician-type letters, Moabite language (Louvre record).
Names Omri king of Israel and his son; names Yahweh (the vessels/altar-hearths taken from Nebo); names Kemosh repeatedly; names 'the men of Gad' as dwelling in Ataroth 'from of old'.
Place names in the text include Medeba, Baal-meon, Kiriathaim, Ataroth, Nebo, Jahaz, Dibon, Aroer, Arnon, Beth-bamoth, Bezer, Beth-diblathan, Beth-baal-meon and Horonaim (Barton 1916 translation).
Line 31 is damaged; Barton's 1916 translation leaves the passage before Horonaim blank. Its reading is the subject of the 'House of David' dispute.
questions: Line 31 'House of David': Lemaire proposed bt[d]wd; Langlois (Semitica 61, 2019) applied RTI to the stone and the 1868 squeeze and judged it 'hypothetical but ... the most probable reading', pointing to a word divider after the group; Lemaire and Delorme (BAR 48, Nov. 2022) state that new photographs 'clearly establish the presence of the first dalet and confirm the last dalet, while only the letter taw remains somewhat unclear'. Finkelstein, Na'aman and Römer (Tel Aviv 46, 2019) examined new photographs of the stone and squeeze and concluded the ruler's name had three consonants starting with b, proposing Balak (Num 22-24).

Timing against 2 Kings: the stele says Omri held Medeba 'his days and half the days of his son, forty years' and that Israel oppressed Moab in the son's days; 2 Kgs 1:1 and 3:5 place Moab's rebellion after Ahab's death. Barton (1916, p. 364) notes that the Bible says nothing of Mesha's revolt as he tells it and Mesha says nothing of the campaign in 2 Kgs 3. How to reconcile 'son' and 'forty years' with the regnal lengths in Kings is an open reading.
Line 12 'rʾl dwdh' (Barton: 'altar-hearth of Duda'): whether dwdh is a divine name, a title, or a personal name is not settled by the text itself.

biblical.tie: Mesha king of Moab, a sheep-breeder (nōqēd), paid tribute to the king of Israel and rebelled after Ahab died. The stele names Mesha, Omri and Omri's son, and Mesha's revolt; it does not describe the Israel-Judah-Edom campaign of 2 Kgs 3.
'Moab rebelled against Israel after the death of Ahab.' The stele places the recovery 'in my day' and during the son's reign; see questions.
Omri as king of Israel: the stele names 'Omri king of Israel' (ʿmry mlk yśrʾl).
Gad and Reuben building/holding Ataroth, Dibon, Aroer, Nebo, Baal-meon, Kiriathaim, Jahaz, Beth-baal-meon. The stele says 'the men of Gad had dwelt in the land of Ataroth from of old'.
Balak king of Moab: the Finkelstein-Na'aman-Römer restoration of line 31.

sites.name: Mount Ebal Structure (el-Burnat) and the Folded Lead Object
sites.subtitle: Late Bronze / Iron I stone installation on Mount Ebal, and a disputed folded lead object from its spoil heap
sites.date: Structure: Zertal's Strata II-I, c. mid-13th to 12th century BCE on pottery and scarabs. Lead object: undated in itself (found in a spoil heap); claimed Late Bronze II by its publishers.
sites.date_basis: Pottery (Zertal: 97% Iron IA, 3% Late Bronze IIB, as summarised by Stripling et al. 2023) and two scarabs (Brandl 1986; re-assessed by Ben-Tor and van der Veen as Thutmose III or soon after). Stripling et al. state that Zertal's organic samples are lost, so no radiocarbon dates exist. The lead object came from a dump pile and carries no stratigraphic date of its own; its publishers assign it to the Stratum II round altar because the east dump held only Area A (altar) material.

discovery.when: Structure found 1980 in survey, excavated 1982-1989; lead object recovered December 2019
discovery.who: Adam Zertal (University of Haifa, Manasseh Hill Country Survey); lead object found by Frankie Snyder in wet-sifting directed by Scott Stripling (Associates for Biblical Research)
discovery.where: el-Burnat (A), second step of Mount Ebal, northeast of Tel Balata (Shechem)

sites.location: Structure in situ on Mount Ebal, northern West Bank. Lead object: held by the Stripling team; no museum inventory number published.

physical.material: Structure: fieldstone. Object: folded lead strip (lead isotopes point to Lavrion, Greece)
physical.dimensions: Rectangular structure (Stratum I) 8.75-9.00 x 7.00 m plus a ramp on the west side; round structure (Stratum II) 2 m diameter beneath its centre; inner enclosure 3.8 dunams (c. 110 x 35 m). Lead object c. 2 x 2 cm, 0.3 cm thick folded, strip c. 0.4 mm thick (all per Stripling et al. 2023, p. 3).
physical.script: Claimed: proto-alphabetic, 48 letters (Stripling et al. 2023); disputed whether any letters exist
physical.language: Claimed: early Hebrew (Stripling et al. 2023); disputed

overview: Adam Zertal of the University of Haifa found a stone installation on the second step of Mount Ebal in 1980 during his Manasseh Hill Country Survey and excavated it from 1982 to 1989. His preliminary report appeared in Tel Aviv 13-14 (1986-87), with a separate faunal report by L. K. Horwitz and a glyptic report by B. Brandl in the same issue. Zertal identified the large rectangular structure, with a ramp on its west side, as an altar, and the smaller round structure under its centre as an earlier altar; he connected the site with the altar Joshua built on Mount Ebal (Josh 8:30-35).

The bone assemblage, as summarised by Stripling et al. (2023), is 65% caprine, 21% bovine, 10% fallow deer and 4% other (snake, tortoise, etc.); they describe 96% as kosher. Ralph K. Hawkins's 2007 Andrews University dissertation (book 2012) tested Zertal's interpretation against domestic, military and cultic parallels and concluded the site 'appears to fit the criteria for a cultic site.'

In December 2019 Stripling's team wet-sifted about 30% of Zertal's discarded spoil. From the east dump, which held altar-area (Area A) material, Frankie Snyder recovered a folded lead object about 2 x 2 cm. It was announced at a press event in March 2022 and published in Heritage Science on 12 May 2023 by Stripling, Galil and a Czech X-ray tomography team, who read 48 proto-alphabetic letters inside it as a curse naming 'yhw'. Published responses from late 2023 and 2024 (Mazar; Maeir and Rollston; Yahalom-Mack; Haughwout) argue that the letters are not present and that the object may be a net sinker or other lead item.

text.quote: Cursed you [are] by the god YHW, cursed. / You will die, cursed; cursed, die, [you will] d[ie]. / [C]ursed you [are] by YHW, [c]ursed.
text.translation: Literal translation (this encyclopedia) of the transliteration published by Stripling et al., Heritage Science 11 (2023) 105, p. 7 ('th 'rwr l'l yhw 'rwr / tmt 'rwr 'rwr mt t[mt] / ['] rwr 'th lyhw [']rwr). Whether these letters exist at all is disputed (see questions).
text.quote_type: own literal translation of a disputed transliteration

evidence: Rectangular Stratum I structure 8.75-9.00 x 7.00 m with a ramp on the west side, over a 2 m round Stratum II structure at its centre (Stripling et al. 2023 p. 3, summarising Zertal).
Structures sit inside a 3.8-dunam foot-shaped enclosure (110 m long, c. 35 m wide) within a larger 14-dunam enclosure (same source).
Pottery: 97% Iron IA, 3% Late Bronze IIB (Zertal, per Stripling et al.); the 2019 sifting gave 268 diagnostic sherds: 95% Iron I, 4.75% Late Bronze, 0.25% Early Roman.
Bones: 65% caprine, 21% bovine, 10% fallow deer, 4% other including snake and tortoise (Stripling et al. 2023, citing the faunal study).
No radiocarbon dates: Zertal's organic samples are reported lost (Stripling et al. 2023 p. 3).
Two scarabs and a seal; Brandl (1986) assigned Scarab 1 to Ramesses II, Ben-Tor and van der Veen to Thutmose III or soon after.
Lead object found in December 2019 in a spoil heap, not in a stratified layer; 0.25% of the sifted sherds were Early Roman, so the dump held some post-Iron Age material.
Lead isotope analysis by N. Yahalom-Mack points to Lavrion (Greece) ore (Stripling et al. 2023 p. 3).
The object has not been unfolded; every claimed letter comes from X-ray tomography reconstructions made at the Czech Academy of Sciences, Telc.
questions: Altar or not? Zertal (Tel Aviv 1986-87; BAR 11/1, 1985) read the rectangular structure with its ramp, the bone assemblage and the enclosure as a cultic altar. Hawkins (dissertation 2007; book 2012) compared it with Iron I domestic and military buildings and religious structures and concluded it fits a cultic site better.

Are there letters inside the lead object? Stripling, Galil et al. (Heritage Science 2023) read 48 letters in three formulaic lines from the tomography slices, with the divine name YHW twice and 'rwr ('cursed') six times. Maeir and Rollston (IEJ 73/2, 2023, per Windle's summary) state that 'the putative 48 letters are simply not present' and that the images show striations, scratches, pitting and indentations in soft lead. Haughwout (Heritage Science 12:70, 2024) reached the same conclusion: there is 'insufficient epigraphic evidence to conclude that writing exists' on the object.

What is the object? A. Mazar (IEJ 73/2, 2023, per Windle; also cited by Haughwout as forthcoming in IEJ) identifies it as a Type L2.3b fishing-net sinker of an Aegean type. Windle (ABR/Bible Archaeology Report, Dec 2023) answers that the Ebal piece is cruder, thicker and heavier than such sinkers and has no rope grooves. Haughwout also lists a clasp on a string (Cargill, Barnea) or a Roman lead tag as possibilities.

Date of the object: Stripling et al. assign it to the Stratum II round altar because the east dump held only Area A material. Haughwout (2024) replies that a spoil heap cannot date an object, since topsoil and later material were also removed; the 0.25% Early Roman pottery in the sifted spoil shows later material was present. Yahalom-Mack's Lavrion lead isotopes fit several periods of mining and so do not decide the date either.

biblical.tie: Moses commands an altar of unhewn stones on Mount Ebal and the curses to be pronounced there. Mount Ebal and the altar command correspond to the site and structure. That this structure is that altar is Zertal's reading, not something written on the site.
Joshua builds the altar on Mount Ebal and reads the blessings and curses. Joshua's name is not on anything found at el-Burnat.

The Ebal ceremony is a series of twelve 'arur ('cursed') formulas. If the lead object's reading stood, its repeated 'rwr would echo this directly. Whether it does depends on whether the letters exist, which is disputed.
Altars are to have no steps. The Ebal structure has a ramp. This agrees with the command but does not show that the builders knew it.

Claims that the lead tablet was 'found in 2022' or 'published in 2022': it was recovered in December 2019, first announced at a press event in March 2022 (Rollston's critique is dated 26 March 2022, per Haughwout's references), and published on 12 May 2023.
Claims that the tablet was 'excavated from the altar': it came from Zertal's spoil heap during wet-sifting, not from a stratified layer.

Claims that the tablet is 'the earliest Hebrew inscription' as a settled fact: no letter is visible on the surface. The reading rests on tomography, and published analyses (IEJ 73/2, 2023; Heritage Science 12:70, 2024) deny that letters are present.

Citation seen in circulation, 'Stripling/Galil vs. Rollston/Mazar': the IEJ critical response is by Maeir and Rollston. Mazar wrote a separate article on the fishing-weight identification, and Yahalom-Mack wrote on the lead source.
Claims that the lead is local Canaanite: isotope analysis points to Lavrion in Greece (Stripling et al. 2023, reporting Yahalom-Mack).

updates.what: Haughwout's refutation published in Heritage Science 12:70. It finds no demonstrable writing and says a spoil-heap object cannot be dated by association.
Shiff (J. Field Archaeology 49/3) treats the Tel Burnat backdirt case as a study in archaeological procedure.
Rouse (JBL 143/2) argues on textual grounds that the MT placement of the Ebal altar episode (Josh 8:30-35) is the earliest.

No new excavation season, no promised second article on the object's 'exterior writing' (announced in Stripling et al. 2023 p. 3), and no museum registration were found in Crossref/OpenAlex searches through Sept 2026. Absence of evidence only; web search budget was exhausted, so press coverage may be missed.

sites.name: Murashu Archive
aka: Business Documents of Murashu Sons of Nippur
sites.subtitle: Cuneiform business archive of a Nippur family under Artaxerxes I and Darius II · c. 454-404 BCE
sites.date: Main span 454-414 BCE, with a few related documents to 404 BCE (Alstola 2020); Hilprecht (1898) gives the reigns of Artaxerxes I and Darius II
sites.date_basis: Every contract carries a regnal date (day, month, year of Artaxerxes I or Darius II) in its colophon; the dates are internal to the tablets.

discovery.when: End of May / June 1893
discovery.who: University of Pennsylvania Babylonian Expedition, field director John Henry Haynes
discovery.where: A single room (5.5 x 2.75 m) about 6 m below the surface on the north-western ridge ('Camp Hill') of Nippur, west of the Inanna temple and Ekur, Iraq

sites.location: Mainly Istanbul Archaeological Museum and the Penn Museum (University of Pennsylvania Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology), Philadelphia; a few in Jena, Yale, the British Museum and elsewhere

physical.material: Clay tablets (plus about twenty clay bullae); many carry seal impressions and some have short Aramaic epigraphs (dockets)
physical.dimensions: About 730 tablets gathered from the room in 1893 (Hilprecht 1898); about 750 texts counted in the archive today (Alstola 2020)
physical.script: Neo-/Late Babylonian cuneiform, with brief Aramaic dockets in alphabetic script on some tablets

overview: In 1893 the Penn expedition at Nippur cleared a small collapsed room and found about 730 clay tablets lying on or near its floor. They were the business records of a Nippur family, the descendants of Murashu son of Hatin, active under the Persian kings Artaxerxes I and Darius II. Hilprecht and Clay published a large part of them in 1898-1912; Stolper (1985) and Donbaz and Stolper (1997, the Istanbul tablets) published most of the rest.

The Murashus were agricultural middlemen in the Persian 'land-for-service' system. Crown land around Nippur was allotted to military and service units (hatru), each under a foreman (shaknu). The Murashus leased these holdings, supplied water, seed and oxen, advanced silver to pay the holders' taxes, took pledges of land, and collected rents in barley and dates. The tablets are promissory notes, receipts, leases and similar legal texts.

The archive names people of many origins living in the Nippur countryside: Babylonians, Persians, Arameans and others. Among them are Judeans, identified mainly by names formed with the divine name Yahweh. Alstola (2020) counts 61 Judean individuals in 64 documents, from 452 BCE (year 13 of Artaxerxes I) to 413 BCE (year 11 of Darius II), mostly as farmers dealing with the Murashus, as witnesses, and a few as minor officials. The tablets are not written in Aramaic and are not the records of a Jewish family.

text.quote: Legal-economic formulae, not narrative. A typical tablet records that a named landholder of a service unit owes the Murashu firm a quantity of barley or dates as rent for a plot on a named canal, or receives silver to pay his tax obligation, and lists witnesses and the scribe, followed by the date in the regnal year of Artaxerxes or Darius. Judeans appear by name in these roles (e.g. Pili-Yama son of Shillimu as witness in several Nippur documents of year 34 of Artaxerxes I).
text.translation: Summary based on Hilprecht and Clay, BE IX (1898) introduction, and Alstola, Judeans in Babylonia (2020), ch. 5

evidence: Hilprecht 1898: 'At the end of May, 1893 ... discovered a room (5.5 X 2.75 m. wide) about 6 m. below the surface'; 730 tablets gathered from the floor in a few hours.
Tablets dated in the reigns of Artaxerxes I and Darius II; BE IX's 120 texts were written by 41 different scribes (Hilprecht 1898).
Main span 454-414 BCE with a handful of related documents to 404 BCE; peak activity 425-417 BCE (Alstola 2020, citing Donbaz and Stolper 1997).
Chief protagonists: Enlil-shum-iddin (active 445/444-421 BCE) and his nephew Rimut-Ninurta (429-415/414 BCE); the family's names honour Enlil and Ninurta, gods of Nippur (Alstola 2020).
61 Judean individuals in 64 documents; earliest BE 9 3 (452 BCE), latest PBS 2/1 148 (413 BCE) (Alstola 2020).

Hilprecht (1898) listed names he read as Hebrew, among them Gadaliama (Gedaliah), Hananiama (Hananiah), Hagga (Haggai), Shabbatai and Zabdiia, noting that many were 'known from the Old Testament, especially from the books of Ezra and Nehemiah'.
A Judean served as shaknu (foreman) of the shushanus of the storehouse (BE 10 65); Judean-held bow and horse lands belong to hatrus of sepirus (scribes), e.g. PBS 2/1 89, 218 (Alstola 2020).
Some tablets carry Aramaic dockets summarizing the content (Hilprecht 1898, e.g. no. 71).

Naming (Alstola 2020, Table 3): of 41 Judean fathers' names, 46% Yahwistic, 24% other West Semitic, 22% Akkadian, 2% Iranian; of 60 Judean first names, 67% Yahwistic, 25% West Semitic, 5% Akkadian, 3% Iranian.
The archive mentions the Kabaru canal (river Chebar): servants of the official Mannukiya were paid for carrying barley from Nippur to the Kabaru canal (Alstola 2020, ch. 5).
questions: Who counts as a Judean? Alstola (Judeans in Babylonia, 2020) identifies Judeans by names containing the Yahwistic element (spelled Ia-a-hu-/-ia-a-ma in cuneiform) and their close kin, and discusses borderline names (e.g. Ardia, Zabdia) that some treat as Yahwistic and others do not. Hilprecht's 1898 list was broader and included names that later work does not accept as Yahwistic. The count of Judeans depends on this rule.

Assimilated or distinct? Alstola (2020, Table 3), following an observation by E. J. Bickerman (1978), finds sons more often bore Yahwistic names (67% of 60 first names) than their fathers did (46% of 41 patronymics), while some Judeans bore Akkadian, other West Semitic and even Iranian names (the last in families dealing with Persian officials). That pattern runs against a simple story of steady assimilation. The tablets record transactions, not worship, so they are silent on Sabbath, temple or ties to Jerusalem.

End of the archive: Stolper (Entrepreneurs and Empire, 1985) and van Driel (1989) differed on when and why the archive stops, as Alstola (2020, n. 877) notes. The room's field record is thin: no excavation report was published, only Haynes's notes and letters.

biblical.tie: The return lists show Judeans leaving Babylonia; the Murashu texts show Judeans who stayed in the Nippur countryside a century after the deportations, under Artaxerxes I and Darius II. Several names in the tablets (e.g. Hananiah, Gedaliah, Haggai) are the same names borne by people in Ezra-Nehemiah, not the same individuals.
Nehemiah serves Artaxerxes I; the archive's main span (454-414 BCE) is the same reign and the next, and documents the tax and land system of the Persian crown in Babylonia at the time.

Exiles settled by canals in Babylonia (the Chebar, Tel-abib, the Ahava canal). The Murashu archive itself names the Kabaru canal, the Babylonian form of 'Chebar', as the waterway to which barley from Nippur was shipped (Alstola 2020): the same canal Ezekiel names, attested in the 5th-century business records.

sources.cite: H. V. Hilprecht and A. T. Clay, Business Documents of Murashû Sons of Nippur Dated in the Reign of Artaxerxes I (464-424 B.C.), The Babylonian Expedition of the University of Pennsylvania, Series A: Cuneiform Texts, vol. IX (Philadelphia, 1898).

corrections: Old entry said the tablets are 'written in Aramaic': they are Akkadian cuneiform clay tablets; only short dockets on some tablets are Aramaic.

Old entry called it the records of 'a Jewish family' and a 'Jewish community': the Murashus were a Babylonian family of Nippur (names honouring Enlil and Ninurta); Judeans appear as clients, witnesses and minor officials, 61 individuals in 64 documents (Alstola 2020).
Old entry said the archive is housed 'in the University of Pennsylvania': the bulk is divided between the Istanbul Archaeological Museum and the Penn Museum, with a few elsewhere.
Old entry described 'production and trade of goods': the business was agricultural credit and management of land-for-service holdings (leases, rents, tax advances, pledges).
Old entry gave 'Date: c. 450 BCE': the dated tablets run from 454 to 414 BCE, with stragglers to 404 BCE.
Old entry listed 'Jeremiah 35 (Rechabites)' as a connection: nothing in the published discussion ties the archive to the Rechabites.

sites.name: Nabonidus Cylinders from Ur (naming Belshazzar)
sites.subtitle: Clay foundation cylinders of Nabonidus, king of Babylon, with a prayer for 'Belshazzar, the eldest son' · 555-539 BCE
sites.date: Reign of Nabonidus (555-539 BCE; Barton 1916 gives 555-538)
sites.date_basis: The text is in Nabonidus's own name as king of Babylon and records his rebuilding of the ziggurat of the moon-god Sin at Ur. It carries no regnal-year date; the reign is fixed by Babylonian chronicles and king lists.

discovery.who: J. E. Taylor, British vice-consul at Basra, working under H. C. Rawlinson (Barton 1916, p. 44)
discovery.where: Tell el-Muqayyar (Ur), temple tower of Sin

sites.location: British Museum, London: four exemplars, BM 91125, BM 91126, BM 91127, BM 91128 (CDLI: RINBE 2, Nabonidus 32, ex. 1-4)

physical.material: Baked clay cylinders

overview: In 1854 J. E. Taylor, British vice-consul at Basra, excavated at Tell el-Muqayyar, the site of Ur, and recovered inscribed foundation cylinders of Nabonidus, the last native king of Babylon. The text records Nabonidus's restoration of the temple-tower (ziggurat) of the moon-god Sin and closes with a prayer to Sin.

In the prayer Nabonidus asks for long life for himself and then prays for 'Belshazzar, the firstborn son, proceeding from my loins'. The cuneiform writes his name dEN-LUGAL-URU3, Bel-sharra-usur. Four exemplars of the same text are in the British Museum and are edited as Nabonidus 32 in The Royal Inscriptions of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, vol. 2 (Weiershäuser and Novotny 2020).

The cylinders, with the Nabonidus Chronicle's notices that 'the son of the king' was in Akkad while Nabonidus stayed at Tema, establish Belshazzar as Nabonidus's eldest son and a figure of state in Babylon.

text.quote: As for Belshazzar, the firstborn son, proceeding from my loins, place in his heart fear of thy great divinity; let him not turn to sinning; let him be satisfied with fulness of life!
text.translation: Nabonidus's prayer to Sin, trans. G. A. Barton, Archaeology and the Bible (Philadelphia, 1916), Part II ch. XVIII, p. 382

evidence: Four exemplars of one text (RINBE 2, Nabonidus 32) in the British Museum: BM 91125, 91126, 91127, 91128; provenance Ur (CDLI records).
Col. ii lines 24-26 of exemplar 1 (CDLI transliteration): u3 sza2 {disz}{d}en-lugal-uru3 / DUMU resz-tu-u2 / s,i-it lib3-bi-ia, 'and of Bel-sharra-usur, the eldest son, offspring of my heart'.
The same prayer asks Sin to keep Nabonidus himself from sin and grant him long days (col. ii 19-23).

The Nabonidus Chronicle (as translated by Barton 1916, p. 382) records for Nabonidus's 9th year that the king was at Tema while 'the son of the king, the princes, and soldiers were in Akkad'; Barton notes similar entries for other years.
Barton (1916, p. 384) reports a contract from Erech, dated in Nabonidus's 12th year, sworn by 'the oath of Nabuna'id, King of Babylon, and of Belshazzar, the king's son' (from Pinches).
questions: Was Belshazzar 'king'? Daniel 5:1 calls him king. The Ur cylinders call him 'eldest son' and the Chronicle calls him 'the son of the king'. Barton (1916, p. 384) notes that an oath sworn jointly by Nabonidus and Belshazzar shows him 'but slightly lower in rank and power than the king himself'. Dan 5:7, 16, 29 offer 'third ruler in the kingdom', which fits a second-in-rank prince. No text yet seen calls Belshazzar šarru (king).

'Nebuchadnezzar his father' (Dan 5:2, 11, 18): the cylinder calls Belshazzar the son of Nabonidus. Barton (1916, p. 382) notes that Nabonidus was not of Nebuchadnezzar's line. Some take 'father' as 'ancestor' or 'predecessor', or propose descent through his mother; no cuneiform text seen here documents Belshazzar's mother.

biblical.tie: Daniel names Belshazzar as ruler in Babylon on the night it fell. The cylinder independently confirms a Belshazzar (Bel-sharra-usur) as Nabonidus's eldest son, from Nabonidus's own inscription.
The offer to make Daniel 'third ruler in the kingdom' fits a regime in which Nabonidus was king and Belshazzar his son held power in Babylon. Reading 'third' that way is an interpretation.
The cylinder names Belshazzar's father as Nabonidus, not Nebuchadnezzar. How to reconcile this with Daniel is an open question (see questions).

corrections: Claims that there is a single 'Nabonidus Cylinder': there are four exemplars of the same text, BM 91125-91128.
Claims that the cylinder calls Belshazzar 'king' or 'co-regent': it calls him 'the eldest son, offspring of my heart'. Co-regency is an inference from the Chronicle and from joint oaths.

sites.name: Early Roman Nazareth (houses and excavations)
sites.subtitle: Excavated Early Roman remains of Jesus' home village · 1st century BCE – 1st century CE
sites.date: Late Hellenistic to Early Roman occupation (late 2nd century BCE to the first third of the 2nd century CE) next to the Church of the Annunciation, following an Iron Age IIA–B stratum
sites.date_basis: Stratigraphy and pottery in the IAA excavation by Y. Alexandre ('Atiqot 98); stratified sequence at the Sisters of Nazareth convent, Nazareth Archaeological Project 2006–10 (Dark 2012).

discovery.when: Sisters of Nazareth site first uncovered 1884 and re-examined 2006–10; Mary's Well excavated by the IAA (published 2012); house next to the Church of the Annunciation excavated by the IAA (published in 'Atiqot 98)
discovery.who: Ken Dark (Nazareth Archaeological Project); Yardenna Alexandre (Israel Antiquities Authority)
discovery.where: Central Nazareth, Lower Galilee

sites.location: In situ, Nazareth, Israel (the Sisters of Nazareth convent; the area next to the Franciscan Church of the Annunciation compound; Mary's Well). 'Nazareth Village' is a separate open-air museum on the edge of town.
overview: Three separate things are mixed together under this name. The first is Nazareth Village, an open-air museum that 'reconstructs and reenacts village life in the Galilee in the time of Jesus' (its own description). Its research is credited to Stephen Pfann's team, with Ross Voss as project archaeologist. It is a modern reconstruction on farmland, not the ancient village centre.

The second is the Sisters of Nazareth convent in the town centre. Found by accident in 1884 and dug informally for decades, it was re-examined by Ken Dark's Nazareth Archaeological Project in 2006–10. Dark identifies a partly rock-cut first-century domestic building, perhaps a courtyard house, as the first surface-built Early Roman house from Nazareth to be published. He notes the area was later used for burial, and that a Byzantine church above it is probably the 'Church of the Nutrition'. A 7th-century pilgrim text says that church stood over the house where Jesus was raised.

The third is an IAA excavation by Yardenna Alexandre next to the Church of the Annunciation compound. It found three strata: Iron IIA–B (10th to early 8th century BCE), a late Hellenistic to Early Roman dwelling (late 2nd century BCE to the first third of the 2nd century CE), and Crusader–Mamluk. The Roman-period house had a three-level complex of underground pits or silos full of discarded potsherds. Alexandre reads this as possibly the Jewish practice of breaking ritually impure pottery. The final report appeared in 'Atiqot 98.
evidence: A late Hellenistic to Early Roman dwelling next to the Church of the Annunciation compound, with a three-level complex of subterranean pits or silos (Alexandre, 'Atiqot 98).
Many potsherds dumped in those pits, similar to deposits at other Early Roman Jewish villages in Galilee (Alexandre, 'Atiqot 98).
An Iron IIA–B stratum (10th to early 8th century BCE) under the same spot (Alexandre, 'Atiqot 98).
At the Sisters of Nazareth convent, a partly rock-cut structure that Dark interprets as a 1st-century CE domestic building, later superseded by burials (Dark, Antiquaries Journal 92, 2012).
A vaulted Byzantine church above the Sisters of Nazareth remains, which Dark identifies as probably the Church of the Nutrition (Dark 2023).
Excavations at Mary's Well found remains from the late Hellenistic to the Ottoman periods, mostly a Crusader fountain house and Mamluk alterations (Alexandre 2012).
questions: Is the Sisters of Nazareth house the house the Byzantines venerated as Jesus' home? Dark (OUP 2023, chs. 3–6) argues the Byzantine church over it is the Church of the Nutrition, which a 7th-century pilgrim says covered the house where Jesus grew up. Bagatti's older view, which Dark says prevailed from the 1930s, treated the convent site as unimportant. Dark's identification of the church rests on the match with the pilgrim text. The first-century house itself carries no inscription or name.

Did Jewish-Christians keep Nazareth's holy places before Constantine? Bagatti and Testa said they did. Taylor (Christians and the Holy Places, OUP 1993, ch. 11) examines that hypothesis and argues it was assembled from scattered literary and archaeological pieces. Her chapter is the counter-case to their reconstruction.

biblical.tie: The Gospels make Nazareth in Galilee the home of Mary and Joseph and the town where Jesus grew up. The excavations show a settlement there in the late Hellenistic to Early Roman period, the right date for that.
Nazareth 'where he had been brought up', built on a hill with a brow. The finds show a village; they do not identify the synagogue or the cliff.
'Can anything good come out of Nazareth?' Nathanael is scorning the town; he is not calling it Jesus' hometown. The finds show a modest Jewish village with ordinary domestic installations.

sites.name: Nebuchadnezzar II's Palace Inscriptions
sites.subtitle: Royal building texts of Nebuchadnezzar II describing his palaces at Babylon · 604-562 BCE
sites.date: Reign of Nebuchadnezzar II, 604-562 BCE; the East India House Inscription belongs to the later part of the reign (Langdon 1905 groups it with the palace-building texts after c. 590)
sites.date_basis: The texts name Nebuchadnezzar son of Nabopolassar; relative order from their contents (which buildings are described as finished) as worked out by Langdon (1905).

discovery.when: East India House Inscription: found before 1803 in the ruins of Babylon and published in London in 1803; palace buildings excavated by the Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft 1899-1917
discovery.who: EIH obtained by Sir Harford Jones Brydges (British Resident in Baghdad); palace excavated by Robert Koldewey
discovery.where: Babylon (Iraq): the Kasr mound (Southern Citadel/palace), with other copies of related texts from Babylon

sites.location: East India House Inscription: British Museum, London (registration 1938,0520.1 per secondary listing; the museum's own record was not reachable). Related cylinders: British Museum 85-4-30,1 and Louvre AO 1506 (Langdon 1905).

physical.material: EIH: dark stone tablet (Langdon 1905: 'black basalt'); related texts on clay cylinders
physical.dimensions: EIH: about 56.5 x 50.2 cm (Langdon: 28 inches square, 4 inches thick); ten columns, 624 lines (Langdon 1905)
physical.script: EIH in archaizing Babylonian cuneiform; cylinders in Neo-Babylonian script

overview: Nebuchadnezzar II left hundreds of building inscriptions - on cylinders, stone tablets and stamped bricks - but almost none report his wars. The largest is the East India House Inscription, a ten-column stone tablet found at Babylon before 1803, which recounts his work on the temples of Esagila and Ezida, the city walls and gates, and above all the rebuilding of the old palace and the building of new palaces 'between the walls' and to the north.

Langdon (1905) showed that the East India House text is an enlarged re-edition of an earlier palace cylinder known in two copies (British Museum 85-4-30,1 and Louvre AO 1506). The palace passages match what Koldewey excavated on the Kasr: a palace raised on a high platform next to his father Nabopolassar's, with thick walls of burnt brick in bitumen and lime mortar.

None of these texts mention Judah or Jerusalem. Barton (1917) noted this directly: 'His inscriptions give no account of these events.' Their biblical interest is the king's own boast of building Babylon, compared with Daniel 4:30. In 2025 two new Nebuchadnezzar cylinders from the ziggurat of Kish and a full edition of 527 administrative tablets from the Babylon palace archives were published.

text.quote: Upon the top of it a great abode for my royal dwelling place with mortar and burnt brick I made high. With the palace of my father I annexed it. In a favorable month, upon a lucky day, I placed its foundation upon the breast of the abyss. Its top I raised like a rocky cliff. In 15 days its work I completed.
text.translation: East India House Inscription col. VIII 59 - IX 1, trans. S. Langdon, Building Inscriptions of the Neo-Babylonian Empire I (1905), p. 139

evidence: EIH: ten columns, 624 lines, archaizing script; first published in London in 1803 (Langdon 1905).
EIH describes restoring Nabopolassar's old palace, whose foundations had been weakened by flood water and whose gates had sunk below the raised street (Langdon 1905, p. 135).
EIH describes a new palace built between the city walls, joined to his father's palace, 'In 15 days its work I completed' (Langdon 1905, p. 139).
EIH describes rebuilding the gates of Imgur-Bel and Nimitti-Bel with bulls and serpents and bronze bulls at their thresholds (Langdon 1905, p. 131) - the Ishtar Gate program.

Koldewey's excavation of the Kasr (1899-1917) found Nebuchadnezzar's palace on a raised platform, with lime mortar used in his latest buildings (Kasr, Principal Citadel, Babil) (Koldewey 1914, p. 31).

Barton's selection of Nebuchadnezzar texts (1917) contains a general claim of conquests 'from the upper sea to the lower sea', the Wadi Brisa (Lebanon) text, and a wall-building text; none mentions Judah (Barton 1917, pp. 379-380).

Pedersén (2025) publishes 527 administrative texts from the South Palace archives of Nebuchadnezzar's reign; its abstract states the largest single oil allotment went to 'the biblical king Jehoiachin'.
questions: Why no Judah? The royal building inscriptions describe buildings and piety; Nebuchadnezzar's 597 BCE capture of Jerusalem is known instead from a separate genre of text, the Babylonian chronicles. Barton (1917, p. 380) states that his inscriptions 'give no account of these events'. Whether this silence reflects genre or choice is a reading, not something the texts say.

Which copy is the 'real' text? Langdon (1905) argued the Louvre cylinder (AO 1506, his 'B') is the earlier original and the British Museum cylinder ('A') a later, Marduk-focused copy, with EIH an enlargement of B. That textual history is Langdon's reconstruction from comparing wording (e.g. 'their lordship' vs 'his lordship'); later editions have not been checked against it for this entry.
The '15 days' claim for the new palace is the text's own figure; nothing in the excavation report tests it.

biblical.tie: 'Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?' The king's inscriptions make exactly this kind of claim about building the palace and the city (e.g. EIH: 'a great abode for my royal dwelling place ... I made high'). The texts do not mention a madness or exile of the king.
Nebuchadnezzar is the conqueror of Jerusalem in the biblical record; these building inscriptions do not mention the campaign (Barton 1917).
The palace's administrative archive (Pedersén 2025) includes the oil lists naming Jehoiachin; see jehoiachin-rations-tablets.

sources.cite: S. Langdon, Building Inscriptions of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, Part I: Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar (Paris: Ernest Leroux, 1905), Nebuchadnezzar No. 15 (East India House Inscription)

corrections: Old entry: the inscriptions 'provide a detailed account of ... the construction of the famed Ishtar Gate and the reconstruction of the Etemenanki ziggurat'. The EIH does describe the walls' gates with bulls and serpents; Etemenanki appears in the related palace cylinder (Langdon's No. 14 lists work on Etemenanki), not in the palace passages quoted here.

sites.name: Nehemiah's Wall
sites.subtitle: Claimed remains of the wall Nehemiah rebuilt · 5th century BCE (disputed)
sites.date: Disputed. Nehemiah's rebuilding is set by the text in the 20th year of Artaxerxes (Neh 2:1), i.e. c. 445 BCE if Artaxerxes I. The masonry proposed as his wall (the 'Northern Tower' and adjoining wall on the crest of the City of David's eastern slope) has been dated by excavators and critics to the Persian period (E. Mazar 2009), to the late Hellenistic / Hasmonean period (Kenyon for the towers; Finkelstein et al. 2007, summarizing Mazar's own 2007 report), or left open.
sites.date_basis: Pottery from fills under and against the tower and wall; no inscription or datable foundation deposit ties any wall segment to Nehemiah. The Artaxerxes identification is fixed by Elephantine: Cowley 30 shows Bigvai as governor of Judah in 408 BCE, so Nehemiah's 32nd year of Artaxerxes (Neh 13:6) must be Artaxerxes I (Cowley 1923).

discovery.when: Wall line exposed by R. A. S. Macalister and J. G. Duncan (1920s) and K. Kenyon (1960s); re-excavated 2005-2008 by Eilat Mazar, who later argued for a Nehemiah date for the Northern Tower (BAR 2009)
discovery.who: Macalister and Duncan; Kathleen Kenyon; Yigal Shiloh; Eilat Mazar
discovery.where: Crest of the eastern slope of the City of David (south-eastern ridge), Jerusalem, above the Stepped Stone Structure

sites.location: In situ, City of David, Jerusalem

physical.material: Dressed and rough stone masonry (tower and city-wall segment); no mudbrick is reported in the sources checked

overview: The book of Nehemiah says that Nehemiah, cupbearer to King Artaxerxes, came to Jerusalem as governor, found its walls broken down and gates burnt, and organized the repair of the whole circuit in 52 days (Neh 6:15), with work gangs assigned to named sections and gates (Neh 3). No inscription naming Nehemiah has been found in any wall.

On the crest of the eastern slope of the City of David stand a stretch of city wall and two towers, excavated in turn by Macalister and Duncan in the 1920s, Kenyon in the 1960s and Shiloh in the 1970s-80s. Kenyon identified a segment of wall north of the northern tower with Nehemiah's fortification; Kenyon and Shiloh dated the Southern Tower to the Hasmonean period, while Macalister and Duncan had called it post-exilic, 5th-4th century BCE (as recorded in Mazar's 2009 endnotes). Eilat Mazar, re-excavating the area from 2005, later argued that the Northern Tower belonged to the Persian period and so to Nehemiah (BAR, March/April 2009, 'The Wall That Nehemiah Built'; the article's evidence section is paywalled and was not read here).

Finkelstein, Herzog, Singer-Avitz and Ussishkin (Tel Aviv 34, 2007) note that Mazar's own 2007 report had assigned the eastern city wall and both towers to the late Hellenistic Hasmonean fortification and that 'no remains were assigned to the Persian period' in the Large Stone Structure. Finkelstein (JSOT 32, 2008) argued the Persian-period settlement was small and that the archaeology, read without the Nehemiah account as a guide, does not show a Persian-period wall. The question is open: the ground shows a wall line reused over centuries; the text shows a rebuilding; no find yet links the two directly.
evidence: A city-wall segment and two towers stand on the crest of the City of David's eastern slope, above the Stepped Stone Structure (Finkelstein et al. 2007, describing Mazar 2007).
Kenyon (1974: 191) identified the wall segment north of the northern tower with Nehemiah's fortifications (as cited in Finkelstein et al. 2007).
Mazar's 2007 preliminary report dated the eastern city wall and its two towers to the late Hellenistic (Hasmonean) fortification (as summarized in Finkelstein et al. 2007).

In BAR 35/2 (March/April 2009) Mazar argued for a Nehemiah-period date; the article's endnotes record that Macalister and Duncan dated the Southern Tower to the 'Post-Exilic period (fifth-fourth century B.C.E.)' while Kenyon and Shiloh dated it Hasmonean.

Renewed Giv'ati Parking Lot excavations found late Iron Age, Persian and Early Hellenistic remains on the western slope; after 586 BCE the city was rebuilt along the summit and north-western slope (Shalev, Shalom, Bocher and Gadot, Tel Aviv 47, 2020).

The mid-slope fortification and retaining wall on the eastern slope were radiocarbon-dated to after the earthquake of c. 760 BCE, reign of Uzziah, not Hezekiah (Regev et al., PNAS 121, 2024). This fixes the date of an Iron Age wall line that a 5th-century rebuilding could have followed or reused; it does not date any Persian-period work.
questions: Is the Northern Tower Persian or Hasmonean? E. Mazar (BAR, March/April 2009) dates it to Nehemiah's time; the evidence she gives there sits behind the paywall and has not been reviewed for this entry. Finkelstein, Herzog, Singer-Avitz and Ussishkin (Tel Aviv 34/2, 2007) cite Mazar's own earlier report assigning the city wall and towers to the Hasmonean fortification and argue that most elements in this area are late Hellenistic, with 'circumstantial evidence' for that date. Pottery under a structure gives only the earliest possible date; neither side has published a sealed foundation deposit for the tower in the sources seen here.

Was Persian-period Jerusalem big enough to need a circuit wall? Finkelstein (JSOT 32/4, 2008) argues activity in the Persian and early Hellenistic City of David was sparse and concentrated south of Mazar's area; the same study opens his book Hasmonean Realities behind Ezra, Nehemiah, and Chronicles, whose title states his view that these books reflect later, Hasmonean-period conditions. Shalev, Shalom, Bocher and Gadot (Tel Aviv 47, 2020) show Persian and Early Hellenistic finds on the western slope and the summit. O. Lipschits' 2024 collected essays include 'Persian Period Finds from Jerusalem: Facts and Interpretations' and a reassessment of the city's Persian-period development. The size of the settlement is still argued from sherds and fills, not from a Persian-period wall line.

Repair or new build? Nehemiah 3 describes repairing existing walls and gates section by section. If Nehemiah followed the Iron Age line, the job was repair of standing ruins, which fits the 52-day figure better than new construction on a new line. That is our reading of the text; the archaeology has not identified which line he used.

biblical.tie: Report that 'the wall of Jerusalem also is broken down, and the gates thereof are burned'; Nehemiah's night inspection. Destruction of 586 BCE is attested in Jerusalem's burnt layers; which walls were still standing in 445 BCE is not known from excavation.

Section-by-section list of repairs and gates (Sheep Gate, Fish Gate, Fountain Gate, 'the wall of the pool of Siloah by the king's garden' 3:15). Mazar used these toponyms to identify buildings; Finkelstein et al. (2007) object to using them for earlier periods. No gate named in Neh 3 has been identified by inscription.
'So the wall was finished ... in fifty and two days.' A 52-day job implies repair of an existing line, not new foundations; the text itself uses 'repaired' throughout ch. 3.

Sanballat the Horonite opposes the work; Elephantine papyrus Cowley 30 (408 BCE) names 'Delaiah and Shelemiah the sons of Sanballat governor of Samaria', which with Bigvai's governorship fixes Nehemiah under Artaxerxes I.

sources.cite: I. Finkelstein, Z. Herzog, L. Singer-Avitz and D. Ussishkin, 'Has King David's Palace in Jerusalem Been Found?', Tel Aviv 34/2 (2007): 142-164. DOI 10.1179/tav.2007.2007.2.142.
sources.verified: Downloaded the 25-page PDF from the archived Tel Aviv University copy. p. 144 summarizes Mazar 2007: city wall and two towers late Hellenistic (Hasmonean); Kenyon (1974: 191) identified the segment north of the northern tower with Nehemiah; 'No remains were assigned to the Persian period.' p. 153: Persian and early Hellenistic activity sparse; n. 5: Mazar uses Nehemiah 3 toponyms for 10th-century buildings.

PNAS radiocarbon chronology re-dated the eastern-slope mid-slope fortification to Uzziah's reign (after c. 760 BCE), clarifying the Iron Age wall line that later builders inherited. It does not identify a Persian-period wall.

corrections: Old entry said the wall was 'uncovered ... in 2007 by archaeologist Eilat Mazar': the wall line and towers were excavated by Macalister and Duncan in the 1920s and by Kenyon and Shiloh later; Mazar re-excavated them and in 2007 proposed a Nehemiah date.

sites.name: Nuzi Tablets
sites.subtitle: Private and official cuneiform records from a Hurrian town near Kirkuk, Iraq · 15th-14th century BCE
sites.date: Mid-2nd millennium BCE, Mitanni period (conventionally 15th-14th century BCE)
sites.date_basis: Tie-in to the Mitanni king Saushshatar, whose letter occurs in the Nuzi material (E. A. Speiser, 'A Letter of Saushshatar and the Date of the Kirkuk Tablets,' JAOS 49, 1929), plus the generations of families traced through the archives. The tablets carry no absolute dates.

discovery.when: Excavation begun 1925; continued from 1927 through the early 1930s
discovery.who: Edward Chiera (1925, Iraq Museum + American School of Oriental Research in Baghdad; 1927, with Harvard University), then R. H. Pfeiffer and R. F. S. Starr as directors; University of Pennsylvania Museum later associated
discovery.where: Yorghan Tepe (ancient Nuzi), near Kirkuk, Iraq; the kingdom of Arrapha

sites.location: Divided between the Iraq Museum and the American partner institutions of the joint expeditions; the present repositories of specific tablets are not confirmed in a published museum record

physical.material: Clay tablets
physical.language: Akkadian, local dialect with heavy Hurrian influence (many Hurrian personal names and terms)

overview: Nuzi (Yorghan Tepe, near Kirkuk) was excavated from 1925 by Edward Chiera for the Iraq Museum and the American School of Oriental Research in Baghdad, and from 1927 with Harvard University; Speiser wrote in 1930 that the Nuzi tablets were already 'one of the largest collections of cuneiform tablets dug up on a single site.' The texts were published in the series 'Joint Expedition with the Iraq Museum at Nuzi' (from 1927) and 'Excavations at Nuzi' (Harvard Semitic Series, from 1929).

The tablets are mostly private legal and economic records of families in a Hurrian town of the kingdom of Arrapha: adoptions (including 'sale-adoptions' used to transfer land), wills, marriage contracts, court cases and loans. They let one follow some families over several generations.

From the 1920s-1950s, scholars compared Nuzi customs with the patriarchal stories in Genesis - a barren wife giving her husband a concubine, adoption of an heir, household gods and inheritance. Later studies (T. L. Thompson 1974; M. Greenberg 1962 on the teraphim) re-examined those parallels text by text.

text.quote: If Gilimninu bears (children), Shennima shall not take another wife; and if Gilimninu does not bear, Gilimninu a woman of the Lullu as wife for Shennima shall take. As for (the concubine's) offspring, Gilimninu shall [not] send (them) away.
text.translation: E. A. Speiser, 'New Kirkuk Documents Relating to Family Laws,' AASOR 10 (1930), text 2 (= HSS V 67), lines 16-23, p. 32

evidence: HSS V 67 (Speiser text 2): an adoption tied to a marriage. If the wife Gilimninu is childless she must provide her husband a Lullu woman; the concubine's children may not be expelled; if Gilimninu has children the husband may not take another wife (Speiser 1930).
Same text: Shurihil's natural son, if born later, would be 'firstborn' and take a double share; the adopted Shennima becomes second heir (Speiser 1930, lines 7-11).
Same text: a handmaid is also given to Gilimninu, with a supervisor assigned (lines 35-37; the handmaid's name is only partly legible in the scan).
Speiser (1930) grouped 40 texts from HSS V as real adoptions, sale-adoptions, wills, and marriage records.
Local Akkadian shows Hurrian influence; Speiser notes pronunciation 'doubtless under the influence of Hurrian' in ancient Arrapha (1930 notes).
questions: Do Nuzi customs date the patriarchs? The 1920s-50s school (e.g. C. J. Gadd, 'Tablets from Kirkuk', RA 23, 1926, cited by Speiser; E. A. Speiser 1930) read Nuzi family law as the background of Genesis 15-31. T. L. Thompson (The Historicity of the Patriarchal Narratives, BZAW 133, 1974, ch. 10 'Nuzi and the Patriarchal Narratives', pp. 196-297) re-examined each proposed parallel and argued that several rest on misreadings of the tablets or occur in other periods too. The HSS V 67 clause is real; whether it fixes the date of Genesis is the argument.

Rachel's teraphim (Gen 31): the proposal that Nuzi household gods served as title to inheritance was re-examined by M. Greenberg ('Another Look at Rachel's Theft of the Teraphim,' JBL 81, 1962) and by M. A. Morrison ('The Jacob and Laban Narrative in Light of Near Eastern Sources,' BA 46, 1983, 155-164). The texts of these articles were not available for this entry, so their exact conclusions are not stated here.

biblical.tie: HSS V 67 obliges a childless wife to give her husband a slave-concubine and protects that woman's children - the same arrangement Sarah makes with Hagar and Rachel and Leah make with Bilhah and Zilpah. That is a documented legal practice, not a Nuzi text about the patriarchs.
The same tablet has an adopted heir displaced to second rank if a natural son is born, comparable to Abram's words about Eliezer and the promise of a son. Correspondence of custom; our reading.
Proposed link between Nuzi household gods and inheritance rights; disputed (Greenberg 1962; Morrison 1983). Not established from sources read here.

Work began in 1925 under Edward Chiera (Iraq Museum and ASOR Baghdad), continued from 1927 with Harvard, with R. H. Pfeiffer and R. F. S. Starr as later directors (Speiser 1930). sites.name: Ophel Pithos Inscription
sites.subtitle: Letters incised on a storage jar before firing, Ophel, Jerusalem · Iron IIA context
sites.date: Context: early Iron Age IIA, which the excavator places in the mid-10th c. BCE; Winderbaum (2022) confirmed the phase; Finkelstein (2022, cited by Vainstub) dissented on the date.
sites.date_basis: Pottery typology of the pithoi (neckless type, Early Iron IIA) and stratigraphy of Building II; no radiocarbon date for the context was located.

discovery.when: 2012 (announced July 2013)
discovery.who: Eilat Mazar, Hebrew University Ophel excavations
discovery.where: Building II, c. 80 m south of the southern wall of the Temple Mount, Ophel, Jerusalem; sherds of seven pithoi reused as fill under the building's second floor

sites.location: Not confirmed in a published museum record.

physical.material: Fired clay; inscription incised on the shoulder below the rim before firing
physical.dimensions: Letters c. 2.5 cm high (press report of editio princeps)
physical.script: Disputed: early Canaanite / proto-Canaanite (Mazar, Ben-Shlomo, Ahituv 2013) or Ancient South Arabian (Vainstub 2023)
physical.language: Disputed: unknown West Semitic, Hebrew (Galil; Petrovich 2015), or Sabaean (Vainstub 2023)

overview: In 2012 Eilat Mazar's Ophel excavation found fragments of seven large storage jars (pithoi) of the neckless Early Iron IIA type, used as fill beneath the second floor of Building II, about 80 m south of the Temple Mount's southern wall. One pithos shoulder carries seven surviving letters, incised before the jar was fired.

The editio princeps (Mazar, Ben-Shlomo and Ahituv, IEJ 63, 2013) read the letters in an early Canaanite script; the press release stated that the letter combination 'has no meaning in known west-Semitic languages' and that its meaning is unknown. It is the earliest alphabetic inscription so far found in Jerusalem.

Close to a dozen readings have followed. Galil read Hebrew 'yyn ḥlq' ('inferior wine'), followed by Petrovich (PEQ 2015); Vainstub (JJAR 4, 2023) reads Ancient South Arabian script in Sabaean: '[ ]šy ladanum 5'.

text.quote: ]šy lḏn ḫ̇  - '[ ]šy ladanum 5' (Vainstub's reading, right-hand group); editio princeps letter sequence (as reported): m, q, p(?), ḥ, n, (possibly) l, n - meaning unknown.
text.translation: D. Vainstub, Jerusalem Journal of Archaeology 4 (2023): 45, fig. 3; editio princeps letters as summarised in the July 2013 press report of Mazar, Ben-Shlomo & Ahituv, IEJ 63 (2013).

evidence: Seven pithoi, neckless type, Early Iron IIA; one inscribed (Vainstub 2023, citing Mazar 2015: 467-468).
Incised before firing, so the writing was done where the jar was made; Vainstub states the vessel was locally made.
Seven letters survive (Vainstub 2023, p. 44); letter height c. 2.5 cm (press report).
Found in secondary use as floor fill, not in the jar's primary use context.
Editors of the editio princeps: script early Canaanite, meaning unknown (press report, 2013).
questions: Script and language: Mazar, Ben-Shlomo and Ahituv (IEJ 63, 2013) classify the script as early Canaanite and give no meaning; Galil and Petrovich (PEQ 147, 2015) read Hebrew 'yyn ḥlq' ('poor wine'), taking the double yod as southern Hebrew spelling; Vainstub (JJAR 4, 2023) reads Ancient South Arabian letters in Sabaean, '[ ]šy lḏn 5' ('ladanum, 5'), linking lḏn with Hebrew šəḥēlet of Exod 30:34.
Direction and letter count: Petrovich (2015) argues sinistrograde reading and restores yod-yod; Vainstub divides the text into a right-to-left group and a left-to-right group (fig. 3).

Date of the context: Mazar (2015) and Winderbaum (2022) place Building II in early Iron IIA (mid-10th c.); Finkelstein (2022) dissents (cited by Vainstub, n. 2); Wightman (PEQ 157, 2024) offers 'a significantly different reconstruction' of the Ophel's 11th-9th c. history; Kleiman (Eretz-Israel 35, 2024) wrote specifically on the inscription's date (text not read).

biblical.tie: The queen of Sheba brings spices to Solomon. Vainstub's Sabaean reading would put a South Arabian writer handling aromatics in 10th c. Jerusalem; that connection depends entirely on his script identification.
šəḥēlet as an incense ingredient; Vainstub equates it with ladanum (lḏn). This is his lexical argument.

The Ophel lies between the City of David and the later Temple Mount. The find shows writing in a 10th c. (on the excavator's date) Jerusalem building; it says nothing on its own about David or Solomon.

sites.name: Persepolis Fortification Tablets
sites.subtitle: Administrative archive of the Persepolis region under Darius I · 509-494 BCE
sites.date: Years 13-28 of Darius I, 509-494 BCE (Hallock 1969, for the Elamite texts)
sites.date_basis: Regnal-year and month dates written on the tablets; Hallock notes the identification of the king as Darius I was settled by a text naming Darius and by the calendar data (intercalations).

discovery.who: Oriental Institute (University of Chicago) Persepolis expedition directed by Ernst Herzfeld
discovery.where: Rooms in the fortification wall at the north-east corner of the Persepolis terrace, Fars, Iran

sites.location: Lent by Iran to the Oriental Institute (now ISAC), University of Chicago, in 1937 for study; much of the collection has been returned to Iran in batches (150 complete tablets in 1948, per Hallock). The balance of the loan's location as of 2026 was Not confirmed in a published museum record.

physical.material: Unbaked clay tablets, fragments and sealed tags/bullae; many sealed with cylinder or stamp seals
physical.dimensions: Remains of perhaps 15,000-18,000 Elamite documents, 700-1,000 Aramaic documents, and 5,000-6,000 sealed but uninscribed tablets (Stolper and Tavernier 2007); 2,087 Elamite texts published by Hallock (PF 1-2087); the US Supreme Court described 'approximately 30,000 clay tablets and fragments' at Chicago
physical.script: Elamite cuneiform (the great majority); Aramaic alphabetic script; single items in Greek, Old Persian cuneiform, Phrygian(?) and a Neo-Babylonian legal text
physical.language: Achaemenid Elamite (majority); Imperial Aramaic; one Old Persian administrative tablet (Fort. 1208-101); one Greek tablet (Fort. 1771)

overview: In 1933-34 Ernst Herzfeld's Oriental Institute team excavated rooms in the fortification wall at the north-east corner of the Persepolis terrace and found tens of thousands of unbaked clay tablets and fragments. They were impregnated with paraffin, shipped to Chicago on loan from Iran, and became available for study in 1937. Richard Hallock published 2,087 Elamite texts in 1969 (OIP 92).

The texts are the day-to-day records of the royal economy of the Persepolis region: issues and transfers of grain, flour, wine, beer, fruit, sheep and cattle as rations to workers, officials, travellers and members of the royal family, across an area reaching at least to Niriz in the south and into Elam in the north. Travellers carried sealed authorizations and the supplier's sealed receipts returned to Persepolis. Letters include orders from Darius himself, e.g. Fort. 6764, where Darius orders 100 sheep to be issued to Irtasduna (Artystone), and PF 1795, 200 marris of wine to her.

Most are in Elamite; a smaller number are in Aramaic, and single tablets are in Greek and Old Persian. The Old Persian tablet (Fort. 1208-101, published by Stolper and Tavernier in 2007) shows Old Persian was written for a routine administrative record, not only for royal monuments. The archive was the subject of Rubin v. Islamic Republic of Iran, in which the US Supreme Court held in 2018 that the collection could not be seized to pay a judgment against Iran.

text.quote: Administrative Elamite formulae. A typical ration text records that a stated quantity of a commodity (grain, wine, sheep), supplied by a named official, was received by named workers or a traveller at a named place in a given month and year. In a letter (Fort. 6764) Darius orders the issuance of 100 sheep to the princess Irtasduna; in PF 1795 he orders 200 marris (about 2,000 quarts) of wine for her.
text.translation: Summary after R. T. Hallock, Persepolis Fortification Tablets (OIP 92, 1969), Introduction, pp. 1-2 and the letter discussion

evidence: Hallock 1969: Elamite texts deal with transfers of food commodities in 509-494 BCE, years 13-28 of Darius I.
Found in the fortification wall at the north-east corner of the Persepolis terrace, excavated 1933/34 by Herzfeld for the Oriental Institute (Hallock 1969, p. 1).
Tablets arrived in Chicago in 2,353 numbered boxes plus tins of fragments; 150 complete tablets were returned to Iran in 1948 (Hallock 1969).
Hallock published PF 1-2087 (Elamite); the Aramaic texts were assigned to R. A. Bowman.
Estimated archive: 15,000-18,000 Elamite documents, 700-1,000 Aramaic, 5,000-6,000 uninscribed sealed tablets (Stolper and Tavernier 2007).

Unique items: one Greek tablet (Fort. 1771, 'two marris of wine, Tebet'), one Old Persian tablet (Fort. 1208-101), a Phrygian(?) tablet (A. 29797), and a Neo-Babylonian slave-sale document (Fort. 11786) (Stolper and Tavernier 2007).
Royal women act in the texts: Irtasduna (Artystone), wife of Darius, receives and orders commodities (PF 730-32, 1835-39).

Rubin v. Islamic Republic of Iran, 583 U.S. 202 (argued 4 Dec 2017, decided 21 Feb 2018): the 'Persepolis Collection' of about 30,000 tablets and fragments at the Oriental Institute is immune from attachment; opinion by Sotomayor, J., Kagan, J., not participating.
questions: Is there any Judean in the archive? The old entry claimed the tablets 'mention Jewish administrative roles'. None of the sources read here (Hallock 1969 introduction; Stolper and Tavernier 2007) identifies a Judean. The archive's personal names are overwhelmingly Iranian and Elamite; whether any bearer of a West Semitic name is a Judean would need the same name-based test used for the Babylonian archives. On what was checked, the sources are silent.

How big was the archive, and how much Aramaic record-keeping is missing? Hallock (1969) raised the 'essentially unanswerable question' of how far records were kept in Aramaic on parchment and are now lost. Stolper and Tavernier (2007) estimate what survives. Both point to a much larger paper trail that did not survive in clay.

Women in the Persian economy: Y. Safaee, Women of the Empire: Life and Labor in the Achaemenid Persepolis Archives (Brill, 2026), builds a study of women's rations, work and status on these texts. That is new work on old tablets.

biblical.tie: Ezra reproduces Aramaic letters between Persian officials and the court, orders to release supplies from royal stores (6:8-9: 'wheat, salt, wine, and oil') and to fund the temple from the tribute of Beyond the River. The Fortification tablets are original examples of the same Persian system of sealed orders and commodity issues, in the heartland under Darius I. They do not mention Judah.

Nehemiah asks for letters to governors so they will let him pass and give him timber: the Persepolis travel texts show travellers carrying sealed authorizations that entitle them to rations on the road. Nehemiah's 'bread of the governor' (5:14) is a ration allowance of the same kind. The link is to the system, not to named persons.

Esther's world of satrapies, royal couriers and sealed documents under a Persian king is the administrative world these tablets document for Darius I (Xerxes' father). The tablets predate Xerxes and do not name Esther, Mordecai or Haman.

Ezra 6 has Darius (I) confirm Cyrus's decree and order supplies for the Jerusalem temple. The Fortification tablets show Darius I personally issuing orders for commodity disbursements, as in Fort. 6764. The Jerusalem order itself is not in the archive.

Old entry dated them '5th century BCE' / 'c. 470 BCE': Hallock's Elamite texts date 509-494 BCE (Darius I years 13-28), mostly late 6th century.

Old entry said they record 'oversight of various construction projects' and 'management of labor' as their subject: they are chiefly records of food and livestock rations and transfers, which include rations to work groups.

Old entry linked 'Daniel 6 (lions' den)': nothing in the archive bears on Daniel 6.

sites.name: House of Peter, Capernaum
sites.subtitle: Late Hellenistic house under a 5th-century octagonal church · venerated as Peter's
sites.date: House built in the Late Hellenistic period; converted to a place of assembly (excavators: late 1st century CE); enclosed and enlarged in the 4th century; octagonal church second half of the 5th century CE, used to the 7th century
sites.date_basis: Stratified excavation by the Franciscan Custody (Corbo and Loffreda) 1968–1986 and 2000–2003; phase dates as published by the Custody. The 1st-century conversion date is the excavators' reading.

discovery.when: 1968 (excavation of the house under the octagon)
discovery.who: Virgilio Corbo and Stanislao Loffreda, Studium Biblicum Franciscanum
discovery.where: Franciscan property at Capernaum (Kfar Nahum), north shore of the Sea of Galilee, south of the limestone synagogue

sites.location: In situ, Capernaum; since 1990 under a modern memorial church (architect Ildo Avetta) with a glass floor
overview: At Capernaum, south of the white limestone synagogue, the Franciscans excavated a Byzantine octagonal church from 1968. Beneath it they found a cluster of simple basalt houses around courtyards. One room in that cluster was singled out, plastered and repeatedly rebuilt as a place of gathering.

The Custody's summary of the results: the house was 'built in the Late Hellenistic period'. 'In the late first century A.D. it was changed into a domus-ecclesia', which in the 4th century was enlarged and enclosed by a wall. 'In the second half of the fifth century A.D. an octagonal church was built upon the house of St. Peter' and remained in use until the 7th century. The walls produced many fragments of painted plaster and graffiti with Christian symbols and invocations.

No inscription in the house names Peter as owner. The identification rests on the room's long special treatment, on the pilgrim graffiti (published by E. Testa, Cafarnao IV, 1972), and on the Gospel statement that Jesus stayed at Simon's house in Capernaum.
evidence: A residential quarter of basalt houses under the octagon; one room was repeatedly replastered and set apart (Custody summary; Corbo's publications).
A 4th-century enclosure wall around the venerated house (Custody summary).
A 5th-century octagonal church built directly over the venerated room, centred on it (Custody summary).
Painted plaster fragments and pilgrims' graffiti with Christian symbols and invocations on the walls (Custody summary; Testa 1972).
Excavation seasons: 19 seasons 1968–1986 (Corbo, Loffreda) and 4 campaigns 2000–2003 (Loffreda).
questions: When did Christian use of the room begin? The excavators (Corbo; Custody summary) put its conversion into a domus-ecclesia in the late 1st century CE, pointing to the replastering and the graffiti. Taylor (Christians and the Holy Places, OUP 1993, ch. 12, pp. 268–294) directly tests the excavators' claim that the octagon was built on a Jewish-Christian house-church, in her wider critique of the Bagatti–Testa hypothesis. Cirafesi (Capernaum, Fortress 2024) returns to the question with a chapter on 'Jewish Christ-Followers in Capernaum before the Fourth Century'.

The graffiti readings: Testa (Cafarnao IV, 1972) published readings that include names and invocations. How many of them can be securely read, and whether any name Peter, is disputed in later discussion (Strange & Shanks, BAR 1982, discuss Testa's volume). The full texts were not available for this entry.

biblical.tie: After the Capernaum synagogue, Jesus goes 'into the house of Simon and Andrew' and heals Simon's mother-in-law. The excavated house lies south of the synagogue on the same Franciscan property. It is in the right town, but the text does not give the house's position.
Parallel accounts of Peter's house and his mother-in-law.

Jesus 'at home' in Capernaum, and the roof dug through to lower a paralysed man. The excavated houses are single-storey basalt structures with light roofs. The dig shows that type of house; it does not identify this episode.
Jesus settles in Capernaum.

corrections: Old subtitle '1st century CE house' is too narrow. The Custody's excavation summary says the house was built in the Late Hellenistic period.

Old claim that the find 'provides tangible evidence of the existence of Peter' goes beyond what was found. No inscription names the owner. The finds show a room given special treatment and later marked by Christian graffiti and churches. The link to Peter is the tradition carried by that treatment.

Old claim it 'aligns precisely with the biblical description of Peter's residence'. The Gospels say only that Simon and Andrew's house was in Capernaum and was entered after the synagogue (Mark 1:29). They give no location or description to match 'precisely'.
Old dimension 'Approximately 10 meters square' and material 'Stone and mudbrick' are unsourced. The houses are basalt-built (Custody). No measurement was verified, so the size is dropped.
Old phrase 'testament to the enduring legacy of ancient Jerusalem' is wrong. Capernaum is in Galilee.
Old 'venerated as Peter's since 1st century' states the excavators' interpretation as fact. The late-1st-century date for the domus-ecclesia is their reading and is disputed (Taylor 1993).

sites.name: Pilate Inscription (Caesarea)
sites.subtitle: Latin building dedication naming Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judaea · 26–36 CE
sites.date: Within Pilate's term as prefect of Judaea (c. 26–36 CE)
sites.date_basis: The text names Pontius Pilatus with the title praefectus Iudaeae; the date comes from his known term of office, not from a date in the text. The block was found in secondary (later) use, so its findspot gives no date.

discovery.who: Italian expedition directed by Antonio Frova
discovery.where: Reused as a step in the Roman theatre, Caesarea Maritima

sites.location: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (IAA inv. 1961-529); replica on site at Caesarea

physical.material: Limestone block
physical.dimensions: 82 × 65 cm; letters c. 6 cm high; surviving inscribed area c. 30 × 31 cm (Taylor 2006)

overview: A limestone building block carrying four lines of a Latin inscription, found in 1961 by Antonio Frova's Italian team at Caesarea Maritima. It was not in its original place: it had been reused as a step in the theatre (Taylor 2006 describes this as its third use; a half-circle 22 cm across cut into its right side points to an earlier reuse, perhaps as a well-head).

The left side is broken away, so every line is missing its beginning. What survives reads [...]S TIBERIEUM / [..PO]NTIUS PILATUS / [PRAEF]ECTUS IUDA[EA]E / [...]É[...]. The certain content is the name Pontius Pilatus and the title 'prefect of Judaea', plus a building or monument called a 'Tiberieum', a word found nowhere else in Latin.
What the Tiberieum was, who or what it was dedicated to, and what verb ended the text are all restorations, and they differ sharply between editors (see questions).

text.quote: [...]S TIBERIEUM / [..PO]NTIUS PILATUS / [PRAEF]ECTUS IUDA[EA]E / [...]É[...]  —  '[...] Tiberieum / [..Po]ntius Pilate / [Pref]ect of Judaea / [...]'
text.translation: Literal translation (this encyclopedia) of the diplomatic text printed by J. E. Taylor, NTS 52 (2006) 564–565 (restorations in square brackets are editorial)

evidence: The name PILATUS and the nomen [PO]NTIUS are on the stone; only the first two letters of PONTIUS are restored.
The title reads [PRAEF]ECTUS IUDA[EA]E: 'prefect', an equestrian military-administrative title, not 'procurator'.
The first surviving word ends ]S; the word before TIBERIEUM is lost and is estimated at 4–6 letters (Taylor 2006, following Lehmann & Holum 1999).
Only an E with an apex survives in line 4; the verb is not preserved.
The block was found reused as a theatre step, not in its original setting.
questions: What was the Tiberieum? Frova (1961) and Degrassi (1964) took it as a cult building for Tiberius, with Degrassi restoring line 1 as [DIS AVGVSTI]S ('to the divine Augusti'); Taylor (NTS 2006) keeps a cultic reading, arguing Pilate dedicated a Tiberieum to the Dis Augustis and linking it to Philo's account of Pilate's shields (Legatio 299–305). Alföldy (SCI 18, 1999, 85–108) reads line 1 as [NAVTI]S ('for sailors') and line 4 as [REF]E[CIT] ('rebuilt'), making the Tiberieum a secular harbour lighthouse tower at Caesarea, on the analogy of the Drusion tower Josephus names there.

The line-1 word: Lehmann & Holum (Inscriptions of Caesarea Maritima, 1999, 68–71) list at least ten proposals (e.g. Dis Augustis, Caesariensibus, Iudaeis, clupeis, munus) and find none fully convincing because most are too long for the 4–6 letter gap (as reported by Taylor 2006, 565).
The verb in line 4: 'dedicavit' (dedicated), 'fecit' (made) and 'refecit' (rebuilt) have all been proposed; the stone shows only an apexed E.

biblical.tie: The Gospels name Pontius Pilate as the Roman governor of Judaea under Tiberius (Luke 3:1 dates by Tiberius' 15th year). The stone names the same man, under a Tiberius-related building, with the title praefectus Iudaeae. Luke 3:1 uses the general verb hēgemoneuontos ('governing'); the stone supplies the exact Latin rank.
Other New Testament mentions of Pontius Pilate; the stone confirms the name and office, nothing about the trial.

sources.cite: A. Frova, 'L'iscrizione di Ponzio Pilato a Cesarea', Rendiconti dell'Istituto Lombardo, Classe di Lettere 95 (1961) 419–434 (editio princeps), as reviewed by A. N. Sherwin-White, Journal of Roman Studies 54 (1964) 258–259
