sites.name: Politarch Inscription (Vardar Gate, Thessalonica)
sites.subtitle: Greek list of Thessalonica's civic officials, headed by six politarchs · Roman period, undated
sites.date: Undated in its text. Burton (1898) places it after 30 BCE and possibly as late as 143 CE or later; the British Museum and later writers give 2nd century CE.
sites.date_basis: No date formula survives. Boeckh's Flavian date rested on a misread name (a 'Flavius Sabinus' that is not on the stone). Burton argued from the number of politarchs: five in an Augustan-era Thessalonica inscription, six in one dated 143 CE, six here.

discovery.when: Known and copied by 1740 (Bimardus, published by Muratori); removed 1876
discovery.who: Stone rescued by Rev. Peter Crosbie with British consul Blunt when the arch was demolished in 1876
discovery.where: Inside face of the Roman arch called the Vardar Gate, on the Via Egnatia at the western entrance to Thessalonica

sites.location: British Museum, London, reg. no. 1877,0511.1

physical.material: Marble building block

overview: A marble block from the Roman arch that stood over the Via Egnatia at the western entrance of Thessalonica, known locally as the Vardar Gate. Travellers copied the text from 1740 onward; in 1866 a photograph was taken of it in place. When the arch was torn down in 1876, Rev. Peter Crosbie saved the main block; it went to the British consulate and then to the British Museum. A second, narrow block with five more letters was carried off with the rubble and lost in the construction of the harbour quay (acting consul Barker's letter of 1877, quoted by Burton 1898).

The text is a list of officials. It opens with the word ΠΟΛΕΙΤΑΡΧΟΥΝΤΩΝ ('while … were politarchs'), then names six politarchs, the city treasurer (tamias tēs poleōs) and the gymnasiarch. It is not a dedication of a statue, and it does not name an emperor.

Its value for the New Testament is the title. Acts 17:6 and 17:8 call the magistrates of Thessalonica politarchai, a word that is almost absent from literary Greek; this stone and others from Thessalonica show it was the city's real official title.

text.quote: ΠΟΛΕΙΤΑΡΧΟΥΝΤΩΝ ΣΩΣΙΠΑΤΡΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΚΛΕΟΠΑΤΡΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΛΟΥΚΙΟΥ ΠΟΝΤΙΟΥ ΣΕΚΟΥΝΔΟΥ ΥΙΟΥ … ΤΑΜΙΟΥ ΤΗΣ ΠΟΛΕΩΣ … ΓΥΜΝΑΣΙΑΡΧΟΥΝΤΟΣ …  —  'While politarchs were Sosipatros son of Kleopatra and Lucius Pontius Secundus, son …; [five more names]; … treasurer of the city …; … being gymnasiarch …'
text.translation: Literal translation (this encyclopedia) of the Greek text printed by E. D. Burton, 'The Politarchs', American Journal of Theology 2 (1898) p. 600

evidence: The first word is the participle ΠΟΛΕΙΤΑΡΧΟΥΝΤΩΝ, 'being politarchs', spelled with ΕΙ (Burton 1898, 600).
Six politarchs are listed, then a treasurer of the city and a gymnasiarch (Burton 1898, 600–602; Boeckh's corrigenda).
Some of the names are Roman (Lucius Pontius Secundus, Aulus Avius Sabinus, Gaius Agilleius Potitus) and some Greek (Sosipatros, Demetrios, Zoilos, Tauros).
The text carries no date formula.
The stone was set in the inside face of an arch on the Via Egnatia, the road Paul would have used between Philippi and Thessalonica (Acts 17:1).
questions: Date: Boeckh (CIG 1967, 1833) put it no earlier than Vespasian because he read a 'Flavius Sabinus' in line 3. Burton (AJT 1898, 601–602) shows that reading came from bad early copies (Bimardus, Pococke), not the stone, and argues from the count of politarchs (five under Augustus per the Kalamari Gate text; six in the dated 143 CE text) that it is later than 30 BCE and may be as late as 143 CE. The British Museum dates it to the 2nd century CE; the basis for that date is not confirmed in a published museum record available here.

How many politarchs in Paul's day? Burton (1898, 627–628) collects a Thessalonica text dated to Augustus' reign with five, and a text of 46 CE with two politarchs that he argues does not come from Thessalonica (it was found in a private courtyard and names no city). Acts gives no number.

biblical.tie: The Jews of Thessalonica drag Jason and some believers 'before the politarchs' (epi tous politarchas). The stone uses the same office title for the city's magistrates.
'They troubled the crowd and the politarchs.' Same title.
The mob seeks to bring Paul before the dēmos (the people's assembly). Burton notes that a dated Thessalonica inscription of 143 CE also names the dēmos and boulē, a separate point from this stone.

sources.cite: E. D. Burton, 'The Politarchs', The American Journal of Theology 2.3 (July 1898) 598–632
sources.verified: Full scan read on archive.org (JSTOR Early Journal Content, stable 3153438): Greek text on p. 600, history of copies pp. 600–604, rescue and removal to the British Museum p. 603, dating argument pp. 607 and 627–628.

sources.cite: British Museum, collection object 1877,0511.1 (marble block from the Vardar Gate, Thessalonica)
sources.verified: URL and summary seen in search results (building block from a Roman gateway at Thessalonika listing six politarchs, the treasurer and the gymnasiarch). The page itself is behind a bot wall and I could not open it.

sources.cite: C. T. Newton, The Collection of Ancient Greek Inscriptions in the British Museum, Part II (London 1883), no. CLXXI
sources.verified: Not seen directly. Burton (1898, 604) cites it as the edition made 'from the marble itself'; the citation is taken from Burton's footnote.

sources.cite: C. Rasmussen, 'Politarchs (Acts 17:6, 8): Luke gets it right—as usual!', HolyLandPhotos' Blog, 3 May 2016
sources.verified: Page read: 2nd century CE date, arch torn down 1876, stone given to British consulate then British Museum; count of 'more than sixty' politarch inscriptions attributed to Fant & Reddish (2008).

corrections: Old entry: 'discovered in 1876 during excavations'. The inscription was never excavated. It stood in a standing arch and was copied from 1740 (Muratori's publication of Bimardus' copy). 1876 is the year the arch was demolished and the stone removed (Burton 1898, 600, 603).

Old text 'The politarchs of the city erected a statue of the emperor' is invented. The stone is a list of officials, six politarchs plus a treasurer and gymnasiarch. It mentions no statue and no emperor (Burton 1898, 600).
Old location 'British Museum, Greece' is wrong. It is in the British Museum in London.
Old date 'c. 50 CE' has no basis in the text. The stone is undated; proposals run from after 30 BCE to the 2nd century CE.
Old dimensions '20 cm × 30 cm' are unsourced, and no measurement could be verified. They are dropped.

Old biblical links: Acts 17:34 is Dionysius the Areopagite and Damaris in Athens, not a 'Council of politarchs'. Acts 17:32 is the Athenian reaction to the resurrection and has nothing to do with Thessalonica. The only verses that use the title are Acts 17:6 and 17:8.

Old claim 'Confirms Luke's terminology' is true in a narrow sense. The title is real and belongs to Thessalonica; this stone may be later than Paul's visit, and the Augustan-era Kalamari Gate inscription (now lost) is the earlier Thessalonica witness (Burton 1898, 604–607).

sites.name: Pool of Siloam
sites.subtitle: Reservoir at the south end of the City of David · dam c. 800 BCE; stepped pool of the late Second Temple period
sites.date: Two different things carry the name. (1) The monumental dam that created the reservoir: radiocarbon 805-795 BCE (68.3%), 809-792 BCE (95.4%) (Regev et al., PNAS 2025). (2) The stepped pool found in 2004: late Second Temple period (Reich and Shukron), destroyed around 70 CE
sites.date_basis: Dam: four radiocarbon dates on uncharred straw and charred twigs from the mortar of dam walls W001 and W114 (RTD 12351, 12352, 12353, 12948), statistically combined. Stepped pool: pottery, coins and architecture reported by the excavators; the detailed coin evidence for its construction date has not been checked for this entry.

discovery.when: June 2004 (stepped pool); dam faces exposed in several excavations, dated 2025
discovery.who: Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron (Israel Antiquities Authority), during work to repair a water/sewer pipe; later IAA and Tel Aviv University excavations (N. Szanton, J. Uziel and others)
discovery.where: Southern end of the City of David ridge, Silwan, Jerusalem, where the Tyropoeon Valley meets the Kidron

sites.location: In situ, City of David, Silwan, Jerusalem

physical.material: Stepped pool: dressed stone steps over an earlier plastered phase. Dam: stone walls bonded with mortar
physical.dimensions: Stepped pool: one side c. 225 ft (c. 69 m), trapezoidal, steps on at least three sides (BAS). Dam: at least 19 m long, 11 m high, 10 m wide (Regev et al. 2025)

overview: The Gihon Spring, Jerusalem's only perennial source, lies in the Kidron Valley on the east side of the City of David. Its water was brought to the south end of the ridge, first through an open or semi-open channel (Channel II) and later through the rock-cut Siloam Tunnel. At the south end a reservoir formed behind a massive dam across the mouth of the Tyropoeon Valley. The name 'Siloam' (Hebrew Shiloah, 'sent') is attached to this whole system and to more than one pool built there over time.

In June 2004, during pipe repair work, Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron exposed stone steps of a large stepped pool south-east of the Byzantine church and pool long pointed out to pilgrims. They identified it as the Pool of Siloam of the late Second Temple period, the pool named in John 9. Most of it lay under an orchard; after 2022 the IAA began exposing more of the site.

In 2025 a radiocarbon study (Regev, Szanton, Vukosavovic, Berko, Shalev, Uziel, Mintz, Regev and Boaretto, PNAS) dated straw and twigs in the mortar of the dam to about 800 BCE, the reign of Jehoash or Amaziah of Judah, and argued that the Gihon Spring tower, Channel II and the reservoir formed one building project. The IAA's own 'Atiqot reports on the dam and pool area show that the dating is not settled: a radiocarbon date on dam plaster came out Persian-Hellenistic, against a stratigraphic date of the 7th century-586 BCE.
evidence: Stepped pool exposed June 2004 by Reich and Shukron during water-pipe repair south of the Temple Mount; trapezoidal, corners slightly over 90 degrees, one side c. 225 ft (BAS).
Dam across the Tyropoeon outlet: vertical and slanting sections, at least 19 m long, 11 m high, 10 m wide (PNAS 2025).
Dam mortar: 3 uncharred straw samples and 1 charred-twig sample, combined 805-795 BCE (68.3%) / 809-792 BCE (95.4%); passes chi-squared test (T = 7.5, 5% = 7.8) (PNAS 2025).
Earlier date estimates for the dam by various excavators ranged from the 8th to the 1st century BCE, including one radiocarbon date of the 4th-3rd century BCE (PNAS 2025 summary).

Plaster from the outer face of the dam wall was radiocarbon-dated to the Persian and Hellenistic periods, which the dating report calls 'difficult to explain' against the stratigraphic date of the 7th century-586 BCE ('Atiqot 101).
Siloam Tunnel floor plaster: a wood sample 810-780 BCE and a short-lived plant 770-550 BCE (Frumkin et al., as summarized in PNAS 2025).

A separate plastered pool just east of the Siloam Pool, along the outer dam wall, is dated by pottery and coins to the later 1st century CE, probably the last year of the Great Revolt ('Atiqot 101, Greenhut and Mazor).
Szanton ('Atiqot 113) identifies the Silwan Pool (the 2004 stepped pool) with the Siloam Pool and Birkat el-Hamra with 'Solomon's Pool' of Josephus, all Early Roman.
questions: When was the reservoir dam built? Regev et al. (PNAS 122/35, 2025) date it to c. 800 BCE from four short-lived plant samples in the mortar, arguing that fresh straw would not have been stored for long before use. E. Boaretto's report on the pool plaster ('Atiqot 101, 2025) got Persian-Hellenistic radiocarbon dates from plaster on the outer dam wall, while the excavators' pottery and stratigraphy pointed to the 7th century-586 BCE. The two may date different parts or repairs of the dam; neither report shows that yet.

Which pool is 'the' Pool of Siloam of Isaiah, Nehemiah and John? The reservoir behind the c. 800 BCE dam is a candidate for the Iron Age pool (Isa 22:9-11 'lower pool', 'reservoir between the two walls'). The 2004 stepped pool is Early Roman. Szanton ('Atiqot 113, 2024) argues from the excavated plan and the written sources that the Silwan Pool = Siloam Pool (for ritual immersion of pilgrims) and Birkat el-Hamra = Solomon's Pool (an open swimming pool). Y. Elitzur (PEQ 140, 2008) argued the Siloam Pool was itself the swimming pool known as 'Solomon's Pool'. The texts give names; the ground gives several pools.
Whether an Iron Age pool lies under the 2004 stepped pool is unknown; the later construction would have removed or buried it, and no excavation has yet reported one there.

biblical.tie: Jesus tells the blind man 'Go, wash in the pool of Siloam'. The 2004 stepped pool is of the right period (late Second Temple) and place; its identification with John's pool rests on name and location, not on an inscription.

'The wall of the pool of Siloah by the king's garden' in the 5th century BCE: a pool at the south end of the city near a royal garden. The orchard over the site was long called the King's Garden. Which structure Nehemiah meant is not known.

'The waters of Shiloah that go softly' (8:6) fits a gentle channel such as Channel II. 22:9-11 speaks of gathering the waters of the lower pool and making a reservoir between the two walls. A dam-built reservoir of c. 800 BCE predates Isaiah and would be the existing 'lower pool' in his day; that is our reading.

Hezekiah 'made a pool and a conduit' and brought the Gihon water down to the west side of the City of David. If the dam and reservoir date to c. 800 BCE, Hezekiah's work would be the tunnel and/or a new pool, not the first reservoir. The tunnel's own date is debated (plaster dates 810-780 and 770-550 BCE).

sites.name: Qumran and the Dead Sea Scrolls
sites.subtitle: Manuscripts from eleven caves near Khirbet Qumran · 3rd century BCE – 1st century CE
sites.date: Individual manuscripts range from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE by radiocarbon and palaeography; the Qumran caves were found 1947–1956.
sites.date_basis: AMS radiocarbon on parchment/papyrus (Bonani et al., Radiocarbon 34, 1992; Jull et al., Radiocarbon 37, 1995; Popović et al., PLOS ONE 20, 2025: 27 valid new dates from 30 samples), plus palaeography of the scripts.

discovery.when: 1947 (Cave 1) to 1956 (Cave 11); new cave (Cave 12) identified 2017
discovery.who: Bedouin shepherds first; then Bedouin and the Jordanian Department of Antiquities, École Biblique and Palestine Archaeological Museum teams
discovery.where: Caves in the cliffs and marl terrace around Khirbet Qumran, north-western Dead Sea

sites.location: Mostly Israel Antiquities Authority (Dead Sea Scrolls lab, Jerusalem) and the Israel Museum's Shrine of the Book (the Cave 1 scrolls including 1QIsaᵃ). Other pieces are held elsewhere; the Copper Scroll (3Q15) is in Amman.

physical.material: Mostly parchment, some papyrus; one text (3Q15) on copper
physical.dimensions: 1QIsaᵃ: 7.34 m long, 25.3–27 cm high, 17 sheets, 54 columns
physical.script: Square Jewish (Aramaic) script, some Paleo-Hebrew, Greek

overview: From 1947 to 1956 about 930 manuscripts, most surviving only as fragments, were recovered from eleven caves near the ruin of Khirbet Qumran on the north-western shore of the Dead Sea (the IAA's Leon Levy Digital Library images about 930). They include copies of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther, other Jewish writings (Enoch, Jubilees, Tobit, Ben Sira), and texts of a particular community such as the Community Rule, the Damascus Document, the War Scroll and the pesharim (running commentaries).

The best-known single scroll is the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ) from Cave 1: complete except for small damaged spots, 7.34 m long, 17 sheets sewn together, 54 columns. The Israel Museum put the whole scroll on display on 24 February 2026 for the first time since 1968. The exhibition closed after four days because of the war, and the scroll went back into a protected vault (Haaretz, 6 April 2026).
Next to the caves, Roland de Vaux excavated Khirbet Qumran itself in 1951–1956. Who lived there, and how the site relates to the scrolls, remains disputed (see questions).
evidence: Cave 1 yielded seven large scrolls in 1947, including 1QIsaᵃ. Caves 4 and 11 yielded thousands of fragments.

1QIsaᵃ contains Isaiah 1–66 in one scroll written by two scribes, one for each half. Enoch's writing-style model dates both halves to 180–100 BCE and shows no time gap between them (Popović et al. 2025, Fig. 2).
Radiocarbon (Bonani et al. 1992; Jull et al. 1995) gave dates for 14 and then 18 texts that fall in the last centuries BCE and 1st century CE.
Popović et al. (2025): 4Q114 (Daniel 8–11) has a 2σ radiocarbon range of 230–160 BCE. Enoch dates 4Q109 (Ecclesiastes) to the 3rd century BCE.
The same study found that manuscripts in 'Herodian' script carry radiocarbon dates spread from the 2nd century BCE to the 2nd century CE, wider than the palaeographic scheme allowed.
A twelfth cave identified in 2017 held scroll jars and a scrap of blank parchment but no written scroll.
questions: Who owned the scrolls and lived at Qumran? Magness (The Archaeology of Qumran and the Dead Sea Scrolls, Eerdmans 2002; 2nd ed. 2021) reads the site as a sectarian settlement tied to the scrolls. Her evidence is the site's layout, its many miqva'ot, communal dining debris and its connection to the caves, and she rejects the villa or manor readings. Hirschfeld (Qumran in Context, Hendrickson 2004) reads Qumran as a Hasmonean fort and later a prosperous estate on the Dead Sea trade route, unconnected to a sect. He places it among contemporary Judean desert estates and Ein Feshkha.

How far can script-dating be trusted? Popović et al. (2025) show several manuscripts are older than their palaeographic dates, with only two younger. Some Hasmonaean and Herodian script types overlap in time rather than following one another. Their AI dates are predictions from 24 radiocarbon-dated training samples with a mean error of about 28–31 years, and experts judged 79% of the 135 predictions for undated scrolls 'realistic'.

Was Daniel written in the 160s BCE? Popović et al. note that the 2σ radiocarbon range for 4Q114 (230–160 BCE) overlaps the 160s date usually assigned to Daniel 8–11 on literary-historical grounds. The earliest part of that range is older than the 160s. The radiocarbon result does not by itself decide the question.

biblical.tie: 1QIsaᵃ is a complete Hebrew Isaiah copied in the 2nd century BCE (Enoch estimate 180–100 BCE), about a thousand years older than the medieval Masoretic codices. It agrees with the later Hebrew text in substance, but it also has many spelling differences and a number of word-level variants.
4Q114 preserves these chapters on a manuscript radiocarbon-dated 230–160 BCE (2σ), within about a generation of the events Daniel 11 describes, or earlier.
4Q109 is dated by Enoch to the 3rd century BCE.

sources.cite: M. Popović, M. A. Dhali, … M. Perla Colombini, E. Tigchelaar et al., 'Dating ancient manuscripts using radiocarbon and AI-based writing style analysis', PLOS ONE 20(6): e0323185 (4 June 2025)

Old 'Israel Museum' as the home of the scrolls is only partly right. The Shrine of the Book holds the Cave 1 scrolls; most fragments are in IAA custody, and the Copper Scroll is in Amman.

Old date range '250 BCE – 70 CE' is out of date. Popović et al. (2025) push several manuscripts earlier (4Q114 to 230–160 BCE; 4Q109 predicted 3rd century BCE) and show Herodian-script manuscripts running from the 2nd century BCE to the 2nd century CE.
The old entry's claim that the scrolls show 'the Jewish community that inhabited the Qumran region' treats a disputed identification (Magness vs Hirschfeld) as settled.

Old biblical link to Psalm 119 as an 'Acrostic prayer' gives no reason why this text matters for the scrolls. No specific Qumran copy is confirmed in the sources cited here, so the link is dropped rather than repeated.

updates.what: Popović et al. publish 27 new radiocarbon dates and the 'Enoch' AI writing-style model. 4Q114 (Daniel) dates to 230–160 BCE, both halves of 1QIsaᵃ to 180–100 BCE, and Herodian-type hands span the 2nd century BCE to the 2nd century CE.
The Israel Museum shows the entire Great Isaiah Scroll for the first time since 1968; the display closes after four days because of the war and the scroll goes to a protected vault.

sites.name: Samaria Ostraca
sites.subtitle: Hebrew ink dockets for wine and oil sent to Samaria · early 8th century BCE (disputed)
sites.date: Probably first half of the 8th century BCE. The texts are dated only by regnal years 9, 10 and 15 of an unnamed king.
sites.date_basis: The ostraca give 'in the 9th year', 'in the 10th year' and 'in the 15th year' but never name the king (Lyon 1924, p. 227). The absolute date rests on letter forms, on the stratigraphy of the find spot, and on which Israelite kings reigned 15 years or more. Faigenbaum-Golovin et al. (2020) narrow this to Joash or Jeroboam II, since proto-Canaanite script still appears in the 9th century.

discovery.who: Harvard Expedition to Samaria (G. A. Reisner, field director; C. S. Fisher; texts published by D. G. Lyon)
discovery.where: Samaria, royal acropolis: rooms 401, 416, 417, 419 and 470-474 on the east side of the palace courtyard, in the building the excavators called the 'Ostraca House'

sites.location: Not confirmed in a published museum record. The excavation was carried out under an Ottoman permit issued on the recommendation of the Imperial Ottoman Museum, Constantinople (Harvard report, 1924). The Harvard Semitic Museum holds the expedition's photographic negatives, which were used for the 2020 handwriting study.

physical.material: Potsherds (ostraca) from jars, jugs, pans and bowls, written in carbon ink
physical.dimensions: Small sherds; Harvard numbered 63 texts (Nos. 1-63), two of them true jar labels (Nos. 62-63); the full assemblage is c. 100 short administrative texts

overview: In 1910 the Harvard expedition found inscribed potsherds in rooms on the east side of the courtyard of the Israelite palace at Samaria. D. G. Lyon published them in the 1924 report. They are short ink notes, each opening with a regnal year (9, 10 or 15), and they record deliveries of 'a jar of old wine' or 'a jar of fine (washed) oil' from named places or clan districts to named men.

Seventeen names follow the preposition 'from'. Lyon pointed out that six of them (Abiezer, Helek, Shechem, Shemida, Noah and Hoglah) are the clan divisions of Manasseh listed in Joshua 17:2-3 and Numbers 26:30-33. The personal names include Yahweh-names ending in -yau (Gaddiyau, Shemaryau, Yeda'yau, Abedyau) and Baal-names (Ba'ala, Meriba'al, Abiba'al, Ba'alzamar).

A 2020 algorithmic handwriting study of 31 of the texts, using Harvard's original negatives, concluded they were most likely written by two scribes working in Samaria, not by many writers out in the villages.

text.quote: "In the 10th year. To Shemaryau. From Be'er-yam. Jar[s ?] of old [wine]. Rage' son of Elisha' ... 2; 'Uzza son of ---- 1; ... Ba'ala son of Elisha' [1] ..."
text.translation: D. G. Lyon in G. A. Reisner, C. S. Fisher and D. G. Lyon, Harvard Excavations at Samaria 1908-1910, vol. I (1924), p. 228, Ostracon No. 1

evidence: Findspot: 'In the eastern part of the courtyard in rooms 401, 416, 417, 419, 470-474, in the lowest part of the debris of occupation' (Lyon 1924, p. 227).
Every text begins with a regnal year: years 9 and 10 (the 'old wine' and 'fine oil' dockets) and year 15 (dockets naming clan districts such as Shemida, Helek, Abiezer, Hoglah, Noah).

Formula types, per Lyon: 'In the 10th year. Wine of Kerm ha-Tell for a jar of fine oil' (Nos. 43, 54, 55?); 'A jar of old wine' (Nos. 4-10, 12, 14, 15, year 9); 'A jar of fine oil' (Nos. 16-19, year 10).
Six of the seventeen 'from' names match Manasseh clan names in Josh 17:2-3 / Num 26:30-33: Abiezer, Helek, Shechem, Shemida, Noah, Hoglah.
Theophoric names: Yahwistic -yau names (Gaddiyau, Shemaryau, Yeda'yau, Marnayau, Abedyau) alongside Baal names (Ba'ala, Meriba'al, Abiba'al, Ba'alzamar).
Lyon judged the letter forms would place them in 'the 8th or 9th century B.C.' on epigraphic grounds alone.
The ostraca are written on already-broken sherds, some shaped to fit and written across the wheel marks, so they are office notes and not jar labels (except Nos. 62-63).
Faigenbaum-Golovin et al. 2020: 31 texts analysed; most likely two hands.
questions: Which king's years 9, 10 and 15? Anson Rainey (BASOR 272, 1988, 'Toward a Precise Date for the Samaria Ostraca') argued for a specific early-8th-century placement. Faigenbaum-Golovin et al. (PLOS ONE 2020) list the only Israelite kings with 15+ years (Ahab, Jehu, Jehoahaz, Joash, Jeroboam II) and exclude the 9th-century kings because proto-Canaanite script was still in use then, leaving Joash or Jeroboam II. Lyon (1924) only bracketed the texts to the life of the palace, 'about 865 to 722 B.C.'

Floor or fill? Lyon (1924) put them 'in the lowest part of the debris of occupation' on the courtyard floor. Rainey (1988), as cited by Faigenbaum-Golovin et al., treats them as coming from a fill laid down before a building went up. Ron E. Tappy's re-study of the excavation records (The Archaeology of the Ostraca House at Israelite Samaria, ASOR Annual 70, 2016) takes a different view of that context. The difference affects whether the building dates the ostraca or the ostraca date the building.

Were the men after 'to' (l-) the recipients or the owners? Yigael Yadin (IEJ 9, 1959, 'Recipients or Owners?') took on that question. Hermann Michael Niemann (Tel Aviv 35, 2008) reread the texts as evidence of a king-clan relationship, not a simple tax system.

Where were they written? The 2020 algorithmic study found about two hands, which points to scribes at Samaria rather than writing spread across the villages. The result depends on the image-based letter reconstructions, which the authors published on figshare.

biblical.tie: Abiezer, Helek, Shechem, Shemida (sons of Gilead) and Noah, Hoglah (daughters of Zelophehad) are Manassite clan names in these genealogies; the same six names appear on the ostraca as districts sending wine and oil to Samaria.
Samaria as the royal capital of Israel. The ostraca are palace deliveries at Samaria.

Hosea's complaint about Baal in Israel. The ostraca carry both Yahweh-names (-yau) and Baal-names among the same people; our reading is that this is onomastic evidence for both cults, not proof of either practice.
'Drink wine in bowls and anoint themselves with the finest oils.' The ostraca record deliveries of 'old wine' and 'fine/washed oil' to the capital; a direct match of commodities, not of events.

corrections: Old entry says they were found in 1910 'by a German archaeologist'. The 1910 season of the Harvard (American) expedition was directed by G. A. Reisner with C. S. Fisher as architect; D. G. Lyon published the ostraca in 1924. Gottlieb Schumacher directed only the first season (1908), before the ostraca were found.
Old entry says they record allocations of 'wine, oil, and grain'. The texts record wine ('old wine') and oil ('fine/washed oil'); no grain is listed in Lyon's formula types.

Old entry dates them 'c. 850 BCE' in the facts box but '8th century' in the text. The years 9, 10 and 15 point to a long reign, and recent work places them in the first half of the 8th century (Joash or Jeroboam II); c. 850 is not supported.

Old entry links them to '1 Kings 20:35-36 (Samaria's governance)', '2 Kings 23:1 (Josiah's reforms)' and 'Nehemiah 11'. None of these relates to the ostraca: 1 Kgs 20:35-36 is a prophet and a lion; Josiah was a Judahite king a century after Samaria fell. The real textual tie is the Manasseh clan list in Josh 17:2-3 / Num 26:30-33.

Old entry says they are housed in 'the Rockefeller Museum in Jerusalem and the Istanbul Archaeological Museum' (facts box: 'Rockefeller Museum, Istanbul'). Current repository not confirmed in the sources cited here; no Rockefeller connection was found.

sites.name: Sargon II Palace Inscriptions (Khorsabad)
aka: Great Display Inscription of Sargon II
sites.subtitle: Royal inscriptions from Sargon II's palace at Dūr-Šarrukīn · c. 710-706 BCE
sites.date: Sargon II reigned 722-705 BCE. The Display Inscription runs 'from the beginning of my reign until my fifteenth regnal year' (707 BCE); the palace at Dūr-Šarrukīn was inaugurated in his 16th year (706 BCE).
sites.date_basis: Internal regnal-year statements: the Display Inscription (RINAP 2 no. 7) says its summary runs to the 15th regnal year. Sargon's accession date comes from the Babylonian Chronicle (12 Ṭebētu, Shalmaneser V's 5th year = 722 BCE), and his regnal years are fixed by the Assyrian eponym list. The RINAP 2 campaign table puts the inauguration of Dūr-Šarrukīn in 706.

discovery.when: March 1843-1844 (P.-É. Botta); 1852-1854 (V. Place with F. Thomas); 1928-1935 (Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago: E. Chiera, H. Frankfort, G. Loud; epigraphist T. Jacobsen)
discovery.who: Paul-Émile Botta, French consular agent at Mosul (not Layard)
discovery.where: Khorsabad (ancient Dūr-Šarrukīn), about 15 km north-east of Mosul, Iraq

sites.location: Dispersed: Louvre (Botta's and Place's shipments), British Museum, Oriental Institute Chicago, Iraq Museum and elsewhere. Many inscribed slabs were lost in the Tigris in 1855 or reburied at the site and survive only in Botta's copies (Monument de Ninive, 1849-50).

physical.material: Carved stone wall slabs (orthostats), stone pavement slabs, human-headed bull colossi; also clay prisms and cylinders from other sites
physical.language: Akkadian (Standard Babylonian literary dialect of royal inscriptions)

overview: In March 1843 Paul-Émile Botta, the French consular agent at Mosul, found carved and inscribed stone rooms at Khorsabad. They were the palace of Sargon II in his new capital Dūr-Šarrukīn ('Fortress of Sargon'). Botta dug until 1844, Victor Place continued in 1852-54, and the Oriental Institute of Chicago excavated again in 1928-35. Botta published his copies in Monument de Ninive (1849-50), thinking he had found biblical Nineveh.

The inscriptions include annals carved room by room on wall slabs (Rooms II, V, XIII, XIV and the throne room), the 'Display Inscription' (a summary of the reign to year 15), texts on the bull colossi and pavement slabs, and short captions over reliefs. Grant Frame's edition (RINAP 2, 2021) covers about 130 historical inscriptions of Sargon.

For biblical history the key passages are the capture of Samaria (see separate entry), the revolt of Hamath with Arpad, Ṣimirra, Damascus and Samaria (720 BCE), the defeat of Hanno of Gaza and an Egyptian army at Raphia, and the Ashdod campaign against Iāmānī in 712/711 BCE. The Ashdod campaign is the event Isaiah 20:1 dates by 'the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him'. Isaiah 20:1 is the only verse in the Bible that names Sargon.

text.quote: (97) In the anger of my heart I did not collect the mass of my troops, (98) I did not rally my forces. (99) With my soldiers, who do not depart from my side, ... (100) I marched against Ashdod. (101) Yamani, who heard from afar (102) the approach of my column, fled to the borders of Egypt, (103) which lies before Melucha, and was seen no more. (104) Ashdod, Gimtu [Gath], Ashdudimmu (105) I besieged [and] conquered.
text.translation: R. W. Rogers, Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament (New York, 1912), pp. 328-329 (Display/'General' Inscription ll. 97-105)

evidence: Display Inscription (RINAP 2 no. 7) ll. 90-109: Azūri of Ashdod stops tribute and is replaced by his brother Aḫī-Mīti; the people put up Iāmānī; Sargon marches 'with (only) my warriors who never leave my side'; Iāmānī flees 'to the (far) edge of Egypt, on the border with the land Meluḫḫa'; Ashdod, Gath and Ashdod-Yam are conquered and resettled under an Assyrian governor.
Display Inscription ll. 109b-112: the king of Meluḫḫa (Nubia) later sent Iāmānī to Assyria in iron fetters.
Khorsabad Annals date the Ashdod campaign to Sargon's 11th regnal year (711 BCE); the Nineveh Prism (RINAP 2 no. 82) puts it in the 9th regnal year (RINAP 2 Introduction, note 96).
Display Inscription l. 33: Ilu-bi'dī (Iaū-bi'dī) of Hamath 'incited the cities Arpad, Ṣimirra, Damascus, (and) Samaria to rebel'; Sargon captured him at Qarqar and flayed him.

Pavement and bull inscriptions give short titularies: 'conqueror of the city Samaria and all of the land Bīt-Ḫumria (Israel)' (RINAP 2 no. 13); Display Inscription of Room XIV: 'I plundered the city Šinuḫtu, the city Samaria, and all of the land Bīt-Ḫumria' (no. 8).

Text preservation: RINAP 2 states that text nos. 1-4, 6-14 and 23-41 are unavailable in the original because the slabs were lost in the Tigris in 1855 or reburied at Khorsabad; for these the edition depends on Botta's copies ('numerous anomalous/unexpected signs') and Winckler's later copies.
Botta's room numbering used Roman numerals for spaces he took to be courts; several (II, V, X, XIII, XIV and 'Court VII', the throne room) were actually rooms (RINAP 2 Introduction).
questions: Who led the Ashdod campaign? Isaiah 20:1 says the turtānu (field marshal) came to Ashdod, sent by Sargon. The Display Inscription has Sargon marching himself 'with (only) my warriors who never leave my side'. RINAP 2 (Frame 2021, n. 118) identifies Isaiah's campaign with the capture of Ashdod in 711 and notes that Isaiah has the army led by the tartan, not the king. Whether the king was actually present, or the royal text credits him with his general's campaign, is not decided by the texts.

711 or 713/712? The Khorsabad Annals put the Ashdod campaign in Sargon's 11th regnal year and the Nineveh Prism in his 9th (RINAP 2 n. 96). Hayim Tadmor (JCS 12, 1958) is the classic chronological study of Sargon's regnal-year (palû) counting; the discrepancy affects how Isaiah 20's 'three years' sign is dated.

How reliable is the received text? For most Khorsabad slabs the originals are gone (Tigris 1855) and editors rely on Botta's 1840s copies. Frame's RINAP 2 lists the problems with those copies; any single reading from a lost slab is only as good as Botta's copy.

biblical.tie: 'In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it.' Sargon's inscriptions record the capture of Ashdod, Gath and Ashdod-Yam after Iāmānī's revolt, with Iāmānī fleeing to the border of Egypt/Meluḫḫa (Kush). Isaiah 20:3-5 addresses Egypt and Ethiopia (Kush) as the failed hope of those who revolted. Our reading: the same revolt and the same Egypt-Kush connection.

Deportation from Samaria and resettlement of foreigners there. Sargon's texts claim he took Samaria, deported its people and 'brought there people from the lands that I had conquered'. See the 'Sargon's Annals - Fall of Samaria' entry for who took the city.
'Is not Hamath as Arpad? is not Samaria as Damascus?' Sargon's Display Inscription groups Arpad, Ṣimirra, Damascus and Samaria as the cities Ilu-bi'dī of Hamath incited to revolt.

corrections: Old entry says the inscriptions were 'unearthed during the excavations ... of Khorsabad in 1843 by the British archaeologist Austen Henry Layard'. Khorsabad was excavated by the French consular agent Paul-Émile Botta (1843-44), then Victor Place (1852-54), then the Oriental Institute of Chicago (1928-35). Layard worked at Nimrud and Nineveh.

Old entry says Isaiah 20:1 describes the prophet walking naked for three years 'as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia' and ties that to Sargon's conquest of Israel. Isaiah 20:1 dates the sign to the tartan's capture of Ashdod, which the Khorsabad texts describe as the Iāmānī revolt (711 BCE per the Annals). It is not about the fall of Israel.

Old entry lists '2 Kings 18-19 (Sargon's campaign)' and '2 Kings 20 (Hezekiah's illness)'. 2 Kings 18:13-19:37 is Sennacherib's 701 BCE campaign and 2 Kings 20 is Hezekiah's illness; neither names Sargon.

Old entry's 'Significance: Only biblical mention of Sargon confirmed by palace' is garbled. The fact is that Isaiah 20:1 is the only biblical verse naming Sargon, and the palace inscriptions are his own records.
Old entry dates the inscriptions 'c. 722 BCE'. 722 is Sargon's accession year; the palace texts summarize events down to his 15th year (707) and the city was inaugurated in 706.

Old entry's 'Material: Stone inscriptions; Dimensions: Various tablets' conflates media: the palace texts are on stone wall slabs, pavement slabs and bull colossi; the clay prisms (e.g. Nimrud, Nineveh, Aššur) are separate documents from other cities.

sites.name: Sargon's Annals: the Fall of Samaria
sites.subtitle: Sargon II's claims to have captured Samaria and deported 27,290 people · 722-720 BCE
sites.date: Events: 'at the beginning of my reign' (Sargon's accession year, 722 BCE) and/or his 2nd regnal year (720 BCE). Texts written c. 720s-706 BCE.
sites.date_basis: Sargon's own texts place the Samaria action 'at the beginning of my reign' (Annals, text no. 1 l. 12b, restored) and group Samaria with the Hamath-led revolt of his 2nd regnal year (720). The Babylonian Chronicle (BM 92502) records that Shalmaneser V died in Ṭebētu of his 5th year and Sargon took the throne on 12 Ṭebētu (722 BCE), and that under Shalmaneser a city read Šamara'in (older reading Shabara'in) was destroyed.

discovery.when: Khorsabad texts 1843-1854 (Botta, Place); Nimrud Prism fragments from the British excavations at Nimrud, published by C. J. Gadd in Iraq 16 (1954)
discovery.who: P.-É. Botta and V. Place (Khorsabad); British excavations at Nimrud (prism)
discovery.where: Khorsabad (Dūr-Šarrukīn) palace slabs and pavements; Nimrud (Kalḫu), clay prism fragments

sites.location: Several objects. The Khorsabad Annals of Room II survive mostly in Botta's copies (originals lost in the Tigris in 1855 or reburied); the Display Inscription is known from five exemplars; the Nimrud Prism fragments were excavated at Nimrud (museum numbers Not confirmed in a published museum record).

physical.material: Stone wall slabs and pavement slabs (Khorsabad); clay prism (Nimrud)

overview: Several of Sargon II's inscriptions claim that he conquered Samaria, capital of the kingdom of Israel, deported its population, took chariots into his army, resettled the city with people from elsewhere and made it an Assyrian province. The fullest versions are the Display Inscription from Khorsabad, the Khorsabad Annals (Room II) and the Nimrud Prism. Shorter titularies on bull colossi and pavements call him 'conqueror of Samaria and all of Bīt-Ḫumria (Israel)'.

The numbers are not uniform. Exemplars of the Display Inscription give 27,290, 27,280 and apparently 24,280 deportees with 50 chariots. The Nimrud Prism has '[20?]+27,280', read tentatively as 47,280, with 200 chariots. In the Annals of Room II the whole passage, number included, is restored from those other texts.

2 Kings 17:3-6 and 18:9-10 name Shalmaneser as the king who besieged Samaria for three years, and say 'they took it'. The Babylonian Chronicle credits Shalmaneser V with destroying a city whose name is usually read Šamara'in. Sargon, who came to the throne within weeks of Shalmaneser's death, claims the conquest for himself.

text.quote: (23) From the beginning of my rule (722 B.C.) to the fifteenth (707 B.C.) of my years of reign I accomplished the defeat of Khumbanigash of Elam in the environs (?) of Dur-ilu; I besieged and captured Samaria; I carried away (24) 27,290 of its inhabitants, I collected there 50 chariots; the remainder of them I permitted to retain their goods (?), put my governors over them, and upon them the tribute of former kings (25) I laid.
text.translation: R. W. Rogers, Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament (New York, 1912), p. 331 (Sargon's 'General' = Display Inscription ll. 23-25)

evidence: Display Inscription (RINAP 2 no. 7) l. 23b-25: URU.sa-me-ri-na al-me ak-šud ... 27 LIM 2 ME 90 UN.MEŠ a-šib ŠÀ-šú áš-lu-la 50 GIŠ.GIGIR.MEŠ ... 'I surrounded (and) conquered the city Samaria. I carried off as booty 27,290 of its inhabitants, conscripted fifty chariots from among them...'
RINAP 2 note: 'Various exemplars of text no. 7 line 24 have 27,290, 27,280, and apparently 24,280.'

Khorsabad Annals, Room II (RINAP 2 no. 1) ll. 11-17: only fragments survive ('LÚ.URU.sa-me]-ri-na-a-a', 'people of Samaria'); the conquest and the '27,280/27,290' figure are restored from nos. 7 and 74. RINAP 2 describes these lines as 'heavily restored from the following texts'.

Nimrud Prism (RINAP 2 no. 74) iv 25-41: the Samarians had allied with a king hostile to Sargon; '[20?]+27,280 people, together with their chariots and the gods who helped them' taken as booty; 200 chariots conscripted; 'I restored the city Samaria and made (it) greater than before. I brought there people from the lands that I had conquered'.

Frame (RINAP 2) on the Prism figure: 'For the proposal that the number in the Nimrud Prism was 47,280, see Na'aman, NABU 2000 ... but note that his reference to the Khorsabad Annals ... is misleading since the number there is totally restored.'
Annals and Display Inscription l. 33: in Sargon's 2nd year Ilu-bi'dī of Hamath 'incited the cities Arpad, Ṣimirra, Damascus, (and) Samaria to rebel against me'.

Room XIV Display Inscription (no. 8) l. 15: 'I plundered (ašlul) the city Šinuḫtu, the city Samaria, and all of the land Bīt-Ḫumria'. Frame notes that ašlul can also mean 'I carried off as booty/captives'.

Babylonian Chronicle (BM 92502) i 27-28, as translated by Rogers 1912: 'On the twenty-fifth day of Tebet Shalmaneser took his seat on the throne in Assyria, and the city of Shabarain was destroyed.' The copy was made in the 22nd year of Darius (Wiseman 1956: 500/499 BCE if Darius I).
questions: Who took Samaria, Shalmaneser V or Sargon II? For Shalmaneser: 2 Kings 17:3-6 and 18:9-10, and the Babylonian Chronicle, which RINAP 1 summarizes as recording that Shalmaneser 'conquered or devastated Samaria'. For Sargon: his inscriptions repeatedly claim the conquest, the deportation and the resettlement. Hayim Tadmor (JCS 12, 1958) credited the 722 capture to Shalmaneser and put Sargon's own action against Samaria in 720, with the Hamath revolt. Bob Becking (The Fall of Samaria, 1992) argued for two captures, one by each king. Eckart Frahm (The Last Days of the Kingdom of Israel, 2018, pp. 55-86) re-examined what Sargon's inscriptions attest. (These positions are summarized from the literature; the three works are cited but not summarized here.) RINAP 2 (Frame 2021) leaves the question open: 'Exactly when Samaria fell ... [has] been [a matter] of intense scholarly discussion.'

Is 'Shabarain/Šamara'in' Samaria? Rogers (1912) printed the Chronicle's city name as 'Shabarain'. The later RINAP 1 overview reads the same line as Shalmaneser having 'conquered or devastated Samaria'. The Chronicle names no region, so the identification rests on the reading of the name and on the biblical parallel.

How many were deported: 27,290, 27,280, 24,280 or 47,280? The Display Inscription exemplars disagree with one another, the Prism's first digit is broken, and the Annals' figure is a modern restoration. Nadav Na'aman (NABU 2000) proposed 47,280 for the Prism. The texts themselves do not settle it.

biblical.tie: Shalmaneser besieges Samaria three years; 'in the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes'. Sargon's texts record the deportation but name no destinations for the Samarians; they name Sargon, not Shalmaneser, as conqueror.

Repeats the three-year siege by Shalmaneser and 'at the end of three years they took it'. The plural 'they' leaves the capturing king unnamed; the Babylonian Chronicle's Shalmaneser line and Sargon's claims are the two external witnesses.

'The king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Ava, and from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria.' Sargon: 'I brought there people from the lands that I had conquered.' A direct correspondence in policy; Sargon's text does not list the origins.

sites.name: Sennacherib throne-room Slab 28 as Jerusalem (Compton 2025)
sites.subtitle: Assyrian palace relief, Southwest Palace, Nineveh, reign of Sennacherib (705-681 BCE) · destroyed 2016; re-identified as Jerusalem in 2025
sites.date: Carved in the reign of Sennacherib (705-681 BCE), after his third campaign (701 BCE) if it shows that campaign
sites.date_basis: The slab belonged to the decoration of Sennacherib's throne room in his Southwest Palace at Nineveh; the reign dates come from the Assyrian eponym chronology. The campaign it shows is inferred from its place in the throne-room sequence; no caption on the slab is reported.

discovery.when: Recorded by Austen Henry Layard around 1850; photographed by John Malcolm Russell in 1990
discovery.who: A. H. Layard (drawings); J. M. Russell (photograph, 1990; publication of the throne room 1998)
discovery.where: Throne room of Sennacherib's Southwest Palace, Nineveh (modern Mosul, Iraq)

sites.location: Destroyed: smashed in situ by Islamic State militants in 2016 (Times of Israel 2026). Known only from Layard's drawings, Russell's 1990 photograph and later studies.

physical.material: Stone palace wall slab (carved relief)

overview: Slab 28 was one of the carved wall slabs of the throne room of Sennacherib's Southwest Palace at Nineveh. It showed a strongly walled city surrounded by the Assyrian army, with a single standing figure on top of a stately building inside, and, unusually for Assyrian siege reliefs, no fighting, looting or burning. Scholars had long taken the throne-room scene in this part of the room as the Assyrian fight at Eltekeh in 701 BCE. The slab was destroyed when Islamic State militants smashed the palace reliefs in Mosul in 2016; it survives only in Layard's mid-19th-century drawings and a 1990 photograph by J. M. Russell.

In the Journal of Near Eastern Studies (October 2025), Stephen Compton of the University of South Africa argued that Slab 28 shows Jerusalem, the city Sennacherib shut in but did not take, and that the figure on the building may be Hezekiah. His points, as reported, are: the lack of any assault; twice-corbelled towers; a wide space between the outer wall and the inner palace, which he reads as a dry moat; a view from the north; and the throne-room entrance bull inscriptions, which he says name only one Phoenician city (Ushu) and one Judahite city (Jerusalem). He proposes the throne-room sequence runs Ushu (Phoenicia), then Philistia, then Judah/Jerusalem, and that the relief previously given to Eltekeh belongs to that sequence differently: the 'misplaced city of Ushu' of his title.

The proposal is contested. Danel Kahn (University of Haifa) told the Times of Israel he thinks Compton is wrong: the flat setting fits a lowland city such as Ekron better than hill-country Jerusalem, the slab sits near the Eltekeh battle scene, and Jerusalem's submission is instead shown on seven slabs near the throne depicting captives against a mountain backdrop. Stefan Maul (Heidelberg) said he did not find the arguments persuasive. Christoph Uehlinger had raised the Jerusalem possibility about two decades earlier without reaching a conclusion.

text.quote: As for Hezekiah, the Jew, who had not submitted to my yoke, 46 of his strong, walled cities and the cities of their environs, which were numberless, I besieged, I captured, I plundered, as booty I counted them. Him, like a caged bird, in Jerusalem, his royal city, I shut up. Earthworks I threw up about it.
text.translation: Sennacherib, Bull Inscription (1) from the palace at Nineveh, Luckenbill, Ancient Records of Assyria and Babylonia II (1927) §312, p. 143 (OCR 'Ishut up' corrected to 'I shut up'). The same bull text (§310) has the kings of Amurru bring tribute 'in the neighborhood of the city of Ushu'. The relief itself carries no reported caption.

evidence: Slab 28 stood in Sennacherib's throne room, Southwest Palace, Nineveh (Times of Israel 2026, reporting Compton).

It showed a walled city surrounded by the Assyrian army, a single standing figure atop a stately building, twice-corbelled towers, a wide space between outer wall and inner structure, and no battle, looting or burning (Times of Israel 2026, reporting Compton's description).
Destroyed by Islamic State militants in 2016; now known from Layard's c. 1850 drawings and Russell's 1990 photograph (Times of Israel 2026).
The long-standing identification of the throne-room scene was Eltekeh: 'scholars long ago concluded depicts the Assyrian siege of the Philistine city of Eltekeh' (Times of Israel 2026).

Luckenbill's Bull Inscription (1) from Nineveh names, for the third campaign: Luli king of Sidon fleeing from Tyre to Cyprus; tribute of the kings of Amurru 'in the neighborhood of the city of Ushu'; Ashkelon; Ekron (Amkaruna); the battle in the plain of Altaka (Eltekeh); and Hezekiah shut up in Jerusalem (ARAB II §§309-312, pp. 142-143).

Sennacherib's final-edition annals (ARAB II §§233 ff.) say of Hezekiah: 'Himself, like a caged bird, I shut up in Jerusalem, his royal city. Earthworks I threw up against him' (ARAB II §240, p. 120). No Assyrian text claims Jerusalem was taken.
No label on Slab 28 identifying the city is reported in any source seen.
questions: Which city Slab 28 shows. Compton (JNES 84:2, 2025: 191-219, as reported by Times of Israel 2026) reads Jerusalem because of the absence of assault, corbelled towers, a dry-moat gap and the bull inscriptions naming Ushu and Jerusalem. Kahn (University of Haifa, quoted by Times of Israel 2026) reads a lowland city, probably Ekron, because of the flat setting and the slab's position beside the Eltekeh battle, and puts Jerusalem's submission on seven slabs of captives with a mountainous backdrop near the throne. Maul (Heidelberg) is unpersuaded. The JNES article itself was not accessible for this entry (publisher access restriction).

The bull-inscription argument. Compton is reported as saying the throne-room entrance bulls 'only name one Phoenician city, Ushu, and one Judahite city, Jerusalem.' In Luckenbill's translation of Bull Inscription (1) from Nineveh (ARAB II §§309-312), Sidon and Tyre also appear (as Luli's city and point of flight), and Ashkelon, Ekron and Eltekeh are named. Whether that is the same bull text as the throne-room entrance bulls Compton means, and whether he counts only captured cities, was not checked. This needs his article to settle.
The figure on the building. Compton proposes Hezekiah. The drawings and one photograph cannot show identifying attributes beyond pose and placement; this is a reading, not something the slab states.

biblical.tie: Sennacherib takes 'all the fenced cities of Judah' and Hezekiah pays tribute. Matches the annals' 46 cities and tribute; the slab, if Jerusalem, would show the capital not stormed.

The Assyrian army before Jerusalem, Hezekiah on the defensive, the city not taken. A walled city surrounded but with no assault shown is what Compton links to this; the tie depends entirely on his identification.
Hezekiah strengthens the wall, raises towers and builds another wall outside. Compton's corbelled towers and inner/outer wall arrangement are the features that would correspond (his reading).

updates.what: Compton's JNES article proposes Slab 28 shows Jerusalem.
Times of Israel report brings the proposal to wide attention with objections from Danel Kahn (Haifa) and Stefan Maul (Heidelberg).

corrections: Some summaries say Compton reads Slab 28 as Jerusalem 'rather than the city of Ushu'. The Times of Israel report states the earlier identification of this throne-room scene was Eltekeh; Ushu is the city Compton moves ('misplaced') to the start of the sequence.
The phrase popularly quoted as 'like a bird in a cage' reads in Luckenbill's 1927 translation 'like a caged bird' (ARAB II §§240, 312).
Destruction is often given as '2015-16'; the Times of Israel report dates the smashing of the palace reliefs to 2016.
The relief carries no caption naming Jerusalem; calling it 'the earliest image of Jerusalem' or 'of Hezekiah' states a proposal as a fact.

sites.name: Sergius Paulus Inscriptions (Soloi, Rome, Pisidian Antioch)
sites.subtitle: Three separate stones bearing a Paul(l)us linked to the proconsul of Acts 13 · 1st century CE
sites.date: Rome cippus: reign of Claudius (41–54 CE; possibly 41–47). Soloi epitaph: undated Roman-period text; the 'Paulus' lines are a later addition. Antioch honorific: lettering of c. 60–100 CE (Ramsay).
sites.date_basis: Rome: acting under the authority of Ti. Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus (EDR). Soloi: the text has a local 'year 13' date, but no era or emperor is named. Antioch: letter forms only (Ramsay 1915, 151).

discovery.when: Soloi: 1870s (Cesnola); Rome: 1887; Pisidian Antioch: 1912
discovery.who: Soloi: L. P. di Cesnola (text by D. Pierides), re-read by D. G. Hogarth in 1888; Rome: found on the Tiber's left bank; Antioch: W. M. Ramsay and J. G. C. Anderson
discovery.where: Soloi (north-west Cyprus), Rome (near S. Biagio della Pagnotta), Salir quarter of Pisidian Antioch

sites.location: Rome cippus: Museo Nazionale Romano, chiostro di Michelangelo, inv. 242. Soloi stone: Hogarth saw it built into a shop threshold at Karavostasi, Cyprus; its present whereabouts are not stated in any source cited here. Antioch stone: not established in the sources cited here.

physical.material: Rome: travertine (lapis tiburtinus) cippus 160 × 80 × 24 cm, letters 3.5–5 cm (EDR). Soloi: marble slab/pedestal (Cesnola; Hogarth).
physical.script: Soloi: Greek; Rome and Antioch: Latin

overview: Acts 13:7–12 names 'the proconsul Sergius Paulus' at Paphos on Cyprus. No stone yet found names 'Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Cyprus' in one text. Three inscriptions are used to build the case, each carrying part of it.

Soloi, Cyprus. A Greek funerary text in which one Apollonius honours his father and his mother Artemidora and lists his civic offices. Lines added later say he also revised the city council 'in the time of the proconsul Paulus' (Hogarth 1889). Cesnola found it in the 1870s. Hogarth recopied it in 1888, built into the threshold of a grain store at Karavostasi where the owner dug it out for paying visitors, and warned it was being worn away.

Rome. A boundary cippus of the Tiber commissioners (curatores riparum et alvei Tiberis) under Claudius names 'L(ucius) Sergius Paullus' among five commissioners. Pisidian Antioch: Ramsay and Anderson copied in 1912 an honorific base for 'L. Sergius Paullus, son of Lucius, the younger', listing early posts of a senatorial career. Ramsay read him as the son of the proconsul of Acts.

text.quote: 'Apollonius to his father … and to his mother Artemidora … consecrated the enclosure and this monument … having filled the offices of clerk of the market, prefect, town-clerk, high priest … He also revised the senate by means of assessors in the time of the proconsul Paulus.'
text.translation: D. G. Hogarth, Devia Cypria (London 1889) p. 115 (Soloi inscription, his no. 36)

evidence: Soloi: the proconsul is named only as 'Paulus'. No praenomen or 'Sergius' survives (Hogarth 1889, 114–115; Cesnola 1877, 425).
Soloi: Hogarth reports that the last two and a half lines, including the Paulus clause, are a later addition in a different letter form. The main text is dated to 'year 13', with no era given.

Rome (CIL VI 31545 = ILS 5926 = EDR127293): 'Paullus Fabius Persicus, C. Eggius Marullus, L. Sergius Paullus, C. Obellius Rufus, L. Scribonius Libo, curatores riparum et alvei Tiberis, ex auctoritate Ti. Claudi Caesaris Aug. Germanici …' marked the bank 'a Trigario ad pontem Agrippae'.
Rome: EDR notes that the verb terminaverunt lacks Claudius' extra letter, which may narrow the date to 41–47 CE, before Claudius' censorship.
Antioch: 'L. Sergio L. f. Paullo filio, IIIIvir. v. c., trib. mil. leg. VI Ferr., quaest. …' (Ramsay 1915, 151). The word filio ('the younger') marks a son of the same name.
questions: Is the Soloi 'Paulus' the Sergius Paulus of Acts? Cesnola's editor D. Pierides (1877, 425) and Hogarth (1889) both say 'may be'. Nothing on the stone gives his nomen, and the local 'year 13' is not tied to an emperor. Any date for this Paulus depends on assumptions the text does not supply.

Is the Tiber commissioner the proconsul? A Tiber commission and a provincial proconsulship both belong to a senatorial career, and the cippus falls under Claudius, the same reign in which Acts places Paul's visit to Cyprus. The stone gives only the name and the commission. It does not say he ever held Cyprus.

Ramsay (1915, 150–172) reads the Antioch Paullus as the proconsul's son and ties the family's estates near Antioch to Paul's route from Cyprus to Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:13–14). That link is Ramsay's inference; the stone does not name the father's office.

biblical.tie: 'the proconsul (anthypatos) Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence'. The Soloi stone uses the same title (anthypatos) with the name Paulus, and the Rome cippus gives a Claudian L. Sergius Paullus.
The proconsul 'believed'. None of the inscriptions bears on his belief. Ramsay's argument about the family's religion is his own interpretation.
Paul goes from Paphos to Pisidian Antioch. The Antioch stone shows a L. Sergius Paullus honoured in that colony.

sources.verified: Full text read on archive.org: p. 229 describes the marble slab naming Soli and 'the Pro-Consul Paulus'; Appendix p. 425 prints the Greek with Pierides' note that he 'may be the Sergius Paulus of the Acts'.

sources.verified: Full text read: new copy and squeezes, threshold at Karavostasi, later-addition argument, English translation quoted here (p. 115).

sources.cite: Epigraphic Database Roma EDR127293 = CIL VI 31545 = ILS 5926 (G. Crimi, 2013, rev. 2024)
sources.verified: Record read: findspot (Tiber left bank, 1887), Museo Nazionale Romano inv. 242, travertine 160 × 80 × 24 cm, full Latin text naming L. Sergius Paullus, date 41–54 CE with the 41–47 note.

sources.cite: W. M. Ramsay, The Bearing of Recent Discovery on the Trustworthiness of the New Testament (London: Hodder & Stoughton, 1915), ch. XII, pp. 150–172
sources.verified: Full text read on archive.org: pp. 150–152 give the 1912 Antioch text, translation and dating by letter forms.

sources.cite: 'Sergius Paulus: An Archaeological Biography', Bible Archaeology Report, 15 Nov 2019
sources.verified: Page read: surveys the Soloi (IGR III 930), Tiber (CIL 6.31545), Antioch and Kythrea texts and calls the identifications 'possible'.

corrections: Old entry: 'discovered in 1887'. Cesnola published the Soloi stone in 1877 (Cyprus, p. 229 and p. 425). Hogarth recopied it in 1888, published 1889. 1887 is the year the Rome cippus came out of the Tiber (EDR127293).

Old text 'Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Cyprus, dedicated this' is invented. The Soloi stone is Apollonius' family monument, and 'the proconsul Paulus' appears only in a later clause. It has no 'Sergius' and no 'dedicated this' by Paulus (Hogarth 1889, 115). The Latin stone that does name L. Sergius Paullus is a Tiber boundary marker in Rome and does not mention Cyprus.

Old location 'Cyprus Museum, Nicosia' is unsupported. Hogarth last saw the Soloi stone in a shop threshold at Karavostasi; no published source gives its present location. The Rome cippus is in the Museo Nazionale Romano.
Old dimensions '25 × 35 cm' are unsourced. The one measured stone, the Rome cippus, is 160 × 80 × 24 cm.
Old date 'c. 45 CE' is not on any of the stones. Only the Rome cippus is datable, to Claudius (41–54 CE).
Old entry treats this as one inscription. It is three different stones in two languages from three places, and none of them alone says 'Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Cyprus'.

sites.name: Shiloh (Khirbet Seilun / Tel Shiloh) excavations
sites.subtitle: Multi-period hilltop site north of Jerusalem · excavated 1926-1963, 1981-1984, 2017-2026
sites.date: Occupation from the Middle Bronze Age through the Iron Age and later periods; ABR's 2026 finds include Middle Bronze Age storage jars, and ABR dates its monumental east-west building to 1177-980 BC
sites.date_basis: The MB date of the 2026 jars is ABR's ceramic typology; ABR says radiocarbon tests on their charred contents are planned, not yet done. The 1177-980 BC date for the monumental building is stated in ABR's 2019 news post without published stratigraphic or radiocarbon data; the peer-reviewed article announced then has not been located for this entry.

discovery.when: Danish excavations 1926, 1929, 1932 and 1963; Tel Aviv University 1981-1984; Associates for Biblical Research (ABR) from 2017, eighth season in 2026
discovery.who: Danish expedition (H. Kjaer and successors); Israel Finkelstein with S. Bunimovitz, Z. Lederman and others; ABR under director Scott Stripling
discovery.where: Khirbet Seilun, north of Jerusalem

sites.location: In situ (site). Finds from the ABR seasons: repository not stated in the sources read.
overview: Tel Shiloh has been dug by three expeditions: a Danish team (1926, 1929, 1932, 1963), a Tel Aviv University team led by Israel Finkelstein (1981-1984, preliminary report in Tel Aviv 12, 1985; monograph 1993), and since 2017 the Associates for Biblical Research (ABR) under Scott Stripling, which finished its eighth season in June 2026.

ABR reports worship-related objects from the area of a large building that runs east-west: three altar horns (2019), a ceramic pomegranate (2018, published in Judea and Samaria Research Studies 28, 2019), murex shells, and a Thutmose III scarab. In 2022 it found the piers and socket stones of a gate in the northern wall. In 2025 it worked on this gate complex. In 2026 it reported three things: more walls showing a bent-axis gate with several rooms; the southern wall of the east-west building; and three Middle Bronze Age storage jars in Area D, two holding charred olives and one holding wheat.

Most of the ABR results so far are season announcements. The only peer-reviewed ABR article located for this entry is the pomegranate study. The building's full dimensions, its stratigraphy, and radiocarbon dates have not yet been published.
evidence: Three restorable Middle Bronze Age pithoi in Area D (the favissa area). Two held charred olives and one held wheat. Radiocarbon testing of the contents is planned (ABR, 22 June 2026).
The southern wall of a 'monumental building' oriented east-west was located in 2026. ABR says this now lets it reconstruct the full dimensions, but it has not yet published them (ABR, 22 June 2026).

Gate complex in the northern fortification: 2022 exposed the gate's piers and socket stones where the glacis against the northern wall ends, with a terraced slope leading up to it; 2026 exposed more walls showing a bent-axis gate with several rooms (ABR 2022; 2026).

Altar horns (2019): horn 1 was 38 x 23.5 cm and was built into an Early Roman wall; horn 2 was 18 x 12.5 cm and lay about 3 m to the southwest; horn 3 was 38 x 20 cm and came from a 'destruction matrix' about 1 m lower. All came from the general area of the east-west building (ABR, 12 Aug 2019).
A ceramic pomegranate from the same area (2018), published by Lopez, Stripling and Ben-Shlomo in JSRS 28 (2019).

Arrowheads that look medieval, together with Islamic pottery and Islamic and Crusader coins, are read as evidence of a possible Frankish raid on the medieval village of Seilun in the 13th century (Seevers, Barber and Campbell, JSRS 34/2, 2025).

A rock-cut pool about 13 x 18 m and 2.5 m deep, about 300 m south of the tell, was built in the Byzantine-Umayyad period and used until the Ottoman period (IAA salvage digs in 2013 and 2022; HA-ESI 138, 2026).
questions: Is the east-west building the tabernacle precinct? ABR (22 June 2026) says the structure 'exhibits proportions similar to those described for the biblical tabernacle (Ex. 26:15-25; 27:13)' and lists altar horns, pomegranates and murex shells found 'in and around' it. Against this, from the published data: the dimensions have not been published, so the proportion claim cannot yet be checked; horn 1 was reused in an Early Roman wall, so its original context is lost; and the only date given (1177-980 BC, ABR 2019) comes without stratigraphic or radiocarbon support. Until a report appears, this stays an announced claim.

Is the northern gate the one where Eli died? ABR (2022) says it 'may have been the gate where Eli died' (1 Sam 4:18). The posts read here give no phase date for the gate, so the tie to Eli rests on the biblical narrative plus the gate's position, not on a dated stratum.

How does ABR's sequence fit the earlier Tel Aviv University stratigraphy (Finkelstein et al., Tel Aviv 12, 1985; monograph 1993)? Neither report has been reviewed in full for this entry. Any agreement or conflict between the two sequences has not been checked here.

biblical.tie: The congregation sets up the tent of meeting at Shiloh. ABR's east-west building is its candidate for the tabernacle area (their reading; dimensions not yet published).

The Shiloh sanctuary has a doorpost and is called hekhal ('temple'), which suggests a built structure there by Eli's time. A monumental building would fit that wording, but no excavated feature has been tied to it by inscription.
Eli falls 'by the side of the gate' and dies. ABR's northern gate is its candidate (their 'may have been').
The tabernacle's board counts and the court width that ABR cites for its proportion comparison.
Shiloh's ruin is remembered as a warning. The published data read here do not establish which destruction layer, if any, corresponds to it.

sites.name: Ketef Hinnom Silver Amulets
sites.subtitle: Two inscribed silver plaques with the Priestly Blessing · late Iron Age, Jerusalem
sites.date: Late pre-exilic, around 600 BCE (Barkay et al. 2004); Israel Museum label: 6th century BCE; E. Waaler 2002 argued 725-650 BCE
sites.date_basis: Palaeography of the incised Palaeo-Hebrew letters (re-read with enhanced imaging by the USC West Semitic Research team) plus the pottery and objects around them in the burial repository, which the tomb's excavator dates from c. 650 BCE into the early 6th century. No date is written on the plaques.

discovery.who: Gabriel Barkay (Tel Aviv University excavation)
discovery.where: Repository beneath Chamber 25 of burial Cave 24, Ketef Hinnom, on the slope of the Hinnom Valley southwest of Jerusalem's Old City

sites.location: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (Israel Antiquities Authority collection, IAA 1980-1495 and 1980-1496)

physical.material: Silver sheet, rolled into small scrolls; letters incised with a fine point
physical.dimensions: Israel Museum: height 3.9-9.7 cm, width 1.1-2.7 cm (the larger, KH1, c. 9.7 x 2.7 cm unrolled; the smaller, KH2, c. 3.9 x 1.1 cm)

overview: Two tiny silver sheets, rolled up like scrolls and evidently worn as amulets, were found in 1979 in the repository (bone pit) under a bench chamber of a rock-cut family tomb at Ketef Hinnom, excavated by Gabriel Barkay. The repository is reported to have held about a thousand objects (pottery, arrowheads, jewellery, bone and glass items); that count comes via secondary summary of the excavators' reports and was not checked in them. The rolled sheets had to be unrolled in a laboratory before the writing could be seen.

Both carry a Hebrew text using the divine name YHWH and a form of the Priestly Blessing known from Numbers 6:24-26. KH2 preserves 'May YHWH bless you, keep you; may YHWH make his face shine upon you and grant you peace' (the middle clause of the Numbers text about lifting up the face and being gracious is not on the plaque). KH1 is more damaged; besides the start of the blessing it contains a phrase about the one who keeps 'the covenant and loving-kindness toward those who love him and keep his commandments', wording known from Deut 7:9 and Dan 9:4 / Neh 1:5.

A 2004 re-edition by Barkay, Lundberg, Vaughn and Zuckerman used new photography and computer enhancement and defended a late pre-exilic date. On that dating they are the oldest known objects carrying wording also found in the Hebrew Bible. They are amulets, not biblical manuscripts: the texts are short devotional and protective formulas, and the phrasing differs from the Masoretic text.

text.quote: ...[bl]essed be he / she by YHWH, the helper and the rebuker of [E]vil. May YHWH bless you, keep you. May YHWH make his face shine [upon] you and grant you peace.
text.translation: Literal translation (this encyclopedia) of the KH2 transliteration as published by Barkay, Lundberg, Vaughn and Zuckerman (BASOR 334, 2004), reached here through a secondary reproduction; not checked against the plates. Broken letters in brackets.

evidence: Two rolled silver plaques, IAA 1980-1495 and 1980-1496, now in the Israel Museum; height 3.9-9.7 cm, width 1.1-2.7 cm.

Found in 1979 in the repository under Chamber 25 of Cave 24 at Ketef Hinnom (Barkay excavation); the deposit reportedly held about a thousand other grave goods (secondary summary, not checked in the excavation report).
Script is Palaeo-Hebrew (pre-exilic letter forms), incised on silver.
Both plaques contain the divine name YHWH.
KH2 carries a short form of the Priestly Blessing: 'YHWH bless you, keep you; YHWH make his face shine upon you and grant you peace'. The middle clause of Num 6:25b-26a is absent.
KH1 includes 'the covenant and loving-kindness toward those who love [him] and those who keep [his commandments]', a formula found in Deut 7:9.
KH2 calls YHWH 'the rebuker of Evil' (ha-go'er ba-ra'), a protective (apotropaic) formula.
questions: Date. Barkay, Lundberg, Vaughn and Zuckerman (BASOR 334, 2004) place the plaques in the late pre-exilic period, just before 586 BCE, on the basis of letter forms visible in enhanced images and the 7th-6th-century pottery around them. E. Waaler (Tyndale Bulletin 53, 2002) puts them earlier, 725-650 BCE, also on archaeological and palaeographic grounds. J. Renz and W. Röllig (Handbuch der althebräischen Epigraphik, 1995) are reported to have argued that the writing was too poorly preserved to date securely and that a 3rd-2nd century BCE date could not be ruled out, because the repository also held later material. That summary comes through secondary reporting and was not checked in the HAE volume itself.

What do they prove about the Pentateuch? Waaler (2002) argues that one scribe drew both the Numbers blessing and the Deuteronomy 7:9 formula from a single source text, so Priestly and Deuteronomic material already stood together before Josiah's reform. Against this, the plaques could draw on liturgical formulas used in worship and not on a written book: the blessing is shortened and the KH1 formula occurs in several biblical books. The objects show the wording existed; they do not show which written book, if any, it came from.

biblical.tie: KH2 (and the damaged end of KH1) give the Priestly Blessing in a shorter form: 'bless and keep', 'make his face shine... and grant you peace'. The clause 'be gracious to you / lift up his countenance' is not present on KH2.
KH1's 'the covenant and loving-kindness toward those who love him and keep his commandments' matches this covenant formula.
Our reading: YHWH's words likened to refined silver and YHWH as the one who keeps/guards. The link is thematic (silver, 'keep') and is not quoted on the plaques.

corrections: Old entry said the plaques are 'approximately 2 cm diameter each': the Israel Museum gives height 3.9-9.7 cm and width 1.1-2.7 cm; rolled up they are small, but the sheets are up to c. 9.7 cm long.

Old entry said the text is 'a direct quotation of the Priestly Blessing': it is a shorter form that leaves out a clause of Num 6:25-26 and adds other formulas ('rebuker of Evil', the Deut 7:9 covenant formula).

Old entry called the script 'among the earliest known examples' of Hebrew: Hebrew inscriptions in the same script are centuries older (e.g. Iron Age ostraca); the plaques are early for biblical wording, not for Hebrew writing.
Old entry listed 'Deuteronomy 6 (Shema)' and 'Exodus 15 (Song of Moses)' as connections: neither text appears on the plaques. The Deuteronomy parallel is 7:9, not chapter 6.

Old entry dated them simply 'c. 600 BCE' as settled: Waaler (2002) argues 725-650 BCE and Renz-Röllig reportedly left a Hellenistic date open; the date rests on palaeography and deposit context, not on a written date.

sites.name: Soleb 'Land of the Shasu of Yhw' Inscription
sites.subtitle: Prisoner-name cartouche in Amenhotep III's temple of Amun-Ra at Soleb, Sudan · c. 1400-1385 BCE
sites.date: Reign of Amenhotep III, 18th Dynasty; carved no later than his Year 30 jubilee (c. 1385 BCE on Kennedy's high chronology; c. 1360s on lower chronologies)
sites.date_basis: The temple was built and decorated for Amenhotep III and carries his Year-30 Heb-Sed scenes, so the prisoner lists were in place by the first jubilee. Kennedy (2019) brackets the lists to c. 1409-1385 BCE using a high 18th-Dynasty chronology; the stone gives only the king, not a regnal year for the list itself.

discovery.when: Temple known since Burckhardt (1813); the Yhw column and wall block uncovered in the 1957-1963 excavations
discovery.who: Mission of Michela Schiff Giorgini (with Clément Robichon, Jean Leclant)
discovery.where: Hypostyle hall (Sector IV), column IV N4; and wall block SB 69 from the 2nd court (Sector III), temple of Amun-Ra, Soleb, west bank of the Nile south of the Third Cataract, Sudan

sites.location: Column IV N4: in situ at Soleb. Wall block SB 69: in storage in Sudan (antiquities department), per Kennedy 2019

physical.material: Sandstone temple column (relief-carved)
physical.dimensions: Name-ring (cartouche) 42 cm x 15 cm, measured on site by Kennedy (2019)
physical.language: Egyptian (rendering a foreign, West Semitic name)

overview: Amenhotep III's temple of Amun-Ra at Soleb in Nubia has columns carved with bound foreign prisoners, each over a fortified name-ring naming a subject people or land. Column IV N4 in the hypostyle hall carries four names of Shasu (Egyptian šꜣsw, 'nomads') groups. The second, N4 a2, reads tꜣ šꜣsw yhwꜣ, 'the land of the Shasu of Yhwꜣ'.

The same phrase appears on a fragmentary wall block (SB 69) from the temple's second court, and again in a later list at Amara West (Ramesside, early 13th century BCE), which appears to copy part of the Soleb list. The column is still standing at Soleb; the drawing is published in the excavation volume Soleb V (1998).

The name is spelled y-h-w-ꜣ. Kennedy (2019), photographing the column, reported that the last sign is the vulture/aleph (G1), not the quail-chick w (G43) printed in the excavation report. No text accompanies the name beyond the list formula: it says nothing about who these Shasu worshipped or where exactly they lived.

text.quote: tꜣ šꜣsw yhwꜣ - 'land of the Shasu (nomads) of Yhwꜣ'
text.translation: Literal translation (this encyclopedia) of the transliteration published by T. Kennedy, Dotawo 6 (2019) 184 (column IV N4 a2)

evidence: Column IV N4 names four Shasu groups: twr byl, yhwꜣ, smt, bt ꜥn[...] (Kennedy 2019, citing Leclant, Les Fouilles de Soleb, p. 214).
Sign sequence of N4 a2: N16 (land) + šꜣ-sw (nomads) + M17-O4-V4-G1 (y-h-wꜣ-ꜣ) (Kennedy 2019, p. 184).
The name carries no city/foreign-land classifier and no 'god' sign (Kennedy 2019).
A second Soleb occurrence is on wall block SB 69, 2nd court, R38 (Soleb III pp. 179-180; Soleb V pls. 206-207, as cited by Kennedy).
The prisoner figure on N4 is headless; the ethnic dress of this particular captive is not preserved (Kennedy 2019).
Amenhotep III's only recorded military campaign is the Year 5 Kush campaign; the Asiatic names in the list are not tied to a recorded campaign (Kennedy 2019, citing Urk. IV 1665-1666).
questions: Is yhwꜣ the divine name YHWH? T. Kennedy (Dotawo 6, 2019) says yes: the name is unique, is not a known place-name, lacks a land classifier, and sits beside other Shasu names he reads as divine (twr byl = 'Bull Baal'; bt ꜥnt = 'house of Anat'); he concludes these Shasu 'could be identified with the early Israelites'. F. Adrom and M. Müller (in The Origins of Yahwism, de Gruyter 2017, 93-114) hold that the sequence cannot be shown to be a tribe, a place or a deity, and caution against tying it to Israelite or proto-Israelite groups. The inscription itself settles the spelling, not the referent.

Where were these Shasu? Egyptian texts of Ramesses II-III place Shasu in the Seir/Edom region; D. B. Redford (Egypt, Canaan, and Israel in Ancient Times, 1992, pp. 269-273, as cited by Kennedy) uses this to locate the Yhw Shasu in the south, in or near Edom. Kennedy widens the field to Sinai, Edom, Moab, Transjordan or Canaan. The Soleb column gives no geography of its own beyond grouping these names as Shasu.

Last sign: the excavation report (Soleb III pp. 122-123) transcribed the final bird as w (G43); Kennedy (2019), from new photographs, reads aleph (G1), matching the Amara West copy. Adrom & Müller (2017) follow the older reading, per Kennedy n. 30.

Date: Kennedy dates the lists 1409-1385 BCE on a high chronology; on the lower chronologies common in Egyptological handbooks Amenhotep III's jubilee falls in the 1360s BCE. The absolute date moves with the chronology chosen, not with anything on the column.

biblical.tie: If yhwꜣ is the divine name, this is the earliest written occurrence of it, attached to a nomadic group east of Egypt, not to a city. That is a reading of the name, not a statement in the text.

These poems have YHWH coming from Seir/Edom/Teman. Egyptian texts put Shasu in Seir; the Soleb list groups a 'land of the Shasu of Yhw' among Shasu. The correspondence is regional, and depends on the Seir location of these particular Shasu, which the Soleb column does not state.

sources.cite: M. Schiff Giorgini, C. Robichon, J. Leclant, ed. N. Beaux, Soleb V: Le temple. Bas-reliefs et inscriptions (Cairo: IFAO, Bibliothèque générale 19, 1998)
