sites.name: Solomon's Wall (Ophel fortification)
sites.subtitle: Iron Age city wall, gatehouse and tower on the Ophel, south of the Temple Mount · date disputed (10th vs 8th-7th century BCE)
sites.date: Disputed. Eilat Mazar (2010): late 10th century BCE. Finkelstein, Herzog, Singer-Avitz and Ussishkin (2007), writing about Mazar's earlier (2006) publication of the same fortification: in use in the 8th-7th centuries BCE.
sites.date_basis: No inscription dates the wall. Mazar's 10th-century date rests on (1) pottery sherds 'within the fill of the lowest floor of the royal building near the gatehouse' and (2) architectural comparison with Iron Age gates at Megiddo, Beersheba and Ashdod (Hebrew University release, 22 Feb 2010). Finkelstein et al. (Tel Aviv 34, 2007: 159) state that the chronological data Mazar had published then showed the fortification 'was in use during the 8th-7th centuries BCE'. No radiocarbon dates for the Ophel wall were located for this entry.

discovery.when: Tower outline recorded 1867; excavated 1986 (B. and E. Mazar); re-excavated and announced February 2010
discovery.who: Charles Warren (1867 underground survey); Benjamin Mazar and Eilat Mazar (1980s, Hebrew University); Eilat Mazar (2009-2010 season, Hebrew University Institute of Archaeology)
discovery.where: The Ophel, between the City of David and the southern wall of the Temple Mount, Jerusalem

sites.location: In situ, Ophel, south of the Temple Mount, Jerusalem (outside the Old City walls; not in the Jewish Quarter)

physical.material: Stone masonry (wall, gatehouse, towers)
physical.dimensions: As announced 22 Feb 2010: wall section c. 70 m long and 6 m high; inner gatehouse 6 m high, symmetrical four-room plan; adjacent tower 24 x 18 m; corner tower 8 m long, 6 m high; an eastern wall section 35 m long, 5 m high

overview: A stretch of city wall with an inner gatehouse, an adjoining 'royal structure' and towers on the Ophel, the saddle between the City of David ridge and the Temple Mount. Charles Warren traced the outline of the large tower in an underground survey in 1867 without assigning it a date. Benjamin and Eilat Mazar excavated in the area in the 1980s (final report: Qedem 29, 1989). Eilat Mazar re-excavated it and on 22 February 2010 the Hebrew University announced it as a city wall of the 10th century BCE, which she connected with Solomon's building of 'the wall of Jerusalem round about' (1 Kings 3:1).

The 2010 release lists a 70 m wall section 6 m high, a four-room gatehouse, a 24 x 18 m tower, storage jars 1.15 m tall burned in a fire, cult figurines, seal impressions reading 'to the king', Hebrew bullae, and a jar with a partial Hebrew inscription that Mazar read as naming a high government official. The date rests on sherds in the fill of the lowest floor of the building beside the gate and on comparison with gates at Megiddo, Beersheba and Ashdod.

The date is disputed. Finkelstein, Herzog, Singer-Avitz and Ussishkin (Tel Aviv 34, 2007) argued, from Mazar's own earlier publication of this 'Solomonic city-wall', that the dated evidence placed its use in the 8th-7th centuries BCE and that the 10th-century attribution came from the biblical text rather than the finds.
evidence: Wall section c. 70 m long and 6 m high; eastern section 35 m long and 5 m high (Hebrew University release, 22 Feb 2010).
Inner gatehouse 6 m high with a symmetrical four-room plan; tower beside it 24 x 18 m; corner tower 8 m long, 6 m high overlooking the Kidron valley (same release).
Storage jars 1.15 m high were found burned; one bears a partial Hebrew inscription that the excavator read as belonging to a high government official (same release).
Finds also include cult figurines, seal impressions reading 'to the king', and Hebrew bullae; the release does not give the stratum of each.
The dating evidence given is: pottery sherds 'within the fill of the lowest floor of the royal building near the gatehouse', plus architectural comparison with gates at Megiddo, Beersheba and Ashdod.
Charles Warren recorded the outline of the large tower in 1867 without attributing it to Solomon (same release).

The Ophel area was excavated in the 1980s by B. and E. Mazar; their report (Qedem 29, 1989) includes Iron Age II figurines, Hebrew inscriptions and seal impressions, and a dendrochronology study from the 1986 season.
No radiocarbon dates specific to this wall were found in the sources checked.
questions: Date of construction. Eilat Mazar (Hebrew University release, 22 Feb 2010) dates the wall to the late 10th century BCE on the basis of sherds in the fill of the lowest floor of the adjoining building and on gate plans like Megiddo, Beersheba and Ashdod. Finkelstein, Herzog, Singer-Avitz and Ussishkin (Tel Aviv 34, 2007: 159) respond, concerning Mazar's 2006 chapter 'The Solomonic Wall in Jerusalem': 'As she admits, the chronological data recovered in her excavations indicate that the sole Iron Age fortification system extending in this area was in use during the 8th-7th centuries BCE,' and that it was dated to Solomon because 'the Solomonic city-wall must have passed here' according to the biblical sources. Evidence to test: sherds in a fill give only the earliest possible date of the floor above them; four-room gates are known in more than one Iron Age phase (our reading). The 2010 finds post-date Finkelstein's critique, and no published response to them was located for this entry.

Whether 'to the king' seal impressions, bullae and burned jars belong to the wall's construction phase or to its later use and destruction: the 2010 release lists them together and does not separate them by stratum.
Reading of the jar inscription: the 2010 release gives only the excavator's reading ('belonged to a high-level government official'); the full published reading was not located for this entry.

biblical.tie: Solomon 'had made an end of building his own house, and the house of the LORD, and the wall of Jerusalem round about.' The 2010 announcement ties the Ophel wall to this verse. The verse names a wall around Jerusalem; it does not describe its route, gate plan or towers.
Solomon builds 'the wall of Jerusalem' and the Millo with levied labour. Same caution: the text gives no location on the Ophel.

Jotham: 'on the wall of Ophel he built much' (KJV); Manasseh encircles the Ophel with a very high wall. These are the only verses naming building on the Ophel wall, and they are 8th-7th century kings, the period Finkelstein et al. assign to the fortification's use (our observation).
The 'wall of Ophel' and 'the great tower that lieth out' in the Persian-period repair list; a tower on the Ophel is part of the city's later description.

sites.name: Stepped Stone Structure
sites.subtitle: Stone revetment on the eastern slope of the City of David, Jerusalem · date disputed (Iron I / Iron IIA / later phases)
sites.date: Disputed and probably multi-phase: proposals range from Iron I (12th-11th century BCE) through Iron IIA (10th-9th century BCE) for the original build, with the upper courses assigned by some to the Hasmonaean (2nd-1st century BCE) period
sites.date_basis: No inscription. The date is bracketed by pottery: Iron I sherds found by Kenyon in the terraces beneath the mantle (Steiner 1994), and pottery of Shiloh's Stratum 14 (10th century on the traditional scheme) on the earliest surface of a house built into it (Cahill 2003), both as reported by Finkelstein et al. 2007: 148. Finkelstein et al. read the same houses' floors differently and note that Kenyon and Shiloh had dated those houses to the 7th century BCE. The upper courses join the late Hellenistic/Hasmonaean city wall (Shiloh 1984: 30). No radiocarbon date taken from the structure itself was found for this entry.

discovery.who: R. A. S. Macalister and J. G. Duncan (Palestine Exploration Fund), who called it the 'Jebusite Ramp'; Kathleen Kenyon (her Area A); Yigal Shiloh (his Area G); Eilat Mazar (excavation on the summit directly west of it)
discovery.where: Upper eastern slope of the southeastern ridge (City of David), Jerusalem, above the Kidron Valley

sites.location: In situ, City of David archaeological park, Jerusalem

physical.material: Stone: a stepped stone 'mantle' laid over a system of earlier stone-and-fill terraces

overview: A stepped stone revetment covering the upper eastern slope of the City of David ridge. Macalister and Duncan (1923-1925) exposed its top and called it the 'Jebusite Ramp'. Kenyon in the 1960s exposed more of it, with houses built over it and the terraces underneath; Yigal Shiloh excavated it as his Area G from 1978. Amihai Mazar (2006) divided the complex into five components: the underlying terraces (Component 1), the stepped mantle itself (Component 2), and three structures in Kenyon's Trench I (Components 3-5) that are not physically connected to the first two.

Iron Age houses (among them the 'Burnt Room House') were later built against and over its lower part. Its top is joined by the city wall and towers that Macalister and Duncan called the 'Maccabean Tower' and 'Great Tower'. Eilat Mazar, excavating on the summit to the west from 2005, argued that the stepped structure and her 'Large Stone Structure' were one building complex of c. 1000 BCE, which she identified with David's palace.

The date is contested. Finkelstein, Herzog, Singer-Avitz and Ussishkin (2007) argue the mantle has at least two building phases: a lower part of small stones running south-north, possibly late Iron IIA or early Iron IIB (9th-8th century BCE), and an upper part of larger stones oriented northwest that is bonded to the Hasmonaean city wall and was built or rebuilt in the late Hellenistic period. The identification with the biblical 'Millo' (a word built on the Hebrew root m-l-' , 'to fill') is a proposal; nothing on the stones names it.
evidence: Macalister and Duncan (1926) exposed the upper edge and labelled it the 'Jebusite Ramp' (their Pl. V), with a southern 'Great Tower' and northern 'Maccabean Tower' beside it (Finkelstein et al. 2007: 143).

Duncan recorded a fissure in the rock scarp at this spot 'filled up with great boulders... for a considerable distance under the foundations of the great Jebusite Eastern Rampart' (Macalister and Duncan 1926: 52, quoted by Finkelstein et al. 2007: 150).
The stepped mantle overlies a system of terraces (Component 1); Kenyon found Iron I pottery under those terraces (Steiner 1994, as reported by Finkelstein et al. 2007: 148).

In the mantle, the lower courses are of smaller stones running south-north; the upper third is of larger stones oriented northwest - the reverse of normal retaining-wall practice (Finkelstein et al. 2007: 151, Fig. 3).
Shiloh observed that 'the line of the "First Wall" and its towers integrated the top of the stepped stone structure' (Shiloh 1984: 30, quoted by Finkelstein et al. 2007: 153).

Houses were built over the lower mantle. Cahill (2003) reported Stratum 14-13 pottery (10th-9th century on the traditional scheme) on the lower floors of the 'Burnt Room House'; Kenyon (1974: 137) and Shiloh (1984: 28) had dated these houses to the second half of the 7th century BCE (Finkelstein et al. 2007: 151-152).

Parts of the complex are modern: Shiloh marked a 'modern retaining wall' at the northern tower, Steiner (2001: 51) notes the northern ramp was partly restored with cement by the Department of Antiquities of Palestine, and the present flat top may be a restoration (Finkelstein et al. 2007: 143, 148).
Kenyon found large building blocks and a proto-Ionic capital at the bottom of her Square A XVIII, just north of the structure (Kenyon 1963: 16, cited by Finkelstein et al. 2007: 154).
No dimension figures for the structure were found in the sources read for this entry.
questions: Date and unity of the mantle. Eilat Mazar (BAR 32:1, 2006, and her 2007 preliminary report, as summarized by Finkelstein et al. 2007: 148) treats the stepped structure and the Large Stone Structure as one Iron IIA complex of c. 1000 BCE, bracketed by Iron I pottery beneath the terraces and 10th-century pottery on the first floor of a house built into the slope (Cahill 2003). Finkelstein et al. (Tel Aviv 34, 2007: 148-153) answer that no clear physical connection between the two structures has been established, that the present top of the stepped structure seems to be a modern restoration, and that the mantle's lower and upper parts differ in stone size and orientation, so the lower part may be 9th-8th century and the upper part Hasmonaean. Kenyon (1974: 192-194) had already suggested a Hellenistic date for the upper part (as reported by Finkelstein et al. 2007: 153).

Floors of the Burnt Room House. Cahill (2003: 56-66) reads the 10th-9th century sherds as lying on the house's lowest floors, which would date the mantle below to before that. Finkelstein et al. (2007: 151) reply that they are sherds from ten loci, not whole vessels, and may come from fills beneath upper floors, noting that neither Kenyon nor Shiloh saw 10th-9th century occupation in these houses.

Is it the Millo? The proposal rests on the name (from the Hebrew root m-l-', 'to fill') and on the structure being a built fill/revetment. The biblical texts give no location or description for the Millo beyond Jerusalem and the city of David; the identification is an interpretation, not something the stones record.

Relation to the 2024 radiocarbon series. Regev et al. (PNAS 2024) dated 103 samples from City of David contexts and found almost 20% (18 dates) fall in the 12th-10th centuries BCE, and extensive building on the southeastern ridge in the 9th century. The samples came from Areas C/U, E and the Givati lot, not from the stepped structure, so they do not date it directly.

biblical.tie: David takes 'the stronghold of Zion' and builds 'round about from Millo and inward'. The stepped structure is one proposed candidate for the Millo or for the stronghold's support; the text gives no description of the Millo's form.
Solomon builds (or 'repaired the breaches' at) the Millo with levied labour. If the stepped structure is the Millo, these verses describe work on it; the identification is a reading.
Joash is killed 'in the house of Millo'. Eilat Mazar used this to argue the Millo was part of a palace complex joining the stepped structure and the Large Stone Structure (her interpretation).
Hezekiah 'repaired Millo in the city of David'. Finkelstein et al.'s 9th-8th century date for the lower mantle would fall before this repair (our observation).

sites.name: Susa Palace Remains
sites.subtitle: Darius I's palace and audience hall at Susa · built late 6th century BCE, rebuilt by Artaxerxes II
sites.date: Built under Darius I (522-486 BCE). Artaxerxes II (404-358 BCE) states that the apadana burned under Artaxerxes I and that he rebuilt it.
sites.date_basis: The royal inscriptions on site: Darius I's building texts, and Artaxerxes II's column-base inscription (A2Sa) naming the builder, the fire and the rebuilding. The Louvre dates its Susa palace objects to Darius I (-522 to -486).

discovery.when: 1884-1886 (Marcel and Jane Dieulafoy, Louvre mission); the palace was re-excavated in the 1970s under Jean Perrot, published 2013
discovery.who: Marcel-Auguste Dieulafoy and Jane Dieulafoy; Jean Perrot
discovery.where: The Apadana mound and royal city at Susa (Shush), Khuzestan, Iran

sites.location: In situ at Shush, Iran (foundations, column bases, gate). Excavated elements in the Louvre, Paris, Room 307 (Sully wing): Frieze of Archers AOD 488; bull capital of the Apadana AOD 1.

physical.material: Mudbrick and gravel-filled terraces, limestone column bases and capitals, glazed siliceous (frit) relief bricks
physical.dimensions: Apadana bull capital (Louvre AOD 1): total height 532 cm, width 374 cm. Frieze of Archers panel (Louvre AOD 488): 475 × 375 × 17 cm (Louvre records).
physical.script: Old Persian, Elamite and Akkadian cuneiform (royal inscriptions)

overview: Susa was an Elamite city long before the Persians. Darius I built a royal palace there, and its audience hall (apadana) was a forest of columns on a raised terrace. Marcel and Jane Dieulafoy excavated the apadana for the Louvre in 1884-1886 and shipped the glazed-brick Frieze of Archers and a column capital with double bull protomes to Paris. Jean Perrot's later excavation of the palace was published as The Palace of Darius at Susa (2013).

The site's own inscriptions give its history. On the column bases, Artaxerxes II states that 'this apadana Darius, my ancestor, made', that 'later under Artaxerxes my grandfather it was burned', and that he rebuilt it. So the hall Darius built stood through the reigns of Xerxes and into that of Artaxerxes I before it burned.

The Book of Esther is set in 'Shushan the palace' under Ahasuerus. Dieulafoy devoted a chapter of his excavation report to Esther, and Perrot's 2013 final publication includes a chapter on 'Susa and the Bible'. The text names a royal gate, inner and outer courts, and a garden pavilion with pillars and coloured pavements, and the palace provides a real setting of that kind. Nothing found at Susa names Esther, Mordecai or Haman.

text.quote: Says Artaxerxes the great king … this apadana Darius, my ancestor made; [later under Artaxerxes my grandfather it was burned; By the grace of Ahura Mazda, Anahita and Mithra I built this apadana; may Ahura Mazda, Anahita and Mithra protect me].
text.translation: H. C. Tolman, Ancient Persian Lexicon and the Texts of the Achaemenidan Inscriptions (Vanderbilt Oriental Series 6; New York: American Book Co., 1908), p. 49, 'Art. Sus. a.' (now A2Sa), 'On four pedestals of column hall; Persian, Elamite, Babylonian.' Tolman's square brackets mark the portion restored from the parallel versions.

evidence: The palace terrace, residence and apadana at Susa were built under Darius I. The Louvre dates the palace objects to 'Achéménide : Darius I (-522 - -486)'.

The Frieze of Archers (Louvre AOD 488) is a panel of four archers flanking a trilingual inscription of Darius, in moulded, polychrome glazed siliceous ceramic, 475 × 375 × 17 cm. It came from the Dieulafoy mission.
The Apadana capital (Louvre AOD 1) is limestone with double bull protomes, 532 cm tall overall. It was acquired 'en mission' and was excavated by Dieulafoy.
Artaxerxes II's column-base inscription (A2Sa) records that the apadana was built by Darius, burned under Artaxerxes I, and rebuilt by Artaxerxes II (Tolman 1908, p. 49).
Excavation reports: the Dieulafoys (1884-1886) published L'Acropole de Suse (1890-1893), and Perrot's team produced The Palace of Darius at Susa (2013).
No inscription or object from the palace names any figure from Esther, Nehemiah or Daniel.
questions: Which Persian king is Ahasuerus? The book of Esther names 'Ahasuerus… from India unto Ethiopia' (Esth 1:1). The Hebrew ʾăḥašwērôš corresponds consonantally to Old Persian Xšayāršā (Xerxes), and the Susa texts show that Darius's apadana was standing in Xerxes' reign. The Septuagint of Esther instead calls the king Artaxerxes. The identification is linguistic, and no Susa find confirms either name in connection with the story.

How closely does the palace plan match the narrative? M. Dieulafoy (L'Acropole de Suse III-IV, 1890-1893, ch. XIII 'Le livre d'Esther') read the book against the palace he excavated. J. Perrot (The Palace of Darius at Susa, 2013, ch. 'Susa and the Bible') revisits the question with the later excavation. The narrative details are a king's gate (Esth 2:19, 21; 5:13), an inner court facing the throne room (5:1), and a garden pavilion with pillars and coloured pavement (1:5-6). How far each maps onto a specific excavated unit is the excavators' interpretation, and neither text has been reviewed in full for this entry.

What burned under Artaxerxes I? A2Sa states the fire but gives no cause or year within the reign (465-424 BCE). The sources are silent on whether that fire relates to anything in Nehemiah, whose master was an Artaxerxes.

biblical.tie: 'Shushan the palace' (bîrâ), a feast 'in the court of the garden of the king's palace', with 'pillars of marble' and a pavement of coloured stones. Susa had a Persian royal palace with columned halls, courts and glazed decoration, so the setting is real. The specific garden pavilion has not been identified with any named find in the sources consulted.

Mordecai 'sat in the king's gate'. The text assumes a gate building where officials sat. Perrot's 2013 publication discusses the Bible and the palace, but it has not been reviewed for this entry, so no specific excavated gate is identified with the text here.

Esther stands 'in the inner court of the king's house, over against the king's house', with the king on his throne. The palace is organized around courts, so that description fits the kind of building the Persians built at Susa.
Nehemiah was 'in Shushan the palace' in Artaxerxes' 20th year. By the A2Sa inscription the apadana burned under Artaxerxes I, but when in his reign is not stated.

Daniel sees himself 'at Shushan in the palace, which is in the province of Elam… by the river of Ulai'. Susa is in Elam and on the rivers of the Khuzestan plain. The vision is set there, and nothing in the palace remains relates to it specifically.

corrections: The old entry dated the palace 'c. 450 BCE' and called it a '5th century BCE' complex. The palace was built under Darius I (522-486 BCE), and the apadana burned under Artaxerxes I and was rebuilt by Artaxerxes II (A2Sa). About 450 BCE is not a construction date.

The old entry said the palace features 'elaborate reliefs' and 'intricate architectural details' generically. The concrete surviving decoration is moulded glazed-brick friezes (the archers, lions, griffins) and giant limestone bull capitals (Louvre AOD 488, AOD 1).

The old entry said 'Script: N/A'. The palace carries trilingual royal inscriptions in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, including the Artaxerxes II column-base text that dates the fire and the rebuilding.

The old entry called it the 'palace where Esther and Daniel narratives occur' as fact. Esther and Nehemiah are set at the Susa palace. Daniel 8 is a vision set 'at Shushan in the palace' in Elam. No find at Susa names any of them, and the correspondences are of setting.
The old entry tied Daniel 9 ('seventy weeks') to Susa. Daniel 9 is set in 'the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus' (Dan 9:1) and does not mention Susa.

The old entry gave the discovery simply as '1884+'. The first systematic excavation of the palace was by Marcel and Jane Dieulafoy for the Louvre (1884-1886). The palace was later re-excavated by Jean Perrot, whose final publication appeared in 2013.

overview: Tall el-Hammam is a large two-tiered tell in the southern Jordan Valley north-east of the Dead Sea, excavated since 2005 by a team led by Steven Collins. The excavators describe a fortified city occupied from the Chalcolithic through the Middle Bronze Age, ended by a thick burned destruction layer and followed by a long gap in regional settlement.

In 2021 T. Bunch and 20 co-authors argued in Scientific Reports that a Tunguska-size cosmic airburst caused the destruction, citing shocked quartz, melted pottery and mudbrick, spherules and metal grains, and linked it to the Sodom story. S. J. Jaret and R. S. Harris (Sci. Rep. 12, 2022) rebutted the mineralogy and geochemistry; M. Boslough and A. Bruno (Sci. Rep. 15, 2025) rebutted the Tunguska comparison. On 24 April 2025 the journal retracted the 2021 article.

What remains is the destruction layer itself - burned debris up to c. 1.5 m thick with high-temperature material - and the argument about what caused it and whether the city is Sodom. The retraction removes the published support for the airburst cause; it does not remove the destroyed city.
evidence: Destruction 'debris matrix' up to ~1.5 m thick across most of the tall, capped in places by a thin laminated 'blow-over layer' with plaster fragments, limestone spherules and charcoal (Bunch et al. 2021).
26 radiocarbon dates from the layer; 20 combine to 1661 ± 21 BCE (Bunch et al. 2021, OxCal 4.4/IntCal20).
Site size claimed: 36 ha fortified + ~30 ha lower settlement, described as >4x Tall Nimrin and >5x Jericho (Bunch et al. 2021).

Materials reported: shocked-quartz candidates, pottery with melted glassy surfaces, melted mudbrick, Fe/Si-rich spherules, metal grains (Bunch et al. 2021) - each of these interpretations is what Jaret & Harris (2022) contest.
The 2021 article received Author Corrections (22 Feb 2022; 22 May 2023) and a Matters Arising (25 March 2022) before its retraction (Scientific Reports article page).

Retraction note (Sci. Rep. 15:14291, online 24 Apr 2025): 'the claims that an airburst event destroyed the Middle Bronze Age city of Tall el-Hammam appear to not be sufficiently supported by the data in the Article.'
questions: Cause of the destruction: Bunch et al. (Sci. Rep. 11:18632, 2021) read the melted materials and shocked-quartz candidates as proof of a >Tunguska airburst above 2000 °C. Jaret & Harris ('No mineralogic or geochemical evidence of impact at Tall el-Hammam', Sci. Rep. 12:5189, 2022) contest the mineralogical and geochemical identifications and methods. Boslough & Bruno (Sci. Rep. 15:13869, 2025) show the Tunguska comparison inherited overestimates of temperature, wind speed and blast. Eleven of the original authors (LeCompte, Burleigh, Hermes, Wolbach, Kletetschka, Witwer, Howard, Moore, Kennett, West, Silvia) disagree with the retraction (retraction note). Other causes (warfare, fire, earthquake) are not tested in the retracted paper; the layer's cause is presently unestablished in the peer-reviewed record.

Is it Sodom? Bunch et al. (2021) note the 'ongoing debate as to whether Tall el-Hammam could be the biblical city of Sodom (Silvia and references therein)' and set it aside. The identification rests on geography - Gen 13:10-12 places Sodom in 'the kikkar of the Jordan', which the excavators equate with the plain north-east of the Dead Sea. Rival proposals place the Cities of the Plain south of the Dead Sea; their publications are not reviewed here. No site has produced an inscription naming Sodom.

Date vs. biblical chronology: a c. 1650 BCE destruction is later than the c. 2000 BCE date for Abraham often derived from the Masoretic numbers (1 Kgs 6:1 + Gen/Exod figures). Anyone equating the two must either move Abraham or reject the equation; the stratigraphy itself says nothing about Abraham.

biblical.tie: The 'kikkar of the Jordan' (the Jordan disk/plain) is where Lot settles and where Sodom lies. Tall el-Hammam is the largest Bronze Age tell in the plain north-east of the Dead Sea (Bunch et al. 2021). This is a geographic correspondence, not an identification.

A city in that plain ended in a thick burned layer with high-temperature material and was followed by a long regional abandonment (per the excavators). The biblical account of fire from heaven and smoke 'like a furnace' matches a fiery destruction in general terms; the cosmic-airburst explanation that tied them tightly has been retracted.

overview: A six-sided clay prism inscribed with the final edition of the annals of Sennacherib, king of Assyria (704-681 BCE): a prologue, reports of his first eight campaigns, and an account of building work on the armoury ('rear palace') at Nineveh. It was a foundation record, buried in the building's structure. Colonel Robert Taylor acquired it in 1830; the British Museum bought it from his widow in 1855. It is not from a documented excavation: its findspot (Nebi Yunus) rests on the report at purchase.

The third campaign (701 BCE) covers Syria-Palestine: the flight of Luli of Sidon, tribute from western kings, the capture of Sidqa of Ashkelon, the battle at Eltekeh against Egyptian and Kushite forces, the punishment of Ekron, and the campaign against 'Hezekiah the Judahite'. The prism claims 46 fortified Judahite towns taken, 200,150 people counted as spoil, and Hezekiah shut up in Jerusalem 'like a caged bird'; Judahite towns were handed to the kings of Ashdod, Ekron and Gaza; Hezekiah later sent 30 talents of gold, 800 talents of silver and other goods, plus his daughters and palace musicians, to Nineveh.

The same text survives on the Chicago (Oriental Institute) prism of 689 BCE, and a near-identical edition (RINAP text no. 23) on the Jerusalem Prism in the Israel Museum. Earlier editions of the same campaign account go back to the Rassam Cylinder of 700 BCE. None of them claims Jerusalem was taken.

text.quote: As for Hezekiah, the Jew, who did not submit to my yoke, 46 of his strong, walled cities, as well as the small cities in their neighborhood, which were without number... I besieged and took (those cities)... Himself, like a caged bird, I shut up in Jerusalem, his royal city.
text.translation: D. D. Luckenbill, Ancient Records of Assyria and Babylonia II (Chicago, 1927), §240, pp. 120-121 (translating the Chicago prism, which carries the same text as the Taylor Prism)

evidence: BM record: hexagonal clay prism, height 38.1 cm, BM 91032 / 1855,1003.1, dated by the eponym Bel-erumanni to 691 BCE, 'said to have been found at Nebi Yunus', purchased by Col. R. Taylor in 1830.
The Jerusalem passage is RINAP 3/1 Sennacherib 22 ii 37-iii 49 (the third campaign).
Names 'Hezekiah the Judahite' (Luckenbill: 'Hezekiah, the Jew') and Jerusalem as 'his royal city'.
Claims 46 strong walled cities and countless small towns taken; 200,150 people and livestock counted as spoil.
Hezekiah 'like a caged bird' shut up in Jerusalem; earthworks thrown up against him; those leaving the city gate turned back.
Tribute: 30 talents of gold and 800 talents of silver, plus precious stones, ivory furniture, his daughters, palace women and musicians, sent after the king to Nineveh.
Padi of Ekron, handed to Hezekiah by Ekron's rebels, is brought out of Jerusalem and restored.
There is no claim that Jerusalem was entered or taken, and no account of the Assyrian army's withdrawal.
questions: Who won in 701? P. S. Evans (Bible and Interpretation, Feb 2025) argues both accounts can be read as victories because the two sides had different war aims: the Assyrian side achieved destroyed towns (Evans cites the destruction of Lachish) and tribute, while 2 Kings 18-19 / Isaiah 36-37 stress that Jerusalem stood and Hezekiah kept his throne. The prism's own silence about capturing the city, which a royal annal would normally claim, is the concrete evidence both readings rest on.

Tribute figures differ: the prism says 30 talents of gold and 800 of silver; 2 Kgs 18:14 says 30 talents of gold and 300 of silver. The gold matches exactly; the silver does not, and the sources give no reason. Any explanation (different talent standards, inclusion of other goods) is conjecture.

Sequence differs: in 2 Kgs 18:14-16 Hezekiah pays at Lachish before the envoys come to Jerusalem; the prism places the payment after the campaign, sent to Nineveh. The sources are silent on how to reconcile the order.

Which edition is earlier, text 22 (Chicago/Taylor) or text 23 (Jerusalem Prism)? Grayson and Novotny (RINAP 3/1, 2012) note the month of the Jerusalem Prism is lost; its shorter building report (one wing of the armoury instead of two) suggests it may be the earlier of the two.

biblical.tie: 'Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fenced cities of Judah, and took them' corresponds to the prism's 46 walled cities taken.
Hezekiah's payment of 30 talents of gold corresponds exactly to the prism's gold figure; the silver differs (300 in Kings vs 800 on the prism).

Jerusalem besieged but not taken: the prism confines Hezekiah in the city and never claims its capture. The Bible's account of the Assyrian withdrawal (2 Kgs 19:35-36) has no counterpart in the prism, which is silent on how the campaign ended.

Chronicles' account of Sennacherib encamping against fenced cities and Hezekiah's defensive works; the prism's 'earthworks' against Jerusalem and the report that his auxiliary troops deserted him are the Assyrian side of the same siege.

sites.name: Judahite Shrine at Tel Arad
sites.subtitle: Shrine inside a Judahite fortress in the Beersheba-Arad valley · 8th century BCE (latest dating)
sites.date: 8th century BCE. The 2020 residue study dates the shrine to c. 750-715 BCE (Stratum X); Aharoni's original scheme gave it a longer life starting earlier.
sites.date_basis: Stratigraphy inside the Iron Age fortress sequence (Aharoni's excavation; revised by Herzog 2002). Arad inscriptions 102-103 came from the shrine courtyard in Locus 394, Stratum X (Lemaire 2024, citing Aharoni 1981). The c. 750-715 BCE range is the Tel Aviv University / Israel Museum dating reported for the 2020 study.

discovery.when: First excavation season 1962; Aharoni's excavation of the fortress mound continued through the 1960s
discovery.who: Yohanan Aharoni (excavation); residue study by Eran Arie (Israel Museum), Baruch Rosen and Dvory Namdar (2020)
discovery.where: Fortress mound of Tel Arad, Beersheba-Arad valley, southern Israel

sites.location: Remains at Tel Arad. The museum repository of the two altars is not stated in the sources cited here.

physical.material: Two limestone monoliths interpreted as altars
physical.dimensions: Smaller altar c. 40 cm high, top c. 20 x 20 cm; larger altar c. 50 cm high, top c. 30 x 30 cm (as reported in the 2020 release)

overview: Yohanan Aharoni's excavation of the Tel Arad fortress mound, which began in 1962, uncovered a small shrine inside the Iron Age Judahite fortress. It had a courtyard with a sacrificial altar, and two limestone monoliths interpreted as incense altars were found inside it. Aharoni's results appeared in preliminary form (e.g. Biblical Archaeologist 1968; Arad Inscriptions 1981). Ze'ev Herzog's 2002 interim report in Tel Aviv revised the stratigraphy of the fortress sequence.

In 2020 Eran Arie, Baruch Rosen and Dvory Namdar published organic residue analyses of dark material on the tops of the two altars. On the smaller altar they found cannabinoids (THC, CBD, CBN) with residue attributed to animal dung, which they read as cannabis burnt at low heat. On the larger altar they found frankincense markers (boswellic acid, norursatriene) with animal fat.

The Arad ostraca come from the same fortress. One, ostracon 18, has the phrase byt yhwh, 'house/temple of YHWH' (line 9), but it dates to about 597 BCE, when the Arad shrine was already out of use. Lemaire (2024), following Aharoni (1981), takes it to mean the Jerusalem temple.

text.quote: Arad ostracon 18, line 9, contains the phrase byt yhwh, 'the house (temple) of YHWH', in a letter whose context is otherwise unclear; the ostracon is dated to early 597 BCE.
text.translation: Paraphrase based on the reading and dating in Lemaire, Jerusalem Journal of Archaeology 7 (2024): 50, citing Aharoni, Arad Inscriptions (1981): 37. No public-domain translation exists (found 1960s).

evidence: Two limestone monoliths interpreted as altars were found in the shrine, each with dark residue on its upper surface (Arie, Rosen and Namdar 2020, abstract).
Smaller altar: Delta9-THC, CBD and CBN plus terpenes, and residue attributed to animal dung (same).
Larger altar: boswellic acid and norursatriene (frankincense markers), plus animal-fat compounds (same).
Two unrelated laboratories ran the analyses using similar extraction methods (same).
Arad inscriptions 102 and 103, plates with two incised signs starting with qoph, came from the shrine courtyard near the sacrificial altar, Locus 394, Stratum X (Lemaire 2024: 54).
Arad inscription 104 is a vessel inscribed qdsh, 'holy' (Lemaire 2024: 52-53, citing Aharoni 1981: 118).
Ostraca 50-52 were found in the sanctuary and bear single personal names. The Meremoth name is on no. 50, and a Pashhur name is on no. 54 (Lemaire 2024: 56, citing Aharoni 1981: 85).
Ostracon 18 names byt yhwh (line 9) and dates to early 597 BCE, after the shrine went out of use (Lemaire 2024: 50).
questions: How long was the shrine in use? Aharoni ('Arad: Its Inscriptions and Temple', Biblical Archaeologist 31, 1968) placed it in a long sequence of fortress strata. Herzog's interim report (Tel Aviv 29, 2002) re-dated the fortress strata, and the 2020 residue study (Arie, Rosen and Namdar) treats the altars as 8th-century, reported as c. 750-715 BCE. Neither Aharoni 1968 nor Herzog 2002 has been reviewed in full for this entry, so their exact stratum assignments for the shrine are not restated here.

What was the cannabis for? The chemistry shows cannabis burnt on the smaller altar. That its use was psychoactive and 'central to the cultic rituals' is the lead author's interpretation (Arie, quoted in the 2020 release), not something the residue itself shows.

Which temple is 'the house of YHWH' in ostracon 18? Aharoni (1981: 37) and Lemaire (2024: 50) read it as the Jerusalem temple, because the Arad shrine no longer existed in 597 BCE. The letter's own context does not name a place.

What do the qoph plates (nos. 102-103) say? Readings compared by Lemaire (2024: 54): q(d)sh 'holy' (Cross 1979); qrbn 'offering' (Aharoni's later view); q(dsh) k(hnm) 'holy to the priests' (Herzog et al. 1984; Herzog 2002; Maeir). The second sign is ambiguous.

biblical.tie: Hezekiah removes the high places and altars outside Jerusalem. An 8th-century YHWH shrine in a royal Judahite fortress is the kind of place this describes. Whether its going out of use was caused by this reform is an inference; the ostraca do not say.
Josiah defiles the high places 'from Geba to Beersheba'. Arad lies inside that range.
The sacred incense includes frankincense (levonah). Frankincense was found on the larger altar. Cannabis appears in no biblical incense recipe.
Frankincense 'from Sheba' offered to YHWH. The Arad residue shows frankincense, an imported South Arabian resin, burnt in a Judahite shrine.

corrections: Descriptions of Arad as a 'Solomonic' (10th-century) temple do not match the latest dating. The 2020 study treats the altars as 8th-century, reported as c. 750-715 BCE.

sites.name: Tel Dan Stele
sites.subtitle: Old Aramaic victory stele fragments naming the "House of David" · 9th century BCE
sites.date: 9th century BCE (Iron Age II); the kings named in the restored text point to c. 841 BCE or shortly after
sites.date_basis: No date survives on the stone and the king who set it up is not named in the preserved text. The date rests on (1) letter forms (Old Aramaic in the Phoenician-derived alphabet, compared with dated 9th-century inscriptions); (2) the find contexts in Area A at Tel Dan, all below/against Iron Age gate architecture; and (3) the restored royal names on fragment B ("...rm son of" / "...yhw son of"), which the editors restored as Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah, both of whom 2 Kings 9 places in the same year. Point (3) depends on the editors' placement of fragment B beside fragment A, which Langlois (IEJ 2024) argues must be abandoned.

discovery.when: Fragment A: 21 July 1993. Fragment B1: 20 June 1994. Fragment B2: 30 June 1994.
discovery.who: Tel Dan excavation of the Nelson Glueck School of Biblical Archaeology, Hebrew Union College-Jewish Institute of Religion, directed by Avraham Biran; fragments A and B2 spotted by the excavation surveyor Gila Cook
discovery.where: Area A, Tel Dan (northern Israel): A in the eastern part of the flagstone pavement in front of the outer gate; B1 in a debris layer 0.80 m above pavement level about 13 m to the northeast; B2 about 8 m north of B1 at the foot of a wall bordering the pavement

sites.location: The Israel Museum, Jerusalem (permanent display; Israel Antiquities Authority numbers 1993-3162 and 1996-125). Lent to the Jewish Museum, New York, 5 Dec 2024 - 5 Jan 2025, and to the Museum of the Bible, Washington DC, 30 Aug - 3 Nov 2025.

physical.material: Basalt
physical.dimensions: Joined fragments H 34 cm, W 32 cm (Israel Museum record). Langlois (2024) notes the original stele was under 50 cm wide.
physical.script: Old Aramaic alphabet (Phoenician-type letter forms) with word dividers

overview: Three inscribed basalt fragments found in the Iron Age gate area (Area A) at Tel Dan. The large fragment A was spotted on 21 July 1993 lying in the flagstone pavement in front of the outer gate; its tip is visible in photographs taken a year earlier. Two smaller pieces, B1 and B2, which physically join each other, were found in June 1994 in debris and at the foot of a wall nearby. Avraham Biran and Joseph Naveh published A in Israel Exploration Journal 43 (1993) and B1+B2 in IEJ 45 (1995), and glued the three together in the arrangement still shown in the museum.

The text is a first-person royal victory inscription in Old Aramaic. The speaker says his father 'lay down' (died), that the king of Israel had earlier entered his father's land, that the god Hadad made him king and went before him, and that he killed kings and chariotry. Fragment A preserves the phrases mlk yśrʾl, 'king of Israel' (line 8), and bytdwd, 'House of David' (line 9). Fragment B preserves the ends of two royal names followed by 'son of' ('...rm br' and '...yhw br'), which the editors restored as [Jeho]ram son of [Ahab] and [Ahaz]iahu son of [Jehoram]. The speaker's own name does not survive; the attribution to Hazael of Damascus is an inference from the content.

In 2024 Michael Langlois (University of Strasbourg), using new RTI imaging, 3D scanning and a letter-by-letter chart, argued that fragment A and fragments B1+B2 were cut with two different ductus (letter-stroke habits) and different line spacing, that A and B1 have no real physical join, and that the editors' side-by-side placement 'must be abandoned.' The words 'king of Israel' and 'House of David' on fragment A are not affected by this; the restored pairing of those titles with the name fragments on B is.

text.quote: Content of the preserved lines (editors' 1995 arrangement): the speaker's father died; the king of Israel had previously entered his father's land; Hadad made the speaker king and went before him; he killed [seve]nty kings with thousands of chariots and horsemen; '...]rm son of [...' king of Israel; '...]yhw son of [...' ... of bytdwd ('House of David'); he laid waste their land; a broken reference to someone ruling over Israel; and a siege.
text.translation: Paraphrase of the Old Aramaic text as published by Biran and Naveh, IEJ 43 (1993) 81-98 and IEJ 45 (1995) 1-18; no public-domain translation exists (the text was found in 1993). Aramaic words mlk yśrʾl (l. 8) and bytdwd (l. 9) as cited by Langlois, IEJ 74/2 (2024) 59.

evidence: Fragment A was found 21 July 1993 in the eastern part of the flagstone pavement before the outer gate in Area A; the pavement had been exposed from 1992 and the fragment's tip shows in earlier photographs (Langlois 2024: 60, citing Biran and Naveh 1993: 81).

Fragment B1 was found 20 June 1994 in debris 0.80 m above the pavement, c. 13 m northeast of A; B2 on 30 June 1994, c. 8 m north, at the foot of a wall (Langlois 2024: 60, citing Biran and Naveh 1995: 2, 5).
The stone is basalt; the joined fragments measure H 34 x W 32 cm (Israel Museum record).
Line 8 of fragment A reads mlk yśrʾl, 'king of Israel'; line 9 reads bytdwd, 'House of David', written as one word string.
Fragment B preserves only the ends of two names followed by br, 'son of'; the full names Joram/Jehoram and Ahaziah are editorial restorations.

B1 and B2 join physically. A and B1 do not: the editors wrote that 'Fragments A and B cannot be joined in an obvious, unequivocal way' (Biran and Naveh 1995: 11, quoted by Langlois 2024: 62), and a restorer who glued them told the 2024 conference they 'do not really join' (Langlois 2024: 63).

Every beth on A has a rounded one-stroke descender; every beth on B1+B2 has two straight strokes meeting at an elbow; lamed, kaph and resh differ in the same A-versus-B split (Langlois 2024: 65-70, RTI close-ups).
Lines on A slope downward and are corrected over the first 7-8 lines; lines on B1+B2 are level and evenly spaced, with spacing that does not match A (Langlois 2024: 70-71).

Paleomagnetic measurement (Yoav Vaknin, reported by Langlois 2024: 72, 75 as personal communication) found A and B1 have the same magnetic orientation, i.e. cut from the same block in the same orientation.
The king who set up the stele is not named in any preserved line.
questions: Placement of the fragments. Biran and Naveh (IEJ 45, 1995) set B1+B2 beside A so that the name endings on B run into 'king of Israel' and 'House of David' on A, a placement they reached by testing and by a join on the back 'corroborated by three experienced restorers.' Langlois (IEJ 74/2, 2024: 59-79) reads A and B as different hands or a changed hand, because every beth, lamed, kaph and resh shows a systematic A-vs-B difference in ductus and the line slope/spacing differs, and concludes B 'does not continue the lines started by frag. A'. Galil (Palestine Exploration Quarterly 133, 2001: 16-21) had earlier put A below B on literary grounds (as reported by Langlois 2024: 75 n. 18). Our reading: if Langlois is right, the stone still says 'king of Israel' and 'House of David', but the restored pairing 'Joram ... king of Israel' / 'Ahaziah ... House of David' is no longer supported by the stone.

Who killed Joram and Ahaziah. The editors' restoration has the Aramaean king claim both deaths ('I killed'). 2 Kings 9:24, 27 has Jehu kill both. Schniedewind (BASOR 302, 1996: 75-90) reads the two accounts together as Jehu acting in collusion with Hazael. The Jewish Museum's 2024 label states the text 'is not consistent with the biblical account of 2 Kings 9.' This dispute rests entirely on the restored names, and so on the placement question above.

Authenticity of the find circumstances. Elgvin (Warrior, King, Servant, Savior, 2022: 14 n. 24, as cited by Langlois 2024: 75) raised the possibility that the fragments are modern forgeries, given the timing and separate findspots. Langlois (2024: 75) answers that the difference in ductus 'is not in itself evidence of forgery' and that the discovery circumstances need further research; the fragment A tip visible in photographs a year before its discovery bears on this.

Author of the stele. Hazael of Damascus is the usual attribution (Schniedewind 1996; the Jewish Museum label says 'Hazael's name is not mentioned in the inscription'). Other Damascene kings (Ben-Hadad/Bar-Hadad) have been proposed; the preserved text names only the god Hadad, the speaker's unnamed father, and the kingdoms.

Whether bytdwd means 'House of David' (a dynasty named after a founder, like 'House of Omri' for Israel in Assyrian texts) or a place-name ('Beth-David'), and whether the one-word spelling matters: Athas (The Tel Dan Inscription, JSOT Sup 360, 2003) reappraised the reading; the arguments were not re-verified for this entry.

biblical.tie: Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah at war with Hazael at Ramoth-gilead, then both killed in Jehu's coup. The stele's restored names match these two kings, but in the stele the Aramaean king claims the killings, while Kings credits Jehu. The name match depends on the contested fragment placement.

Hazael takes the throne of Damascus after Ben-Hadad's death. The stele's speaker says his father 'lay down' and that Hadad made him king; if the speaker is Hazael, this is his own presentation of the succession (our reading).
Hazael 'cut Israel short' and struck Israel's territory in Jehu's days; the stele is an Aramaean boast of victories over Israel from the same arena (inference: the author is not named).
Ben-Hadad of Damascus strikes Dan: the town where the stele was set up was contested between Aram and Israel.
'House of David' as the name of the Judahite royal line. The stele uses bytdwd as the name of a kingdom/dynasty alongside 'king of Israel'; it does not mention David as an individual.

corrections: Old entry files it under 'United Monarchy Period'. The stele is 9th century BCE, a century and more after the United Monarchy; the kingdoms named are Israel and bytdwd as separate states.

Old entry presents the restored line '[Jo]ram son of [Ahab] ... [Ahaz]iahu son of [Jehoram kin]g of the House of David' as the inscription. The stone preserves only '...rm son of' and '...yhw son of' on fragment B; the names are restorations, and their pairing with 'king of Israel' / 'House of David' on fragment A depends on a placement that the editors themselves said has no unequivocal join and that Langlois (IEJ 2024) argues is wrong.
Old entry lists 'Erected by Hazael' as settled. The preserved text does not name its author (Jewish Museum label, 2024: 'Hazael's name is not mentioned in the inscription').
Old entry dimensions 'Fragments up to 32 cm x 22 cm'. The Israel Museum record gives the joined fragments as H 34 x W 32 cm.

Old entry says it 'confirms David as a historical figure'. The stone contains the phrase bytdwd naming a kingdom/dynasty; it does not refer to David as an individual. What it attests is a 9th-century Aramaean scribe's use of that name for Judah or its dynasty.
Old entry omits that the stele's claim ('I killed') conflicts with 2 Kings 9:24, 27, where Jehu kills Joram and Ahaziah.

Old entry says 'three fragments... discovered in 1993 and 1994' without dates or places; fragment A lay in the gate pavement (seen 21 July 1993), B1 in debris c. 13 m to the northeast and B2 c. 8 m north of B1 at the foot of a wall (June 1994).

sites.name: Concealed standing stone at Tel 'Eton
sites.subtitle: Household standing stone laid down and built into a platform before the Assyrian destruction · late 8th century BCE
sites.date: Stone erected in the building's first phase (the building itself dated late 11th-10th century BCE by radiocarbon); laid down and embedded in a platform at an undetermined time before the Assyrian destruction of the late 8th century BCE
sites.date_basis: Stratigraphy: the platform (F1489) holding the laid-down stone was in use when Building 101 was destroyed, and a cooking pot lay on top of it (Faust 2026: 45). The destruction layer is attributed by the excavator to the Assyrian army in the late 8th century BCE. Faust states: 'how long before the destruction did the dismantling take place, we cannot, at this stage, determine' (2026: 45), and notes radiocarbon is imprecise for the late 8th century because of the Hallstatt plateau (2026: n. 14). The building's founding date rests on 14C samples from a foundation deposit and floor make-up (Faust and Sapir, Radiocarbon 60, 2018).

discovery.when: Stone layer and the larger fragment exposed in the 2014 season; rest of Room 101B and the second fragment in 2015
discovery.who: Tel 'Eton Archaeological Project, Bar-Ilan University, directed by Avraham Faust
discovery.where: Room 101B (the largest room, 16.7 sq m, south-western part) of Building 101, the 'governor's residency', Area A on top of Tel 'Eton, south-eastern Judean Shephelah

sites.location: In situ as excavated (the large fragments were left in place; Faust 2026 figs. 6, 8); no museum record located

physical.material: Worked stone (lithology not given in the article)
physical.dimensions: ca. 140 x 70 x 36 cm, ca. 750 kg; broken into two fragments that match in dimension and indentation (Faust 2026: 38)

overview: Building 101 at Tel 'Eton is a large four-space ("four-room") house on the summit of the mound, excavated over ten seasons (2006-2015) and sealed under a massive late 8th century BCE destruction layer. The excavators sifted all sediment and excavated much of the floor on a 20 x 20 cm grid, which let them reconstruct the use of every room on the eve of destruction.

In Room 101B, the largest and one of the innermost rooms, the 2014 season found a dense layer of small-to-medium stones (F1489) with one exceptionally large worked stone in it. In 2015 the layer turned out to be a platform covering only the south-western part of the room, not collapse. The large stone (in two pieces, F1476) was the only worked stone in it, far larger than the rest, and it lay on a continuous foundation (F1387) that crosses the room, the only place in the building where such a foundation crosses a room rather than continuing a wall.

Avraham Faust (Jerusalem Journal of Archaeology 9, 2026) reads the stone as a massebah that originally stood on that foundation near wall F1381, positioned so that it was visible from the building's entrance and much of the courtyard, and that was later laid down and 'concealed' inside a platform built around it. He proposes, as a plausible context, the cult changes attributed to Hezekiah (2 Kgs 18:4, 22), while stating that the date evidence allows but does not prove that link.
evidence: Building 101 was excavated over 10 seasons (2006-2015); walls stood 1.0-1.5 m high; hundreds of vessels were found in place (Faust 2026: 35).
Room 101B measures 16.7 sq m, the largest in the building (other rooms 3.8-13.5 sq m) (Faust 2026: 40, 42).
The stone layer F1489 covers only the south-western part of Room 101B; the floor beneath it held no complete vessels, unlike most other rooms (Faust 2026: 36-38).
The two large fragments F1476 are one worked stone, ca. 140 x 70 x 36 cm and ca. 750 kg; they are the only worked stones in the layer (Faust 2026: 38).
The large stone lies on continuous foundation F1387, which crosses the room; this is the only such crossing recorded in the building (Faust 2026: 38-39).
The platform was in use at the time of the Assyrian destruction; a cooking pot was found on top of it (Faust 2026: 45).
The excavator judges the break in the stone accidental, occurring when it was laid down (Faust 2026: n. 6).
Large chunks of wood were found below the platform; the wood was not identified (Faust 2026: n. 7).
A bench runs along the room's southern wall (Faust 2026: n. 3).
Radiocarbon samples from a foundation deposit and floor make-up place the building's earliest phase in the late 11th-10th century BCE (Faust and Sapir 2018 abstract).
questions: Whether the stone was a cult object at all. Faust (JJAR 9, 2026) reads it as a massebah because it had no practical function, sat on a foundation built for it, and was placed to be seen from the entrance. The article records no inscription, carving or offering deposit on the stone itself; the cultic reading rests on size, position and the special foundation (our observation from the published description).

When and by whom it was laid down. Faust (2026: 45) states only that it happened before the destruction and that how long before 'we cannot, at this stage, determine'; the link to Hezekiah is his proposal from the date range plus similar changes at Beersheba, Arad and Lachish. He himself says the Arad and Lachish evidence is 'not unequivocal' and that the changes 'need not have been contemporaneous' (2026: 48, 50).

Reform or war. Faust (2026: 49) reports that Edelman (2008), Fried (2002) and Handy (1988) explain dismantled cult places as consequences of, or precautions against, Sennacherib's 701 BCE campaign. Faust answers that at Beersheba and Tel 'Eton the dismantled items were built into structures that were in use when the Assyrians arrived, so the dismantling preceded the campaign. These opposing works have not been reviewed directly for this entry; their positions are given as Faust reports them.

Date of the building's first phase. Faust and Sapir (Radiocarbon 60, 2018) put its founding in the late 11th-10th century BCE from 14C and argue for an 'old-house effect'; their 2021 paper in Palestine Exploration Quarterly 153 is titled as a response to a Low Chronology critique of that date. The critique itself has not been located for this entry.

biblical.tie: Hezekiah 'removed the high places, and brake the images (Hebrew matstsebot, standing stones), and cut down the groves' (KJV). The find is a standing stone taken out of use before the late 8th-century destruction. Its date range fits Hezekiah's reign; nothing on the site names a king or a decree (Faust's proposal, labelled as such).

Standing stones broken throughout Judah and Benjamin after Hezekiah's Passover. At Tel 'Eton the stone was not smashed but laid down whole (the break judged accidental) and enclosed in a platform; that differs from 'brake the images in pieces' (KJV) in the text.

Standing stones set up by patriarchs and leaders as memorials; cited by BAS as background for what a massebah was. The Tel 'Eton stone stood inside a house, a domestic setting none of these texts describes.
Eglon, a Shephelah city of Judah. BAS calls Tel 'Eton 'likely biblical Eglon'; the 2026 article does not argue the identification, and no inscription from the site names it.

corrections: Press framing that the stone shows 'coordinated religious transformation across Judah' with Arad, Beersheba and Lachish goes further than the article. Faust says the Arad and Lachish evidence is 'not unequivocal' and that the changes 'need not have been contemporaneous'; he claims only that the pattern 'hints at a coordinating hand' (JJAR 9, 2026: 48, 50).

Headlines tying the stone directly to Hezekiah treat a proposal as a finding. The only fixed point is that it was laid down before the late 8th-century destruction; Faust writes that the dates 'are insufficient for us to suggest that the dismantling actually did take place at the time of Hezekiah' without further argument (2026: 45).

Descriptions of the stone as 'buried' or 'concealed' should be read with the article's own quotation marks: it was laid on its original foundation and a platform of small stones was built around it, not interred in a pit (2026: 38-40).

sites.name: Tel Shimron cultic megastructure and favissa
sites.subtitle: Middle Bronze Age monumental complex on the acropolis of a Jezreel Valley city · c. 1750-1650 BCE
sites.date: Middle Bronze Age; the monumental acropolis phase is contemporary with the domestic phase radiocarbon-dated to MB IIB (c. 1750-1650 BCE). Press reports round this to 'around 1800 BCE'.
sites.date_basis: Excavation report (Master and Martin, Hadashot Arkheologiyot 2021): radiocarbon evidence places the earlier domestic phase in Grid 92 in MB IIB (1750-1650 BCE) and the later in MB IIC (1650-1550 BCE); the pottery from the monumental Grid 33 is contemporary with Grid 92 (c. 1750 BCE). Radiocarbon sampling by E. Boaretto. The 'c. 1800 BCE' in BAS/Haaretz coverage is not the report's figure.

discovery.when: Tel Aviv University / Wheaton College excavation seasons from 2017 (reported for 2017 and 2019; favissa and megastructure announced Nov 2024)
discovery.who: Daniel M. Master (Wheaton College) and Mario A. S. Martin (Tel Aviv University), under IAA licenses G-43/2017 and G-24/2019
discovery.where: Grid 33, eastern acropolis of Tel Shimron, western Jezreel Valley, northern Israel

sites.location: In situ (Tel Shimron, Jezreel Valley); finds with the excavation / Israel Antiquities Authority
overview: Tel Shimron is a large mound on the northwestern edge of the Jezreel Valley, excavated since 2017 by Wheaton College and Tel Aviv University under Daniel Master and Mario Martin. Their published report for the 2017 and 2019 seasons describes, on the eastern acropolis (Grid 33), 'walls built of huge boulders' supporting a multi-story structure and large mudbrick walls running parallel to the slope, between which 'tens of thousands of bones and pottery fragments were recovered', including miniature vessels and several 'bowl with seven cups' vessels of a type known from the high place at Nahariya.

In November 2024 the excavators announced that these elements belonged to one monumental complex: a cone-shaped, white-chalk-surfaced structure rising nearly 20 feet (about 6 m) above the ancient mound, and an open-air favissa (a pit for discarded offerings) of over 700 square feet with thick mudbrick walls and two staircases. The favissa held about 40,000 animal bones (mainly cattle, sheep and goat, burned at high temperatures) and about 57,000 potsherds, with two bronze bull figurines and miniature jugs and bowls. A corbelled vault found in an earlier season is part of the same complex.

The site's ancient name is Shimron (Hebrew Bible, Masoretic Text) or Shim'on (Old Greek). A 2026 Tel Aviv article by Deirdre Fulton and Michelle Hunt argues that the form without /r/ is the older one. The monumental complex is Middle Bronze Age, centuries before any setting the book of Joshua describes.
evidence: Grid 33 (eastern acropolis): 'walls built of huge boulders supported a multi-story structure'; large mudbrick walls parallel to the slope; 'tens of thousands of bones and pottery fragments' between them (Master and Martin, HA 2021).
Grid 33 pottery includes miniature vessels and multiple 'bowl with seven cups' forms, compared by the excavators to the cultic high place at Nahariya (HA 2021).
Grid 92 domestic phases: radiocarbon places them in MB IIB (1750-1650 BCE) and MB IIC (1650-1550 BCE); Grid 33 pottery is contemporary with Grid 92 c. 1750 BCE (HA 2021).
Cone-shaped structure 'rising nearly 20 feet above the ancient mound', surfaced in white chalk (BAS 2025, reporting the excavators).

Favissa 'over 700-square-foot', originally unroofed, thick mudbrick walls, two staircases; about 40,000 animal bones (cattle, sheep, goat, burned at high temperature) and about 57,000 sherds; two bronze bull figurines; miniature jugs and bowls (BAS 2025).
A corbelled vault 'had been discovered in an earlier excavation season before the team realized that the entire complex was part of a single megastructure' (BAS 2025).
A hematite cylinder seal of North Syrian style, MB IIA-B, came from the first season (Rossberger, BASOR 385, 2021).

Later occupation on the mound includes an 11th-century BCE silo with whole vessels comparable to Megiddo VI, a Persian-Hellenistic village with an Antiochus III coin hoard abandoned in the mid-2nd c. BCE, and Roman houses with ritual baths (HA 2021).
No inscription naming the site has been reported from the excavation.
questions: Function of the complex. Daniel Master (quoted by BAS 2025) calls it 'very much an intentional, monumental thing designed to be seen from very far away'; the excavators read the burned animal bones, miniature vessels and seven-cup bowls as cultic (sacrificial) refuse. The full final publication of the megastructure was not located; the reading so far rests on the 2021 preliminary report and press interviews.
Date. The preliminary report ties the acropolis pottery to c. 1750 BCE via radiocarbon from Grid 92; press coverage gives 'around 1800 BCE'. No radiocarbon dates from the favissa itself were seen.

Name of the city. The Masoretic Text of Joshua 11:1, 12:20 and 19:15 reads Shimron; the Old Greek reads Shim'on. Fulton and Hunt (Tel Aviv 53:1, 2026: 103-116) argue from ancient Near Eastern sources and regional memory that the name lacked the /r/, and that the MT form is a scribal harmonisation with Shimron son of Issachar (Gen 46; Num 26; 1 Chr 7).

biblical.tie: Jabin king of Hazor 'sent to Jobab king of Madon, and to the king of Shimron, and to the king of Achshaph' (KJV). The excavated MB city is centuries earlier than this setting; the find shows Shimron as a major Bronze Age center, not the king of Joshua's day.
'The king of Shimronmeron, one' in the list of defeated kings (KJV).

sites.name: Tell es-Safi / Gath: the late 9th-century siege and destruction
sites.subtitle: Philistine city with a siege trench, wall breach and destruction layer attributed to Hazael of Aram · late 9th century BCE
sites.date: Destruction late 9th century BCE (c. 830 BCE in the excavators' popular accounts); siege trench cut in Iron Age IIA
sites.date_basis: Stratigraphy and pottery of the Iron IIA destruction level. Radiocarbon and ceramics for the trench fill (Ackermann, Bruins and Maeir, Geoarchaeology 20, 2005: 'Iron Age IIA (ca. 1000-800 B.C.E.)'). Namdar et al. (J. Archaeological Science 38, 2011) studied the 9th-century destruction layer. The link to Hazael is historical: 2 Kgs 12:17 is the only recorded conqueror of Gath in that period.

discovery.when: Bar-Ilan University excavations 1996 to July 2021 (the last large-scale season, per the final-report series)
discovery.who: Aren M. Maeir (director), Tell es-Safi/Gath Archaeological Project, Bar-Ilan University
discovery.where: Tell es-Safi (Tel Zafit), at the edge of the Shephelah and the coastal plain, central Israel

sites.location: In situ (site); finds with the project and the Israel Antiquities Authority (repository details not stated in the sources read)
overview: Tell es-Safi, identified with Philistine Gath, was excavated by a Bar-Ilan University team under Aren Maeir from 1996. The final-report series (Ägypten und Altes Testament 69, 105, 122) says the last large-scale season was in July 2021.

Aerial photographs showed a feature encircling the tell on three sides. Excavation showed it is a man-made trench over 2 km long, 5-6 m deep and more than 8 m wide, cut through bedrock, with the spoil dumped on one side as a berm. It was dug in Iron Age IIA and is read as part of a siege system (Ackermann, Bruins and Maeir 2005). A destruction level of the late 9th century BCE covers the Iron IIA city. Maeir (Vetus Testamentum 54, 2004) takes the siege system and destruction as the physical trace of Hazael of Aram's capture of Gath (2 Kgs 12:17), after which the site was of little importance until the end of the Iron Age. In 2021 the team reported a breach of about 30 feet in the city wall, read as the point where the attackers broke in.

The site's earlier Iron Age finds include a late Iron I/early Iron II inscription on a bowl sherd with two names, read 'lwt and wlt[...] (Maeir, Wimmer, Zukerman and Demsky, BASOR 351, 2008), and a 9th-century horned altar.
evidence: A trench over 2 km long, 5-6 m deep and more than 8 m wide, cut through bedrock around three sides of the tell, with the spoil heaped as a berm on one side (Ackermann, Bruins and Maeir 2005, abstract).
The trench fill has two phases, Iron Age IIA and Byzantine, separated by a soil-formation horizon. The digging is dated to Iron IIA (ca. 1000-800 BCE) (same).
A destruction level and siege system dated to the late 9th century BCE, after which the site is 'of little significance until the end of the Iron Age' (Maeir 2004, abstract).
A 9th-century BCE destruction layer studied with combined macro- and micro-archaeological methods (Namdar, Zukerman, Maeir, Katz and Cabanes 2011).
A breach of nearly 30 feet in the fortification, found in the 2021 season (BAS, 12 Aug 2021, reporting Maeir).

An inscribed sherd from a red-slipped, hand-burnished bowl in a clear late Iron I/early Iron II context, read as two personal names, 'lwt and wlt[...], judged by the editors to be Philistine names of Greek or Anatolian origin (Maeir et al. 2008, abstract).
questions: Was it Hazael? The dates fit: a late-9th-century destruction (Maeir 2004; Namdar et al. 2011), and 2 Kgs 12:17 records Hazael taking Gath in the reign of Jehoash of Judah. No inscription at the site names the attacker. The attribution rests on that date match plus the biblical notice.

Trench date: broad or narrow? The geoarchaeological study (Ackermann et al. 2005) dates the trench to Iron IIA, 'ca. 1000-800 B.C.E.', and calls it 'apparently' part of a siege system. Maeir (2004) ties the siege system specifically to the late-9th-century destruction. The two fit together, but the trench fill alone gives the broader range.

Amos 6:2. Maeir (VT 54, 2004) argues that Amos's 'go down to Gath of the Philistines' refers to cities destroyed by Hazael, and so dates the oracle soon after Gath's destruction, while it was fresh in memory. This is a reading of the biblical text in light of the dig, not something the stratigraphy itself shows.

The 'lwt / wlt inscription and Goliath. The editors (BASOR 351, 2008) discuss how these two names relate to the biblical Philistine names and do not claim either is Goliath. Popular 'Goliath inscription' headlines go beyond the article's own framing.
The horned altar: two horns or four? Eitam (Academia Letters, 2022) takes up the question (title only seen).

biblical.tie: 'Hazael king of Syria went up and fought against Gath and took it'. The late-9th-century siege works and destruction are the excavators' match to this verse.
'Then go down to Gath of the Philistines'. Maeir (2004) dates the oracle close to the city's destruction.

Goliath and the giants 'of Gath'. The site is Gath, but no find names Goliath. The Iron I/IIA 'lwt and wlt names are Philistine names that the editors discuss alongside the biblical onomasticon, not the same name.
Uzziah 'broke down the wall of Gath'. This comes after the Hazael destruction, when Maeir (2004) describes the site as of little significance.
'Tell it not in Gath'. Gath still serves as a name to conjure with in the late 8th century.

sites.name: Temple Mount Platform (Herodian enclosure)
sites.subtitle: Herod's enlarged temple esplanade in Jerusalem · begun c. 20/19 BCE, work continuing to the 60s CE
sites.date: Begun in Herod's 18th regnal year, about 20/19 BCE (Josephus, Ant. 15.380). Josephus says the temple works were 'finished' under the procurator Albinus, about 62–64 CE (Ant. 20.219). Excavation shows building and alterations around the enclosure well into the 1st century CE.
sites.date_basis: Josephus' regnal-year dating; coins and radiocarbon from excavations along the walls (e.g., Western Wall Tunnels 2018–2020, Levy and Weksler-Bdolah, 'Atiqot 119, 2025; Regev et al., PLOS ONE 2020 for Wilson's Arch).

discovery.when: Standing monument; measured by the Palestine Exploration Fund survey (Warren's shafts 1867–70); excavated along the south and south-west walls 1968–1978 and in many later campaigns
discovery.who: Charles Warren (PEF); Benjamin Mazar (1968–78); Israel Antiquities Authority teams (Reich, Baruch, Weksler-Bdolah, Uziel and others)
discovery.where: Eastern ridge of the Old City of Jerusalem

sites.location: In situ, Jerusalem

physical.material: Limestone ashlar retaining walls with drafted margins, earth and vault fill
physical.dimensions: PEF survey (1884): west wall 1,601 ft (c. 488 m); east wall 1,530 ft (c. 466 m); south wall 922 ft (c. 281 m); north wall 1,042 ft (c. 318 m); c. 35 acres

overview: The Temple Mount platform is the huge artificial esplanade Herod the Great built around the Jerusalem temple. His builders ran retaining walls down the slopes of the eastern ridge, filled and vaulted the space behind them, and levelled the top. The modern Haram al-Sharif keeps this outline on the west, south and east.

The Survey of Western Palestine's Jerusalem volume (1884, p. 119) measured the enclosure: south wall 922 ft, west wall 1,601 ft, east wall 1,530 ft, north wall 1,042 ft, about 35 acres. It is an irregular four-sided figure, not a square. Warren's shaft 90 ft east of the south-west angle exposed 24 courses, 87 ft 6 in of masonry, with the foundation course bedded on rock (SWP Jerusalem, p. 169–170).

Josephus describes the project (Whiston's translation, Ant. 15.11.3). Herod 'built a wall below, beginning at the bottom… and at the south side he laid rocks together, and bound them one to another with lead… and made it a level on the external upper surface'. He gives the circuit as four furlongs, 'each angle containing in length a furlong'. The excavated walls are longer than a furlong on the west and east. That is the difference between his figure and the measured outline. (Josephus quotations: W. Whiston, 1737, public domain.)
evidence: Irregular quadrilateral: W 1,601 ft, E 1,530 ft, S 922 ft, N 1,042 ft; about 35 acres (SWP Jerusalem 1884, p. 119 and in the section on Arab measurements).
At the south wall, 24 courses of 3 ft 6 in to 3 ft 9 in masonry, 87 ft 6 in in all, run down to bedrock 90 ft east of the south-west corner (SWP Jerusalem, pp. 169–170).
Buried courses have drafted margins with rough, unfinished bosses that were never exposed to weather. The joints are so tight a knife blade can scarcely go in (SWP Jerusalem, p. 170).
A pavement and drainage channel of the 1st century CE were found west of Warren's Gate, probably linked to a north-western Herodian gate (Onn & Weksler-Bdolah, 'Atiqot 106, 2025).

Plastered channels cut only in the Herodian courses of the western and southern walls are dated before 70 CE and read as runoff collectors feeding water installations (Szanton & Weksler-Bdolah, 'Atiqot 119, 2025).

In the Western Wall Tunnels, a Herodian dam wall (latter half of the 1st century BCE) was later topped by a paved triclinium building. A coin of Tiberius (17–25 CE) sealed under its fountain floor gives a terminus post quem of 17 CE for it ('Atiqot 119, 2025).
questions: When was the enclosure finished? Josephus dates the start to Herod's 18th year (Ant. 15.380) and says the work was 'finished' only under Albinus, with 18,000 workmen then laid off (Ant. 20.219). Regev, Uziel et al. (PLOS ONE 2020) date Wilson's Arch as begun under Herod and enlarged under the Roman procurators, including Pilate, within about 70 years. Levy ('Atiqot 119, 2025) moves the triclinium building beside the wall from Herod's reign to after 17 CE. Together these show construction going on around the platform through the first half of the 1st century CE.

The north edge: the SWP (1884, p. 119) records a 30 ft rock scarp forming 350 ft of the north boundary at the north-west. How far north the Herodian platform ran, and how it met the Antonia fortress, is not settled by the sources cited here. Patrich (The Jerusalem Temple and the Temple Mount, Mohr Siebeck 2024) re-evaluates the literary and archaeological evidence for the enclosure's development. Only the publisher's abstract is cited here, so his conclusions are not stated.

biblical.tie: 'Forty-six years was this temple in building.' Counted from Herod's 18th year (c. 20/19 BCE), 46 years lands about 27/28 CE. The excavated evidence for work continuing through the 1st century CE fits a project still under way then.

'What manner of stones and what buildings!' The disciples point out the great stones. The platform walls are built of those very large drafted ashlars (Josephus Ant. 15.392 gives stones of 25 × 8 × 12 cubits).
The cleansing of the temple took place in the outer courts that stood on this platform. The platform is the ground of the event; nothing excavated identifies the spot.
'Solomon's Porch/Colonnade' on the east. Josephus (Ant. 20.221) describes the eastern cloisters in the deep valley, built of stones twenty cubits long.
