corrections: Old dimensions 'approximately 150 meters by 50 meters' / '150 m long, 50 m high' are wrong. The enclosure's sides are about 488, 466, 281 and 318 m (SWP 1884, p. 119), covering about 35 acres.

Old claim that the platform 'has been under continuous construction and expansion for centuries' mixes periods. The Herodian enclosure was begun c. 20/19 BCE and, per Josephus, finished in the 60s CE. Later Islamic and other work on top is a separate matter.

Old 'discovery of the Temple Mount Platform' framing is wrong. It is a standing monument. What has been 'discovered' is its buried courses, gates, streets and dating evidence through excavation (Warren 1867–70; Mazar 1968–78; IAA work to the present).

Old 'Mark 13 (Jesus on the Mount of Olives)' and 'Luke 21 (signs of the end)' are loose links. The relevant verses are Mark 13:1–2 / Luke 21:5–6, where the disciples admire the stones. John 2:20 (46 years in building) is the verse that bears directly on the construction and was missing.

Old 'Massive platform Jesus walked on' is a reasonable inference from the Gospels, which place Jesus teaching in the temple courts (e.g., John 10:23). But the platform's full extent was still under construction in his day (see questions).

updates.what: Onn & Weksler-Bdolah publish a 1st-century CE pavement and drain at Warren's Gate, probably the approach to a north-western Herodian gate.

'Atiqot 119 publishes the 2018–2020 Western Wall Tunnels excavation (a Herodian dam wall and a triclinium building after 17 CE), its coins, and a new pre-70 CE date for the gutter-like channels on the Herodian walls.
Patrich's collected study of the Temple and Temple Mount appears (Mohr Siebeck).

sites.name: Three previously unknown Assyrian kings (Edmonds and Frahm 2026)
aka: Assur-uballit, Tiglath-pileser and Shalmaneser missing from the Assyrian King List
sites.subtitle: Kings erased from the Assyrian King List, reconstructed from a grant, a ritual text and a recut stela · 10th-8th century BCE
sites.date: Proposed reigns: Assur-uballit c. 913-912 BCE; Tiglath-pileser c. 763-762 BCE; Shalmaneser c. 747-745 BCE (Edmonds and Frahm 2026)
sites.date_basis: Absolute dates hang on the Assyrian Eponym Chronicle, anchored by the solar eclipse it records in the eponymy of Bur-Saggile (763 BCE; identified with the eclipse of 15 June 763 BCE in the ORACC edition notes). The Rm 75 grant is dated by eponym to 762 BCE (Yale report). The other two reigns are placed by the authors from the political context; the specific reasoning was not read in the JCS article itself.

discovery.when: Argument published June 2026 (JCS 78); the objects themselves are old finds: the Tell Abta stela was found in 1894; Rm 75 is a British Museum tablet; VAT 10136 is a Berlin tablet
discovery.who: Alexander Johannes Edmonds (University of Münster) and Eckart Frahm (Yale University)
discovery.where: Tell Abta (Dur-Bel-Harran-belu-usur) on the Wadi Tharthar for the stela; Nineveh for Rm 75 (per BAS); VAT 10136 find-spot not given in the sources read

sites.location: Tell Abta stela: Istanbul Archaeological Museums, Ist 01326 (ORACC RIAo). Rm 75: British Museum (Yale News). VAT 10136: Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin (by the VAT prefix; no museum record seen).

physical.material: Tell Abta stela: stone (ORACC catalogue); 'alabaster' per Luckenbill 1926. Rm 75 and VAT 10136: clay tablets

overview: In Journal of Cuneiform Studies 78 (2026) Alexander Edmonds and Eckart Frahm argue that three men ruled Assyria briefly but were left out of the Assyrian King List (AKL). No new excavation is involved; the case is built from long-known texts and objects, read together with the Eponym Chronicle.

The three: (1) an Assur-uballit, c. 913-912 BCE, named in a text (VAT 10136) that lists rulers who restored a silver ritual vessel for beer dedicated to the god Ashur; (2) a Tiglath-pileser, c. 763-762 BCE, in whose name a royal land grant (British Museum Rm 75) is dated to 762 BCE, during the years the Eponym Chronicle records 'rebellion in the Inner City (Ashur)'; (3) a Shalmaneser, c. 747-745 BCE, whose name, the authors argue, is the one erased on the Tell Abta stela of the palace herald Bel-Harran-belu-usur and replaced by the name of Tiglath-pileser III.

The Tell Abta stela is the most concrete piece. Its line 9 now reads 'Bel-Harran-belu-usur, the palace herald of Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria', with the royal name cut over an erasure. Since Unger (1917) the erased name has been read as Shalmaneser IV (782-773 BCE). Edmonds and Frahm assign it instead to a later, unlisted Shalmaneser just before Tiglath-pileser III, citing among other things the official's robe, which BAS reports they date to the mid-8th century.

text.quote: me, Bél-harran-bél-usur, the major-domo of Tiglath-pileser (written over Shalmaneser), king of Assyria, who fears the great gods
text.translation: Luckenbill, Ancient Records of Assyria and Babylonia I (1926), §824, p. 295 (Tell Abta stela)

evidence: Tell Abta stela, Ist 01326, line 9: 'Bel-Harran-belu-usur, the palace herald of Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria'; the signs of the royal name are marked damaged in the ORACC transliteration, and the king's name is cut over an erased Shalmaneser (ORACC RIAo Shalmaneser IV 2; Luckenbill 1926 §824).
The stela's upper part carries divine symbols and a standing human figure in profile, most likely the herald himself (ORACC RIAo introduction).

In the stela the herald, not the king, founds the city of Dur-Bel-Harran-belu-usur, builds its temple and grants it freedom from grain and straw taxes and corvée (ORACC translation lines 9-22; Luckenbill §§824-826).
Eponym Chronicle 763 BCE (Bur-Saggile): 'rebellion in the Inner City; in the month of Simanu an eclipse of the sun took place'; 762 BCE: 'rebellion in the Inner City' (ORACC SAAo Q007771).
Eponym Chronicle 746 BCE: 'rebellion in Kalhu'; 745 BCE: 'in the month of Ayyaru, [day] 13, Tiglath-pileser took the throne' (ORACC SAAo Q007771).
Eponym Chronicle 741 BCE lists Bel-Harran-belu-usur, palace herald, as eponym; ORACC notes he had been replaced as herald by 751 and reinstated under Tiglath-pileser III.

Rm 75 obverse: fragment of a royal land grant dated 762 BCE issued in the name of a Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria (Yale News caption). The authors note the grant 'was likely not made in the name of Adad-nerari III, as the name of that king is written differently in other texts' (Yale News).
VAT 10136: a text listing rulers who restored a silver beer vessel for Ashur, naming an Assur-uballit with implied royal status (Yale News; BAS).
questions: Whose name was erased on the Tell Abta stela. Unger (1917, as reported by Luckenbill 1926 §824 n.) and the RIMA 3 / ORACC edition (A.0.105.2, filed under Shalmaneser IV, 782-773 BCE) read it as Shalmaneser IV, with Bel-Harran-belu-usur serving him first and Tiglath-pileser III later. Edmonds and Frahm (JCS 78, 2026) read it as an otherwise unknown Shalmaneser of c. 747-745 BCE; BAS reports their evidence includes the figure's 'tartan' robe, which they date to the mid-8th century. The eponym entries (herald removed by 751, reinstated 741) are compatible with either reading; the robe dating is the new element. The JCS text has not been reviewed for this entry.

Whether a single dated grant makes a king. The Tiglath-pileser of 763-762 rests on Rm 75 plus the Eponym Chronicle's two years of 'rebellion in the Inner City'. The chronicle entries do not name the rebel. The case is cumulative ('textual, chronological, archaeological, and artistic evidence', BAS); what else the authors bring was not seen here.

The Assur-uballit of c. 913-912 depends on VAT 10136 naming him in a list of restorers of a cult vessel; whether that list implies he was king (BAS: 'implied royal status') or a crown prince is the point to test against the JCS text.

biblical.tie: Pul / Tiglath-pileser III, who took Menahem's tribute and later deported Galileans and Transjordanians. The Tell Abta stela shows his name cut in over a predecessor's; if Edmonds and Frahm are right, a Shalmaneser held the throne in the two years before Tiglath-pileser's accession (Ayyaru 745 BCE). It does not change the date of that accession, which is fixed by the Eponym Chronicle.

Shalmaneser king of Assyria who besieged Samaria is Shalmaneser V (727-722 BCE), the son of Tiglath-pileser III. The proposed Shalmaneser of 747-745 is a different, earlier man; the two should not be confused.

Israel under Jeroboam II, Zechariah and Shallum (mid-8th century) coincides with the Assyrian rebellions of 763-759 and 746 in the Eponym Chronicle. The Bible does not mention Assyrian interventions in those years; this is a chronological overlap only.

corrections: Headlines saying three kings were 'discovered' or 'uncovered' imply new finds. The evidence is long-known: the Tell Abta stela was found in 1894 and published by Scheil (1894) and Unger (1917), with the recut royal name already noted by Unger (Luckenbill 1926 §§823-824; ORACC RIAo). What is new is the reading of the erased name as a separate Shalmaneser of 747-745 and the assembling of the three cases.

The erasure on the Tell Abta stela is not a new observation: the standard edition already reads a Shalmaneser under Tiglath-pileser III's name, assigning it to Shalmaneser IV (782-773). The dispute is which Shalmaneser, not whether one was erased.

The Shalmaneser proposed for 747-745 BCE is not the biblical Shalmaneser of 2 Kgs 17:3 and 18:9 (Shalmaneser V, 727-722 BCE, who took the throne after Tiglath-pileser III per the Eponym Chronicle entry for 727).

sites.name: Tiglath-pileser III Records
sites.subtitle: Assyrian royal inscriptions naming Menahem, Pekah, Hoshea and Ahaz · 744-727 BCE
sites.date: Reign of Tiglath-pileser III, 745-727 BCE (RINAP 1 dates his inscriptions 744-727). Menahem's payment falls in 738 BCE; the Damascus-Israel campaigns in 734-732 BCE.
sites.date_basis: The annals are arranged by regnal year (palû), anchored to the Assyrian Eponym Chronicle, which says he became king in Ayyāru of 745 after a revolt in Kalḫu in 746. RINAP 1's campaign table puts the western tribute list with 'Menahem of Samaria' in year 7 (738) and the siege and annexation of Damascus, with Gilead and Galilee, in 733-732. Summary inscriptions are undated retrospectives, so their events are dated by the annals and eponym entries.

discovery.when: 1845-1847 (Layard's excavations at Nimrud); further inscriptions in the 1950s British excavations at Nimrud (published by D. J. Wiseman in Iraq 13, 1951; 18, 1956; 26, 1964); the stele with provenience given as Luristan (Iran), one fragment in a private collection
discovery.who: Austen Henry Layard (Nimrud); later British excavations at Nimrud under Max Mallowan
discovery.where: Nimrud (ancient Kalḫu), Central Palace slabs (many later reused or displaced); a stele reportedly from Luristan, western Iran

sites.location: Dispersed. Examples: Annals slab BM 124961 (+) Detroit Institute of Arts 50.32 (RINAP 1 no. 14); Summary Inscription tablet ND 4301+4305 (no. 49); tablet K 3751 (no. 47); Iran stele IMJ 74.049.0096a (+) 0096b, Israel Museum, plus a fragment in a private collection (no. 35).

physical.material: Stone wall slabs with reliefs (annals and summary texts), a stone stele, clay tablets (summary inscriptions)

overview: Tiglath-pileser III (745-727 BCE) turned Assyria from a kingdom exacting tribute into an empire of annexed provinces. His inscriptions come in two forms: annals carved in sequence across slabs of his palace at Kalḫu (Nimrud), and 'summary' inscriptions that list conquests geographically. Many slabs were shifted or broken in antiquity and in the 19th century, and several key texts survive only in fragments or in early copies. RINAP 1 (Tadmor and Yamada, 2011) is the current edition.

Four Israelite and Judahite kings appear. 'Menahem of the city Samaria' is on the tribute list of 738 (annals and the Iran stele). Summary Inscription 4 says of Bīt-Ḫumrî (Israel) that Peqah (Pekah) was killed and Hoshea set up as king, paying 10 talents of gold. The summary tablet K 3751 lists 'Jehoahaz of the land Judah', the full form of the biblical name Ahaz, among the western tributaries. The texts also record the annexation of Damascus and of Gilead and Abil-šiṭṭi 'on the border of Bīt-Ḫumrî'.

text.quote: 816. The land of Bit-Humria ...... all of its people, together with their goods I carried off to Assyria. Pakaha, their king they deposed and I placed Ausi' (Hoshea) over them as king. 10 talents of gold, x talents of silver, as their tribute I received from them and to Assyria I carried them.
text.translation: D. D. Luckenbill, Ancient Records of Assyria and Babylonia I (Chicago, 1926), §816, p. 293

evidence: Annals (RINAP 1 no. 14 l. 10, slab BM 124961 (+) Detroit 50.32): ... mme-ni-ḫi-im-me URU.sa-me-ri-na-a-a, 'Menahem of the city Samaria', in a list of western rulers paying tribute alongside Rezin (Raḫiānu) of Damascus and Hiram of Tyre.
Iran stele (RINAP 1 no. 35 iii 5, IMJ 74.049.0096a+b): the same tribute list, with 'Menahem of the land Samaria'.

Summary Inscription 4 (RINAP 1 no. 42 ll. 15'b-19'a): 'As for the land Bīt-Ḫumrî (Israel), I brought to Assyria [...] (and) all of its people ... [I/they] killed Peqah, their king, and I placed Hoshea [as king o]ver them. I received from them ten talents of gold, ... talents of silver'.

RINAP 1 note to no. 42 l. 17': the verb before Peqah is damaged: '[i]-du-ku-ma' ('they killed') or '[a]-du-uk-ma' ('I killed') are both possible restorations, and G. Smith's draft shows space for more signs than either. Luckenbill (1926) rendered 'they deposed'.

Summary tablet ND 4301+4305 (RINAP 1 no. 49 rev. 9-11): '[I conquered the land Bīt-Ḫumr]î (Israel) in [its] entirety' (restored), '[I placed Hoshea as] king over them', and tribute brought to the city Sarrabānu.

Summary tablet K 3751 (RINAP 1 no. 47 rev. 11'): mia-ú-ḫa-zi KUR.ia-ú-da-a-a, 'Jehoahaz of the land Judah', among the western tributaries (with Mitinti of Ashkelon, Qauš-malaka of Edom, Hanūnu of Gaza).

No. 42 l. 5'b-6' and no. 49 rev. 3-4: annexation of '[...]nite, Gil[ead, and] Abil-šiṭṭi, which are (on) the border of the land Bīt-Ḫumrî', and of 'the extensive [land of Bīt-Ḫazā-i]l (Damascus)'. Where Luckenbill (1926, §815) printed 'the wide land of Naphtali', RINAP 1 restores 'the extensive land of Bīt-Ḫazā'il (Damascus)'.

RINAP 1 campaign table: 738 (year 7), tribute of the western kings including Rezin and Menahem; 733-732, siege and conquest of Damascus, campaigns to Gilead and Galilee (with the editors' cross-references to 2 Kgs 15:29; 16:5-9; Isa 7:1).
questions: Who killed Pekah? 2 Kings 15:30 says Hoshea son of Elah conspired against Pekah and killed him. The Assyrian verb is broken and can be restored as 'they killed' or 'I killed' (RINAP 1 no. 42 n. 13); Luckenbill (1926) read 'they deposed'. The text is too damaged to say whether Tiglath-pileser claimed the killing himself.

'Naphtali' or 'Bīt-Ḫazā'ili'? The older reading (Luckenbill 1926) had Tiglath-pileser annexing 'the wide land of Naphtali', which matches 2 Kgs 15:29 ('all the land of Naphtali'). RINAP 1 restores the damaged passage as the land of Damascus (Bīt-Ḫazā'ili). The 2 Kgs 15:29 parallel for Galilee now rests on the Gilead/Abil-šiṭṭi and Galilee entries, not on the word 'Naphtali'.

Is 'Pul' (2 Kgs 15:19) Tiglath-pileser? 2 Kgs 15:19-20 has Menahem pay 1,000 talents of silver to 'Pul king of Assyria'; 1 Chr 5:26 names 'Pul king of Assyria' and 'Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria' together. The Assyrian texts call the king only Tiglath-pileser and give no amount for Menahem's payment. Identifying Pul with Tiglath-pileser is our reading here; no Assyrian royal inscription cited here uses the name Pul.

biblical.tie: Menahem pays tribute to 'Pul king of Assyria'. Assyrian annals and the Iran stele list 'Menahem of Samaria' among tributaries in 738 BCE. The Bible gives 1,000 talents of silver; the Assyrian texts give no figure for Menahem.

In Pekah's days Tiglath-pileser took Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee and Naphtali and deported the people. The Assyrian summaries record annexing Gilead and Abil-šiṭṭi on Israel's border and carrying Bīt-Ḫumrî's people to Assyria.

Hoshea kills Pekah and reigns. Assyria: Peqah killed (subject damaged) and 'I placed Hoshea as king over them'. Both put Hoshea on the throne in place of Pekah; the Assyrian text claims the appointment.

Rezin of Damascus and Pekah attack Ahaz; Ahaz sends tribute to Tiglath-pileser, who takes Damascus. Assyrian texts list 'Jehoahaz (Ahaz) of Judah' as a tributary, and record the siege and annexation of Damascus (733-732).

sites.name: Timna Copper Mines
sites.subtitle: Copper mining and smelting district in the southern Arabah · Chalcolithic to Islamic, with a major smelting peak in the 11th-9th centuries BCE
sites.date: Mining from the Chalcolithic period onward; Egyptian New Kingdom (Late Bronze Age) activity at the Hathor shrine (Site 200); the main smelting camps Site 30 and Site 34 radiocarbon-dated to the early Iron Age (11th-9th century BCE), Site 34's Slag Mound 19 to the 10th century BCE
sites.date_basis: High-resolution AMS radiocarbon dating of short-lived seeds from stratified slag mounds (Ben-Yosef et al., BASOR 367, 2012 for Site 30; eleven AMS dates from Slag Mound 19 at Site 34, all 10th century BCE, per the Central Timna Valley Project); OSL dating of sediments filling mines (Merkavot 1 and 2); earlier Egyptian New Kingdom dating from the Hathor shrine (Site 200) excavated by Rothenberg's Arabah Expedition in 1969.

discovery.when: Surveyed 1934 (Glueck); Arabah Expedition surveys 1959-1961 and excavations from the 1960s (Hathor shrine 1969); Central Timna Valley Project from 2012 (field seasons from 2013, latest listed 2025)
discovery.who: Nelson Glueck (survey); Beno Rothenberg and the Arabah Expedition; Erez Ben-Yosef, Central Timna Valley (CTV) Project, Tel Aviv University
discovery.where: Timna Valley, southern Arabah (Aravah), southern Israel; the copper ore district measures c. 10 x 12 km

sites.location: In situ, Timna Valley (Timna Park), southern Arabah, Israel

physical.material: Copper ore-bearing sandstone and conglomerate; mines (open pits and shaft-and-gallery workings); smelting camps with slag mounds, furnace remains, tuyeres, charcoal, textiles and organic refuse

overview: The Timna Valley in the southern Arabah holds thousands of ancient mine shafts and several large smelting camps. Nelson Glueck surveyed it in 1934. Beno Rothenberg's Arabah Expedition surveyed from 1959 and in 1969 excavated a shrine of the Egyptian goddess Hathor (Site 200); from that find the main mining and smelting was assigned to the Egyptian New Kingdom (the 'Egyptian paradigm').

Since 2012 the Central Timna Valley Project of Tel Aviv University, directed by Erez Ben-Yosef, has re-excavated the smelting camps with radiocarbon dating of short-lived seeds. Site 30 is now dated to the early Iron Age (11th-9th century BCE) (Ben-Yosef et al. 2012). At Site 34, the 'Slaves' Hill', a 1 m section through Slag Mound 19 contains 32 layers representing about 150 years of smelting, and eleven AMS dates from it fall in the 10th century BCE. Extraordinary dryness preserved seeds, textiles (wool, goat hair and linen), rope and cordage.

OSL dating of mine fills showed open-pit mining at Merkavot 1 in the Chalcolithic and again at the end of the 2nd millennium BCE, and a shaft at Merkavot 2 in the Chalcolithic-Early Bronze Age, overturning the assumption that simpler mining techniques are always older. The Iron Age industry relied on local white broom and acacia charcoal, and its end has been linked to fuel exhaustion. The Hebrew Bible never names Timna; the tie to Solomon is a modern label.
evidence: Site 30 radiocarbon-dated to the early Iron Age, 11th-9th century BCE, replacing the Late Bronze/New Kingdom date (Ben-Yosef et al. 2012, as summarized by the CTV Project).

Site 34, Slag Mound 19, Square 19A: deposit slightly over 1 m thick, 32 layers, c. 150 years of operation; eleven AMS radiocarbon dates on short-lived seeds, all 10th century BCE (CTV 2013 season report).
The slag's high copper content and a two-piece tuyere at Site 34 fit Late Bronze / early Iron Age smelting technology (CTV 2013 season report).

The Hathor shrine (Site 200) was excavated by the Arabah Expedition in 1969; on that basis Type C shaft-and-gallery mines (cut with metal chisels) were dated to the Egyptian New Kingdom (CTV mines page).
OSL: Merkavot 1 Area A open-pit mine is Chalcolithic; Merkavot 1 Area B was mined at the end of the 2nd millennium BCE; the Merkavot 2 Area C shaft is Chalcolithic-Early Bronze Age (CTV mines page).
Late Bronze Age copper production is also attested at Site 3 (Yagel, Ben-Yosef and Craddock, Levant 48, 2016).
About 100 textile and cordage fragments from the 2013-2014 seasons at Site 34: wool, goat hair and linen, some with coloured designs (CTV textile page).

Charcoal from two stratified waste heaps of the 11th-9th century industry is mostly local white broom (Retama raetam) and acacia; later layers include less suitable taxa, read by the authors as a widening search for fuel (Cavanagh, Ben-Yosef and Langgut 2022).
In Timna the smelting ores were almost exclusively the Amir/Avrona type in the Late Bronze-Early Iron cycle (Bode et al. 2024).
Heavy-metal enrichment of soil at two Timna smelting camps is confined to the production areas (Yagel et al. 2024).
questions: Who ran the Iron Age industry? Ben-Yosef (Vetus Testamentum 69, 2019) argues that a complex society of largely nomadic people ran the Arabah copper centers, and that archaeologists of all schools have missed such polities because they rely on stone architecture ('architectural bias'). Eshel et al. (PLoS One 2025) call it 'the Arabah copper polity' and propose Faynan and Timna were 'possibly controlled by a joint polity'. Whether this polity is biblical Edom, a Judahite/Israelite enterprise, or something else is not settled by any inscription from the sites; it is an inference from location (1 Kings 9:26 places Ezion-geber 'in the land of Edom') and date.

Egyptian or local? Rothenberg's Arabah Expedition dated the main mining and smelting to the Egyptian New Kingdom from the Hathor shrine (Site 200). Ben-Yosef et al. (BASOR 367, 2012) show from radiocarbon that the largest camps (Site 30, Site 34) operated in the 11th-9th centuries BCE, after Egyptian control of Canaan ended. Both phases are real; the dispute is over which phase the thousands of shafts belong to, which the CTV Project calls 'now insecure'.

Link to Solomon. The radiocarbon peak at Site 34 overlaps the 10th century BCE that the biblical chronology gives Solomon. No object, inscription or trade record found at Timna links its copper to Jerusalem; 1 Kings 7:46 places the casting of the temple bronze in the Jordan plain, not the Arabah.

biblical.tie: 'a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills thou mayest dig brass' (KJV; 'brass' = copper/bronze). General statement about the land; does not name Timna.

Hiram casts the temple bronzes; 'in the plain of Jordan did the king cast them... between Succoth and Zarthan' and the weight of the brass 'was not found out'. The text says where casting happened, not where the copper came from. Radiocarbon dates for Site 34 fall in the same century as the traditional Solomonic date; no direct link is attested.

Solomon's fleet at Ezion-geber 'beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red sea, in the land of Edom'. This places Solomonic activity near the Gulf of Aqaba, c. the southern end of the Arabah where Timna lies; the texts mention gold from Ophir, not copper.

David puts garrisons in Edom. If the 10th-century Arabah copper producers were Edomite, this is the biblical claim of Israelite control over their territory (inference; no Timna find names Edom or Israel).

'kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel.' Ben-Yosef's case for a complex nomadic polity in the Arabah bears on whether an early Edomite kingdom is plausible (our reading).

corrections: Old entry dates the site 'c. 1000 BCE' as a whole. Mining at Timna runs from the Chalcolithic onward (OSL at Merkavot 1-2), with Late Bronze/New Kingdom activity (Hathor shrine, Site 3) and an early Iron Age smelting peak (11th-9th century BCE; Site 34 slag mound 10th century).

Old entry calls it evidence of 'Solomonic economic activity' and says Timna supplied copper for Solomon's building projects. No find at Timna names Solomon, Israel, Judah or Jerusalem, and 1 Kings 7:46 places the temple bronze-casting in the Jordan plain without naming the copper's source.

Old entry describes 'administrative structures' and an 'Israelite economy'. The excavators describe smelting camps, slag mounds and a gate complex at Site 34 and attribute the industry to an Arabah polity with a large nomadic component (Ben-Yosef 2019; Eshel et al. 2025), not to Israel.

Old entry cites 1 Kings 10:22 (ships of Tarshish bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, peacocks) and 2 Chronicles 8:1 (twenty years of building) as connections; neither mentions copper or the Arabah. The relevant Ezion-geber verses are 1 Kings 9:26-28 and 2 Chronicles 8:17-18.
Old entry omits the Egyptian New Kingdom Hathor shrine (Site 200, excavated 1969) and the resulting 'Egyptian paradigm', which the radiocarbon work since 2012 revised.

sites.name: Tobiah Inscription
sites.subtitle: The name 'Tobiah' cut beside two cave entrances at ʿIraq al-Amir, Jordan · date disputed, 6th to 2nd century BCE
sites.date: Disputed, by palaeography only: 2nd-3rd century BCE (Clermont-Ganneau 1896; Dalman; Vincent), 4th century BCE (Cross 1961; Naveh 1971; Gera), 5th century BCE (Albright), or 6th / early 5th century BCE (Mazar 1957), as tabulated by Ji (1998)
sites.date_basis: Letter forms only. The inscription is a single name cut into the living rock, with no stratified context and no associated datable object. Conder (1889) dated it to Hyrcanus the Tobiad (d. 176 BCE) by linking the caves to Josephus' account, not by the letters.

discovery.when: Known to 19th-century travellers. Copied by de Vogüé; recorded and photographed for the PEF Survey of Eastern Palestine (Conder, Lt. Mantell), published 1889.
discovery.who: Melchior de Vogüé (copy); C. R. Conder and Lt. Mantell, R.E. (survey)
discovery.where: Rock-cut cave façade (two tiers of caves) about 200 m NW of the ancient village at ʿIraq al-Amir, Wadi es-Sir, c. 17 km west of Amman

sites.location: In situ, cut into the cliff beside two cave entrances at ʿIraq al-Amir, Jordan

physical.material: Letters cut into the living rock of the cliff
physical.script: Early Jewish/Aramaic square script (Mazar calls it among the earliest examples of the official Aramaic square script)
physical.language: A personal name, ṭwbyh ('Tobiah', meaning 'YHWH is good'), in Hebrew/Aramaic form

overview: At ʿIraq al-Amir in the Wadi es-Sir, west of Amman, two tiers of caves are cut into a cliff. Beside the entrances of two of them the same five-letter name is carved in large letters: ṭwbyh, 'Tobiah'. Below the cliff stand a village and the monumental Hellenistic building Qasr al-ʿAbd. Josephus (Antiquities 12.4.11) describes a fortress built of white stone with animals carved on it, a moat, and caves 'of many furlongs in length', built by Hyrcanus son of Joseph the Tobiad, who ruled there until his suicide under Antiochus IV. The site has been identified with that fortress.

The inscription says nothing but the name. It has no title (not 'governor', not 'servant'), no patronymic and no date. Its date therefore depends entirely on how the letter shapes are placed in the development of the Aramaic and Jewish scripts. As C. C. Ji (1998) tabulates, proposals run from the 6th / early 5th century BCE (B. Mazar) to the 2nd-3rd century BCE (Clermont-Ganneau, Dalman, Vincent).

The reading itself took time to settle. Conder's Survey of Eastern Palestine (1889) records that Euting read the name as 'Turiah' ('Tyre') and de Vogüé as 'Arabiah', and Conder offered his own reading. Later epigraphers read ṭwbyh, 'Tobiah', and Ji (1998) summarizes the site's scholarship on that reading.

text.quote: ṭwbyh — 'Tobiah'
text.translation: Literal rendering (this encyclopedia) of the name as read in the literature summarized by Ji, Liber Annuus 48 (1998): 417-440. The inscription consists of this single name. No public-domain translation of the modern reading exists; Conder (1889) printed a different reading.

evidence: Two inscriptions of the one word ṭwbyh are cut near the entrances of two caves in the cliff at ʿIraq al-Amir (Ji 1998, p. 419).
Conder (1889, section 'Tyrus', pp. 76-77) places one 'to the right of the door, high up' at cave No. 13. His copy agreed with de Vogüé's and is backed by Lt. Mantell's photograph (Series No. 26).
The text is a bare personal name, with no title, patronymic or date.
The caves lie in two tiers, the upper reached by a rock-cut gallery about 300 yards long (Conder 1889).

The settlement below had occupation in the late Iron Age / Persian period: Ulvoczky (2017), restudying P. W. Lapp's original sherds, dates Stratum V to Iron IIC/Persian. Ji (1998) cites French excavators for early-Persian-period building phases and for Persian walls reused in the Hellenistic period.
The Zenon papyri (C.P.Jud. 1, 4-5, as cited by Ji 1998) show 3rd-century BCE Tobiads as influential Jewish landowners in Transjordan who commanded a cavalry garrison.
questions: Is this the Tobiah of Nehemiah? B. Mazar (1957, 141-142) dated the letters to the 6th or early 5th century BCE, and Albright (as cited by Ji) to the 5th, which would bring the carving near Nehemiah's time (c. 445 BCE). F. M. Cross (1961), J. Naveh (1971) and D. Gera (1990) date the script to the 4th century BCE. Clermont-Ganneau (1896), Dalman (1921) and Vincent (1923) put it in the 2nd-3rd century BCE, which would fit the Tobiads of the Zenon papyri and of Josephus (Ji 1998, nn. 37-38). The disagreement is over letter forms in a five-letter word, which is a very small sample for palaeography.

Was the family already at ʿIraq al-Amir in the Persian period? P. W. Lapp dated Stratum V to Iron I, with a gap before the Hellenistic period. C. C. Ji (1998) and D. Ulvoczky (2017) argue from the pottery for late Iron II / Persian occupation, which is compatible with a Persian-period Tobiah at the site. No Persian-period object at the site bears the name.
What was the inscription for? Tomb markers, property marks and dedicatory labels for the caves have all been proposed. The inscription gives no function, and the sources are silent.

biblical.tie: 'Tobiah the servant (hāʿebed), the Ammonite' opposes Nehemiah and later lodges in a temple chamber. The inscription gives the same name, ṭwbyh, in Ammonite territory (ʿIraq al-Amir lies west of Rabbath-Ammon). The name and the region correspond. Whether this is the same man or a family name repeated over generations depends on the date.

Tobiah's son Jehohanan married into a Jerusalem family, and Tobiah had sworn allies in Judah. Josephus' later Tobiads (Joseph, Hyrcanus) are tied to the Jerusalem priesthood. That is a family pattern across the sources, not something the inscription shows.
The 'children of Tobiah' among returnees who could not prove their descent. This is another biblical occurrence of the name group. It has no direct connection to the carving.

corrections: The old entry said the inscription names Tobiah 'as a governor'. It is the bare name ṭwbyh with no title. In Nehemiah, Tobiah's title is 'the servant (ʿebed), the Ammonite', not governor.

The old entry dated it firmly to the '3rd century BCE' (and 'c. 200 BCE'). Published dates range from the 6th / early 5th century BCE (Mazar) to the 2nd-3rd century BCE (Clermont-Ganneau and others), all on palaeography (Ji 1998). No single date is established.

The old entry called it a 'stone inscription… approximately 1 meter tall'. It is cut into the cliff face beside the cave entrances, not on a separate stone. No measurement was found in the sources read.

The old entry claimed it was 'written in a form of Hebrew script' and 'provides valuable insights into… administrative… practices'. It is a single personal name in early square (Aramaic-derived) script and contains no administrative content.

The old entry said it 'confirms the existence of' Nehemiah's Tobiah. The name and region match, but only the earliest proposed dates (Mazar, Albright) would make the carving contemporary with Nehemiah. On the 4th-2nd century dates it would belong to later members of a Tobiad family.
The old entry referred to 'the Tobiah Inscription' in the singular. There are two carvings of the same name, at two caves (Ji 1998, p. 419).

updates.what: C. Nihan re-examines Josephus' account of the Tobiads and Ptolemaic administration (the main literary source for the family at ʿIraq al-Amir). This is a new study of the texts, not a new find at the site.

sites.name: Wadi Daliyeh Papyri
sites.subtitle: Aramaic legal deeds from Persian-period Samaria, hidden in a cave c. 332/331 BCE
sites.date: Written c. 375-335 BCE. The oldest explicitly datable deed is WDSP 22 (c. 375-365 BCE). The latest dated is WDSP 1, 19 March 335 BCE (20 Adar, year 2 of Arses/Artaxerxes IV, at the start of Darius III's reign). WDSP 36 frg. 1 may be later, 335-332 BCE.
sites.date_basis: Regnal-year dating formulas in the deeds themselves (Artaxerxes II, Artaxerxes III, Arses/Darius III). The latest pre-Alexander coin in the cave was struck at Tyre in 334 BCE, in year 15 of Ozimilk (Puech 2003, reviewing Gropp 2001; Dušek 2020).

discovery.when: Found by Taʿâmireh Bedouin in or before 1962. Purchased 19 Nov 1962 and 7 Aug 1963. Cave excavated 1963-1964.
discovery.who: Taʿâmireh Bedouin (finders); dealer Kando; Yusef Saad, Roland de Vaux and Paul W. Lapp (acquisition); P. W. and N. L. Lapp (ASOR excavations); F. M. Cross (first study)
discovery.where: Mughâret Abū Shinjeh, a cave in Wadi ed-Daliyeh, about 14 km north of Jericho

sites.location: Rockefeller Museum (formerly Palestine Archaeological Museum), Jerusalem. A few further fragments are in the Schøyen Collection (Dušek 2020).

physical.material: Papyrus, with clay bullae (sealings), some still attached
physical.dimensions: None complete. The best-preserved deed, WDSP 1, is about half of its original length. WDSP 28-37 are groups of fragments (Dušek 2020). Gropp's edition (DJD 28) presents 37 entries, 18 of them substantial enough to call papyri (Puech 2003).
physical.script: Aramaic cursive (the bulla WD 22 is in palaeo-Hebrew script)
physical.language: Aramaic (legal formulary with Neo-Babylonian loans); the bulla is Hebrew

overview: In 1962 Taʿâmireh Bedouin brought papyri, bullae and coins from a cave in Wadi ed-Daliyeh, north of Jericho, to the antiquities dealer Kando. The lot was bought for the Palestine Archaeological Museum (now the Rockefeller Museum) in November 1962 and August 1963. Paul and Nancy Lapp then excavated the cave, Mughâret Abū Shinjeh, for ASOR in 1963-1964 and found more fragments, bullae, and the remains of a large number of people.

The documents are Aramaic legal deeds written 'in Samaria the fortress/city, in Samaria the province' in the last decades of Persian rule (c. 375-335 BCE). Most are sales of slaves, single men, women or groups. Others record a loan (WDSP 17), a lawsuit (WDSP 11 verso), a house sale and other contracts. Dušek distinguishes three successive family archives among them. Witness lists and sealings name governors of Samaria: Ḥananyah (WDSP 7, dated 4 March 354 BCE) and a bulla (WD 22) of '[Dela]yahu son of [Sanba]llat, governor of Samaria'.

The excavators and editors explain the deposit by the events of 332/331 BCE. Quintus Curtius (4.8.9-11) reports that the Samarians burned Alexander's governor Andromachus alive and that Alexander returned to punish them. Refugees from Samaria carrying their deeds would have fled to the cave. Cross (1974) proposed that they were found there and suffocated by a fire lit at the entrance. The cave's contents fit that sequence, but no text in the cave records it.

text.quote: [lDl]yhw bn [sbʾ]blṭ pḥt šmr[n] — '[Belonging to Dela]yahu son of [Sanba]llat, governor of Samar[ia]'
text.translation: Literal translation (this encyclopedia) of the transliterated Hebrew legend of bulla WD 22 as given (in Hebrew characters) by J. Dušek, Religions 11/2 (2020): 63, citing Dušek 2007, p. 316. Square brackets mark restored letters.

evidence: Findspot: Mughâret Abū Shinjeh, Wadi ed-Daliyeh, about 14 km north of Jericho. The papyri were bought for the Palestine Archaeological Museum on 19 Nov 1962 and 7 Aug 1963 (Dušek 2020).
Place of writing: 'Samaria the fortress/city' in 'Samaria the province' (šmryn byrtʾ/qrytʾ, šmryn mdyntʾ) (Dušek 2020).
Dated deeds run from c. 375-365 BCE (WDSP 22) to 19 March 335 BCE (WDSP 1). The kings named are Artaxerxes II, Artaxerxes III and Arses/Darius III (Puech 2003; Dušek 2020).

Content: at least half are slave sales. There are also a house sale (pap. 15), rooms in a public building (pap. 14), a vineyard (pap. 16), a loan receipt (pap. 17) and a lawsuit (WDSP 11v) (Puech 2003; Dušek 2020).

Governors of Samaria named: Ḥananyah or ʿAnanyah, as witness in WDSP 7 (4 March 354 BCE), and the bulla WD 22 of '[Dela]yahu son of [Sanba]llat, governor of Samaria', attached to WDSP 16 (Dušek 2020).
The latest coin is from Tyre, 334 BCE (year 15 of Ozimilk), which gives a terminus post quem for the deposit (Puech 2003).

Human remains: Lapp's early report, from Bedouin interviews, gave about 205 skeletons, and after excavation about 300 men, women and children were reported (as summarized by Mendonça 2024, citing Lapp 1965 and Lapp & Lapp 1974). Signs of fire were found at the cave entrance.
questions: How many Sanballats? F. M. Cross (JBL 94, 1975) used the Daliyeh material to reconstruct a line of governors that repeats the name Sanballat across generations, to fit Josephus' Sanballat in Alexander's time. This summary of Cross comes from secondary accounts; the article was not read. J. Dušek (2007; Religions 11, 2020) reads bulla WD 22 as probably belonging to Delayah son of Sinʾuballiṭ, the same Delayah named with his father in the Elephantine letter of 407 BCE. He argues that Josephus confused events, dating the Gerizim sanctuary a century too late, so no second or third Sanballat is needed. The evidence is one broken bulla legend with the patronym restored, the Elephantine letter, and Josephus Ant. 11.

Who died in the cave, and how? Cross (1974) proposed Samarian refugees trapped and suffocated by Alexander's troops, using Curtius 4.8.9-11 and the fire at the entrance. The documents are deeds carried by their owners and do not describe the event. The link to Alexander rests on the terminal dates (335 BCE deed, 334 BCE coin) and Curtius's report.

What faith did the Samarian owners hold? Dušek (2020) analyses the personal names in the deeds and finds them largely Yahwistic or West Semitic. That is evidence for Samarian religion before the Samaritan–Jewish split. The deeds themselves contain no cultic texts.

biblical.tie: Sanballat the Horonite, Nehemiah's opponent, whose daughter married into the high-priestly family. Bulla WD 22 names '[Dela]yahu son of [Sanba]llat, governor of Samaria'. On Dušek's reading this is Sanballat's son, known also from Elephantine (407 BCE). The Bible never calls Sanballat 'governor', but in Neh 4:2 he speaks 'before… the army of Samaria'.
Persian-period letters about Samaria written in Aramaic. The Daliyeh deeds show Aramaic as the working legal language of the province of Samaria in the 4th century BCE.

The account of Samaria's mixed population and worship. The papyri's many Yahwistic personal names in Samaria are data for the religion of the province. How they bear on this passage is an interpretation.

sites.name: Western Wall and Robinson's Arch
sites.subtitle: Herodian western retaining wall of the Temple Mount, with its great arches · late 1st century BCE – 1st century CE
sites.date: Herodian and later 1st-century CE construction. Wilson's Arch was begun under Herod and enlarged under the Roman procurators within about 70 years (radiocarbon, Regev et al. 2020).
sites.date_basis: Josephus' account of Herod's work (Ant. 15.11); radiocarbon on charred material in building fills beneath Wilson's Arch (Regev et al., PLOS ONE 2020); coins and stratigraphy in the Western Wall Tunnels ('Atiqot 119, 2025) and along the Western Wall foundations (Baruch, Reich, Hagbi & Uziel 2023).

discovery.when: Standing wall; Robinson identified the arch springer in 1838 (published 1841); Warren's shafts 1867–70; excavations 1968–78 and continuing
discovery.who: Edward Robinson; Charles Warren; Benjamin Mazar; IAA teams (Reich & Baruch; Hagbi & Uziel; Weksler-Bdolah; Uziel, Solomon & Lieberman)
discovery.where: West side of the Temple Mount enclosure, Jerusalem

sites.location: In situ, Jerusalem

physical.material: Limestone ashlars with drafted margins
physical.dimensions: Whole west wall of the enclosure 1,601 ft (c. 488 m) (SWP 1884). Robinson's Arch springer: 51 ft along the wall, its south side 39 ft from the south-west corner; stones up to 24½ ft long (Robinson 1841).

overview: The Western Wall is the western retaining wall of Herod's Temple Mount enclosure, 1,601 ft (about 488 m) long by the Palestine Exploration Fund survey (1884). The open-air prayer area is only a short stretch of it; most of its length runs behind and under later buildings and is reached through the Western Wall Tunnels.

In 1838 Edward Robinson noticed three courses of huge curved stones jutting from the wall near its south-west corner. He wrote (Biblical Researches in Palestine I, 1841, p. 425): 'their external surface is hewn to a regular curve; and being fitted one upon another, they form the commencement or foot of an immense arch, which once sprung out from this western wall in a direction towards Mount Zion, across the Valley of the Tyropoeon.' He took it for the bridge Josephus mentions between the temple and the Xystus. Further north, Wilson's Arch still stands and carried a causeway across the valley.

Recent work has dated these structures directly. Radiocarbon from building fills shows Wilson's Arch was begun under Herod and enlarged under the procurators, Pilate among them (Regev et al. 2020). The 2018–2020 Western Wall Tunnels excavation found a Herodian dam wall across the valley, later topped by a paved triclinium building after 17 CE ('Atiqot 119, 2025).
evidence: Robinson's Arch: three surviving courses of curved voussoirs, one 5 ft 4 in thick; a chord of 12 ft 6 in on the surviving arc; 350 ft from the arch to the rock scarp opposite (Robinson 1841, p. 425).
Buried courses near the south-west corner keep fine drafted margins and rough projecting bosses, never weathered. Four courses match 'those at the Wailing Place' (SWP Jerusalem 1884, p. 170).

Wilson's Arch: charred material in the construction fills dates the first phase to Herod and an enlargement to the procurators; a theatre-like structure beneath is Hadrianic and was left unfinished before 132–136 CE (Regev et al. 2020).

Western Wall Tunnels 2018–2020: a Herodian dam wall with drainage channels, a later paved triclinium building with a fountain (after 17 CE by a sealed Tiberius coin), and a miqweh of the time of the First Revolt (67/68 CE) (Weksler-Bdolah; Levy, 'Atiqot 119, 2025).
Plastered horizontal channels cut only in the Herodian courses, dated before 70 CE (Szanton & Weksler-Bdolah, 'Atiqot 119, 2025).
questions: What did Robinson's Arch carry? Robinson (1841, p. 425) identified it with the bridge Josephus names between the temple and the Xystus, measuring 350 ft across the valley to the opposite rock. A different reading, that the arch topped a monumental stair running down south to the street below, is attributed to B. Mazar's 1968–78 excavations at its foot. Their final reports (Qedem series) were not available for this entry, so the stair reading is flagged here as unverified, not stated as fact.

How long did the building take? Josephus (Ant. 20.219) says the temple works were 'finished' under Albinus (c. 62–64 CE). Radiocarbon at Wilson's Arch (Regev et al. 2020) and coins in the Western Wall Tunnels (Levy 2025) show construction around the western wall continuing well after Herod's death in 4 BCE. How much of the western wall's visible masonry is from after Herod is not settled in the sources cited here.

biblical.tie: Jesus says of the temple buildings, 'There shall not be left one stone upon another.' The Western Wall is a retaining wall of the platform, not the temple building. The temple itself was destroyed in 70 CE, and these lower walls still stand.
'Forty-six years was this temple in building.' The dated construction phases at Wilson's Arch and the tunnels show the complex was still being built through the early 1st century CE.

corrections: Old dimensions 'up to 47 meters high, 60 meters long' are unsourced. The western wall of the enclosure is about 488 m long (SWP 1884). The prayer plaza exposes only a short stretch of it. No source cited here gives the 47 m or 60 m figures, so they are dropped.
Old location 'Jewish Quarter' is imprecise. The wall is the western side of the Temple Mount. The prayer plaza lies beside the Jewish Quarter, and the wall runs north under the Muslim Quarter.
Old 'Discovery: 1838 (Robinson's Arch)' is right in substance: Robinson recognised the springer in 1838 and published it in 1841. His identification of it as the bridge to the Xystus is his reading.
Old 'The discovery of the Western Wall' framing is wrong. It is a standing wall that was never lost.
Old link 'John 15 (Jesus walks on Temple Mount)' is wrong. John 15 is the vine discourse. The Temple Mount links are passages like John 10:23 and Mark 13:1–2.

Old 'Mark 13 (Jesus predicts temple destruction)' needs precision. The prophecy concerns the temple buildings. The Western Wall is part of the platform's retaining wall and was not what Jesus pointed at.

sites.name: Yeda'yah (son of) Asayahu bulla
aka: Temple Mount Sifting Project Josiah-era bulla
sites.subtitle: Paleo-Hebrew clay sealing from Temple Mount soil · late 7th - early 6th century BCE
sites.date: Late 7th to early 6th century BCE (late First Temple period)
sites.date_basis: Palaeography only: the letter forms were dated by the epigrapher to the second half of the 7th / beginning of the 6th century BCE. The object has no stratified context; it came from soil removed from the Temple Mount by bulldozer in 1996-1999 and dumped in the Kidron Valley, later wet-sifted by the Temple Mount Sifting Project.

discovery.when: Recognised c. early July 2025 (about three weeks before the 30 July 2025 announcement); the soil had been sifted about two years earlier
discovery.who: Mordechai Ehrlich (Temple Mount Sifting Project), while going through containers of sifted bones; read by Dr. Anat Mendel-Geberovich and Zachi Dvira
discovery.where: Temple Mount soil removed during 1996-1999 construction on the Mount, dumped in the Kidron Valley, salvaged and sifted by the Temple Mount Sifting Project (Emek Tzurim, Jerusalem)

sites.location: Temple Mount Sifting Project, Jerusalem (no museum inventory number published as of Sept 2026)

physical.material: Clay (bulla, i.e. a lump of clay pressed with a seal)

overview: A small clay bulla bearing a seal impression in Paleo-Hebrew script, recognised in 2025 by Mordechai Ehrlich of the Temple Mount Sifting Project among bones that had been sifted about two years before. The soil it came from was dug out of the Temple Mount during 1996-1999 construction and dumped in the Kidron Valley, so the object has no archaeological layer; only its script dates it.

The epigrapher Anat Mendel-Geberovich and project co-director Zachi Dvira, using RTI (reflectance transformation) photography, read it as ליד[ע]יה (בן) עשיהו, 'Belonging to Yed[a']yah (son of) Asayahu'. The square brackets mark the ayin as restored; the round brackets mark the word 'son of' as supplied by the readers, i.e. the seal gives two names in a row, as is common on Judahite seals. The sealing preserves a fingerprint, and marks on its back show it closed a bag or container.

The project announced that the father's name Asayahu is the long form of Asaiah, the 'servant of the king' whom Josiah sent to Huldah (2 Kings 22:12, 14; 2 Chronicles 34:20), and called the link 'highly plausible' but not certain. A paper was announced for submission in August 2025; the find was presented at the 50th Archaeological Congress in Israel in June 2026, and the project says full details await the article. No peer-reviewed publication had been located as of Sept 2026.

text.quote: lyd['y]h ('s)yhw -- 'Belonging to Yed[a']yah, (son of) Asayahu'
text.translation: Our literal rendering of the reading published by the Temple Mount Sifting Project (Mendel-Geberovich and Dvira), 30 July 2025: ליד[ע]יה (בן) עשיהו. No public-domain translation exists (found 2025).

evidence: Reading as published by the excavators: ליד[ע]יה (בן) עשיהו, 'Belonging to Yed[a']yah (son of) Asayahu' (TMSP, 30 July 2025).
The ayin of Yeda'yah is restored, not read (bracketed in the published reading).
The word 'son of' (bn) is not on the seal; it is supplied in round brackets by the readers.

The father's name is written in the long form -yahu (Asayahu); the Masoretic text of 2 Kings 22:12 / 2 Chronicles 34:20 spells the official's name in the short form 'Asaiah'. Dvira: 'The longer and shorter versions of the name were often used interchangeably' (Times of Israel, 30 July 2025).
Date is palaeographic: late 7th-early 6th century BCE (TMSP; JNS: 'second half of the 7th century BCE to the beginning of the 6th century BCE').
No stratigraphic context: the soil was removed from the Temple Mount by construction machinery in 1996-1999 and dumped in the Kidron Valley (Times of Israel, 30 July 2025).
A fingerprint is preserved on the sealing; impressions on the back show it sealed a bag or container (TMSP; BAS 2025).
Dvira: only the second time in the project's 20+ years that a sealing with so complete an inscription has been found (Times of Israel, 30 July 2025).
Dimensions have not been published in any source located.
questions: Is this Asayahu the Asaiah of 2 Kings 22? The Temple Mount Sifting Project (Mendel-Geberovich and Dvira, announcement 30 July 2025; Armstrong Institute report) calls it 'highly plausible' because the date by script matches Josiah's reign (c. 640-609 BCE) and the object came from Temple Mount soil, but they state it is not 'entirely certain'. The seal itself carries no title (no 'servant of the king') and the Asaiah of Kings has no recorded son; by the criteria the Jerubba'al editors cite from Mykytiuk (2004) for a firm identification (a matching patronymic, title or epithet), the match here is a name plus a date range only. The Bible also names other men called Asaiah (1 Chr 4:36; 6:30; 9:5; 15:6, 11), though none of them in Josiah's court.
Whose fingerprint? The fingerprint belongs to whoever pressed the clay; the seal owner named is Yeda'yah, not Asayahu. Nothing on the object identifies the person who left the print.

Full technical publication (dimensions, photographs, reverse, palaeographic argument) was still pending as of the June 2026 congress report; the reading and date cannot yet be checked against a peer-reviewed edition.

biblical.tie: Josiah sends 'Asahiah a servant of the king's' (KJV) with Hilkiah, Shaphan, Ahikam and Achbor to Huldah after the book of the law is found. The bulla names an Asayahu as the father of the seal owner. The match is the name and the 7th-6th century date; no title or further link is on the seal.
Parallel account: 'Asaiah a servant of the king's'. Same correspondence and same limits as above.

The name Yedaiah (Jedaiah) occurs in the Bible for a priestly course and for later individuals; the bulla shows the name in use in late monarchic Jerusalem. No identification with any biblical Jedaiah is claimed.

corrections: Some press (e.g. the Greek Reporter headline 'Biblical fingerprint discovered on 2,600-year-old Temple Mount seal', seen in search results; Daily Mail 'fingerprint seal linked' headline) implies the fingerprint is the biblical official's. The sealing names Yeda'yah as owner and Asayahu only as his father; nobody can say whose finger pressed it, and the Asayahu identification itself is unconfirmed (TMSP 2025; BAS 2025).

Headlines such as Israel365 News 'First Temple clay seal validates biblical history' (seen in search results) overstate the find: the excavators call the link to Josiah's Asaiah 'highly plausible' but not certain, because the seal has no title and the name recurs in the Bible (TMSP 30 July 2025).

Reports that print the reading as a continuous 'Yedayah son of Asayahu' (e.g. the Biblical Archaeology Society summary 'Yeda'yah son of Asayahu') drop the editors' brackets: the ayin is restored and the word 'son of' is not written on the seal (TMSP reading ליד[ע]יה (בן) עשיהו).
